per_choice_rationale.D: Implies brief, casual visits, contradicting the dawn-to-dusk intensity (goal_minimizing_verb).

why_correct_md: The original verb vividly conveys **dense, urgent crowding**, exactly the emphasis the writer requests.
why_tempted_md: The neutral options are accurate statements of fact, so literal-minded readers accept them.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's stated goal in your own words. 2) For each verb, describe the picture it creates. 3) Eliminate neutral or mismatched pictures. 4) Keep the verb whose connotation matches the goal exactly.

subject: act-english
context_html: The engineering notebook reflects the team's discipline: after each test, members <u>recorded the trial conditions and quantified every result</u> before proposing modifications.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the formal, technical tone established in the sentence?

choices.label: totally geeked out over the numbers
scribbled some quick notes on stuff

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the precise, technical diction matches the notebook's formal register.
per_choice_rationale.B: Vague and offhand, clashing with the precise language around it (tone_casual_vague).
per_choice_rationale.C: Injects slang into measured technical prose (tone_slang).
per_choice_rationale.D: Suggests haste and carelessness, contradicting the discipline the sentence asserts (tone_careless_informal).

why_correct_md: The original phrase's precise, technical diction **matches** the notebook's formal register.
why_tempted_md: The friendly, natural sound of the casual options is easily mistaken for good style.
rule_md: 1) Identify the passage's register from surrounding word choices. 2) Rate each option: slang, casual, neutral, or formal. 3) Keep the option matching the passage's rating, regardless of which sounds most natural alone.

subject: act-english
context_html: To validate the autonomous routine, the programmers ran the robot from the same starting position forty times in a single afternoon. They logged each run's final coordinates and flagged any trial that ended more than five centimeters from the target. After adjusting one turning constant, the routine hit its mark in nineteen of the final twenty runs.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the second sentence of the paragraph: 'The team's spring bake sale had raised almost four hundred dollars for new batteries.' Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it shows that the team succeeds at more than just engineering.
Yes, because it explains how the team paid for its testing equipment.
No, because it fails to say which students organized the bake sale.
No, because it interrupts the account of the testing process with an unrelated fundraising detail.

per_choice_rationale.A: Approves the addition for boosting the team's image, which is not the paragraph's job (add_flattering_but_offtopic).
per_choice_rationale.B: Invents a funding question the paragraph never raises (add_false_relevance).
per_choice_rationale.C: Rejects the sentence for missing trivia rather than for being off-topic (delete_wrong_reason).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the sentence breaks the step-by-step testing narrative with an off-topic fact.

why_correct_md: The bake-sale sentence **breaks** the step-by-step testing narrative with an off-topic fact, so it should not be added.
why_tempted_md: The battery connection in one 'yes' option sounds logical because the tests really do use batteries.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's job in one sentence. 2) Ask whether the proposed sentence advances that job. 3) If not, choose 'no' — then verify the stated reason targets relevance, not a trivial flaw.

subject: act-english
context_html: When I joined the robotics team as a sophomore, I could not tell a hex key from a screwdriver. Over one season I learned to read a match schedule, to lose gracefully, and to ask older students for help without embarrassment. By the banquet in April, the trophy case mattered far less to me than the people I had built things with.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to provide a technical guide explaining how to construct a competition robot. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because the essay refers to technical tools such as hex keys and screwdrivers.
Yes, because the narrator describes an entire season from joining the team to the banquet.
No, because the essay is a personal narrative about a single season rather than a technical guide.
No, because a technical guide would need to mention trophies and match schedules.

per_choice_rationale.A: Mistakes a passing mention of tools for actual instruction (purpose_stray_vocabulary).
per_choice_rationale.B: Confuses complete time coverage with coverage of the required topic (purpose_scope_confusion).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the essay recounts one student's growth and never explains construction, so it fails the goal for this reason.
per_choice_rationale.D: Reaches the right verdict with a nonsensical requirement about trophies (purpose_wrong_reason).

why_correct_md: The essay is a first-person account of growth over one season and **never explains construction**, so it fails the stated goal for exactly that reason.
why_tempted_md: The hex-key option tempts students who equate mentioning tools with explaining their use.
rule_md: 1) Restate the hypothetical goal. 2) Summarize what the essay actually does. 3) Compare: match or mismatch? 4) Among same-verdict options, pick the reason that accurately describes the essay.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] In the hour before each match, the drive team follows a strict routine. [2] The operator recalibrates the arm presets while the driver walks the field to note any new wear in the carpet. [3] Our school's cafeteria began offering a vegetarian lunch line this year. [4] Finally, the coach reviews the opposing alliance's scouting data and assigns defensive priorities.
stem_md: The writer wants this paragraph to stay focused on how the drive team prepares before each match. Which sentence should be deleted to preserve that focus?

per_choice_rationale.A: Deletes the topic sentence that frames every step in the routine (delete_topic_sentence).
per_choice_rationale.B: Removes a direct example of pre-match preparation, weakening the focus (delete_on_topic_support).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the cafeteria news has no connection to pre-match preparation.
per_choice_rationale.D: Cuts an on-topic preparation step because it appears last and adds new names (delete_final_support).

why_correct_md: The cafeteria news has **no connection** to pre-match preparation, so deleting it preserves the paragraph's focus.
why_tempted_md: Some students target the final sentence because it introduces new people and data at the end.
rule_md: 1) Write the paragraph's focus in one phrase. 2) Test each sentence: does it show that focus? 3) Delete the one sentence that fails the test — never the topic sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: The robot stalled at <u>midfield the battery</u> connector had vibrated loose during the first hard collision.
stem_md: Which choice creates a complete and correctly joined sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: Fuses two independent clauses with no boundary at all (fused_sentence).
per_choice_rationale.B: Glues the two independent clauses with only a comma, creating a comma splice (comma_splice).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the semicolon legally joins the two independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.D: Adds a subordinator after the semicolon, leaving a fragment on the right side (semicolon_plus_fragment).

why_correct_md: The **semicolon** legally joins the two independent clauses that were fused together.
why_tempted_md: The comma version tempts students who hear a pause and assume any mark can hold two sentences together.
rule_md: 1) Find each subject-verb pair. 2) Ask whether each clause could stand alone. 3) If both can, join them with a semicolon, a period, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction — never a bare comma or nothing at all.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Although</u> the scrimmage ended in a lopsided loss, the drive team came home with a full page of tuning notes.
stem_md: Which choice most logically connects the two parts of the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the concessive subordinator sets the loss against the surprising upside in the main clause.
per_choice_rationale.B: Claims the loss caused the useful notes, a false cause-effect link (subordinator_false_cause).
per_choice_rationale.C: Turns one specific scrimmage into a recurring pattern, changing the meaning (subordinator_wrong_time).
per_choice_rationale.D: Uses a preposition that cannot head a full subject-verb clause (preposition_before_clause).

why_correct_md: The original subordinator correctly **concedes** the loss while the main clause delivers the surprising upside.
why_tempted_md: 'Because' attracts students who assume any two joined clauses must be cause and effect.
rule_md: 1) Read both clauses and label their relationship: contrast, cause, condition, or time. 2) Match the connector to that label. 3) Check grammar: prepositions like 'despite' cannot introduce a full clause.

subject: act-english
context_html: In bench tests, the new intake's grip strength consistently exceeded <u>the old design.</u>
stem_md: Which choice makes the comparison logical and clear?

per_choice_rationale.A: Compares a strength measurement to an entire design, a category mismatch (illogical_comparison).
per_choice_rationale.B: Swaps in a physical part, so strength is still compared to an object rather than to a measurement (comparison_wrong_object).
per_choice_rationale.C: Substitutes a vague clause about the design's identity instead of its strength (comparison_vague_clause).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the stand-in phrase makes the sentence compare strength with strength.

why_correct_md: **That of** makes the comparison logical: the new strength is measured against the strength of the old design.
why_tempted_md: The original sounds complete because everyday speech routinely compares a measurement to a thing.
rule_md: 1) Name the two items the sentence compares. 2) Confirm they belong to the same category. 3) If they do not, insert 'that of' or 'those of' so the second item matches the first.

subject: act-english
context_html: Before the regional, the mechanical and software subteams <u>combined</u> their separate checklists into a single pit binder.
stem_md: Which choice is the most effective for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the verb alone carries the complete idea of joining the checklists.
per_choice_rationale.B: Adds 'together,' which merely repeats meaning already inside the verb (redundant_adverb).
per_choice_rationale.C: Stacks a synonym onto the verb, doubling the same idea (redundant_synonym_pair).
per_choice_rationale.D: Layers two redundant modifiers onto the verb at once (redundant_double_layer).

why_correct_md: The single verb already expresses the full idea; every alternative adds words that **repeat** its built-in meaning.
why_tempted_md: 'Combined together' is so common in casual speech that the redundancy is invisible to most readers.
rule_md: 1) Define the verb precisely. 2) Test every added word: does it repeat part of that definition? 3) Delete each word that does. 4) Keep the version with zero repeats.

subject: act-english
context_html: The match ended early <u>due to the fact that</u> the servo controlling the lift overheated.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most concise?

choices.label: in light of the fact that

per_choice_rationale.A: Uses a five-word filler phrase where one word does the same job (filler_fact_that).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: a single conjunction delivers the entire causal meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: Swaps one padded formula for an even more formal-sounding one (filler_formal_variant).
per_choice_rationale.D: Trims halfway but still drags the empty 'of the fact that' along (filler_partial_trim).

why_correct_md: The one-word conjunction delivers the **entire causal meaning** of the padded five-word phrase.
why_tempted_md: The half-trimmed version feels like a safe compromise since it keeps the familiar opening word.
rule_md: 1) Spot formula phrases built on 'the fact that.' 2) Replace the whole phrase with a one-word conjunction. 3) Re-read to confirm no meaning was lost. 4) Reject any option that still contains removable words.

subject: act-english
context_html: The scouting app <u>has the ability to</u> rank every alliance pairing by projected score within seconds.
stem_md: Which choice expresses the idea most efficiently?

per_choice_rationale.A: Stretches a simple capability into a four-word idiom (wordy_capability_idiom).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: one modal verb conveys the full capability with nothing lost.
per_choice_rationale.C: Inflates the diction without adding any meaning (inflated_diction).
per_choice_rationale.D: Trims some fat but still uses three words where one identical-meaning word exists (partial_concision).

why_correct_md: One **modal verb** conveys the full capability, so every longer equivalent fails the concision test.
why_tempted_md: 'Is able to' tempts students because it is shorter than the original and feels like an improvement.
rule_md: 1) List what each option literally means. 2) Group the options that mean exactly the same thing. 3) Within that group, keep the fewest words. 4) Only keep extra words when they add real meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: A downward-facing color sensor <u>notices</u> changes in floor brightness as the robot crosses the white gaffer-tape line.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely describes the sensor's function?

per_choice_rationale.A: Attributes casual human awareness to an electronic component (verb_personification).
per_choice_rationale.B: Imports a bystander, almost legal connotation that misfits an instrument (verb_wrong_connotation).
per_choice_rationale.C: Implies touch or emotion, which a color sensor has neither of (verb_literal_mismatch).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: this is the standard, precise verb for an instrument registering a signal.

why_correct_md: It is the **standard, precise verb** for an instrument registering a signal.
why_tempted_md: The original tempts readers because we casually personify machines in everyday speech.
rule_md: 1) Identify the subject's nature: person or device? 2) Strike verbs implying consciousness or touch when the subject is a device. 3) Choose the verb used in technical writing for that exact operation.

subject: act-english
context_html: In their scouting reports, rival teams described our defensive robot as <u>stubborn</u>, praising the way it refused to surrender its zone even against double-teams.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely conveys the admiring judgment described in the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: Shares the core meaning of refusing to yield but tilts toward criticism, clashing with 'praising' (connotation_negative_synonym).
per_choice_rationale.B: Frames persistence as a flaw, nearly an insult, inside a sentence built on praise (connotation_insult).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: it means admirably persistent, matching both the meaning and the praising tone.
per_choice_rationale.D: Describes inflexibility of form or attitude rather than determined effort, with a faint negative shade (connotation_wrong_nuance).

why_correct_md: The key word means **admirably persistent**, matching both the meaning and the praising tone of the sentence.
why_tempted_md: The original shares the core meaning of refusing to yield, so students who check denotation alone keep it.
rule_md: 1) Pin down the required meaning from context. 2) Check each synonym's connotation: positive, neutral, or negative. 3) Match the connotation to the sentence's attitude — here, explicit praise. 4) Keep the word that passes both checks.

subject: act-english
context_html: In her follow-up story on the zoning dispute, the reporter <u>cited the mayor's principal aide</u>, who confirmed that the variance had been granted without a public hearing.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: 'cited' means quoted as a source, and 'principal' means chief, so both spellings match their intended meanings.
per_choice_rationale.B: Swaps in 'sited,' which means placed at a location — the site/cite homophone confusion.
per_choice_rationale.C: Swaps in 'principle,' a noun meaning a rule or belief, for the adjective meaning chief — the principal/principle confusion.
per_choice_rationale.D: Commits both homophone errors at once, treating sound-alike spellings as interchangeable when their meanings differ.

why_correct_md: The sentence needs **cite** (to quote as a source) and **principal** (chief), and the original supplies exactly those spellings.
why_tempted_md: 'Principle' attracts students because the two words sound identical and both feel formal in a news story.
rule_md: 1) Circle each sound-alike word in the span. 2) Say what the sentence needs it to mean (quote? place? rule? chief?). 3) Match meaning to spelling: cite = quote, site = place; principal = chief or person in charge, principle = rule. 4) Re-read the sentence with those meanings substituted and keep only the pair that fits.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>The stack of press releases sits</u> on the copy desk until an editor sorts through it each afternoon.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: The stack of press releases sit
The stacks of press releases sits
The stack of press releases are sitting

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the subject is the singular 'stack'; 'of press releases' is only a prepositional phrase, so the singular verb agrees.
per_choice_rationale.B: Matches the verb to 'releases,' the plural noun nearest the verb, instead of to the true subject — nearest-noun attraction.
per_choice_rationale.C: Rewrites the subject as plural while keeping a singular verb, trading one agreement error for another.
per_choice_rationale.D: Uses the plural verb 'are' with the singular subject 'stack,' the same attraction error in progressive form.

why_correct_md: The subject is the singular **stack** — the phrase 'of press releases' is only a prepositional modifier — so 'sits' agrees.
why_tempted_md: 'Sit' tempts students who match the verb to 'releases,' the plural noun sitting closest to it.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb. 2) Ask 'who or what does it?' to find the subject. 3) Cross out prepositional phrases (of..., on..., with...) between subject and verb. 4) Match the verb to the remaining head noun. 5) Re-read the trimmed sentence to confirm it sounds right.

subject: act-english
context_html: At the awards banquet, the publisher thanked the intern <u>who had organized</u> fifty years of photo negatives into a searchable archive.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: 'who' is the subject performing 'had organized,' so subject case is required.
per_choice_rationale.B: Hypercorrect 'whom' places an object form in the subject seat of its clause.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Which' cannot refer to a person; the antecedent is 'the intern.'
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Whomever' is both object case and an open-ended pronoun, and neither feature fits a specific intern doing the verb.

why_correct_md: **Who** is correct because the pronoun is the subject of 'had organized' — the he/him test yields 'he had organized.'
why_tempted_md: 'Whom' tempts students who assume the fancier form is safer after a verb like 'thanked.'
rule_md: 1) Isolate the clause the pronoun starts. 2) Replace the pronoun with 'he' or 'him' and read the clause alone. 3) If 'he' works, use who/whoever; if 'him' works, use whom/whomever. 4) Confirm the pronoun refers to a person, not a thing. 5) Re-read the full sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: After the county fair edition came back smeared, the editor phoned the pressroom manager, and <u>she promised that</u> a corrected run would be delivered by noon.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence's meaning clearest?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'She' could be either the editor or the manager, so the reference is ambiguous.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: naming 'the manager' gives the verb one unmistakable doer in a sentence with two possible referents.
per_choice_rationale.C: Names the speaker but shifts to present tense inside a past-tense narrative.
per_choice_rationale.D: Changes the tense while keeping the ambiguous pronoun, so the real problem survives.

why_correct_md: Replacing the pronoun with **the manager** gives the promise one unmistakable maker in a sentence containing two women.
why_tempted_md: The original tempts readers who assume a pronoun automatically points to the nearest or most recently mentioned person.
rule_md: 1) Circle the pronoun. 2) List every earlier noun it could point to. 3) If more than one candidate fits, the pronoun is ambiguous — replace it with the intended noun. 4) Keep the verb tense consistent with the surrounding narrative. 5) Re-read to confirm one clear meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: The Gazette's print circulation has fallen for nine straight years. <u>Similarly,</u> its free email newsletter now reaches three times as many readers as the printed paper did at its peak.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Similarly' claims the two facts run in the same direction, but decline and growth pull opposite ways.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Therefore' invents a cause-effect link the sentences never state.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For example' would make the newsletter's growth an instance of print's decline, which it is not.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it signals the reversal between shrinking print readership and booming digital readership.

why_correct_md: Only this transition matches the **logical turn** from a shrinking print run to a growing digital readership.
why_tempted_md: 'Similarly' tempts readers because both sentences describe the same newspaper's audience, so they feel parallel.
rule_md: 1) Summarize the sentence before the transition in five words. 2) Summarize the sentence after it. 3) Name the relationship: same direction, reversal, cause, or example. 4) Test the transition by reading both sentences with it. 5) Keep only the transition that matches the named relationship.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each week, Rosa Alvarez interviews the family of every person who has died in Harper County, asking about nicknames, recipes, and small kindnesses. The finished obituaries often run longer than the front-page stories. Readers say they clip and save them, and some families frame them.
stem_md: The writer wants to open the paragraph with a sentence that introduces its main focus. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Newspapers have printed obituaries for hundreds of years.
Rosa Alvarez has worked at the Ledger longer than any other employee.
Harper County has been losing population for decades.
At the Harper County Ledger, obituaries are treated as the paper's most careful journalism.

per_choice_rationale.A: Too broad — it promises a history of obituaries in general, not this paper's distinctive practice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Wrong emphasis — it narrows the paragraph to one employee's tenure, which the details never discuss.
per_choice_rationale.C: Off-topic — population decline never appears anywhere in the paragraph.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it names the paper and frames obituaries as its signature work, the idea every following sentence supports.

why_correct_md: It states the exact idea the details develop: this paper gives its obituaries **extraordinary care**, shown by the interviews, the length, and the readers who save them.
why_tempted_md: The tenure sentence tempts students because Rosa Alvarez stars in the paragraph's first body sentence.
rule_md: 1) Read the body sentences and state their shared subject in one phrase. 2) Ask what each opener promises the paragraph will discuss. 3) Eliminate openers broader or narrower than the shared subject. 4) Eliminate openers introducing facts the body never touches. 5) Keep the opener whose promise every body sentence helps keep.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Most stories at the Bugle begin with a call to the newsroom tip line. [2] A reporter first checks the caller's claim against public records. [3] If the documents support it, the reporter schedules interviews with everyone involved. [4] Only after that groundwork does the editor assign the story a slot in an upcoming edition. [5] Those interviews often uncover details the records leave out.
stem_md: For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, Sentence 5 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Leaves 'Those interviews' stranded after a sentence about the editor, two steps past its referent.
per_choice_rationale.B: Opens the paragraph with a pointing phrase that refers to nothing the reader has seen.
per_choice_rationale.C: Places the comment about interviews before any interviews have been mentioned.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: 'Those interviews' directly follows the sentence that introduces the interviews.

why_correct_md: The sentence's pointer phrase **'Those interviews'** must sit immediately after the step that introduces the interviews.
why_tempted_md: Leaving it in place tempts students because the sentence is true anywhere; only the dangling pointer reveals the problem.
rule_md: 1) Find the moved sentence's pointing words ('those,' 'this,' 'it'). 2) Locate the sentence that introduces what they point to. 3) Place the moved sentence immediately after that referent. 4) Re-read the paragraph to confirm each step still follows the last.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] New carriers at the Bugle spend their first Saturday riding the delivery route with manager Dot Pruitt. [2] By their third week, most can finish the route alone in under two hours. [3] She points out which porches flood, which dogs only bluff, and which subscribers want the paper tucked inside the storm door. [4] Veterans say that single morning teaches more than the carrier handbook ever could. [5] Perhaps that is why the Bugle has not missed a delivery day in forty years.
stem_md: For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, Sentence 3 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Rewinds the paragraph's clock: carriers are already working alone in week three when the first-morning details suddenly return.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the first-Saturday details follow the sentence that introduces the ride-along, and 'She' sits next to Pruitt.
per_choice_rationale.C: Files the tour's details after veterans have already delivered their verdict on the morning's value.
per_choice_rationale.D: Opens the paragraph with 'She' before Pruitt has been named.

why_correct_md: Placing the tour details right after the ride-along is introduced keeps the **chronology** intact and puts 'She' beside its antecedent, Dot Pruitt.
why_tempted_md: The current spot tempts students because the sentence still reads grammatically there; only the timeline jump gives it away.
rule_md: 1) Find the sentence's time cues and pronouns. 2) Match the pronoun to its antecedent and keep them close. 3) Order events by the paragraph's clock: first morning before third week. 4) Re-read the whole paragraph to confirm time moves forward.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] For sixty years, the Ledger's press run ended with a ritual: the night foreman inked his thumb and pressed it beside the masthead of the first copy off the press. [2] The smudged copies were never sold; they went onto a nail in the pressroom wall. [3] By the time the paper moved out, more than three thousand hung there in yellowing rows. [4] The building's new owners planned to gut the pressroom for loft apartments. [5] When word spread, former carriers and pressmen drove in from three states to claim a thumbprinted copy. [6] Startled by the turnout, the developers agreed to frame two hundred of them in the lobby instead.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide this paragraph into two paragraphs, separating the account of the pressroom ritual from the account of what happened after the paper moved out. The most logical place to begin the second paragraph is at:

per_choice_rationale.A: Splits the ritual from its immediate result, stranding the thumbprinted copies one sentence into a new paragraph.
per_choice_rationale.B: Tempting because it mentions the move, but Sentence 3 still describes the collection's growth — the ritual's own story.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: Sentence 4 introduces the new owners and their plan, the first sentence that belongs wholly to the aftermath.
per_choice_rationale.D: Leaves the owners' demolition plan attached to the ritual half, though it launches the aftermath.

why_correct_md: The topic genuinely **turns** when the new owners and their demolition plan enter; everything before that still portrays the tradition.
why_tempted_md: Sentence 3 tempts students because its opening time phrase mentions the move, even though its main clause still describes the tradition's scale.
rule_md: 1) State each half's job from the stem. 2) Label every sentence with the half it serves, judging by its main clause. 3) Find where the labels flip and stay flipped. 4) Begin the new paragraph at the first sentence of the second job. 5) Re-read both halves to confirm each is self-contained.

subject: act-english
context_html: The Ledger's oldest <u>machine, a 1948 flatbed press that once printed ration books,</u> still turns out the holiday edition every December.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English punctuation?

choices.label: machine, a 1948 flatbed press that once printed ration books
machine a 1948 flatbed press that once printed ration books,
machine, a 1948 flatbed press, that once printed ration books,

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the nonessential appositive is set off by a matched pair of commas, and the restrictive 'that' clause stays glued to 'press.'
per_choice_rationale.B: Opens the appositive but never closes it before the main clause resumes at 'still.'
per_choice_rationale.C: Closes an interruption that was never opened, leaving 'machine a 1948 flatbed press' run together.
per_choice_rationale.D: Adds an extra comma that severs the restrictive 'that' clause from the noun it defines.

why_correct_md: A nonessential appositive needs **paired commas** — one at its entrance, one at its exit — with no comma inside splitting the 'that' clause from 'press.'
why_tempted_md: Dropping the second comma tempts students because the pause feels finished once the description ends.
rule_md: 1) Find the interrupting description. 2) Test it: delete the phrase — if the sentence still works, it is nonessential. 3) Give a nonessential interrupter punctuation on BOTH sides. 4) Check that no comma separates a noun from a 'that' clause that defines it. 5) Re-read with the phrase removed to confirm the frame is matched.

subject: act-english
context_html: The Bugle's sports section relies on its stringers<u>—three high schoolers and a retired coach—</u>to cover every varsity game in the county.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: —three high schoolers and a retired coach,
, three high schoolers and a retired coach—
—three high schoolers and a retired coach

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the interrupting appositive is framed by a matched pair of dashes.
per_choice_rationale.B: Opens with a dash but closes with a comma — a mismatched frame.
per_choice_rationale.C: Opens with a comma but closes with a dash — the same mismatch reversed.
per_choice_rationale.D: Opens the interrupter with a dash and never closes it at all.

why_correct_md: Paired punctuation must **match**: an interrupter opened with a dash must be closed with a dash.
why_tempted_md: The dash-comma mix tempts students because each mark looks acceptable on its own side of the phrase.
rule_md: 1) Spot the interrupting phrase. 2) Note the mark that opens it. 3) Require the identical mark to close it: dash pairs with dash, comma with comma, parenthesis with parenthesis. 4) Delete the interrupter and re-read to be sure the outer sentence flows. 5) Reject any mixed or missing frame.

subject: act-english
context_html: Applicants for the Courier's summer internship <u>must bring:</u> a notebook, two clippings of their own writing, and a pen that works.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: Places a colon between a verb and its objects; a colon requires a complete statement before it.
per_choice_rationale.B: Uses a semicolon to introduce a list, but semicolons join independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.C: Inserts an unnecessary comma between the verb and the items it governs.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the list completes the verb 'bring,' so no punctuation belongs at that spot.

why_correct_md: The list is the **direct object** of 'bring,' so the verb should flow straight into it with no mark at all.
why_tempted_md: The colon tempts students trained to put a colon before every list, whether or not a complete clause precedes it.
rule_md: 1) Cover everything after the possible colon spot. 2) Ask: is what remains a complete, standalone statement? 3) If yes, a colon may introduce the list; if no, use no mark. 4) Never let any mark separate a verb from its objects. 5) Re-read the sentence straight through to confirm the flow.

subject: act-english
context_html: When the flood cut off the east side of town, volunteers <u>hauled</u> bundles of the emergency edition across the railroad bridge on foot.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize the physical effort the volunteers' task required. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the verb connotes dragging heavy weight, putting the volunteers' exertion front and center.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Took' is colorless and says nothing about strain.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Moved' records only a change of place, not the labor involved.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Transported' is precise but clinical — logistics language, not sweat.

why_correct_md: The original verb builds **strain and weight** into its very meaning, exactly the emphasis the stated goal demands.
why_tempted_md: 'Transported' tempts students who equate the most formal-sounding word with the best word.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's stated goal in your own words. 2) For each verb, ask what a reader pictures. 3) Score each verb against the goal, not against formality. 4) Eliminate verbs that are neutral about the goal's key quality. 5) Pick the one whose connotation delivers the goal.

subject: act-english
context_html: The council's audit of the paving contract, released Tuesday and summarized on the Sentinel's front page, <u>was a total train wreck for</u> the mayor's downtown plan.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the formal, reportorial tone established in the passage?

choices.label: was kind of a bummer for

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Total train wreck' is casual slang that clashes with the measured news-report register.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: measured and precise, matching the passage's reportorial diction.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Kind of a bummer' is even more conversational than the original.
per_choice_rationale.D: Grammatical but melodramatic — editorializing overstatement rather than neutral reporting.

why_correct_md: It keeps the sentence in the passage's **measured, reportorial register** while still conveying that the audit hurt the plan.
why_tempted_md: The melodramatic option tempts students because its forcefulness sounds impressively decisive.
rule_md: 1) Sample the passage's diction from the non-underlined parts. 2) Label the register: formal report, casual talk, or dramatic commentary. 3) Read each option in the sentence and label its register the same way. 4) Reject any option whose label differs from the passage's. 5) Keep the one that blends in.

subject: act-english
context_html: This spring, the Millbrook Courier began scanning a century of back issues, some so brittle they crumble at a touch. The project's biggest obstacle is not equipment but labor: each page must be flattened, photographed, and labeled by hand. The editor hopes the archive will be searchable online within two years.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the second sentence: "Last month, twelve volunteers from the historical society began labeling pages every weekend." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it explains what the project's equipment costs.
Yes, because it shows how the project's main obstacle is being addressed.
No, because it shifts the main focus away from the editor.
No, because it repeats the paragraph's earlier description of the obstacle.

per_choice_rationale.A: Right verdict, wrong warrant — the new sentence says nothing about equipment or costs.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the paragraph names labor as the bottleneck, and the volunteer crew answers exactly that problem.
per_choice_rationale.C: The paragraph's focus is the scanning project, not the editor, so no shift occurs.
per_choice_rationale.D: The sentence adds new information — who is now doing the labeling — rather than repeating anything.

why_correct_md: The paragraph names hand labor as the project's bottleneck, and the added sentence supplies **direct progress** on that exact problem.
why_tempted_md: The equipment-costs option tempts students because its 'yes' verdict feels right and they skim past the stated justification.
rule_md: 1) Decide the verdict: does the new sentence serve the paragraph's focus? 2) Then audit the justification: does it describe what the sentence actually does? 3) Reject any option whose justification misstates the sentence's content, even if its verdict matches yours. 4) Confirm the surviving justification names the real connection.

subject: act-english
context_html: The Deer Creek Bugle once printed twice a week; now it prints only on Thursdays. Yet the paper's newsroom is busier than ever. Last fall, its two reporters began recording a weekly podcast in the old darkroom, answering listener questions about county government. The Bugle's website now posts game scores the same night they happen, and its email edition follows readers who moved away decades ago.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to show how a small-town newspaper is adapting to a changing media landscape. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it argues that print is superior to new media like podcasts.
No, because it describes the specific efforts of only one paper rather than the whole industry.
Yes, because it describes specific changes the Bugle has made to reach new audiences.
No, because it never explains why the Bugle made these changes to its operations.

per_choice_rationale.A: Misreads the essay — it never compares print's merits to any other medium, let alone argues superiority.
per_choice_rationale.B: Over-demands: a goal about 'a small-town newspaper' is satisfied by one paper's story.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the podcast, same-night scores, and email edition are exactly the adaptations the stated goal asks for.
per_choice_rationale.D: Invents a requirement; the goal concerns how the paper is adapting, not why it cut a print day.

why_correct_md: The essay catalogs concrete **adaptations** — podcast, instant scores, email edition — which is precisely what the supposed goal requests.
why_tempted_md: The one-paper objection tempts students who assume a broad-sounding goal requires industry-wide evidence.
rule_md: 1) Restate the supposed goal precisely, noting its scope ('a small-town newspaper,' singular). 2) List what the essay actually does, sentence by sentence. 3) Match: does the essay's content fit the goal's scope and subject? 4) Check each option's stated warrant against both the goal and the essay. 5) Keep the option whose verdict and warrant are both accurate.

subject: act-english
context_html: Loyal readers often say they subscribe to the Sentinel mainly for its community calendar. The calendar lists every gathering in the county, from pancake breakfasts to school-board meetings, and it appears in the same spot on page three each week.
stem_md: The writer wants to add a sentence that most strongly supports the paragraph's claim that the calendar keeps subscribers loyal. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: The Sentinel's calendar has been edited by the same staff member for eleven years.
In a recent survey, half of the Sentinel's subscribers named the calendar as the top reason they renew.
Subscribers can renew by mail, by phone, or at the newspaper's front counter.
One recent addition to the calendar is a listing of library story hours.

per_choice_rationale.A: Describes the calendar's staffing, which says nothing about why subscribers stay.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it gives direct evidence tying the calendar to subscribers' decisions to renew.
per_choice_rationale.C: Lists renewal methods, not motives — the calendar never enters the sentence.
per_choice_rationale.D: Adds calendar content but draws no link to subscriber loyalty.

why_correct_md: It is the only option that **links both ends** of the claim — the calendar and subscribers' decisions to stay.
why_tempted_md: The staffing detail tempts students because an editor's longevity feels like proof of quality, which they mistake for proof of loyalty.
rule_md: 1) Underline the claim to be supported ('the calendar keeps subscribers loyal'). 2) For each option, ask: does it connect the calendar to subscribers' staying? 3) Discard sentences about the calendar alone or about subscribing alone. 4) Prefer concrete evidence of the link over adjacent facts. 5) Re-read the paragraph with the winner inserted.

subject: act-english
context_html: The deadline passed at <u>midnight the presses</u> were already humming in the basement.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Fuses two independent clauses with no boundary at all.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: a semicolon legally joins the two closely related independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.C: A comma alone between independent clauses creates a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'However' with only a comma still splices the clauses — a conjunctive adverb is not a conjunction.

why_correct_md: A **semicolon** is a legal boundary between two independent clauses, which is exactly what these two complete statements need.
why_tempted_md: The comma tempts students because the pause feels sufficient when the two clauses are short and related.
rule_md: 1) Find each subject-verb pair. 2) Ask whether each could stand alone as a sentence. 3) Two standalones need a real boundary: period, semicolon, or comma plus a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS). 4) A comma alone — or comma plus 'however' — is not a boundary. 5) Re-read each clause separately to confirm.

subject: act-english
context_html: In its final issue of the year, the Courier endorsed the school <u>bond, and its editorial board</u> had opposed the same measure only a year earlier.
stem_md: Which choice most effectively signals the logical relationship between the two clauses?

choices.label: bond even though its editorial board

per_choice_rationale.A: 'And' treats a striking reversal as mere addition, hiding the tension between the clauses.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'So' claims this year's endorsement caused last year's opposition — backward causation.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: it subordinates the earlier opposition as a concession, capturing the surprising reversal.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'For' asserts the old opposition was the reason for endorsing, which inverts the logic.

why_correct_md: The clauses pull against each other, so the joint must signal **concession** — an endorsement made despite the board's earlier opposition.
why_tempted_md: 'And' tempts students because it is never ungrammatical, so the flattened logic slips past them.
rule_md: 1) State each clause's point in plain words. 2) Name the logical link: addition, cause, result, or concession/surprise. 3) Pick the connector built for that link. 4) Watch direction: cause words point from reason to result. 5) Re-read to confirm the connector matches the meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: According to the press association's annual tally, the Sentinel's letters page draws more submissions <u>than the Tribune</u>, its only competitor in the county.
stem_md: Which choice makes the comparison in the sentence logical and grammatically correct?

per_choice_rationale.A: Compares submissions to an entire newspaper — a category mismatch.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the possessive stands in for 'the Tribune's letters page,' balancing the comparison.
per_choice_rationale.C: Adds an s without an apostrophe, creating a plural rather than a possessive.
per_choice_rationale.D: Swaps in 'then,' a time word, where the comparison word is required.

why_correct_md: The **possessive** makes the sentence compare like with like — one paper's submissions against the other paper's.
why_tempted_md: The original tempts students because speech routinely shortens comparisons this way, masking the category mismatch.
rule_md: 1) Find the two things compared. 2) Ask: are they the same category (page vs. page, count vs. count)? 3) If not, repair with a possessive or 'that of / those of.' 4) Confirm 'than' (comparison), not 'then' (time). 5) Re-read the comparison with both halves spelled out.

subject: act-english
context_html: The two editors <u>collaborated</u> on the investigation for six months before publishing a single word.
stem_md: Which choice is most concise while preserving the meaning of the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the verb already contains the idea of working together, so nothing more is needed.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Together' repeats meaning built into the verb itself — a redundant modifier.
per_choice_rationale.C: Stacks two redundant modifiers that both restate the verb's core idea.
per_choice_rationale.D: Adds two more ways of saying what the verb already says, tripling the same idea.

why_correct_md: **Collaborated** already means worked together, so any added modifier only repeats it.
why_tempted_md: 'Collaborated together' tempts students because the pairing is common in casual speech and sounds emphatic rather than repetitive.
rule_md: 1) Define the underlined verb precisely. 2) Ask what each added word contributes beyond that definition. 3) Delete any word whose meaning the verb already carries. 4) Prefer the leanest version that keeps the full meaning. 5) Re-read to confirm nothing was lost.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Due to the fact that</u> the press broke down on Wednesday, the weekend edition shipped a day late.
stem_md: Which choice most effectively eliminates wordiness?

choices.label: In light of the fact that

per_choice_rationale.A: Five words doing one word's job — bureaucratic padding around a simple cause.
per_choice_rationale.B: Swaps one padded 'the fact that' formula for an equally padded one.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a single standard conjunction carries the full causal meaning.
per_choice_rationale.D: A colloquialism that standard written English rejects as a cause connector.

why_correct_md: One standard **conjunction** expresses the entire causal link that the five-word formula labors to state.
why_tempted_md: The original tempts students because official-sounding phrases feel more formal and therefore more correct.
rule_md: 1) Ask what logical job the underlined phrase performs (here: cause). 2) List the shortest standard word for that job. 3) Compare candidates: same meaning, fewer words wins. 4) Reject phrases containing 'the fact that.' 5) Re-read with the lean version to confirm nothing changed but length.

subject: act-english
context_html: Asked about the missing festival funds, the county treasurer <u>gave a response in which she declined</u> to comment.
stem_md: Which choice best expresses the idea in the clearest, most economical way?

per_choice_rationale.A: Wraps one working verb inside an empty 'gave a response in which' frame.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: one verb carries the complete meaning of the whole span.
per_choice_rationale.C: Names the refusal twice — 'gave her refusal' and 'declined' describe one act.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'By way of' pads the sentence without adding any information.

why_correct_md: A single verb preserves **every shade of meaning** in the span, so all longer versions lose on economy.
why_tempted_md: The original tempts students because its roundabout frame sounds like careful, official reporting.
rule_md: 1) Identify the single action the span reports. 2) Try expressing it as one verb. 3) If the one-verb version keeps every shade of meaning, longer versions lose. 4) Watch for empty frames ('gave a response,' 'by way of'). 5) Re-read the sentence with the shortest survivor.

subject: act-english
context_html: Over one winter, the Gazette's archivist <u>invented</u> a catalog of every photograph the paper had published since 1946.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely describes the archivist's work?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Invented' means created from nothing, but the photographs already existed and only needed organizing.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it means gathered and arranged existing items — exactly the archivist's task.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Concocted' implies improvised mixtures or schemes, with a shady connotation wrong for archival work.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Imagined' would mean the catalog exists only in her head, not on paper.

why_correct_md: The archivist **gathered and organized existing photographs**, and only this verb means precisely that.
why_tempted_md: 'Invented' tempts students because inventing and creating feel interchangeable when something new is produced.
rule_md: 1) Pin down what literally happened (existing photos were organized into a list). 2) Define each verb candidate precisely. 3) Reject verbs implying creation from nothing, deception, or unreality. 4) Choose the verb whose core meaning matches the literal event. 5) Re-read for fit.

subject: act-english
context_html: Without naming anyone, the unsigned letter to the editor <u>indicated</u> that a council member had leaked the sealed bids.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely describes how the letter made its charge?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Indicated' is flat and neutral, missing the letter's sly, indirect accusation.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it means to suggest something discreditable indirectly — matching 'without naming anyone.'
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Announced' means declared openly, the opposite of an unsigned, nameless hint.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Disclosed' means revealed verified information, which an anonymous accusation is not.

why_correct_md: The context — unsigned, accusatory, naming no one — demands a verb of **indirect, discreditable suggestion**, and only one choice carries that exact shade.
why_tempted_md: 'Indicated' tempts students because it is a safe, general-purpose verb that never sounds wrong.
rule_md: 1) Collect the context clues ('without naming anyone,' 'unsigned,' an accusation). 2) Profile the needed verb: indirect, suggestive, accusatory. 3) Define each candidate and score it against all three features. 4) Eliminate verbs that are too open, too neutral, or too factual. 5) Keep the verb matching every clue.

subject: act-english
context_html: In a classic beurre blanc, the sharpness of the reduced white wine <u>compliments</u> the sweetness of the slowly whisked butter.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Confused homophone: the spelling with i means 'praises,' but the flavors complete and enhance each other, so the praise word is wrong.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the spelling with e means 'completes or enhances,' the intended meaning, and the present tense matches the sentence's timeless description.
per_choice_rationale.C: Doubles the error: it keeps the praise meaning and also shifts into past tense, clashing with the present-tense description.
per_choice_rationale.D: Right word, wrong tense: the past tense clashes with the sentence's present-tense account of how the sauce always works.

why_correct_md: The verb meaning **completes or enhances** (spelled with an e) fits the flavor relationship, and its present tense matches the rest of the sentence.
why_tempted_md: The praise spelling with *i* is far more common in everyday writing, so it looks correct by sheer familiarity.
rule_md: 1) Ask what the sentence means: is one thing praising another, or completing it? 2) If it means praise, use the spelling with *i* (as in 'I pay a compliment'). 3) If it means to complete or enhance, use the spelling with *e* (as in compl*e*te). 4) Finally, confirm the verb tense matches the surrounding sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: Every morning, the <u>batch of croissants rise</u> unevenly if the layered butter softens before the trays reach the oven.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Nearest-noun trap: the verb has been matched to the plural 'croissants' inside the prepositional phrase instead of to the singular subject 'batch.'
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the true subject is the singular 'batch,' so it takes the singular verb; 'of croissants' is only a modifier.
per_choice_rationale.C: Uses a plural verb and needlessly shifts into a progressive form, both of which fail with the singular, habitual subject.
per_choice_rationale.D: Rewrites the subject instead of fixing the verb — and the new plural 'batches' still disagrees with the singular verb.

why_correct_md: The subject is the singular **batch**, so it needs a singular verb; the prepositional phrase 'of croissants' cannot control agreement.
why_tempted_md: The plural noun sitting directly beside the verb makes a plural verb sound natural to the ear.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb. 2) Ask 'who or what does this?' 3) Cross out any prepositional phrase ('of ___') between subject and verb. 4) Match the verb to the head noun that remains. 5) Reread the sentence to confirm it sounds right without the crossed-out phrase.

subject: act-english
context_html: The saucier <u>who the head chef trusted</u> with the evening's consommé had apprenticed for a decade in Marseille.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: whom the head chef trusted him

per_choice_rationale.A: Case error: the pronoun is the object of 'trusted' (the head chef trusted *her*), so the subject form fails.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the relative pronoun receives the action of 'trusted,' so it must take the object case.
per_choice_rationale.C: Uses a relative pronoun reserved for things to refer to a person.
per_choice_rationale.D: Pronoun doubling: the relative pronoun already fills the object slot, so adding 'him' names the object twice.

why_correct_md: The pronoun is the **object** of 'trusted' — the head chef trusted *her* — so the object-case relative pronoun is required.
why_tempted_md: Because the pronoun appears right where a subject usually sits, before 'the head chef,' the subject form sounds natural.
rule_md: 1) Isolate the relative clause. 2) Rearrange it into a plain sentence: 'the head chef trusted ___.' 3) Test with he/him: if *him* fits, use the object-case relative pronoun; if *he* fits, use the subject form. 4) Confirm the pronoun refers to a person, not a thing. 5) Check that no extra pronoun repeats the same slot.

subject: act-english
context_html: After the milk is scalded and the yolks are whisked with sugar, <u>the custard base</u> must rest overnight before it is churned into ice cream.
stem_md: Which choice makes the reference clearest for the reader?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: with milk, yolks, and sugar all in play, only the specific noun makes the subject unmistakable.
per_choice_rationale.B: Ambiguous reference: 'it' could point to the milk or to the sugar as easily as to the finished mixture.
per_choice_rationale.C: Vague demonstrative: a bare 'this' after a clause full of nouns names nothing in particular.
per_choice_rationale.D: Wrong number and wrong referent: the plural seems to grab 'the yolks' and misstates what actually rests and gets churned.

why_correct_md: With **three candidate nouns** in the opening clause, only the concrete noun phrase identifies what must rest overnight.
why_tempted_md: After a long opening clause, a short pronoun feels less repetitive and more graceful than restating a noun.
rule_md: 1) Circle the pronoun or noun in question. 2) List every earlier noun it could point to. 3) If more than one noun could claim it, a pronoun is ambiguous. 4) Replace an ambiguous pronoun with the specific noun. 5) Reread as a first-time reader to confirm only one interpretation survives.

subject: act-english
context_html: Baking soda is inert on its own and must borrow an acid from the batter before it can lift anything. <u>Likewise,</u> baking powder arrives with its own acid built in, needing only moisture and heat to fire.
stem_md: Which transition most logically connects the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: Wrong-logic transition: 'Likewise' promises similarity, but one leavener must borrow an acid while the other carries its own — a difference.
per_choice_rationale.B: Wrong-logic transition: the second sentence is not an example of the first claim; it presents an opposing design.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the two sentences oppose each other on the key point — needing an outside acid versus carrying one built in.
per_choice_rationale.D: Wrong-logic transition: nothing in the sentences claims the first fact caused the second.

why_correct_md: The two leaveners **differ** on the crucial point — borrowed acid versus built-in acid — so the connector must signal opposition.
why_tempted_md: Both sentences describe leaveners and acids, so the surface similarity of topic makes a similarity word feel right.
rule_md: 1) Summarize the sentence before the transition in five words. 2) Summarize the sentence after it in five words. 3) Name the true relationship: same direction, example, cause-effect, or opposition. 4) Check that the transition's job matches that relationship. 5) If not, pick the connector whose job does.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] The paragraph then explains how heat unravels those coils. [2] As the egg white climbs past sixty degrees Celsius, the proteins bond into a mesh that traps water and turns the liquid opaque and firm. [3] <u>________</u>
stem_md: The writer wants a concluding sentence that captures the paragraph's main idea about why egg whites set when cooked. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Egg whites, of course, have been used in kitchens for centuries in dishes far too numerous to list here.
Sixty degrees Celsius is a temperature easily reached by most home stovetops within a minute or two.
Chefs sometimes add a pinch of salt to egg whites, though opinions differ on whether it truly helps.
In short, cooking sets an egg white by prompting its unraveled proteins to link into a solid, water-holding network.

per_choice_rationale.A: Off-topic conclusion: it drifts into the history of egg whites rather than summarizing the protein science just explained.
per_choice_rationale.B: Wrong focus: it seizes on a stray number instead of restating the paragraph's central cause-and-effect idea.
per_choice_rationale.C: Adds a new tangent about salt that the paragraph never developed, so it fails to summarize the main point.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it restates the paragraph's core idea — heat links proteins into a firm, water-holding mesh — as a clean conclusion.

why_correct_md: A strong conclusion **restates the paragraph's central point**, and only this option summarizes the heat-driven protein bonding the paragraph described.
why_tempted_md: The temperature detail was mentioned in the paragraph, so a sentence built around that number feels grounded in the text.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's single main idea in one sentence. 2) For each option, ask 'Does this echo that main idea, or introduce something new?' 3) Eliminate any option that adds a fact the paragraph never developed. 4) Keep the option that summarizes the central point. 5) Confirm it would make sense as the last line a reader remembers.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] A good stock begins with cold water, not hot. [2] Cold water draws proteins and impurities out slowly, letting them rise as a scummy raft the cook can skim away. [3] Hot water, by contrast, seals those impurities inside, clouding the finished broth. [4] The result is a stock that stays clear enough to read a printed word through.
stem_md: For the sake of logic and cohesion, where should the writer place the sentence 'The result is a stock that stays clear enough to read a printed word through' (currently sentence 4)?

per_choice_rationale.A: Misplaced: sitting after the 'hot water clouds the broth' sentence, the clarity 'result' seems to follow the clouding, which reverses the cause.
per_choice_rationale.B: Wrong slot: a 'result' sentence cannot open the paragraph before any cause has been given.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the clear-broth result follows directly from the cold-water skimming described in sentence 2, so it belongs right after it.
per_choice_rationale.D: Wrong slot: placed here, the 'result' interrupts before the reader learns what cold water actually does.

why_correct_md: A **result belongs immediately after its cause**; the clear broth is the payoff of the cold-water skimming in sentence 2, so it slots in right there.
why_tempted_md: Leaving the sentence last feels natural because concluding lines often close paragraphs, and it already sits at the end.
rule_md: 1) Identify what the movable sentence is a result of. 2) Locate the sentence that states that cause. 3) Place the result immediately after its cause. 4) Read the reordered paragraph to confirm no later sentence now seems to cause the result instead. 5) Check that the transitions still line up.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Caramelization and the Maillard reaction are often confused, yet they brown food by different routes. [2] Caramelization is the breakdown of sugar alone under high heat. [3] The Maillard reaction, by contrast, needs both sugars and amino acids, which is why it flavors seared meat and toasted bread rather than plain melted sugar. [4] Understanding which reaction is at work helps a cook aim heat and timing with real intent.
stem_md: For the sake of logic and cohesion, where should the writer place the sentence 'Understanding which reaction is at work helps a cook aim heat and timing with real intent' (currently sentence 4)?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the takeaway about applying the distinction rightly closes the paragraph, once both reactions have been contrasted.
per_choice_rationale.B: Wrong slot: the payoff about 'which reaction' lands before the second reaction has even been introduced.
per_choice_rationale.C: Wrong slot: a closing takeaway cannot precede the topic sentence that frames the comparison.
per_choice_rationale.D: Wrong slot: placed here, the takeaway interrupts the caramelization–Maillard contrast midstream.

why_correct_md: A **synthesizing takeaway belongs last**, after both reactions have been laid out, so it can rest on the full contrast.
why_tempted_md: Because the sentence names 'which reaction,' it seems to belong near the first mention of a reaction, tempting an earlier placement.
rule_md: 1) Decide whether the movable sentence introduces the topic or draws a conclusion from it. 2) A conclusion depends on the details before it, so it belongs after them. 3) Check that every idea the sentence refers to has already appeared. 4) Place it where nothing it relies on comes later. 5) Reread to confirm the paragraph builds to it.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Sourdough rises without commercial yeast because wild microbes colonize the flour-and-water starter. [2] Lactic acid bacteria and native yeasts settle in, feeding on sugars and releasing gas and tangy acids. [3] Feeding the starter daily keeps this community balanced and vigorous. [4] Shaping the dough is a separate craft altogether. [5] The baker folds and tensions the loaf to build a skin that traps the gas the microbes produce. [6] A well-shaped loaf holds its dome instead of spreading flat.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide this passage into two paragraphs so that each covers a distinct stage. Where should the new paragraph begin?

per_choice_rationale.A: Premature break: sentence 3 still concerns the microbial starter, so splitting here divides one topic in two.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: sentences 1–3 cover the living starter, while sentence 4 explicitly turns to shaping, a distinct stage — the natural fault line.
per_choice_rationale.C: Late break: sentence 4 already announces the shift to shaping, so beginning the new paragraph at 5 orphans that topic sentence.
per_choice_rationale.D: Too late: sentence 6 merely concludes the shaping discussion, leaving the shaping topic sentence stranded above the break.

why_correct_md: A new paragraph should start where the **topic changes**, and sentence 4 openly pivots from the microbial starter to the craft of shaping.
why_tempted_md: Sentence 5 gives the vivid, concrete details of shaping, so it feels like where the 'real' new topic begins.
rule_md: 1) Label each sentence with its subtopic. 2) Find the exact sentence where the subtopic first changes. 3) The new paragraph begins with that pivoting sentence, not the one after it. 4) Confirm the sentence before the break still fits the first subtopic. 5) Confirm the break does not separate a topic sentence from its supporting details.

subject: act-english
context_html: The pastry chef sharpened all of her <u>knive's</u> before the dinner service began.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Apostrophe error: the word is a simple plural, not a possessive, so no apostrophe belongs.
per_choice_rationale.B: Wrong plural form: 'knife' pluralizes to 'knives,' not 'knifes.'
per_choice_rationale.C: Double error: it uses the wrong plural stem and adds a possessive apostrophe the sentence does not need.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the sentence needs the plain plural of 'knife,' which is 'knives,' with no apostrophe.

why_correct_md: The chef sharpened more than one knife — a **plain plural** — so the correct form is 'knives' with no apostrophe.
why_tempted_md: Writers often reach for an apostrophe whenever a word ends in -s, mistaking every -s ending for a possessive.
rule_md: 1) Ask whether the word shows ownership or just names more than one thing. 2) If it merely counts more than one, use a plain plural with no apostrophe. 3) For nouns ending in -fe, change the ending to -ves. 4) Reserve the apostrophe for possession or contraction. 5) Reread to confirm nothing is being owned.

subject: act-english
context_html: Three humble ingredients <u>flour, water, and salt)</u> become bread once wild yeast and time go to work.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence's punctuation correct?

per_choice_rationale.A: Unpaired mark: a closing parenthesis appears with no opening one, so the aside is not enclosed.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: paired parentheses open and close the parenthetical list, enclosing it cleanly.
per_choice_rationale.C: Same flaw as the original: only the closing parenthesis is present, leaving the opener missing.
per_choice_rationale.D: Opposite half-pair: it supplies the opening parenthesis but drops the closer, so the aside never ends.

why_correct_md: Parentheses are **paired punctuation**: an enclosed aside needs both an opening and a closing mark.
why_tempted_md: Because the closing parenthesis already sits in the sentence, adding nothing feels like leaving well enough alone.
rule_md: 1) Spot any parenthesis, dash, or bracket used to set off an aside. 2) Confirm it comes as a matched pair — one to open, one to close. 3) If only one mark appears, add its partner or delete it. 4) Check that the sentence still reads correctly if the aside is removed. 5) Reread to confirm the enclosure is complete.

subject: act-english
context_html: A well-stocked spice drawer rewards the patient cook with one essential <u>virtue: freshness,</u> since ground spices surrender their aroma within months.
stem_md: Which choice uses punctuation correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: Extra comma: the colon correctly introduces 'freshness,' but the trailing comma wrongly splits it from the clause that explains it.
per_choice_rationale.B: Wrong mark: a semicolon must join two independent clauses, yet 'freshness' is a single word, not a clause.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a complete clause precedes the colon, and the colon introduces the single item 'freshness' with no stray comma to break the flow.
per_choice_rationale.D: Weak substitute: a comma cannot do the announcing work the colon does before a spotlighted term, and the second comma compounds the choppiness.

why_correct_md: A colon follows a **complete clause** to spotlight what comes next, and 'freshness' should flow straight into its explanation with no extra comma.
why_tempted_md: The trailing comma looks like a natural breath before the 'since' clause, so the original punctuation seems balanced.
rule_md: 1) Confirm the words before the colon form a complete sentence. 2) Confirm the colon introduces a list, term, or explanation. 3) Do not drop a comma between the introduced term and the clause that modifies it unless grammar demands one. 4) Reserve semicolons for joining two independent clauses. 5) Reread to hear whether the spotlighted term flows into its explanation.

subject: act-english
context_html: When the sear hit the ribeye, the surface <u>changed</u> from dull red to a lacquered mahogany crust in seconds.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize how dramatic and rapid the transformation looked. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: Too flat: 'changed' is accurate but neutral, conveying no drama or speed.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: 'erupted' delivers the sudden, vivid intensity the writer wants to emphasize.
per_choice_rationale.C: Too mild: 'shifted' suggests a gentle, gradual move, the opposite of a dramatic burst.
per_choice_rationale.D: Weakest: 'was different' is static and vague, capturing neither drama nor motion.

why_correct_md: The goal is **drama and speed**, and 'erupted' carries explosive suddenness that a neutral verb cannot.
why_tempted_md: 'Changed' is perfectly accurate and grammatical, so it feels safe even though it conveys none of the requested intensity.
rule_md: 1) Underline the goal words in the stem — here, dramatic and rapid. 2) Rank each option for intensity and speed. 3) Discard verbs that are neutral or gradual. 4) Keep the word that most vividly matches the stated goal. 5) Reread the sentence to confirm the chosen word delivers the intended punch.

subject: act-english
context_html: The lab notebook describes the emulsion precisely: as oil is added drop by drop, lecithin molecules coat each droplet and <u>prevent the fat and water from separating</u>.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the passage's measured, scientific tone?

choices.label: stop the greasy mess from splitting apart
keep everything from totally falling to pieces
boss the fat and water into behaving

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the neutral, precise wording matches the notebook's measured scientific register.
per_choice_rationale.B: Register clash: 'greasy mess' is colloquial and dismissive, breaking the clinical tone.
per_choice_rationale.C: Too loose: 'totally falling to pieces' is casual hyperbole out of place in a lab notebook.
per_choice_rationale.D: Figurative slang: 'boss ... into behaving' personifies the molecules in a jokey, informal way.

why_correct_md: The passage keeps a **measured scientific register**, and only the neutral, precise phrasing sustains it.
why_tempted_md: The livelier phrasings feel more engaging, and students often assume vivid always beats plain, even in a technical context.
rule_md: 1) Name the passage's established tone — here, precise and scientific. 2) Read each option and flag any slang, hyperbole, or joking figure. 3) Eliminate options whose register clashes with the passage. 4) Keep the wording that blends in seamlessly. 5) Reread the full sentence to confirm the tone holds steady.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Blanching vegetables briefly in boiling water, then plunging them into ice, locks in their bright color. [2] The quick heat deactivates the enzymes that would otherwise dull the green, while the ice bath halts cooking before the texture goes soft. [3] Cooks use this two-step trick before freezing produce for the winter.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after sentence 2: 'The shock of the ice bath is what preserves the crispness that freezing alone would ruin.' Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it introduces the new topic of freezing that the paragraph goes on to develop.
Yes, because without it the paragraph never explains why blanching is done at all.
No, because it contradicts the earlier claim that the ice bath halts cooking.
No, because it repeats the point sentence 2 already makes about the ice bath protecting texture.

per_choice_rationale.A: False justification: the sentence dwells on the ice bath and crispness, not on freezing as a new topic.
per_choice_rationale.B: False justification: sentence 2 already explains the purpose, so this reason misreads the paragraph.
per_choice_rationale.C: Misreads the logic: the new sentence agrees with sentence 2 rather than contradicting it.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: sentence 2 already states the ice bath protects texture, so the addition is redundant.

why_correct_md: The addition merely **restates** sentence 2's point that the ice bath preserves texture, so it should be left out as redundant.
why_tempted_md: The sentence sounds informative and on-topic, and its mention of freezing seems to tie neatly to the last sentence.
rule_md: 1) Read the proposed sentence and state its single point. 2) Scan the paragraph for any sentence already making that point. 3) If the point is already present, the addition is redundant and should be cut. 4) If the point is new and relevant, keep it. 5) Match your yes/no to a reason that survives a careful reread.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] This essay walks through a single day in a fermentation lab, from the morning pH readings to the evening taste tests. [2] It follows the technicians as they nudge temperature and salt to steer colonies of bacteria toward the flavors a client ordered. [3] By closing time, a batch of miso has deepened a shade and gained a savory edge that no recipe could have promised in advance.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to argue that home fermentation is safer than most people fear. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: No, because the essay documents a day of professional lab work rather than making a case about home-fermentation safety.
No, because the essay focuses on the taste of miso instead of on bacteria.
Yes, because the essay shows technicians controlling bacteria without any accidents.
Yes, because the essay proves that fermentation is a widespread and ancient practice.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the essay is a descriptive account of a professional lab day, never arguing anything about home safety, so it misses the proposed goal.
per_choice_rationale.B: Wrong reason: the essay covers far more than miso's taste, and taste focus is not why it fails the safety goal.
per_choice_rationale.C: Overreach: an accident-free description of experts is not an argument that home fermentation is safe.
per_choice_rationale.D: False claim: the essay never addresses fermentation's history or prevalence at all.

why_correct_md: The essay is **descriptive, not argumentative**, and says nothing about home safety, so it cannot accomplish a persuasive safety goal.
why_tempted_md: Because the technicians handle bacteria smoothly with no mishaps, it can seem to imply that fermentation is safe.
rule_md: 1) State the proposed goal in your own words. 2) Identify what the essay actually does — describe, argue, or narrate. 3) Match the essay's real purpose against the goal. 4) Answer yes only if the essay genuinely pursues that goal. 5) Then choose the reason that accurately describes the mismatch or match.

subject: act-english
context_html: The paragraph explains why bread staling is not simply drying out. As a loaf cools, its starch molecules slowly recrystallize, hardening the crumb even inside a sealed bag. ________ A quick warm-up in the oven can reverse the process by melting those crystals back into softness.
stem_md: Which sentence, if inserted at the blank, best supports the paragraph's focus on the chemistry of staling?

choices.label: Many bakeries sell day-old loaves at a discount to avoid throwing them away.
This recrystallization, called retrogradation, continues even in humid conditions where drying cannot be the cause.
Sourdough has become a popular hobby among people who bake at home on weekends.
Some cooks prefer to slice bread thin so that each piece toasts more evenly.

per_choice_rationale.A: Off-focus: bakery pricing is a business detail, not part of the staling chemistry.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it names and reinforces the recrystallization mechanism, tying directly to the paragraph's chemical focus.
per_choice_rationale.C: Off-focus: the popularity of a hobby has nothing to do with the molecular process.
per_choice_rationale.D: Off-focus: slicing and toasting is a serving preference, unrelated to why bread stales.

why_correct_md: The paragraph is about the **chemistry of staling**, and only this sentence extends that mechanism by naming the recrystallization process.
why_tempted_md: The other options are all true statements about bread, so they feel relevant even though they drop the chemical thread.
rule_md: 1) Name the paragraph's specific focus in a phrase. 2) For each option, ask whether it advances that exact focus. 3) Reject any sentence that is merely about the same broad topic. 4) Keep the sentence that deepens the stated focus. 5) Reread with the insertion to confirm the thread stays unbroken.

subject: act-english
context_html: The candy thermometer is essential for <u>caramel work the sugar</u> passes through narrow temperature stages that the eye alone cannot judge.
stem_md: Which choice best corrects the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Fused sentence: two independent clauses run together with no punctuation or conjunction.
