rule_md: 1) List the meaning units the underlined portion must convey. 2) Strike every word that repeats a unit. 3) Choose the option carrying all units in the fewest words. 4) Re-read for grammar and fit.

subject: act-english
context_html: To keep the dye bath at a steady temperature, Elena <u>looked at</u> the thermometer every few minutes.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely conveys Elena's deliberate, repeated checking?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Looked at' is serviceable but vague; it misses the purposeful, ongoing attention described.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Glanced toward' suggests a casual flick of the eyes, weaker than the careful checking intended.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Witnessed' describes observing an event happen, not tracking an instrument over time.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the verb means to watch something systematically over time, matching the steady-temperature purpose.

why_correct_md: **Precision**: the right verb encodes systematic, purposeful watching — exactly what tending a dye bath requires.
why_tempted_md: 'Looked at' tempts because it is not wrong, merely weak; precision items reward the exact verb over the adequate one.
rule_md: 1) Identify what the sentence needs the word to convey (manner, purpose, duration). 2) Define each option in a phrase. 3) Eliminate words whose definitions add wrong shades or drop needed ones. 4) Pick the definition that matches the context exactly.

subject: act-english
context_html: In her artist's statement for the fiber-arts fellowship, Maya wrote that hand-spinning her own yarn <u>lets her mess around with</u> texture in ways commercial thread cannot.
stem_md: Which choice is most appropriate for the formal context of the sentence?

choices.label: gives her a shot at playing with
furnishes her the wherewithal to manipulate

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Mess around with' is casual slang, out of place in a formal fellowship statement.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'A shot at playing with' swaps one colloquialism for two.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: plain, professional wording suited to an application read by a review committee.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Furnishes her the wherewithal' is stiff, antique phrasing that overcorrects into pomposity.

why_correct_md: **Register** must fit audience and occasion: a fellowship statement calls for straightforward professional diction.
why_tempted_md: The ornate version tempts students who equate formal writing with fancy words, but overdressed prose misses the register just as slang does.
rule_md: 1) Name the document and its audience. 2) Decide the register they expect. 3) Sort each option: too casual, too stiff, or fitting. 4) Choose the phrasing the audience would not notice — appropriate register is invisible.

subject: act-english
context_html: At its annual fan appreciation night, the Meadowlark Falls Owls handed out <u>not only free caps and</u> vouchers for discounted season tickets.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: not only free caps as well as
not only free caps, and also
not only free caps but also

per_choice_rationale.A: Leaves 'not only' hanging without its required partner conjunction; a plain 'and' cannot complete the correlative pair.
per_choice_rationale.B: Substitutes the near-synonym 'as well as' for the fixed partner that 'not only' demands (correlative_wrong_partner).
per_choice_rationale.C: Adds a comma and 'also,' but the correlative pair is still broken because the fixed partner phrase never appears.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: 'not only' must be completed by its fixed correlative partner, which this choice supplies.

why_correct_md: **Correlative** conjunctions come in fixed pairs, and this choice completes the pair that 'not only' opens.
why_tempted_md: 'As well as' sounds natural in everyday speech, so students accept it as an interchangeable substitute for the fixed pair.
rule_md: 1) Spot a pair-opener such as 'not only,' 'either,' 'neither,' or 'both.' 2) Recall the one fixed partner that opener requires. 3) Scan ahead in the sentence for that exact partner. 4) If any other connector sits in its place, replace it with the fixed partner. 5) Confirm the two joined elements are parallel in form.

subject: act-english
context_html: The lineup of giveaway promotions <u>were announced</u> at a press event before the home opener.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Matches the verb to the nearby plural 'promotions' instead of the true singular subject 'lineup' (sv_nearest_noun).
per_choice_rationale.B: Repeats the nearest-noun error in the perfect tense: plural 'have' still agrees with the wrong word.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the head noun 'lineup' is singular, so it takes the singular past verb.
per_choice_rationale.D: Wrong on two counts: the verb is plural and present tense, but the subject is singular and the event already happened.

why_correct_md: The **subject** is the head noun 'lineup,' which is singular, so the verb must be singular and past to match the completed press event.
why_tempted_md: The plural noun 'promotions' sits right next to the verb, so the ear locks onto it instead of the true subject.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb. 2) Ask 'who or what does this?' and find the head noun, not the closest noun. 3) Cross out any prepositional phrase between subject and verb. 4) Match the verb's number to the head noun. 5) Check the tense against the sentence's time cues.

subject: act-english
context_html: The scout <u>whom the Owls hired last April</u> once pitched in a winter league in the Dominican Republic.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

choices.label: who the Owls hired last April
whom was hired by the Owls last April
which the Owls hired last April

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: inside the clause, the Owls did the hiring and the pronoun receives the action, so the object form is required.
per_choice_rationale.B: Uses the subject form even though the pronoun is the object of 'hired' (who_in_object_position).
per_choice_rationale.C: Hypercorrection: the pronoun is the subject of 'was hired,' so the object form cannot serve there (case_hypercorrect).
per_choice_rationale.D: Applies 'which' to a person; standard English reserves 'which' for things and animals (which_for_person).

why_correct_md: The pronoun is the **object** of 'hired' — the Owls hired *him* — so the object-case relative pronoun is exactly right as written.
why_tempted_md: Students who rarely hear 'whom' in conversation assume the subject form is always the safe modern default.
rule_md: 1) Isolate the relative clause. 2) Rewrite it as a plain sentence using 'he' or 'him.' 3) If 'him' fits (the Owls hired him), use the object form; if 'he' fits, use the subject form. 4) Separately confirm the pronoun type matches the antecedent: people take who/whom, things take which.

subject: act-english
context_html: After the hitting coach reviews video with each young slugger, <u>the coach</u> records the agreed-upon swing adjustments in a shared notebook.
stem_md: Which choice makes the meaning of the sentence clearest?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: with two possible people in the first clause, repeating the noun is the only way to make the recorder unmistakable.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'He' could refer to either the coach or the slugger, leaving the doer ambiguous (pronoun_two_referents).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'They' either invents a joint actor the sentence never establishes or leaves the recorder vague (vague_plural_pronoun).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'This' is a bare demonstrative with no noun to stand for, so the doer disappears entirely (demonstrative_no_antecedent).

why_correct_md: With two candidates in the opening clause, only the **repeated noun** leaves zero doubt about who keeps the notebook.
why_tempted_md: Students trained to avoid repetition reach for 'he,' overlooking that two males in the sentence make the pronoun ambiguous.
rule_md: 1) Circle every person or thing named before the pronoun. 2) If more than one could grammatically be the referent, the pronoun is ambiguous. 3) Test each candidate in the pronoun's slot; if two readings both make sense, replace the pronoun with the specific noun. 4) Re-read to confirm one, and only one, meaning survives.

subject: act-english
context_html: Cold rain washed out six home dates in April, and announced attendance sagged to a five-year low. <u>Therefore,</u> souvenir sales that month set a franchise record.
stem_md: Which transition word or phrase is most logical in context?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Therefore' claims the sales record resulted from the attendance slump, reversing the actual logic (transition_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: record sales despite a slump is a contrast, and this transition signals exactly that reversal.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Consequently' makes the same cause-effect error in a different word: a slump would not produce record sales.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'For example' would require the sales record to illustrate the slump, but it contradicts it (transition_example_misfit).

why_correct_md: The two sentences pull in opposite directions, so a **contrast** transition is the only logical bridge.
why_tempted_md: Students see two connected facts and default to a cause-effect word without testing whether the second fact actually follows from the first.
rule_md: 1) State sentence one in your own words. 2) State sentence two. 3) Name the true relationship: cause, contrast, example, addition, or time. 4) Check that the transition on the page signals that same relationship. 5) If not, swap in one that does and re-read.

subject: act-english
context_html: [The writer will add an introductory sentence here.] Hours before the gates open, he drags and waters the infield until the clay is uniform. Next he mows the outfield in alternating stripes and repaints the batter's boxes. Finally, he walks the foul lines with a string level, checking for the slightest crown. By the national anthem, every surface has met his exacting standard.
stem_md: The writer wants to open the paragraph with a sentence that introduces its main focus. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Corliss Park hosts more than sixty home games every season.
Corliss Park's infield grass is a hybrid variety bred to survive humid summers.
Ray Delgado attended games at Corliss Park long before he worked there.
Each home date at Corliss Park begins with the same demanding checklist for groundskeeper Ray Delgado.

per_choice_rationale.A: A schedule statistic never mentions the worker or his tasks, so it fails to preview the paragraph and leaves 'he' unexplained (intro_too_broad).
per_choice_rationale.B: A turf-botany detail points the paragraph toward grass science rather than the worker's pregame labor (intro_wrong_emphasis).
per_choice_rationale.C: Introduces the right person but frames his past as a fan, while the paragraph chronicles his present duties (intro_wrong_angle).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it names the worker and previews the sequence of pregame tasks that every following sentence describes.

why_correct_md: An effective introduction must **preview** the paragraph's content, and only this choice names the worker and sets up his pregame tasks.
why_tempted_md: The biography option mentions the right person, so students accept it without checking whether it sets up what the paragraph actually does.
rule_md: 1) Read the body of the paragraph first and summarize its focus in five words. 2) Ask what a reader must know for sentence two to make sense. 3) Test each opener: does it name that focus and point forward to it? 4) Eliminate openers that are broader, narrower, or angled at a different subject. 5) Pick the one that forecasts the body.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] In 2009, the Owls' front office needed a cheap between-innings attraction. [2] An intern proposed a footrace in which staffers dressed as giant condiments would sprint from third base to home plate. [3] Fans began arriving early just to claim seats along the third-base line. [4] Local businesses soon paid to have their logos stitched onto the costumes. [5] Today the race has its own theme song and a highlight reel on the video board.
stem_md: The writer wants to add the following sentence to the paragraph: "The prize was nothing grander than a plastic trophy kept on a shelf in the press box." To make the paragraph most logical, the sentence should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: At that point no race has been described, so 'the prize' has nothing to refer to (placement_before_referent).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the humble-stakes detail belongs right after the race is described, before the paragraph turns to its growing popularity.
per_choice_rationale.C: Interrupts the string of popularity details with origin-era information, breaking the paragraph's arc (placement_breaks_arc).
per_choice_rationale.D: Attaches an origin-era fact to the present-day conclusion, muddling the chronology (placement_wrong_era).

why_correct_md: The trophy detail describes the race's **original** humble stakes, so it must sit immediately after the race is introduced and before the growth story begins.
why_tempted_md: The end of the paragraph feels like a natural home for a leftover detail, so students park the sentence there without checking its time frame.
rule_md: 1) Identify what the new sentence refers to ('the prize' points to a contest). 2) Find where that referent first appears. 3) Note the paragraph's arc — origin, growth, present. 4) Place the sentence in the era it describes, immediately after its referent. 5) Re-read the paragraph to confirm smooth chronology.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Big-league clubs routinely send injured stars to minor-league affiliates to sharpen their timing. [2] Last June, the Owls hosted all-star pitcher Dana Whitfield for two rehab starts. [3] Ticket demand tripled within hours of the announcement. [4] Whitfield threw four scoreless innings in her opening outing and signed autographs afterward. [5] The windfall from those ticket sales paid for a fresh coat of paint on the aging concourse.
stem_md: The writer wants to improve the logic and cohesion of the paragraph. To accomplish that goal, Sentence 5 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Leaves 'those ticket sales' stranded two sentences from its referent, implying the pitching performance produced the money (placement_far_referent).
per_choice_rationale.B: Mentions a windfall before Whitfield's visit or any demand exists, so the reference has no antecedent (placement_before_cause).
per_choice_rationale.C: At that point the paragraph has not yet described any surge in tickets, so 'those ticket sales' still points at nothing (placement_before_cause).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the revenue sentence directly follows the demand spike that generated it, keeping cause and result adjacent.

why_correct_md: 'Those ticket sales' points back to the demand spike, so **cause and result** must sit side by side.
why_tempted_md: The sentence reads like a wrap-up, so students leave it at the end even though its pointer word reaches back past an unrelated sentence.
rule_md: 1) Find pointer words in the movable sentence ('those,' 'this,' 'such'). 2) Locate the exact sentence they refer to. 3) Place the movable sentence immediately after that referent. 4) Confirm nothing between cause and result changes the meaning. 5) Re-read the paragraph for flow.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Corliss Park opened in 1951 as the summer home of the Ridgeline Miners. [2] Its hand-painted outfield signs advertise businesses that closed decades ago. [3] Generations of fans learned to keep score in its shaded grandstand. [4] Even the park's oddities, like the flagpole standing in fair territory, became beloved. [5] Next spring, contractors will begin a two-year modernization of the property. [6] The flagpole will be relocated beyond a rebuilt outfield wall, and the signs will be preserved behind glass. [7] Club officials insist the grandstand's character will survive the upgrade.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide this paragraph into two paragraphs, the first about the park's past and the second about its future. The most logical place to begin the second paragraph is at:

per_choice_rationale.A: Breaks after a single opening fact, stranding the rest of the history in the future-focused paragraph (division_too_early).
per_choice_rationale.B: Fan memories in the grandstand are still past-focused, so a break there splits the history in two (division_mid_topic).
per_choice_rationale.C: Sentence 4 continues cataloging cherished old features; 'Even' extends the list rather than pivoting (division_false_pivot).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: 'Next spring' is the first look ahead, so the future-focused paragraph begins there.

why_correct_md: The **time frame** flips from past to future exactly at 'Next spring,' making that sentence the natural start of the second paragraph.
why_tempted_md: The word 'Even' at Sentence 4 feels like a rhetorical turn, so students mistake an extension of the list for a change of topic.
rule_md: 1) Label each sentence with its time frame or subtopic. 2) Find the first sentence whose label differs from everything preceding it. 3) Confirm every sentence past that point shares the new label. 4) Begin the new paragraph at that sentence. 5) Re-read both halves to verify each is unified.

subject: act-english
context_html: The visiting <u>players' lockers</u> line a narrow hallway behind the third-base dugout.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the lockers belong to multiple visiting players, so the plural possessive with the apostrophe after the s is right.
per_choice_rationale.B: Drops the apostrophe entirely, leaving two stacked nouns with no ownership marked (apostrophe_omitted).
per_choice_rationale.C: Claims a single owner, but a whole visiting roster shares the hallway of lockers (singular_for_plural_owner).
per_choice_rationale.D: Puts the apostrophe on the owned noun instead of the owners (apostrophe_wrong_noun).

why_correct_md: Many players own the lockers, so the **plural possessive** — apostrophe after the s — is exactly right as written.
why_tempted_md: Students who memorize "apostrophe-s shows possession" default to the singular form without asking how many owners there are.
rule_md: 1) Ask: who owns what? 2) Decide whether the owner is singular or plural. 3) Write the owner in its correct number first (player vs. players). 4) Add the possessive mark: apostrophe-s for singular, apostrophe after the s for regular plurals. 5) Confirm the apostrophe sits on the owner, never the thing owned.

subject: act-english
context_html: The club's bat dog<u>—a patient golden retriever named Biscuit,</u> trots onto the field to collect lumber between at-bats.
stem_md: Which choice provides the correct punctuation for the underlined portion?

choices.label: , a patient golden retriever named Biscuit—
, a patient golden retriever named Biscuit

per_choice_rationale.A: Opens the interrupter with a dash but closes it with a comma; paired punctuation must match (mismatched_pair).
per_choice_rationale.B: Reverses the mismatch — comma in, dash out — which is still an unmatched frame (mismatched_pair).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a matched pair of dashes encloses the appositive on both ends.
per_choice_rationale.D: Opens with a comma but never closes the interrupter, fusing 'Biscuit trots' into the main clause (unclosed_interrupter).

why_correct_md: An interrupting appositive must be **enclosed by a matched pair** of marks, and only this choice uses the same mark at both ends.
why_tempted_md: Students judge each mark separately, so a dash on one side and a comma on the other both look individually acceptable.
rule_md: 1) Bracket the interrupting phrase and read the sentence without it. 2) If the sentence still works, the phrase must be set off at both ends. 3) Check the opening mark and the closing mark. 4) Make them twins — two commas, two dashes, or two parentheses. 5) Never mix one kind with another.

subject: act-english
context_html: The promotions calendar saves the season's three biggest <u>draws for July: a drone light show,</u> a jersey auction, and the mascot's birthday bash.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

choices.label: draws for July; a drone light show,
draws for July, they include a drone light show,
draws for July, such as: a drone light show,

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: a complete statement precedes the colon, which then introduces the list of three named draws.
per_choice_rationale.B: A semicolon joins two independent clauses; it cannot introduce a list (semicolon_before_list).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'They include' starts a new independent clause after only a comma, creating a splice (comma_splice).
per_choice_rationale.D: A colon cannot interrupt the phrase 'such as,' and 'such as' wrongly implies examples rather than the full slate of three (colon_after_such_as).

why_correct_md: A **colon** may introduce a list when a complete statement comes before it — exactly the structure already on the page.
why_tempted_md: Many students believe a semicolon is simply a fancier list-introducer, so the second version looks equally formal and safe.
rule_md: 1) Cover everything past the mark and ask: is what remains a complete statement? 2) If yes and a list or explanation follows, a colon is legal. 3) Reject a semicolon unless full clauses sit on both sides. 4) Reject any colon glued to 'such as' or 'including.' 5) Reject a bare comma if a new subject-verb pair follows.

subject: act-english
context_html: Called up from rookie ball only two days earlier, Marcus <u>walked</u> toward the mound for his first professional start.
stem_md: The writer wants to suggest that Marcus is nervous as he approaches the mound. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Walked' is emotionally neutral and conveys nothing about nerves (goal_neutral_word).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: halting, reluctant movement is exactly the connotation the stated goal requires.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Strode' connotes confidence and command — the opposite of the goal (goal_opposite_emphasis).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Bounded' radiates eager energy, not anxiety (goal_wrong_emotion).

why_correct_md: The goal is nervousness, and only a verb connoting **hesitant, reluctant** movement delivers that feeling.
why_tempted_md: 'Strode' sounds vivid and athletic, so students pick the most impressive verb instead of the one matching the stated emotion.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's goal in one word (here: nervousness). 2) For each verb, name the emotion it radiates. 3) Eliminate neutral verbs — no emotion means no goal met. 4) Eliminate verbs radiating a different or opposite emotion. 5) Choose the verb whose connotation matches the goal word.

subject: act-english
context_html: Baseball historians admire Corliss Park's hand-operated scoreboard, which <u>is a seriously cool leftover</u> from the park's earliest seasons.
stem_md: Which choice is most consistent with the style and tone of the sentence?

choices.label: is an awesome blast from the past

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Seriously cool' is conversational slang that clashes with the scholarly frame 'historians admire' (tone_slang).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: measured, formal phrasing matches the sentence's scholarly register.
per_choice_rationale.C: Doubles down on slang with an exclamation-worthy cliché (tone_cliche).
per_choice_rationale.D: A casual idiom plus the vague exaggeration 'forever' undercuts the historian's precise voice (tone_idiom_hyperbole).

why_correct_md: The frame 'historians admire' sets a **formal register**, and only this choice keeps the description at that level.
why_tempted_md: The lively cliché feels more engaging than the original, so students mistake added energy for improved style.
rule_md: 1) Read the non-underlined words and label the register: formal, neutral, or casual. 2) Label each option the same way. 3) Eliminate any option whose register differs from the frame. 4) Among register matches, prefer precise wording over vague. 5) Re-read the full sentence in one voice.

subject: act-english
context_html: Life in the low minors is defined less by the games than by the miles between them. The Owls log more than eleven thousand bus miles each season, often rolling into town at dawn on the day of a game. Players nap in luggage racks, eat gas-station dinners, and learn to stretch in a moving aisle.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence at the end of the paragraph: "After one fourteen-hour ride last August, the team took batting practice without having slept at all." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it offers a vivid specific incident that supports the paragraph's picture of grueling travel.
Yes, because it explains why the league schedules so many road games.
No, because it repeats information already provided earlier in the paragraph.
No, because it introduces a topic unrelated to the paragraph's discussion of travel.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: a single dramatic episode makes the paragraph's general hardships concrete, so both verdict and reason hold.
per_choice_rationale.B: The sentence never touches scheduling decisions, so this justification is false even though its verdict matches (right_verdict_wrong_reason).
per_choice_rationale.C: The paragraph states hardships generally; this dated episode is new material, not repetition (mislabels_new_as_repeat).
per_choice_rationale.D: A sleepless team stumbling from a long bus ride sits squarely on the travel topic (misjudges_relevance).

why_correct_md: The new sentence turns the paragraph's general hardship into one **concrete** episode, which is exactly what a reason for adding must claim.
why_tempted_md: Students skim for repetition, see 'dawn arrivals' mentioned generally, and conclude the anecdote merely restates it.
rule_md: 1) Summarize the paragraph's focus in a phrase. 2) Ask whether the new sentence advances that focus. 3) Decide yes or no on that basis alone. 4) Then test each stated reason as a factual claim about the sentence and paragraph. 5) Select the option whose verdict AND reason are both true.

subject: act-english
context_html: The Owls measure their success in more than wins. Each spring, players visit every elementary school in the county to hand out reading challenges, and the club stocks a downtown food pantry with unsold concessions. Season-ticket holders vote on which neighborhood league receives the team's annual equipment donation, and the stadium's community garden supplies its own concession stand.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to write a brief passage showing how one minor-league team builds ties with its community. Would this passage accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it lists the corporate sponsors that fund the Owls' promotions.
Yes, because it details the club's ongoing partnerships with schools, charities, and neighborhood groups.
No, because it focuses mainly on the team's win-loss record.
No, because it describes outreach programs run by teams across several leagues.

per_choice_rationale.A: Right verdict, false reason: no sponsor is named anywhere in the passage (right_verdict_wrong_reason).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the passage catalogs one club's community programs, so both the verdict and the reason match the text.
per_choice_rationale.C: The passage explicitly sets winning aside in its first sentence and never tallies results (misreads_focus).
per_choice_rationale.D: Every program named belongs to the Owls alone, so the scope claim is false (wrong_scope).

why_correct_md: The passage stays on one club's community programs, so a yes-verdict is right only when its **reason** matches that content.
why_tempted_md: Students verify only the yes-or-no verdict and grab the first 'Yes' option without fact-checking its stated reason.
rule_md: 1) Restate the proposed goal in your own words. 2) Summarize what the passage actually covers. 3) Decide yes or no by comparing the two. 4) Treat each option's reason as a factual claim and verify it against the text. 5) Choose the option where verdict and reason are both accurate.

subject: act-english
context_html: Preparation for a fireworks night begins the moment the schedule is printed. The operations staff files permits with the city, hires a licensed pyrotechnics vendor, and briefs the grounds crew on postgame cleanup.
stem_md: The writer wants to add one more sentence with information most relevant to the paragraph's focus on how the ballpark prepares for fireworks nights. Given that all the choices are true, which one should the writer add?

choices.label: The Owls' mascot costume was redesigned by a local art student in 2018.
Crews rope off a landing zone in the outfield and soak the warning track before the first pitch.
Fireworks were invented in China well over a thousand years ago.
Many fans prefer afternoon games during the chilly early weeks of April.

per_choice_rationale.A: A mascot's makeover is trivia unconnected to show-night readiness (detail_offtopic).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it adds another concrete preparation task, matching the paragraph's list of readiness steps.
per_choice_rationale.C: Ancient origins are background trivia, not a preparation step (detail_trivia).
per_choice_rationale.D: Fan seating preferences describe atmosphere, not the staff's readiness work (detail_wrong_focus).

why_correct_md: The paragraph is a list of **preparation tasks**, and only this choice adds another task to that list.
why_tempted_md: The historical fact is genuinely interesting, so students confuse an engaging fact with a relevant one.
rule_md: 1) Name the paragraph's focus in five words or fewer. 2) For each option, ask: does this perform the same job the other sentences perform? 3) Reject options that add background, trivia, or a different subject, however true. 4) Keep the one that extends the paragraph's specific work. 5) Re-read the paragraph with it inserted.

subject: act-english
context_html: The tarp crew sprinted onto the <u>field the</u> rain was already sheeting down by the second out.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Two independent clauses sit back-to-back with nothing between them — a fused sentence (fused_sentence).
per_choice_rationale.B: A lone comma cannot join two independent clauses (comma_splice).
per_choice_rationale.C: A conjunctive adverb after a mere comma still splices the clauses, and it falsely claims the rain resulted from the sprint (adverb_splice).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: a semicolon legally joins two closely related independent clauses.

why_correct_md: Each half can stand alone, so the join needs a **semicolon-strength** boundary rather than a comma or nothing.
why_tempted_md: A comma matches the pause students hear when reading aloud, so the splice sounds punctuated correctly.
rule_md: 1) Find every subject-verb pair. 2) Test each clause: can it stand alone as a sentence? 3) If two can, check what joins them. 4) Legal joins: a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. 5) A bare comma, a bare adverb, or nothing at all fails — repair with a legal join.

subject: act-english
context_html: Although their bus broke down outside Dayton, <u>but the Owls</u> still reached the ballpark an hour ahead of batting practice.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Although' already links the clauses, so 'but' double-marks the contrast and leaves no true main clause (double_connector).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'And' also duplicates the connection and flattens the contrast into mere addition (double_connector_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'So' duplicates the link and miscasts the contrast as a result (double_connector_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: a subordinate opener attaches directly to the main clause with no added conjunction.

why_correct_md: One clause relationship gets **one connector**: 'Although' already does the linking, so the main clause must follow unassisted.
why_tempted_md: Speech often pairs 'although' with 'but,' so the doubled contrast sounds natural to the ear.
rule_md: 1) Find the opening connector (Although, Because, While...). 2) Recognize the first clause as subordinate — it is already attached. 3) Check the start of the main clause for a second connector. 4) If one appears, delete it. 5) Re-read: subordinate clause, comma, bare main clause.

subject: act-english
context_html: Hoping to spark a late-season rally, <u>the manager shuffled the batting order</u> ahead of Friday's doubleheader.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

choices.label: the batting order was shuffled by the manager
the manager's batting order was shuffled
a shuffle of the batting order was made by the manager

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: 'the manager,' the one doing the hoping, immediately follows the introductory modifier.
per_choice_rationale.B: The passive rewrite makes 'the batting order' the subject, but an order cannot hope — dangling modifier (dangling_passive).
per_choice_rationale.C: A possessive is not a doer; the head noun is still the order, so the modifier dangles (possessive_not_subject).
per_choice_rationale.D: Nominalizes the action and buries the doer at the end, leaving the modifier dangling and the sentence bloated (dangling_nominalization).

why_correct_md: An introductory modifier must be followed **immediately** by the person it describes, and the hopeful manager is right there as written.
why_tempted_md: The passive version keeps the manager in the sentence, so students assume the modifier is still anchored even though the subject changed.
rule_md: 1) Find the opening modifier and ask who performs it (who is hoping?). 2) Look at the noun right after the comma. 3) If that noun is not the performer, the modifier dangles. 4) Reject possessives and passives that displace the performer. 5) Choose the version whose subject is the performer.

subject: act-english
context_html: With Sunday's extra-inning win, the Owls <u>returned back</u> to first place in the Valley Division.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most concise while preserving its meaning?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Back' duplicates the meaning already built into the 're-' verb (redundant_particle).
per_choice_rationale.B: Piles a second duplicate, 'again,' onto the first (double_redundancy).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the verb alone carries the entire idea of going back.
per_choice_rationale.D: A wordy nominalization that keeps the same redundancy (nominalization_plus_redundancy).

why_correct_md: **Redundancy** check: the 're-' verb already means going back, so every added word repeats it.
why_tempted_md: 'Returned back' is common in casual speech, so the doubled idea sounds normal rather than repetitive.
rule_md: 1) Define the verb in plain words. 2) Compare each neighboring word to that definition. 3) Cross out any word whose meaning the verb already contains. 4) Re-read the trimmed sentence and confirm no meaning was lost. 5) Prefer the version where every word earns its place.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Due to the fact that</u> the game stretched into a twelfth inning, the concession stands ran out of soft pretzels.
stem_md: Which choice expresses the idea most concisely?

choices.label: In light of the fact that

per_choice_rationale.A: 'The fact that' is pure padding — five words doing the work of one (fact_that_padding).
per_choice_rationale.B: Swaps in an equally bloated formula that adds no meaning (formal_sounding_padding).
per_choice_rationale.C: Keeps the same 'fact that' scaffolding under a different opener (fact_that_padding).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: a single subordinating conjunction expresses the entire cause-link.

why_correct_md: One **subordinating** word carries the whole cause-link, so every 'the fact that' formula is dead weight.
why_tempted_md: The longer formulas sound more formal and academic, so students equate extra words with extra polish.
rule_md: 1) Spot formulas built around 'the fact that.' 2) Ask what relationship the phrase signals (cause, contrast, time). 3) Swap in the single conjunction that signals the same relationship. 4) Re-read to confirm identical meaning. 5) Keep the shorter version unless meaning changed.

subject: act-english
context_html: The new scoreboard operator <u>has the ability to</u> update out-of-town scores within seconds of each final.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most direct without changing its meaning?

per_choice_rationale.A: Unfolds a single modal idea into a four-word phrase with no added meaning (ability_phrase_padding).
per_choice_rationale.B: A vague idiom that is both roomier and fuzzier than a plain statement of ability (vague_idiom).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: one modal verb states the ability completely.
per_choice_rationale.D: The most inflated version — grand vocabulary disguising the same simple idea (inflated_diction).

why_correct_md: A single **modal** verb expresses ability completely, so the multi-word ability phrases are padding.
why_tempted_md: 'Possesses the capability' sounds sophisticated, so students mistake its formality for precision.
rule_md: 1) Find ability-phrases ('has the ability to,' 'is able to,' 'is capable of'). 2) Replace the phrase with a single modal helper. 3) Re-read: did any meaning vanish? 4) If not, the shorter version wins. 5) Repeat for other unfolded phrases in the sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: As the runner rounded third, the roar of the crowd <u>inflated</u> until the press box windows rattled.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely describes what the crowd's roar did?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Inflated' belongs to balloons and prices — things filled with air or artificially increased — not sound (wrong_collocation).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Bloated' drags in connotations of sickness and unhealthy excess (negative_connotation).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the conventional verb for a sound rising steadily in volume and force.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Enlarged' applies to physical dimensions and images, not audio (category_mismatch).

why_correct_md: Precision means matching the verb to its noun's **category**, and this is the verb English customarily pairs with rising sound.
why_tempted_md: 'Inflated' shares the general grow-bigger meaning, so students accept it without testing what kinds of things actually inflate.
rule_md: 1) Identify the noun the verb acts on (a roar — a sound). 2) List what each candidate verb usually happens to. 3) Eliminate verbs tied to the wrong category (air-filled objects, body tissue, physical size). 4) Check connotation: positive, neutral, negative. 5) Choose the verb whose habits and tone both fit.

subject: act-english
context_html: In a statement released Tuesday, the league office <u>approved</u> the franchise's request to relocate its Class A affiliate.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the formal style established in the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the verb matches the official register of a formal league statement.
per_choice_rationale.B: A breezy gesture idiom that clashes with institutional language (casual_idiom).
per_choice_rationale.C: A slang intensifier plus a conversational idiom — two register violations at once (slang_register).
per_choice_rationale.D: Informal clipped verb that dips below press-release diction (colloquial_clip).

why_correct_md: The frame — an official statement — sets a formal **register**, and the original verb is the only option written at that level.
why_tempted_md: 'Okayed' is short and clear, so students mistake its brevity for appropriate directness despite its casual register.
rule_md: 1) Identify the sentence's setting from its non-underlined words (an official statement). 2) Label the required register: formal, neutral, or casual. 3) Label each option's register. 4) Eliminate every mismatch, even vivid ones. 5) Keep the option that could appear in the original document's own prose.

subject: act-english
context_html: The bookmobile serves <u>not only the rural families who lack transportation but also the retirees</u> at the Riverbend senior center.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: not only the rural families who lack transportation but also serving the retirees
not only the rural families who lack transportation and also the retirees
neither the rural families who lack transportation but also the retirees

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: 'not only … but also' is the properly matched correlative pair, and each half introduces a parallel noun phrase.
per_choice_rationale.B: Breaks parallelism by pairing the noun phrase 'the rural families' with the participial phrase 'serving the retirees.'
per_choice_rationale.C: Substitutes the non-standard pairing 'not only … and also' for the required 'not only … but also.'
per_choice_rationale.D: Mixes two different correlative pairs: 'neither' demands 'nor' and reverses the sentence's positive meaning.

why_correct_md: The **correlative pair** 'not only … but also' is correctly matched, and both halves introduce parallel noun phrases.
why_tempted_md: 'And also' sounds smoothly additive to the ear, so students accept it without checking that correlatives come in fixed partnerships.
rule_md: 1) Find the first half of the correlative pair (not only, either, neither, both). 2) Recall its required partner (but also, or, nor, and). 3) Confirm that exact partner appears. 4) Read the words immediately after each half. 5) If both halves introduce the same grammatical form, the sentence is parallel; if not, revise.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each of the branch libraries <u>keeps</u> a binder of local bus schedules behind its reference desk.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the subject is the singular pronoun 'Each,' so the singular verb agrees.
per_choice_rationale.B: Matches the verb to 'libraries,' the nearest noun, but that noun is the object of 'of,' not the subject.
per_choice_rationale.C: Doubles the error: the plural helper 'are' clashes with singular 'Each,' and progressive aspect misfits a routine habit.
per_choice_rationale.D: Uses the plural helper 'have' with the singular subject and shifts a present routine into the perfect tense.

why_correct_md: The true subject is **Each**, which is always singular, so the singular verb is required.
why_tempted_md: The plural noun 'libraries' sits right next to the verb, so students match the verb to the nearest noun instead of the true subject.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb. 2) Ask 'who or what does this?' 3) Cross out prepositional phrases such as 'of the branch libraries.' 4) Match the verb to the remaining head word — each, one, and everyone are singular. 5) Re-read the sentence with the phrase removed to confirm.

subject: act-english
context_html: The archivist publicly thanked the volunteers, <u>who she believed had rescued</u> the water-damaged maps from the flooded basement.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: with the interrupter 'she believed' set aside, the pronoun is the subject of 'had rescued,' so subject case is required.
per_choice_rationale.B: Hypercorrects to the object case because 'she believed' looks like a verb needing an object, but the pronoun actually performs 'had rescued.'
per_choice_rationale.C: Uses the relative pronoun reserved for things and ideas to refer to human volunteers.
per_choice_rationale.D: Places 'that' after a comma, but 'that' cannot introduce a nonrestrictive clause — and 'who' is preferred for people.

why_correct_md: Bracketing the interrupter 'she believed' shows the pronoun is the **subject** of 'had rescued,' so the subject form is correct.
why_tempted_md: Students hypercorrect to the object case because the pronoun follows a comma and seems to be the object of 'believed.'
rule_md: 1) Bracket off interrupters like 'she believed.' 2) Read the clause without them. 3) If the pronoun performs the clause's verb, use the subject form; if it receives an action or follows a preposition, use the object form. 4) Confirm the pronoun type fits the antecedent: people take who/whom, not which. 5) Re-read the full sentence to verify.

subject: act-english
context_html: When the renovation crew finally met with the library board, <u>they</u> approved the plan to move the teen section upstairs.
stem_md: Which choice provides the clearest sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'They' could point to either the renovation crew or the library board, so the reader cannot tell who approved the plan.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: naming the approving party outright removes the ambiguity created by two competing plural antecedents.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'They themselves' adds emphasis but leaves the same two-way ambiguity untouched.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'This group' is still ambiguous, since both the crew and the board qualify as groups.

why_correct_md: Replacing the pronoun with the specific noun eliminates the **ambiguous reference**, since two plural nouns compete to be its antecedent.
why_tempted_md: 'They' sounds natural aloud because readers silently supply an antecedent that the sentence never actually pins down.
rule_md: 1) Circle every pronoun. 2) List every earlier noun it could point to. 3) If more than one candidate is plausible, the pronoun is ambiguous. 4) Replace it with the specific noun, or rewrite, so only one reading survives. 5) Re-read to confirm a single clear meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: The main branch stays open until nine on weeknights. <u>Similarly,</u> the storefront branch in the mill district locks its doors at five.
stem_md: Which transition word or phrase is most logical here?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Similarly' claims the two branches behave alike, but staying open until nine and closing at five are opposites.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'In fact' intensifies or confirms the previous claim; it cannot signal that the second branch does the opposite.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'As a result' invents a cause-effect link — the storefront's early closing is not caused by the main branch's late hours.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the two sentences present opposing facts, so an opposition transition is required.

why_correct_md: The sentences present **opposing** facts — late hours versus early closing — so the transition must signal opposition.
why_tempted_md: 'As a result' tempts students who assume adjacent sentences must always be linked by cause and effect.
rule_md: 1) Read the sentence before and the sentence after the transition. 2) State their relationship in your own words: agree, oppose, cause, example, or sequence. 3) Match the transition to that stated relationship. 4) Re-read with your choice inserted to confirm the logic clicks.

subject: act-english
context_html: Patrons start by checking out up to five paper packets from a wooden card catalog near the garden window. After the growing season, they harvest seeds from their strongest plants and bring a portion back in labeled envelopes. Staff then sort the envelopes and restock the drawers for the next spring.
stem_md: The writer wants to open the paragraph with a sentence that introduces its focus on how the library's seed exchange operates. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Public libraries across the country have expanded far beyond lending books.
The seed exchange at the Fairview branch runs on a simple borrow, grow, and return cycle.
Tomato and zinnia seed packets disappear from the drawers faster than any others.
Gardening and the seed exchange surged in popularity nationwide during the past decade.

per_choice_rationale.A: Too broad: it introduces libraries in general, while the paragraph explains one specific process.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it names the program and previews the step-by-step process the following sentences describe.
per_choice_rationale.C: A narrow detail about popular packets that belongs mid-paragraph, not an introduction to the process.
per_choice_rationale.D: Background about national trends, which the paragraph never discusses.

why_correct_md: An effective opener must **preview** the paragraph's actual content, and this one announces the exact process the sentences go on to detail.
why_tempted_md: The broad opening about libraries in general feels safe and essay-like, though the paragraph never supports a claim that wide.
rule_md: 1) Read the paragraph and state its focus in one phrase. 2) Check each candidate opener's scope against that focus. 3) Reject options that are broader, narrower, or about a different aspect. 4) Confirm the winner previews what the following sentences actually deliver.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] The library converted an unused study room into a small recording booth. [2] Staff lined its walls with foam panels to muffle hallway noise. [3] Patrons can now reserve the booth to record interviews with elderly relatives. [4] The completed recordings join a growing oral-history collection kept at the reference desk.
stem_md: The writer wants to add the following sentence to the paragraph: "They also installed a compact mixing console beside the microphone." To preserve the paragraph's logical sequence, the sentence should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Before the paragraph begins, 'They' has no antecedent and 'also' has no earlier action to add to.
per_choice_rationale.B: After Sentence 1, 'They' misreads as 'the library,' and no first installation exists yet for 'also' to echo.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: 'They' picks up 'Staff' and 'also' adds a second setup action, keeping all preparation before patron use.
per_choice_rationale.D: Placing setup work after the collection description breaks chronology, since the console was installed before recording began.

why_correct_md: The pronoun and the word **also** both need Sentence 2's staff action directly before them, and setup must precede patron use.
why_tempted_md: The spot right after the opening sentence attracts students because installation feels like part of the initial conversion.
rule_md: 1) Circle backward-pointing words in the added sentence (pronouns, 'also,' 'this'). 2) Find what each must refer to. 3) Place the sentence immediately after those referents. 4) Check the paragraph's timeline — setup, use, results — still flows. 5) Re-read the paragraph with the sentence inserted.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] The library's newspaper archive stretches back to 1902. [2] For decades, its only copies existed on brittle rolls of microfilm. [3] A single balky reader machine offered the only way to view them. [4] Researchers can now search a century of headlines from home. [5] Last spring, a grant funded a high-speed scanner that converted every roll into searchable digital files.
stem_md: The writer wants Sentence 4 placed so that the paragraph unfolds in logical order, with each development following the event that made it possible. The best placement for Sentence 4 is:

per_choice_rationale.A: In its current spot, the home-searching outcome appears before the scanning project that made it possible.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the outcome logically follows the grant-funded digitization that produced it, closing the paragraph's problem-to-solution arc.
per_choice_rationale.C: Moving it even earlier detaches 'now' from both the old limitations and the change that explains it.
per_choice_rationale.D: Opening with the outcome strands 'now' with no earlier situation to improve upon.

why_correct_md: An **effect must follow its cause**: remote searching only makes sense after the scanner has converted the microfilm.
why_tempted_md: Leaving the sentence where it is tempts students because it sits beside other sentences about access, masking the cause-effect reversal.
rule_md: 1) Label each sentence as background, problem, change, or result. 2) Find the sentence that causes the moved sentence to be true. 3) Place the result directly after its cause. 4) Check that words like 'now' have a clear before-picture earlier in the paragraph. 5) Re-read the paragraph in the new order.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] The Granville Public Library opened in 1908 with funds from a Carnegie grant. [2] Its limestone facade and oak reading tables made it the grandest building in the county. [3] Generations of farm families rode into town on Saturdays just to climb its wide front steps. [4] This year, a careful renovation is preparing the old building for its second century. [5] Crews are restoring the original skylights while adding ramps, elevators, and charging stations. [6] The county has promised that the reading tables, sanded and resealed, will remain exactly where they have always stood.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide this paragraph into two paragraphs, the first focused on the library's early history and the second on its current renovation. The best place to begin the second paragraph is at:

per_choice_rationale.A: Sentence 3 still narrates the library's early decades, so cutting there drags history into the renovation paragraph.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: 'This year' pivots the paragraph from past grandeur to the present-day project, so the shift begins there.
per_choice_rationale.C: Sentence 5 continues renovation details begun in Sentence 4, so cutting there strands the pivot with the history.
per_choice_rationale.D: Sentence 6 is the renovation discussion's closing promise; starting there leaves most of the project in the history paragraph.

why_correct_md: A paragraph break belongs at the **first sentence of the new topic**, and the 'This year' sentence is where the time period shifts.
why_tempted_md: The sentence about crews and skylights sounds like fresh action, so students cut there even though the pivot was announced one sentence earlier.
rule_md: 1) Label each sentence with its topic or time period. 2) Find where the labels switch. 3) Begin the new paragraph at the first sentence carrying the new label. 4) Verify each resulting paragraph is single-topic. 5) Re-read both paragraphs to confirm neither strands a sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: Fresh murals now brighten the <u>childrens' section</u> on the library's ground floor.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Places the apostrophe after an -s that the irregular plural 'children' never takes.
per_choice_rationale.B: Drops the apostrophe entirely, leaving a possessive unmarked and a nonexistent word.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: 'children' is an irregular plural, so its possessive is formed with apostrophe + s.
per_choice_rationale.D: Omits the possessive marker altogether, leaving an ungrammatical noun stack.

why_correct_md: Because 'children' is an **irregular plural** with no plural -s, its possessive is formed by adding apostrophe + s.
why_tempted_md: Students overapply the 'plural possessives end in s-apostrophe' rule without checking whether the plural was formed with -s at all.
rule_md: 1) Ask who owns or is associated with the noun. 2) Write the owner word in full. 3) If the owner is a plural ending in -s, add just an apostrophe. 4) If the owner is any other word — including irregular plurals like children, women, men — add apostrophe + s. 5) Re-read to confirm the owner word is spelled normally.

subject: act-english
context_html: The library's oldest <u>treasure—a hand-drawn 1911 map of the harbor—hangs</u> behind glass in the local-history room.
stem_md: Which punctuation choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: treasure—a hand-drawn 1911 map of the harbor, hangs
treasure, a hand-drawn 1911 map of the harbor—hangs
treasure—a hand-drawn 1911 map of the harbor; hangs

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the appositive is enclosed by a matched pair of dashes, and the sentence reads cleanly without it.
per_choice_rationale.B: Opens the interruption with a dash but closes it with a comma, mismatching the pair.
per_choice_rationale.C: Opens with a comma and closes with a dash — the same mismatch reversed.
per_choice_rationale.D: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but what follows here is only the sentence's verb phrase.

why_correct_md: An interrupting appositive must be sealed by a **matched pair** of marks, and here both boundaries use dashes.
why_tempted_md: Mixed comma-dash pairs sound fine when read aloud, so students miss that the opening and closing marks disagree.
rule_md: 1) Find the interrupter and read the sentence without it. 2) If the sentence still works, the interrupter must be enclosed by a matched pair: two commas, two dashes, or parentheses. 3) Check that the opening and closing marks are the same type. 4) Reject any mark, like a semicolon, whose job is different. 5) Re-read the full sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: The bookbinding workshop <u>includes: cleaning</u> leather covers, re-sewing loose bindings, and pressing warped boards.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: A colon may follow only a complete independent clause, and 'The bookbinding workshop includes' is incomplete without its objects.
per_choice_rationale.B: A semicolon here severs the verb from its objects; semicolons join two independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.C: A comma between a verb and its object list is unnecessary punctuation.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: no mark may separate the verb from the objects it governs.

why_correct_md: No punctuation may separate a **verb from its objects**, and the words before the mark do not form a complete clause.
why_tempted_md: Lists feel like they deserve a colon, so students insert one without testing whether the words before it can stand alone.
rule_md: 1) Find the mark before the list. 2) Read only the words before the mark. 3) If they form a complete stand-alone sentence, a colon is allowed. 4) If they end in a verb or preposition that needs the list to finish the thought, use no punctuation at all. 5) Never separate a verb from its objects with any mark.

subject: act-english
context_html: Wearing white cotton gloves, the conservation technician <u>yanked</u> each brittle letter from its protective sleeve.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize the technician's careful, unhurried handling of the fragile letters. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Yanked' conveys sudden force — the opposite of the careful handling the writer wants to stress.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: both the adverb and the verb depict slow, protective handling, fully serving the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Carefully' gestures at the goal, but 'snatched' still describes a quick, rough grab.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Deliberately' suggests intent, yet 'grabbed' remains abrupt and forceful.

why_correct_md: Both words must serve the goal, and this pairing makes the **entire action** slow and protective rather than patching a rough verb with a soft adverb.
why_tempted_md: The adverb 'carefully' seems to satisfy the goal even though the verb it modifies contradicts it.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's stated goal in your own words. 2) Test the verb first: does its core action match the goal? 3) Then test the modifier: does it reinforce or fight the verb? 4) Reject any option in which either word contradicts the goal. 5) Pick the option where verb and modifier both serve it.

subject: act-english
context_html: Colleagues describe the retiring reference librarian as a calm, methodical researcher who was <u>super pumped about</u> the library's new atlas collection.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the sentence's measured, professional tone?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Super pumped' is gym-class slang that clashes with the sentence's formal description of a methodical researcher.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Totally stoked' swaps one slang phrase for another, leaving the register broken.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Crazy about' is milder but still a conversational idiom, not professional prose.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it expresses the same excitement in diction that matches the sentence's measured, professional voice.

why_correct_md: A sentence must keep one **register** throughout, and only this phrasing matches the formal diction of 'calm, methodical researcher.'
why_tempted_md: 'Crazy about' feels tame compared with the original slang, so students accept it without testing it against the sentence's formal frame.
rule_md: 1) Identify the passage's register from surrounding word choices. 2) Flag any underlined words that feel like casual speech. 3) Test each option by asking whether it could appear in a formal written profile. 4) Reject every option with slang or conversational idioms. 5) Confirm the survivor preserves the original meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: The tool-lending counter at the Dockside branch has become one of the library's busiest services. Wait lists for ladders and hedge trimmers stretch weeks into the season, and staff field calls about cordless drills before the doors even open.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the last sentence of the paragraph: "A single post-hole digger was checked out forty-one times last summer." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it supplies a concrete statistic that supports the paragraph's point about the counter's popularity.
Yes, because it explains why the library first decided to lend tools.
No, because it repeats information given earlier in the paragraph.
No, because it introduces a level of detail inconsistent with the paragraph's general overview.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the hard number is new, specific evidence that reinforces the paragraph's claim about heavy demand.
per_choice_rationale.B: Right verdict, wrong reason — the sentence documents usage and says nothing about the program's origins.
per_choice_rationale.C: The checkout figure appears nowhere earlier, so nothing is repeated.
per_choice_rationale.D: The paragraph is already built on specifics like wait lists and morning calls, so one more figure fits the established pattern.

why_correct_md: The sentence adds fresh, specific **evidence** for exactly the idea the paragraph is developing — the counter's heavy use.
why_tempted_md: The 'yes' option with the origin-story reason attracts students who judge only the verdict and never test whether the reason describes the sentence.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's main idea in one phrase. 2) State what the proposed sentence actually does — not what the reasons claim. 3) Decide add or omit based on whether it advances the main idea. 4) Then check that the chosen reason accurately describes the sentence. 5) Reject any option whose reason misdescribes it, even if the verdict matches yours.

subject: act-english
context_html: For eleven years, the Maple Street branch has run a delivery route for patrons who cannot travel to the building. Twice a month, a librarian loads crates of requested novels, audiobooks, and large-print mysteries into a small van. At each stop, she collects finished books, takes new requests, and often stays a few minutes to chat about what to read next. Riders who once felt cut off from the library now plan their calendars around her visits.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to show how one public library serves patrons who cannot visit in person. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it lists every outreach service the library system offers.
Yes, because it describes the branch's delivery route and its effect on the patrons it reaches.
No, because it centers on the library's annual budget negotiations.
No, because it mentions patrons only in its final sentence.

per_choice_rationale.A: Right verdict, wrong reason — the essay follows one program closely rather than cataloging every service.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the essay details exactly how one branch brings books to homebound readers and how those readers respond.
per_choice_rationale.C: Budgets, funding, and negotiations never appear anywhere in the essay.
per_choice_rationale.D: The homebound readers are present from the opening sentence onward, not just at the end.

why_correct_md: The essay's every sentence develops **one program for homebound readers**, which is precisely what the supposed goal requires.
why_tempted_md: The 'yes' option claiming a full list of services tempts students who match the verdict without checking whether the reason describes the essay.
rule_md: 1) Restate the supposed goal in your own words. 2) Summarize what the essay actually spends its sentences on. 3) Decide yes or no by comparing the two. 4) Then verify the chosen reason is factually true of the essay. 5) Eliminate any option whose reason misstates the essay, even when its verdict matches yours.

subject: act-english
context_html: Every Saturday morning, three certified therapy dogs settle onto quilts in the story room, where beginning readers take turns reading aloud to them. The dogs never correct a mispronounced word or sigh at a slow page, so children who freeze up in class often relax within minutes. Parents report that the sessions have changed how their kids feel about books.
stem_md: The writer wants to add a sentence giving a specific example of the confidence the sessions build in young readers. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Golden retrievers were first bred in Scotland during the nineteenth century.
The story room's carpet was replaced shortly after the sessions began.
Nationwide, roughly two-thirds of households own at least one pet.
After four Saturday visits, one second grader who once whispered every word now reads to the spaniel in a clear, steady voice.

per_choice_rationale.A: Dog-breed history is trivia about the animals, not evidence of a child's growing confidence.
per_choice_rationale.B: Facility upkeep has nothing to do with the goal of illustrating a young reader's progress.
per_choice_rationale.C: National pet-ownership data is off-goal background that says nothing about these children.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it shows one named child's measurable change, exactly the specific illustration the goal requests.

why_correct_md: The goal demands a **specific example** of a child's growing confidence, and only this sentence shows an individual reader's change.
why_tempted_md: The pet-ownership figure sounds authoritative and on-topic about animals, so students mistake broad data for a specific example.
rule_md: 1) Underline the goal's key requirements (here: specific, an example, about young readers' confidence). 2) Test each option against every requirement, one at a time. 3) Eliminate options that are about something else, however true. 4) Eliminate broad data when a single case is requested. 5) Confirm the survivor satisfies all requirements at the same time.

subject: act-english
context_html: The book drop jammed late on <u>Friday night it stayed</u> full until the Monday crew pried it open.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Fuses two independent clauses together with no punctuation or conjunction at all.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: a comma plus the coordinating conjunction legally joins the two independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.C: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.D: The semicolon is a legal joiner, but 'it staying' has no finite verb, leaving a fragment on the right side.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses require a **comma plus a coordinating conjunction**, a semicolon, or a period — this option supplies the first.
why_tempted_md: The comma-only version sounds like a natural breath when read aloud, so students miss that both halves are complete sentences.
rule_md: 1) Find each subject-verb pair and test whether each half could stand alone. 2) If both halves are independent, check the joint. 3) Accept only a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. 4) Reject bare contact or a lone comma. 5) Confirm both sides still have finite verbs after the fix.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Because the roof leaked during the thunderstorm, the librarians rolled</u> the rare-book carts into an interior hallway.
stem_md: Which choice provides the clearest and most grammatical sentence?

choices.label: The roof leaked during the thunderstorm, the librarians rolled
Because the roof leaked during the thunderstorm, so the librarians rolled
Because the roof leaking during the thunderstorm, the librarians rolled

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: a subordinate cause clause is properly attached to a complete main clause.
per_choice_rationale.B: Removing the subordinator leaves two independent clauses joined by only a comma — a splice.
per_choice_rationale.C: Doubles the connector: with both 'Because' and 'so,' no independent clause remains.
per_choice_rationale.D: The '-ing' form 'leaking' leaves the subordinate clause without a finite verb.

why_correct_md: One **subordinating conjunction** marks the cause clause, which then leans on a complete main clause — exactly the required structure.
why_tempted_md: 'Because … so' mirrors how many students speak, so the double connector sounds natural even though it strands both clauses.
rule_md: 1) Identify the cause and the effect. 2) Mark the relationship with exactly one connector — a subordinator on the cause or a coordinator between clauses, never both. 3) Confirm the subordinate clause has a tensed verb. 4) Confirm one clause can still stand alone. 5) Re-read the full sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: Hoping to finish before closing time, <u>the cart of returned novels was pushed by Mara</u> toward the fiction aisles.
stem_md: Which choice best corrects the underlined portion?

choices.label: the cart of returned novels was moved by Mara
Mara pushed the cart of returned novels
Mara's cart of returned novels was pushed

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening modifier attaches to 'the cart,' but a cart cannot hope — the modifier dangles.
per_choice_rationale.B: Swapping the verb leaves the same inanimate subject after the comma, so the modifier still dangles.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the person who was hoping now sits directly after the comma, so the modifier attaches logically.
per_choice_rationale.D: The possessive buries the person inside the noun phrase; the grammatical subject is still the cart.

why_correct_md: An opening modifier must describe the **first noun after the comma**, and only this option puts the hopeful person there.
why_tempted_md: The possessive version mentions the person early, so students believe the modifier has something human to attach to.
rule_md: 1) Find the opening modifier and ask who performs it. 2) Look at the first noun after the comma. 3) If that noun is not the performer, the modifier dangles. 4) Rewrite so the performer sits immediately after the comma. 5) Re-read the pair to confirm the match.

subject: act-english
context_html: The Friends of the Library gather <u>each month on a monthly basis</u> to plan the spring used-book sale.
stem_md: Which choice best corrects the underlined portion?

choices.label: on a monthly basis each month
each and every month on a monthly basis

per_choice_rationale.A: States the meeting frequency twice — 'each month' and 'on a monthly basis' mean the same thing.
per_choice_rationale.B: Reorders the two frequency phrases without removing the duplication.
per_choice_rationale.C: Piles the emphatic doublet 'each and every' onto the duplicate phrase, tripling the repetition.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it states the frequency exactly once with no loss of meaning.

why_correct_md: **Redundancy** is the error: the frequency must be stated once, and this option does exactly that.
why_tempted_md: The reordered version sounds revised, so students assume the problem was word order rather than duplication.
rule_md: 1) Ask what fact the underlined words convey. 2) Count how many times that same fact is stated. 3) If more than once, cut until it appears exactly once. 4) Re-read to confirm no meaning was lost. 5) Reject any option that keeps or multiplies the duplicate.

subject: act-english
context_html: The director explained that the new catalog system <u>has the ability to give patrons the option of being able to renew</u> loans from their phones.
stem_md: Which choice best corrects the underlined portion?

choices.label: gives patrons the ability to have the option to renew
is capable of offering patrons the opportunity to renew

per_choice_rationale.A: Buries one simple action under four stacked filler constructions.
per_choice_rationale.B: Reshuffles the same padding — 'ability' and 'option' still duplicate one idea.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a single direct verb delivers the full meaning with no filler.
per_choice_rationale.D: Swaps in equally bloated phrasing dressed up in formal-sounding words.

why_correct_md: **Wordiness** is the error: one direct verb expresses the entire idea that the padded versions bury.
why_tempted_md: The 'is capable of offering … the opportunity' version sounds official and polished, so students mistake formality for quality.
rule_md: 1) Find the buried action — here, renewing. 2) Ask who does it. 3) Rewrite as actor + strong verb + action. 4) Delete scaffolding like 'has the ability to' and 'the option of.' 5) Keep the shortest version that preserves the full meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: Patrons <u>who are waiting in expectation of</u> reserved titles receive a text alert the moment their items reach the hold shelf.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Waiting in expectation of' is swollen — expectation is already built into waiting for something.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: one participle carries the complete meaning and keeps the sentence grammatical.
per_choice_rationale.C: Grammatical but longer — 'who are' adds nothing that the bare participle doesn't already convey.
per_choice_rationale.D: Deletion smashes 'Patrons' directly into 'reserved titles,' garbling the sentence.

why_correct_md: On concision questions the **shortest grammatical option that preserves the meaning** wins, and the single participle does exactly that.
why_tempted_md: The longer relative-clause version sounds complete and correct, so students stop before testing whether a shorter equivalent works.
rule_md: 1) Identify the idea the underlined words must preserve. 2) Line the options up from shortest to longest. 3) Test the shortest: does the sentence stay grammatical and keep the full meaning? 4) If yes, take it; if no, step up one length. 5) Never delete words the sentence's grammar depends on.

subject: act-english
context_html: Using a soft sable brush, the archivist worked to <u>rub</u> a century of dust from the photograph's surface.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most precise word for the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Rub' implies pressure and friction that could grind dust into a fragile print.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Scour' means abrasive scrubbing — far too harsh for archival conservation.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: it matches the light, gliding stroke of a soft brush moving dust off a surface.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Erase' takes marks or writing as its object, not loose dust.

why_correct_md: **Precision** means matching the verb to the tool and task, and only this verb captures a soft brush's light stroke.
why_tempted_md: 'Rub' is an all-purpose cleaning verb students accept without picturing the pressure it implies.
rule_md: 1) Picture the exact physical action the sentence describes. 2) Note the tool and the goal — a soft brush, removing dust without damage. 3) Test each verb against that picture: force, motion, and typical object. 4) Reject verbs whose force or object type doesn't fit. 5) Choose the verb whose picture matches exactly.

subject: act-english
context_html: The library's new circulation policy states that patrons <u>gotta hang onto</u> their date-due receipts until all items are returned.
stem_md: Which choice is most appropriate for the formal register of the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Gotta' and 'hang onto' are both casual speech, clashing with the formal policy language.
per_choice_rationale.B: Fixes the nonstandard verb but keeps the conversational idiom 'hang onto.'
per_choice_rationale.C: Keeps 'gotta,' a spoken contraction that never belongs in a written policy.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: both words match the formal register of an official circulation policy.

why_correct_md: A formal document requires **formal diction in every word**, and only this option replaces both casual elements.
why_tempted_md: Replacing the most glaring slang word feels like enough, so students keep the informal idiom that remains.
rule_md: 1) Identify the document's register from its context — here, an official policy. 2) Flag every casual word or idiom in the underlined portion. 3) Replace all flagged items with standard formal equivalents, not just the worst one. 4) Re-read the sentence in the document's voice to confirm consistency.

subject: act-english
context_html: The kangaroo rat survives the harshest dunes by drawing moisture <u>not only from its seeds and also</u> from the metabolic water its own body produces.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: both from its seeds and also
not only from its seeds but instead
not only from its seeds but also

per_choice_rationale.A: Opens the pair with 'not only' but closes it with 'and also,' which is not the fixed partner of 'not only' (correlative_mismatch).
per_choice_rationale.B: Pairs the starter 'both' with a finishing 'also,' mixing two different correlative sets (correlative_mismatch).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'But instead' signals replacement, yet the sentence keeps both moisture sources as true at once (correlative_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: 'not only ... but also' is the complete, matched correlative pair that adds a second true source.

why_correct_md: The correlative that begins with **not only** must be completed by its fixed partner **but also**.
why_tempted_md: 'And also' sounds like a natural way to tack on a second idea, so students accept it as the second half of the pair.
rule_md: 1) Spot the opening half of a paired connector (not only, both, either, neither, whether). 2) Recall its one fixed partner (but also, and, or, nor, or). 3) Check that the finishing word actually matches that partner. 4) Confirm the two halves signal the intended logic (adding, not replacing). 5) Re-read the whole pair to hear that it locks together.

subject: act-english
context_html: A cluster of towering barrel cacti <u>stores</u> enough water in its ribbed trunks to outlast a season-long drought.
