stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the singular subject 'cluster' governs the verb, so the singular verb form is right.
per_choice_rationale.B: Agrees with the nearest plural noun 'cacti' inside the prepositional phrase rather than the true subject (sv_nearest_noun).
per_choice_rationale.C: Uses a plural progressive verb, again matching 'cacti' instead of the singular head noun (sv_nearest_noun).
per_choice_rationale.D: Shifts to a plural present-perfect verb that disagrees with the singular subject 'cluster' (sv_nearest_noun).

why_correct_md: The subject is the singular noun **cluster**, not the plural 'cacti' buried in the prepositional phrase, so a singular verb is required.
why_tempted_md: The plural noun 'cacti' sits right before the verb, so students match the verb to the nearest word instead of the real subject.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb. 2) Ask who or what does it. 3) Cross out any prepositional phrase ('of ... cacti') between the subject and verb. 4) Read the bare subject and verb together. 5) Choose the verb form that agrees with that head noun's number.

subject: act-english
context_html: The field ecologist <u>who</u> the university had hired analyzed every water sample twice before recording her results.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Uses the subject form, but the pronoun is the object of 'had hired,' which calls for the object form (case_subject_for_object).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the pronoun is the direct object of 'had hired' ('the university had hired her'), so the object form is required.
per_choice_rationale.C: A possessive form that would signal ownership the sentence never expresses (possessive_for_object).
per_choice_rationale.D: A contraction of 'who is,' which cannot serve as the object of the verb (contraction_for_pronoun).

why_correct_md: The pronoun functions as the **object** of 'had hired' (the university hired her), so the objective case form is required.
why_tempted_md: The pronoun sits near the front of the clause where subjects usually appear, so it feels like a subject even though a later verb acts on it.
rule_md: 1) Isolate the clause the pronoun belongs to. 2) Find that clause's own subject and verb (here: 'the university had hired'). 3) Ask whether the pronoun does the action or receives it. 4) If it receives the action, use the object form; if it does the action, use the subject form. 5) Replace with 'he/him' to test: 'him' means use the object form.

subject: act-english
context_html: At first glance the saguaro seems utterly defenseless against thirsty grazers. <u>In addition,</u> its dense armor of spines turns away nearly every animal that might tear into its flesh for water.
stem_md: Which transition provides the most logical connection between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'In addition' signals another similar point, but the second sentence reverses the impression the first creates (transition_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the plant looks defenseless yet is actually well protected, so a contrast transition names the turn accurately.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Therefore' claims the protection results from seeming defenseless, a false cause-and-effect link (transition_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'For instance' promises an example of defenselessness, but the sentence gives evidence of the opposite (transition_false_example).

why_correct_md: The second sentence **overturns the expectation** raised by 'seems defenseless,' so only a contrast transition fits.
why_tempted_md: Both sentences discuss the saguaro's defenses, so an adding transition feels safe even though the second sentence flips the first's impression.
rule_md: 1) Put each sentence into a plain claim. 2) Notice the first says 'appears defenseless' and the second says 'is protected.' 3) Name that relationship: it is a reversal, not an addition or a result. 4) Match the transition to a reversal. 5) Re-read the pair with your pick to confirm the turn sounds right.

subject: act-english
context_html: A rare winter downpour soaks the cracked desert floor for a single afternoon. <u>Similarly,</u> dormant seeds that have waited years for moisture erupt within days into a carpet of blossoms.
stem_md: Which transition provides the most logical connection between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Similarly' claims the two sentences describe parallel events, but the blossoming follows from the rain (transition_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Nevertheless' signals contrast, yet the second sentence agrees with and follows from the first (transition_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Meanwhile' frames the events as merely simultaneous, hiding the cause-and-effect link (transition_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the downpour causes the seeds to bloom, so a cause-and-effect transition names the relationship.

why_correct_md: The blossoming happens **because** of the downpour, so a consequence transition captures the cause-and-effect link.
why_tempted_md: Both sentences describe striking desert events, so a comparison transition feels natural even though one event triggers the other.
rule_md: 1) Turn each sentence into a plain claim. 2) Ask whether the second event would happen without the first. 3) If the first triggers the second, the logic is cause and effect. 4) Reject comparison, contrast, and time-only transitions that hide that link. 5) Re-read the pair with the consequence transition to confirm.

subject: act-english
context_html: The saguaro does far more than tower over the Sonoran Desert. Gila woodpeckers drill nest holes in its trunk, and when they abandon them, elf owls and purple martins take up residence. Insects tunnel through its pulp, and hawks perch on its crown to scan the flats for prey.
stem_md: The writer wants to close the paragraph by emphasizing the saguaro's role as a home for many different kinds of creatures. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: A mature saguaro can keep growing for more than two centuries before it finally topples.
In this way a single saguaro becomes a crowded apartment tower, housing birds, insects, and mammals under one spiny roof.
The Gila woodpecker, in particular, could not raise its young without the cactus.
The saguaro also hoards enormous reserves of water inside its pleated trunk.

per_choice_rationale.A: Shifts to the plant's lifespan, ignoring the requested emphasis on the many creatures it shelters (add_offtopic).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it sums up the paragraph by stressing the wide variety of animals the cactus shelters at once.
per_choice_rationale.C: Narrows to a single species, undercutting the goal of stressing many different creatures (goal_too_narrow).
per_choice_rationale.D: Redirects to water storage, an emphasis the goal does not ask for (goal_wrong_emphasis).

why_correct_md: The goal asks for a close that stresses **variety of inhabitants**, and only this option gathers birds, insects, and mammals together.
why_tempted_md: The water-storage line sounds impressively factual and stays on the saguaro, so students grab it even though it drops the habitat focus.
rule_md: 1) Restate the stated goal in a few words (here: shelters many kinds of creatures). 2) Read each option and ask whether it delivers that exact emphasis. 3) Cross out any option that changes the topic, narrows to one case, or shifts the emphasis. 4) Keep the one that captures the full breadth named in the goal. 5) Re-read it against the goal to confirm the match.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Desert pavement is a mosaic of tightly packed pebbles that armors bare ground against the wind. [2] Beneath that stony crust lies a soft layer of fine, wind-blown silt. [3] Over many centuries the wind lifts loose grains away while heavier stones settle and lock together at the surface. [4] The finished crust can look almost as though a mason had paved it by hand.
stem_md: The writer wants to add the sentence 'Each pebble presses against its neighbors like tiles set in a floor.' To best develop the mosaic introduced at the start of the paragraph, where should this sentence be placed?

per_choice_rationale.A: Placed first, the sentence describes a mosaic no reader has met yet, leaving 'each pebble' without a referent (placement_no_antecedent).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it elaborates the pebble mosaic named in Sentence 1, so it belongs immediately after that introduction.
per_choice_rationale.C: Dropping it here interrupts the shift to the buried silt layer that Sentence 2 opens (placement_breaks_flow).
per_choice_rationale.D: Placed here, it cuts into the step-by-step account of how the crust forms in Sentence 3 (placement_breaks_sequence).

why_correct_md: The new sentence expands on the **pebble mosaic** first named in Sentence 1, so it reads best right after that sentence.
why_tempted_md: Sentence 3 also talks about stones locking together, so the pebble sentence seems to belong there rather than beside its true introduction.
rule_md: 1) Identify what the movable sentence is about (packed pebbles). 2) Find where that idea is first introduced. 3) A detail sentence belongs right after the sentence it develops. 4) Check that no closer sentence interrupts a different train of thought. 5) Read the paragraph with the sentence inserted to confirm smooth flow.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] The desert bighorn sheep rarely needs to drink from open water. [2] Even then, a single animal can gulp gallons in minutes and rebound almost at once. [3] Most of its moisture comes instead from the tough plants it browses at first light. [4] Only a punishing, weeks-long heat wave finally drives the herd on a long trek to a hidden spring.
stem_md: For the sake of logic and coherence, Sentence 2 would most logically be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: The phrase 'Even then' has no prior drinking situation to refer to right after Sentence 1 (placement_dangling_reference).
per_choice_rationale.B: Sentence 3 is about browsing for moisture, so 'Even then' still lacks the drinking event it points back to (placement_dangling_reference).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: 'Even then' refers to the rare trek to a spring described in Sentence 4, so Sentence 2 belongs right after it.
per_choice_rationale.D: Moving it to the very front strands the back-reference with nothing before it at all (placement_dangling_reference).

why_correct_md: The opener **'Even then'** signals a rare drinking occasion, which only Sentence 4's trek to a spring supplies, so Sentence 2 must follow Sentence 4.
why_tempted_md: Leaving Sentence 2 in place feels safe because it sits near the opening claim about drinking, even though its back-reference has nothing to attach to yet.
rule_md: 1) Notice any back-reference cue in the movable sentence ('Even then'). 2) Ask what earlier situation that cue must point to (a rare drinking event). 3) Find the sentence that supplies that situation. 4) Place the movable sentence immediately after it. 5) Re-read to confirm the reference now resolves.

subject: act-english
context_html: The shaded oasis sheltered <u>date palms tall reeds and</u> restless flocks of migrating songbirds.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Runs three list items together with no commas at all (missing_series_commas).
per_choice_rationale.B: Separates the first two items but drops the comma before 'and,' leaving the series incomplete (missing_serial_comma).
per_choice_rationale.C: Places a single comma before 'and' but fails to divide the first two items (misplaced_series_comma).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: commas separate all three items of the series, including the one before 'and.'

why_correct_md: A list of three or more items needs a **comma between each item**, including before the final 'and.'
why_tempted_md: The version with a comma only before 'and' looks tidy, so students accept it even though the first two items still run together.
rule_md: 1) Count the items in the list (here: palms, reeds, songbirds). 2) If three or more, put a comma after every item except the last. 3) Include the comma before the closing 'and.' 4) Make sure no two items are jammed together without a comma. 5) Re-read the series to hear each item stand apart.

subject: act-english
context_html: A fennec <u>foxs</u> oversized ears radiate body heat into the cool night air, cooling the animal without a drop of sweat.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Adds no apostrophe, so it is neither a valid possessive nor a correct plural (missing_apostrophe).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: one fennec owns the ears, so the singular possessive with apostrophe-s is required.
per_choice_rationale.C: The plural possessive implies many animals, but the sentence names a single one (wrong_number_possessive).
per_choice_rationale.D: A plain plural shows more than one animal and no ownership at all (plural_for_possessive).

why_correct_md: The ears belong to one animal, so the **singular possessive** form is required before 'oversized ears.'
why_tempted_md: The plural-looking spelling seems to match 'ears,' so students make the possessive plural to agree with the thing owned.
rule_md: 1) Ask whether the underlined word owns the noun that follows it. 2) If it does, decide how many owners there are. 3) One owner takes apostrophe-s. 4) More than one owner ending in s takes an apostrophe after the s. 5) Re-read to confirm the number of owners matches the sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: The roadrunner<u>—a swift, ground-dwelling bird,</u> rarely takes to the air, sprinting after lizards on foot instead.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Opens the interrupter with a dash but closes it with a comma, so the paired marks do not match (mismatched_pair).
per_choice_rationale.B: Opens with a parenthesis and closes with a dash, mixing two different enclosing marks (mismatched_pair).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a dash before and a dash after enclose the interrupting phrase with matching marks.
per_choice_rationale.D: Opens with a comma and closes with a dash, again failing to match the two enclosing marks (mismatched_pair).

why_correct_md: An interrupting phrase must be enclosed by a **matching pair** of marks — a dash on each side.
why_tempted_md: A dash paired with a comma looks acceptable because both marks can set off phrases, so students overlook that the two ends must match.
rule_md: 1) Find the phrase that interrupts the main sentence. 2) Note the mark that opens it. 3) The mark that closes it must be the same kind (dash-dash or paren-paren). 4) Reject any version that opens with one mark and closes with another. 5) Re-read the sentence to confirm the pair matches.

subject: act-english
context_html: The burrowing owl <u>nests, in</u> tunnels that prairie dogs have long since abandoned.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Drops a comma between the verb and the prepositional phrase it needs, breaking the flow for no reason (intrusive_comma).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: no punctuation belongs between the verb and the phrase that completes it.
per_choice_rationale.C: Moves the stray comma after 'in,' still separating the phrase from the noun it introduces (intrusive_comma).
per_choice_rationale.D: A semicolon cannot join a verb to a prepositional phrase; it links independent clauses (semicolon_misuse).

why_correct_md: Nothing should separate a verb from the **prepositional phrase** that completes its meaning, so no mark belongs here.
why_tempted_md: A brief pause seems natural after the verb, so students insert a comma even though the phrase attaches tightly to it.
rule_md: 1) Identify the verb and the phrase right after it. 2) Ask whether that phrase completes the verb's meaning. 3) If it does, do not separate them with any mark. 4) Reject commas or semicolons dropped between tightly linked words. 5) Re-read to confirm the verb and phrase flow together.

subject: act-english
context_html: As dusk settled over the valley, the dry evening wind <u>moved</u> the fine sand in slow, curling ribbons across the crest of the dune.
stem_md: Which choice best suggests the sand's gentle, unhurried motion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Moved' is accurate but flat, conveying none of the gentle, unhurried quality the goal asks for (word_too_neutral).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Hurled' implies sudden, forceful motion that contradicts the calm image the goal wants (word_wrong_connotation).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: it evokes the soft, continuous, unhurried motion the goal calls for.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Slammed' suggests abrupt violence, the opposite of the gentle movement described (word_wrong_connotation).

why_correct_md: The goal asks for words that convey **gentle, continuous motion**, and only this verb carries that soft connotation.
why_tempted_md: The forceful verb sounds vivid and energetic, so students who equate vividness with strength pick it despite its harsh connotation.
rule_md: 1) Read the goal and name the exact feeling wanted (gentle, unhurried). 2) List the connotation of each option: neutral, forceful, or soft. 3) Cross out any verb whose feeling clashes with the goal. 4) Keep the one whose connotation matches. 5) Re-read the sentence to confirm the tone fits.

subject: act-english
context_html: In her formal field report, the geologist characterized the canyon's layered walls as <u>a meticulous record</u> of nearly ten million years of seasonal flooding.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the tone established in the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the precise, formal phrasing matches the scientific register of a field report.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Totally awesome scrapbook' drops into slang that clashes with the report's formal tone (register_too_casual).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Neat old photo album' uses casual, conversational diction out of keeping with the passage (register_too_casual).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Pretty cool wall calendar' mixes slang and a trivial image, breaking the formal register (register_too_casual).

why_correct_md: A formal field report calls for **precise, elevated diction**, which the original phrasing supplies.
why_tempted_md: The casual comparisons feel friendly and concrete, so students pick them for vividness without checking the passage's formal tone.
rule_md: 1) Identify the passage's register from its context (a formal field report). 2) Read each option and label its tone: formal or casual. 3) Reject any option whose diction is slangy or conversational. 4) Keep the phrasing that matches the established register. 5) Re-read the full sentence to confirm the tone stays consistent.

subject: act-english
context_html: Many desert plants seem to sense a coming storm before the first drop falls. Ocotillo, leafless for months, unfurl fresh green within hours of a downpour. Certain seeds break their long dormancy only after a soaking heavy enough to rinse away the chemicals that keep them asleep.
stem_md: At this point the writer is considering adding the following sentence: 'The nearest paved highway runs some forty miles to the west.' Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it helps readers picture how remote this stretch of desert is.
Yes, because it explains how the plants sense that a storm is coming.
No, because the essay has already described the region's roads earlier.
No, because it adds information unrelated to the paragraph's subject of how plants react to moisture.

per_choice_rationale.A: Endorses adding an off-topic geographic fact for a reason the paragraph never pursues (add_offtopic).
per_choice_rationale.B: Claims the highway sentence explains the plants' sensing, which it plainly does not (false_justification).
per_choice_rationale.C: Rejects the sentence for a reason the passage does not support, since no roads were mentioned before (false_premise).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the highway's distance has nothing to do with the paragraph's subject of plants reacting to moisture, so it should be left out.

why_correct_md: The proposed sentence introduces a fact **irrelevant** to the paragraph's subject, so it should not be added.
why_tempted_md: The remoteness reason sounds plausible because vivid setting details often enrich writing, so students accept it without testing relevance.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's single subject (how plants react to moisture). 2) Read the proposed sentence and ask whether it advances that subject. 3) If it does not, the sentence should be cut regardless of how interesting it is. 4) Then check that the reason given matches the true problem. 5) Choose the yes/no answer whose reason is both correct and accurate.

subject: act-english
context_html: To outlast months without rain, desert animals have evolved striking ways to hold on to water. The kangaroo rat manufactures moisture inside its own body and never sweats a drop. The camel packs fat, not water, into its hump and can cross weeks of dune country between drinks. Even the plodding desert tortoise carries a reservoir of stored water it slowly reabsorbs through a dry spell.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to explain several ways that desert animals hold on to water. Does this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it lays out the specific water-saving methods of more than one animal.
Yes, because it proves that the desert is the harshest habitat on the planet.
No, because it only tells readers where these animals happen to live.
No, because it never explains how the animals end up losing water in the first place.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the essay walks through the distinct water-holding strategies of the kangaroo rat, camel, and tortoise, exactly matching the goal.
per_choice_rationale.B: Judges the essay against a claim it never makes about the desert being the harshest habitat (false_justification).
per_choice_rationale.C: Denies success on the false grounds that the essay only gives locations, which it does not (false_premise).
per_choice_rationale.D: Faults the essay for omitting water loss, a topic the goal never asked it to cover (goal_wrong_standard).

why_correct_md: The goal asks for **several methods**, and the essay supplies a distinct strategy for each of three animals.
why_tempted_md: The water-loss answer sounds rigorous because it demands more information, tempting students who assume a fuller essay is always better.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's goal precisely (show several ways animals hold water). 2) Skim the essay for whether it delivers that. 3) Match the yes/no verdict to what the essay actually does. 4) Reject any reason that misstates the essay's content or judges it by a standard the goal never set. 5) Pick the verdict whose reason is both true and on point.

subject: act-english
context_html: The roadrunner ranks among the desert's most capable predators. Fast and endlessly alert, it patrols open ground on foot from first light until the midday heat drives it into shade. Few small creatures that wander across its path survive once the bird locks them in its gaze.
stem_md: Which detail, if added to the paragraph, would most clearly support its focus on the roadrunner's skill as a hunter?

choices.label: Its mottled brown feathers and long tail make it hard to spot against the brush.
The bird ranges across open country from Kansas down into central Mexico.
With lightning jabs of its beak, it can seize a fleeing lizard and even kill a young rattlesnake.
Cartoon versions of the bird made it famous long before most viewers saw a real one.

per_choice_rationale.A: Describes camouflage rather than the paragraph's focus on how the bird catches prey (add_offtopic).
per_choice_rationale.B: Gives geographic range, which does not develop the point about hunting skill (add_offtopic).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: it shows the bird's speed and lethal precision in taking prey, directly supporting the hunting focus.
per_choice_rationale.D: Adds a pop-culture aside unrelated to the bird's abilities as a predator (add_offtopic).

why_correct_md: Only this detail demonstrates the roadrunner's **prey-catching ability**, which is the paragraph's stated focus.
why_tempted_md: The camouflage detail feels connected because it also concerns survival, so students accept it without checking that the focus is hunting, not hiding.
rule_md: 1) Pin down the paragraph's focus (the roadrunner as a skilled hunter). 2) Read each candidate detail and ask whether it develops that exact focus. 3) Discard details about looks, range, or fame, however interesting. 4) Keep the one that shows the bird actually catching prey. 5) Re-read the paragraph with it added to confirm the focus tightens.

subject: act-english
context_html: By late morning the sun blazed straight down over the salt flats<u>, the sand grew</u> too scorching for even a lizard to cross.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Joins two complete independent clauses with only a comma, creating a comma splice (comma_splice).
per_choice_rationale.B: A colon should introduce an explanation or list, not link two equal independent clauses (colon_misuse).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a semicolon properly links two closely related independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.D: Removing all punctuation fuses the two independent clauses into a run-on (fused_sentence).

why_correct_md: Two complete independent clauses of equal weight are correctly joined by a **semicolon**.
why_tempted_md: The comma marks the natural pause between the clauses, so students accept it without noticing that both sides could stand alone.
rule_md: 1) Test each side of the junction: can it stand alone as a sentence? 2) If both can, they are independent clauses. 3) A comma alone cannot join them, and no punctuation fuses them. 4) Use a semicolon (or period, or comma-plus-conjunction) to join equal clauses. 5) Confirm the second clause is not merely explaining the first, which a colon would require.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Because</u> the cactus wren weaves several bulky nests across its territory each spring, only one of them will ever cradle a clutch of eggs.
stem_md: Which choice most logically joins the two parts of the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Because' claims building many nests causes only one to be used, but the two facts stand in contrast, not cause and effect (subordinator_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Since' asserts the same false causal link in a different word (subordinator_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the concession word fits the contrast — despite building many nests, the wren fills only one.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'So' frames the second clause as a result and produces an ungrammatical opening (coordination_misuse).

why_correct_md: The two clauses are in **contrast** — many nests but only one used — so a concession word, not a cause word, fits.
why_tempted_md: 'Because' feels natural because the sentence pairs two facts, and students assume any paired facts share a cause-and-effect link.
rule_md: 1) State each clause as a plain fact. 2) Ask whether the first causes the second or merely contrasts with it. 3) Building many nests does not cause only one to be used; the facts clash. 4) A contrast calls for a concession word, not 'because' or 'since.' 5) Re-read with your connector to confirm the logic holds.

subject: act-english
context_html: Scanning the ridgeline for the shadow of a circling hawk, <u>the ground squirrel froze</u> at the mouth of its burrow.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: there was a sudden, wary stillness
freezing in place seemed the only choice

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the squirrel is the one scanning, so it correctly follows the opening modifier as the subject.
per_choice_rationale.B: Makes 'the burrow' the scanner, but a burrow cannot scan a ridgeline (dangling_modifier).
per_choice_rationale.C: Supplies no actor at all for the opening phrase, leaving the modifier dangling (dangling_modifier).
per_choice_rationale.D: Puts an abstract idea in the subject slot, so 'scanning' has no logical doer (dangling_modifier).

why_correct_md: An opening -ing modifier must be followed by the **noun that performs its action**, and only the squirrel can do the scanning.
why_tempted_md: Each rewrite sounds smooth on its own, so students judge the fragment in isolation and miss that the opening phrase needs a specific doer.
rule_md: 1) Read the opening modifier and ask who or what is doing that action. 2) Look at the noun that starts the main clause. 3) Check that this noun could logically perform the modifier's action. 4) If it cannot, the modifier dangles. 5) Keep the version whose subject truly does the opening action.

subject: act-english
context_html: The pallid bats stream out of the cavern to hunt <u>at night after dark</u>, combing the canyon walls for sleeping moths.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: during the nighttime hours of darkness

per_choice_rationale.A: 'At night' and 'after dark' say the same thing, so the pair is redundant (redundant_synonym).
per_choice_rationale.B: Stacks 'nighttime,' 'hours,' and 'darkness,' which all repeat one idea in an even wordier way (redundant_synonym).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: it states the time once, with no repetition.
per_choice_rationale.D: Merely reorders the same two synonymous phrases, keeping the redundancy (redundant_synonym).

why_correct_md: 'At night' and 'after dark' name the **same time**, so only one of them is needed.
why_tempted_md: Doubling the time phrase feels like helpful emphasis, so students keep both parts instead of spotting the repetition.
rule_md: 1) Read the underlined phrase and list the ideas it contains. 2) Ask whether any two words or phrases mean the same thing. 3) If they do, keep only one. 4) Reject options that repeat or merely rearrange the synonyms. 5) Re-read to confirm the meaning survives with no loss.

subject: act-english
context_html: The survey team rationed every canteen carefully <u>due to the fact that</u> the next reliable spring lay a full three days' march to the north.
stem_md: Which choice most effectively reduces the wordiness of the sentence?

choices.label: on account of the fact that
in light of the fact that

per_choice_rationale.A: A five-word phrase does the work of a single causal conjunction (wordy_phrase).
per_choice_rationale.B: Swaps in an equally bloated phrase for the same simple idea (wordy_phrase).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: one causal conjunction expresses the link concisely with no lost meaning.
per_choice_rationale.D: Replaces one padded phrase with another just as long (wordy_phrase).

why_correct_md: A single causal conjunction conveys the same 'cause' relationship that the **padded phrase** buries in five words.
why_tempted_md: The long phrase sounds formal and careful, so students mistake its bulk for precision instead of trimming it.
rule_md: 1) Spot any multi-word phrase that signals cause ('due to the fact that,' 'on account of the fact that'). 2) Ask what single word it stands for. 3) Replace the padded phrase with that one word. 4) Confirm the meaning is unchanged. 5) Reject any option that keeps the extra words.

subject: act-english
context_html: The great dunes <u>shift</u> a little with every strong gust that sweeps across the open basin.
stem_md: Which choice best states the idea in the fewest words while keeping its meaning?

choices.label: are subject to a shifting motion

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: a single precise verb conveys the whole idea with nothing to spare.
per_choice_rationale.B: Pairs the verb with a synonym that repeats the same action (redundant_synonym).
per_choice_rationale.C: Turns the verb into a noun phrase, adding words without adding meaning (nominalization).
per_choice_rationale.D: Wraps the idea in a wordy passive construction that says no more than the verb (wordy_passive).

why_correct_md: One exact verb already carries the full meaning, so the **shortest** version that works is best.
why_tempted_md: The longer phrases sound more descriptive, so students equate extra words with richer meaning rather than clutter.
rule_md: 1) Identify the core action the sentence needs. 2) Check whether a single verb already expresses it. 3) Compare each longer option to see if it adds meaning or only words. 4) If the extra words add nothing, prefer the shortest accurate form. 5) Re-read to confirm no meaning is lost.

subject: act-english
context_html: For nearly three centuries, the hidden spring <u>gave</u> water to every weary caravan lucky enough to stumble upon it.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely conveys that the spring furnished water dependably over time?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Gave' is too general to capture the steady, dependable provision the sentence describes (imprecise_word).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it precisely names the reliable, ongoing furnishing of a needed resource.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Granted' implies bestowing permission or a favor, not furnishing a physical resource (wrong_connotation).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Donated' suggests a charitable, one-time gift rather than steady provision (wrong_connotation).

why_correct_md: The context calls for a verb meaning to **furnish a resource steadily**, which the precise choice captures and 'gave' does not.
why_tempted_md: 'Gave' is broadly correct and familiar, so students settle for it instead of the verb that names dependable provision exactly.
rule_md: 1) Pin down the exact shade of meaning the sentence needs (steady furnishing of a resource). 2) Test each verb's precise connotation. 3) Rule out verbs implying permission, charity, or vague giving. 4) Keep the verb whose meaning matches the context exactly. 5) Re-read to confirm the nuance fits.

subject: act-english
context_html: When the wall of sand swallowed the horizon in minutes, the seasoned expedition <u>totally freaked out</u> and scrambled to lash down the tents.
stem_md: Which choice best fits the formal style of the passage?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Totally freaked out' is slang that clashes with the passage's measured, formal tone (register_too_casual).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Kind of lost it' is vague, conversational filler unsuited to the passage (register_too_casual).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the phrasing is composed and formal, matching the surrounding style.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Was bugging out' is slang out of keeping with the formal narrative (register_too_casual).

why_correct_md: The passage's **formal narrative style** calls for composed diction rather than slang.
why_tempted_md: The slang phrase vividly conveys panic, so students choose it for energy without checking that it clashes with the formal tone.
rule_md: 1) Judge the passage's register from its surrounding diction (formal, composed). 2) Label each option as slang, casual, or formal. 3) Discard any slangy or conversational phrasing. 4) Keep the option whose tone matches the passage. 5) Re-read the sentence to confirm the register stays consistent.

subject: act-english
context_html: At the Herrera family's bakery, success depended <u>not only on the quality of the flour but also on</u> the patience of whoever tended the ovens.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: not only on the quality of the flour but also
not only on the quality of the flour and also on
not only on the quality of the flour as well as on

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — 'not only on X but also on Y' keeps the correlative pair intact and places 'on' after both halves, so the two phrases stay parallel.
per_choice_rationale.B: Drops the second 'on,' so the phrase after 'but also' no longer matches the prepositional phrase after 'not only' (parallel_dropped_prep).
per_choice_rationale.C: Pairs 'not only' with 'and also,' a mismatch; that opener must be completed by 'but also' (correlative_mismatch_and).
per_choice_rationale.D: Pairs 'not only' with 'as well as,' another broken correlative pair (correlative_mismatch_aswellas).

why_correct_md: The pair **not only … but also** is complete, and both halves begin with 'on,' keeping the two phrases parallel.
why_tempted_md: Dropping the second 'on' sounds natural in speech, so many students accept the unbalanced version without noticing the broken parallel.
rule_md: 1) Find the first half of the correlative pair (e.g., *not only*). 2) Check that its partner is the exact required match. 3) Compare what follows each half — the two pieces must have the same grammatical shape. 4) If either the partner word or the shapes differ, revise.

subject: act-english
context_html: The <u>row of braided challahs on the top shelf glistens</u> under the display lights every Friday afternoon.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: row of braided challahs on the top shelf glisten
row of braided challahs on the top shelf are glistening
rows of braided challah on the top shelf glistens

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — the subject is the singular 'row,' so the singular verb 'glistens' agrees; 'of braided challahs' is only a prepositional phrase.
per_choice_rationale.B: Matches the verb to the nearest noun 'challahs' instead of the true subject 'row' (sv_nearest_noun).
per_choice_rationale.C: Commits the same attraction error with a plural helping verb 'are' for a singular subject (sv_nearest_noun_aux).
per_choice_rationale.D: Switches the subject to plural 'rows' but keeps a singular verb, creating a fresh mismatch (sv_flipped_number).

why_correct_md: The true subject is the singular **row**, so it takes a singular verb no matter what plural nouns sit between subject and verb.
why_tempted_md: 'Challahs' sits right next to the verb, so the plural verb form sounds correct to the ear.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb. 2) Ask 'who or what is doing this?' to find the subject. 3) Cross out prepositional phrases between subject and verb. 4) Match the verb to the remaining subject's number. 5) Reread the stripped sentence to confirm.

subject: act-english
context_html: Customers still ask about the great-aunt <u>whom the family insists</u> invented the bakery's molasses rye.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Whom' is a hypercorrection here — the pronoun is the subject of 'invented,' not an object of 'insists' (case_hypercorrect).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — set aside the interrupting clause 'the family insists,' and the pronoun must serve as the subject of 'invented,' which requires the subject form.
per_choice_rationale.C: Commas around 'the family insists' do not repair the case error; the pronoun still needs the subject form (comma_fix_case).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Which' cannot refer to a person; a relative pronoun for the great-aunt must be a personal one (which_for_person).

why_correct_md: Ignore the interrupter 'the family insists' — the pronoun is the **subject** of 'invented,' so subject case is required.
why_tempted_md: The pronoun directly follows 'ask about the great-aunt,' so it feels like the object of a verb and pulls students toward the object form.
rule_md: 1) Bracket off interrupting clauses like 'she said' or 'the family insists.' 2) See what job the pronoun does in the clause that remains. 3) Doing the action = subject form; receiving it = object form. 4) Restore the interrupter and reread.

subject: act-english
context_html: The bakery's storefront is barely wide enough for two customers to stand side by side. <u>As a result,</u> the family manages to display more than forty kinds of bread in the tiny space.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'As a result' claims the crowded display is caused by the narrow storefront, but the second sentence works against the first, not because of it (transition_false_cause).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'For example' promises an illustration of the first sentence, yet the second sentence is a surprising contrast, not an instance (transition_false_example).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In other words' signals a restatement, but the second sentence adds new, contrasting information (transition_false_restatement).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — the tiny storefront makes the huge selection unexpected, so a concessive transition fits.

why_correct_md: The second sentence is true **despite** the first, so the transition must concede the obstacle before delivering the surprise.
why_tempted_md: Cause-and-effect transitions feel safe because the two sentences are clearly related — just not causally.
rule_md: 1) Read the sentence before and the sentence after with the transition blanked out. 2) Name the relationship in your own words (cause? example? contrast? restatement?). 3) Pick the transition that names that same relationship. 4) Reread with your pick inserted.

subject: act-english
context_html: Rosa spends every Sunday testing small adjustments to the croissant dough. <u>For instance,</u> last month she swapped half the butter for browned butter to deepen the flavor.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most effective transition?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — the second sentence gives a specific instance of the 'small adjustments' the first sentence describes.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'However' signals contrast, but the butter swap confirms rather than contradicts the first sentence (transition_false_contrast).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In conclusion' signals a summary or ending, but the second sentence narrows to one example instead of wrapping up (transition_false_summary).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Meanwhile' signals two things happening at the same time, but the sentences describe a general habit and one instance of it (transition_false_time).

why_correct_md: The butter swap is a concrete **example** of the small adjustments, so an illustrating transition fits.
why_tempted_md: 'Meanwhile' feels harmless because both sentences involve time words like 'Sunday' and 'last month.'
rule_md: 1) Blank out the transition. 2) Ask: is sentence two an example, a contrast, a result, a restatement, or a time shift relative to sentence one? 3) Choose the transition that matches your label. 4) Reread the pair to confirm the logic clicks.

subject: act-english
context_html: By four in the morning, the mixers are already turning, and the first trays of rolls are proofing beside the warm ovens. An hour later, the pastry team pipes fillings and glazes fruit tarts. Only when the cases are full does anyone unlock the entrance.
stem_md: The writer wants to open the paragraph with a sentence that establishes its focus on the tasks completed prior to opening time. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: The bakery sells rolls, tarts, and several kinds of bread.
Customers often ask why fresh bread costs more than supermarket loaves.
The family bought its first commercial mixer in 1989.
Most of the work at Solano & Sons is finished before the front door ever opens.

per_choice_rationale.A: Lists products, so it frames the paragraph as an inventory rather than a timeline of pre-opening tasks (intro_wrong_focus_inventory).
per_choice_rationale.B: Raises a pricing question the paragraph never answers, steering readers off the stated focus (intro_offtopic).
per_choice_rationale.C: Offers a historical fact about equipment, not a frame for the morning routine that follows (intro_wrong_focus_history).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — it announces that the labor happens early, exactly the idea the paragraph's timeline of pre-opening tasks develops.

why_correct_md: It previews the paragraph's controlling idea — the **pre-opening** labor — which every following sentence illustrates.
why_tempted_md: The product list feels connected because rolls and tarts appear later in the paragraph, but it promises an inventory the paragraph never delivers.
rule_md: 1) Read the body sentences first and state their shared idea in one phrase. 2) Test each opener: does it promise exactly that idea? 3) Reject openers that promise a different topic, however related. 4) Confirm the winner by reading it straight into sentence two.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] The Okafor family opens its market stall with the same routine every Saturday. [2] First, Chidi stacks the sourdough boules into a pyramid at the center of the table. [3] Nneka then clips price cards to small stands beside each variety. [4] A cash box, a stack of paper bags, and a scale complete the setup.
stem_md: The writer wants to add the following sentence: "Next, he fans the seeded batards in a half circle around that pyramid." For the sake of the logic and coherence of the paragraph, the sentence should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Placed there, 'that pyramid' and 'Next' point back to nothing, because the pyramid is not built until later (placement_no_antecedent).
per_choice_rationale.B: The setup is declared 'complete' in Sentence 4, so adding another arranging step afterward contradicts the paragraph's close (placement_after_close).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct — 'he' follows Chidi, 'Next' follows 'First,' and 'that pyramid' points to the pyramid just built.
per_choice_rationale.D: After Sentence 3, 'he' seems to follow Nneka and the sequence 'First … then … Next' falls out of order (placement_pronoun_mismatch).

why_correct_md: Every cue in the new sentence — 'Next,' 'he,' and 'that pyramid' — hooks onto Sentence 2 and **nothing else**.
why_tempted_md: Placing it after Sentence 3 keeps it near the middle of the routine, which feels balanced even though the pronoun no longer matches its person.
rule_md: 1) Circle the new sentence's pointing words (pronouns, 'this/that' phrases, sequence words). 2) Find the one sentence that supplies each pointer's target. 3) Slot the new sentence immediately after that target. 4) Reread the paragraph in order to confirm the chain.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] When their flour supplier raised prices last spring, the Bellamys considered shrinking the bakery's menu. [2] Instead, they rebuilt it around what the wood-fired oven does best. [3] The new menu drew longer lines than the old one ever had. [4] Fewer offerings meant less waste, and each remaining bread received more of the bakers' attention.
stem_md: For the sake of the logic and coherence of the paragraph, Sentence 4 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Left at the end, the explanation of the rebuilt menu arrives after its result, so the paragraph doubles back on itself (order_explanation_after_result).
per_choice_rationale.B: As an opener, 'Fewer offerings' has nothing to refer to, since no menu change has been mentioned yet (order_no_referent).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct — Sentence 4 explains what the rebuilt menu meant, and Sentence 3 then reports the payoff of those changes.
per_choice_rationale.D: Between Sentences 1 and 2, the sentence describes results of a decision not yet made and severs 'Instead' from the option it rejects (order_breaks_instead).

why_correct_md: The paragraph flows problem → decision → **what the decision meant** → payoff once Sentence 4 follows Sentence 2.
why_tempted_md: The sentence reads smoothly at the end because it elaborates on the menu, so the backtracking in logic is easy to miss.
rule_md: 1) Label each sentence's role: problem, decision, explanation, result. 2) Order the roles chronologically and logically (causes ahead of effects). 3) Check connector words ('Instead,' 'The new…') still point to the right neighbors. 4) Read the reordered paragraph straight through.

subject: act-english
context_html: Every Saturday the display case fills with trays of <u>lemon bars, almond croissants, and, cinnamon knots</u> before the first customers arrive.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most effective punctuation?

choices.label: lemon bars almond croissants and cinnamon knots
lemon bars, almond croissants and, cinnamon knots
lemon bars, almond croissants, and cinnamon knots

per_choice_rationale.A: Places a comma after 'and,' splitting the conjunction from the final item (comma_after_and).
per_choice_rationale.B: Runs the three items together with no separating commas at all (series_no_commas).
per_choice_rationale.C: Drops the comma before 'and' and inserts one after it, misplacing the pause (comma_misplaced_and).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — commas separate the items, with the final comma placed before 'and,' not after it.

why_correct_md: In a series, commas go **between** items — including one just before the conjunction — never after 'and.'
why_tempted_md: Students who hear a pause around 'and' sometimes attach the comma to the wrong side of the conjunction.
rule_md: 1) Count the items in the list. 2) Place a comma after each item except the last. 3) Keep the final comma before the conjunction. 4) Make sure no comma follows 'and' itself. 5) Reread the list rhythm.

subject: act-english
context_html: Amara and Dele wrote down every recipe they perfected, and the <u>sisters' battered recipe box</u> now sits on a shelf above the proofing cabinet.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — the box belongs to both sisters, so the plural 'sisters' takes an apostrophe after the final s.
per_choice_rationale.B: Uses the singular possessive even though the sentence names two owners (possessive_singular_for_plural).
per_choice_rationale.C: Omits the apostrophe entirely, leaving a plural noun with no possession marked (possessive_missing_apostrophe).
per_choice_rationale.D: Adds 's to a regular plural already ending in s, an over-marked form (possessive_double_s).

why_correct_md: Two owners make **sisters** plural, and a regular plural shows possession with an apostrophe alone after the s.
why_tempted_md: The apostrophe-before-s pattern is so common that the singular possessive looks right at a glance.
rule_md: 1) Ask who owns it — one owner or more? 2) Write the owner noun in the correct number. 3) If the plural ends in s, add just an apostrophe; otherwise add 's. 4) Reread to check the owner count matches the sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: The <u>starter—a sour, bubbling culture the family has fed daily since 1972, lives</u> in a ceramic crock behind the register.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most effective punctuation?

choices.label: starter, a sour, bubbling culture the family has fed daily since 1972—lives
starter—a sour, bubbling culture the family has fed daily since 1972 lives
starter—a sour, bubbling culture the family has fed daily since 1972—lives

per_choice_rationale.A: Opens the interrupter with a dash but closes it with a comma; paired punctuation cannot be mixed (paired_dash_comma_mix).
per_choice_rationale.B: Reverses the mismatch, opening with a comma and closing with a dash (paired_comma_dash_mix).
per_choice_rationale.C: Opens with a dash and never closes the interrupter, letting it crash into the main verb (paired_unclosed).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — matching dashes fence off the interrupting description on both sides.

why_correct_md: An interrupter must be enclosed by a **matching pair** — dash with dash — so the main clause 'The starter … lives' reads cleanly.
why_tempted_md: The opening dash is so noticeable that the quiet comma at the other end slips by unchecked.
rule_md: 1) Find the interrupting chunk and read the sentence without it. 2) Check the mark before the chunk and the mark after it. 3) Make the two marks match (both commas, both dashes, or parentheses). 4) Reread with the chunk removed to confirm the frame.

subject: act-english
context_html: Under his grandmother's eye, Tomas <u>learned to fold the pastry dough</u> in thirds without tearing a single layer.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

choices.label: learned, to fold the pastry dough
learned to fold, the pastry dough
learned to fold the pastry dough,

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — the verb, its infinitive, and its object flow without interruption, so no internal punctuation is needed.
per_choice_rationale.B: Splits the verb 'learned' from the infinitive that completes it (comma_verb_complement).
per_choice_rationale.C: Separates 'fold' from its direct object, 'the pastry dough' (comma_verb_object).
per_choice_rationale.D: Inserts a comma before the essential phrase 'in thirds,' severing how the folding is done from the folding itself (comma_before_essential).

why_correct_md: No rule calls for a comma here — the chain **verb → infinitive → object → essential phrase** should run unbroken.
why_tempted_md: Students who add commas wherever a speaker might breathe often insert one before 'in thirds.'
rule_md: 1) For each comma, name the rule that requires it (series, intro element, interrupter, joining clauses). 2) If no rule fits, the comma is intrusive — remove it. 3) Never separate a verb from its object or its complement. 4) Reread the stripped sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: Before the family bought a spiral mixer, Etta <u>fought the stiff bagel dough with both fists, bracing her heels against the floor tiles</u>.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize the physical strain of mixing bagel dough by hand. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: mixed the bagel dough by hand each morning
prepared the bagel dough in the traditional manner
handled dough that many bakers find difficult

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — 'fought,' 'both fists,' and 'bracing her heels' render the bodily effort in concrete, muscular detail.
per_choice_rationale.B: States the fact of hand-mixing and its schedule but conveys no effort (goal_states_fact_no_emphasis).
per_choice_rationale.C: Gestures at tradition, shifting emphasis from strain to heritage (goal_wrong_emphasis_tradition).
per_choice_rationale.D: Reports other bakers' opinion of the dough instead of showing Etta's exertion (goal_secondhand_opinion).

why_correct_md: Vivid physical verbs and body details — fists, braced heels — **show** the strain the writer wants to stress.
why_tempted_md: The plain hand-mixing statement mentions 'by hand,' which echoes the goal's wording without delivering any actual strain.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's goal in your own words. 2) For each option, underline the words that directly serve that goal. 3) Discard options whose words serve a different idea (schedule, tradition, reputation). 4) Pick the option with the most goal-serving detail.

subject: act-english
context_html: My grandfather kept the bakery's ledgers in a careful, slanting hand, noting each day's sales beside remarks on the weather. When the entries thinned during the drought years, <u>he got pretty worked up about</u> the sugar orders.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the essay's tone?

choices.label: he was devastated beyond all consolation by

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Got pretty worked up' is conversational slang that clashes with the essay's measured, reflective voice (tone_colloquial).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Devastated beyond all consolation' is melodramatic overstatement, exceeding the essay's quiet restraint (tone_overwrought).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Stressed out over' is casual idiom, too informal for the reflective register (tone_casual_idiom).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — plain, restrained wording that matches the essay's careful, understated voice.

why_correct_md: The essay's voice is quiet and precise, so the revision must stay **measured** — concerned but neither slangy nor theatrical.
why_tempted_md: The melodramatic option sounds 'formal' because of its elevated vocabulary, which masks its excess.
rule_md: 1) Read two or three surrounding sentences and label the voice (formal? conversational? restrained? playful?). 2) Label each option's register the same way. 3) Eliminate options that are more casual OR more dramatic than the passage. 4) Choose the register twin.

subject: act-english
context_html: In the two weeks before the winter holidays, the Vachon family runs its bakery like a relay team. Orders are logged on a whiteboard the moment they arrive, and each night the next day's bake list is sorted by oven temperature. Pickup times are staggered in fifteen-minute blocks so the small front room never overflows.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence to the paragraph: "The bakery's building was once a hardware store owned by an unrelated family." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it explains how the family adapted the building for holiday baking.
Yes, because it provides historical background about the bakery's location.
No, because the paragraph has already described the building's past.
No, because it strays from the paragraph's focus on how the family manages the holiday rush.

per_choice_rationale.A: Says yes with a justification the sentence cannot support — it never mentions adaptation or baking (add_yes_false_reason).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correctly labels the sentence as background but wrongly assumes background automatically belongs (add_yes_background_fallacy).
per_choice_rationale.C: Rejects the sentence for a false reason — the paragraph says nothing about the building's past (add_no_false_reason).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — the sentence is off-topic trivia that would interrupt the paragraph's account of the family's holiday system.

why_correct_md: The paragraph is tightly about the family's **holiday workflow**, and a stray fact about the building's previous owner serves none of it.
why_tempted_md: 'Historical background' sounds enriching, so students accept the addition without checking whether it serves this particular paragraph.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's main idea in one phrase. 2) Ask whether the proposed sentence advances that idea. 3) Then check the reason: even a correct yes/no fails if its justification misdescribes the sentence or the paragraph. 4) Pick the option whose verdict AND reason are both true.

subject: act-english
context_html: When Priya Anand took over her parents' bakery, she kept the notebook of recipes her mother had written out by hand. She still measures cardamom with the brass spoon her grandfather carried from Surat, and she teaches her daughter the same lamination folds she learned at twelve. Even the shop's opening ritual—lighting a small lamp by the register—has passed unchanged through three generations.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to show how a family business keeps its traditions alive across generations. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it details specific practices that have been handed down and are still in use.
Yes, because it explains how the bakery has stayed profitable in a changing market.
No, because it concentrates on a single recipe rather than on the family's habits.
No, because it is mainly about the technique of laminating dough.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — the recipes, spoon, folds, and lamp ritual are inherited practices shown continuing across three generations.
per_choice_rationale.B: Reaches the right verdict for a reason the essay never supports; profit and markets are never discussed (purpose_yes_wrong_reason).
per_choice_rationale.C: Misreads the scope — the essay surveys several inherited habits, not one recipe (purpose_false_narrow).
per_choice_rationale.D: Mistakes one detail for the main subject; lamination is a single example among many (purpose_detail_as_main).

why_correct_md: Every sentence supplies an inherited, still-living practice — exactly what the stated goal requires — and the **reason** cites that evidence.
why_tempted_md: The profitability answer matches the correct verdict, so students grab it without checking whether its reason appears anywhere in the essay.
rule_md: 1) Restate the hypothetical goal. 2) List what the essay actually does, sentence by sentence. 3) Judge the verdict (yes/no) against that list. 4) Then verify the reason — it must describe the essay accurately. 5) Reject any option whose verdict or reason fails.

subject: act-english
context_html: Nothing baked at Ferraro's goes to waste, and the neighborhood knows it. Each evening, unsold loaves are marked down during the final hour of business, and whatever remains is packed up for donation.
stem_md: The writer wants to add a sentence here that supports the paragraph's focus on how the bakery's leftover bread benefits the surrounding neighborhood. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: The family also sells branded tote bags near the register.
A volunteer from the food pantry two blocks away collects the boxes at closing each evening.
Day-old loaves can become croutons, panzanella, or bread pudding.
The bakery's ovens are switched off by seven each evening.

per_choice_rationale.A: Tote bags are merchandise, unrelated to leftover bread or neighborhood benefit (detail_offtopic_merch).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — it shows the donated loaves actually reaching a nearby neighborhood organization, completing the paragraph's point.
per_choice_rationale.C: Recipe ideas describe uses for old bread in general, not this bakery's effect on its neighbors (detail_generic_not_local).
per_choice_rationale.D: An operations fact about oven schedules, with no link to leftover bread helping anyone (detail_irrelevant_ops).

why_correct_md: It extends the donation detail to a concrete **neighborhood** recipient, which is precisely the paragraph's stated focus.
why_tempted_md: The recipe option stays on the topic of day-old bread, so it feels relevant even though it drops the neighborhood angle entirely.
rule_md: 1) Write down the paragraph's focus as 'topic + angle' (here: leftover bread + helping neighbors). 2) Test each option against BOTH parts. 3) Reject options that hit the topic but miss the angle, or vice versa. 4) Choose the option serving both.

subject: act-english
context_html: The walk-in cooler failed on the hottest weekend of July<u>, so the family</u> hauled every tub of butter to a neighbor's restaurant before sunrise.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — a comma plus the coordinating conjunction 'so' legally joins the two independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.B: Joins two complete sentences with only a comma, creating a comma splice (comma_splice).
per_choice_rationale.C: Fuses the two complete sentences with no punctuation or conjunction at all (fused_sentence).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Therefore' is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction, so a comma before it still splices the clauses (splice_conjunctive_adverb).

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses may be joined by a comma **plus a coordinating conjunction**, which is exactly what the sentence does.
why_tempted_md: 'Therefore' feels like a connector strong enough to justify a comma, but it lacks a conjunction's joining power.
rule_md: 1) Check each side of the junction: can it stand alone as a sentence? 2) If both can, they need a period, a semicolon, or comma + FANBOYS. 3) Treat words like 'therefore' and 'however' as adverbs — they need semicolon support. 4) Reread the join.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Although the flood ruined the storefront's tin ceiling, the</u> family reopened the bakery within six weeks.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: Because the flood ruined the storefront's tin ceiling, the
The flood ruined the storefront's tin ceiling, the
Although the flood ruined the storefront's tin ceiling, but the

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — 'Although' concedes the setback, logically setting up the surprising quick reopening.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Because' claims the flood caused the reopening, reversing the logic (subordinator_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.C: Removing the subordinator leaves two independent clauses joined by a comma — a splice (splice_dropped_subordinator).
per_choice_rationale.D: Doubles the connection with both 'Although' and 'but,' so the contrast is marked twice and no main clause remains (double_connector).

why_correct_md: The sentence needs a **concession**: despite the flood's damage, the family reopened fast — exactly what 'Although' signals.
why_tempted_md: 'Although … but' mirrors how some speakers talk, so the doubled contrast can sound natural to the ear.
rule_md: 1) Identify the logical relationship between the clauses (cause, contrast, concession, time). 2) Pick one connector that encodes it. 3) Never stack a subordinator and a coordinator on the same pair of clauses. 4) Confirm one clause remains fully independent.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Piping the last row of rosettes, the oven timer startled Junia</u>, and the icing bag slipped across the cake board.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: Piping the last row of rosettes, Junia's grip was loosened by the oven timer
Piping the last row of rosettes, the oven timer's buzz startled Junia
As Junia piped the last row of rosettes, the oven timer startled her

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening phrase attaches to 'the oven timer,' absurdly making the timer the one piping (dangling_modifier).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Junia's grip' is a thing, not a person, so the piping phrase still has no doer to attach to (dangling_possessive).
per_choice_rationale.C: Swapping in 'the oven timer's buzz' leaves the modifier dangling — a buzz cannot pipe rosettes (dangling_new_noun).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — converting the phrase to a clause with its own subject puts Junia at the piping and the timer at the startling.

why_correct_md: Giving the opening idea its own **subject and verb** removes the dangling phrase entirely, so nothing attaches to the wrong noun.
why_tempted_md: The possessive fix puts Junia's name right after the comma, which looks like a repair even though 'grip' is the actual head noun.
rule_md: 1) Find the opening verbal phrase. 2) Ask: who is doing that action? 3) Check the noun right after the comma — it must be that doer. 4) If it is not, either move the doer there or rewrite the phrase as a full clause. 5) Reread for sense.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each January, the cousins <u>collaborate together</u> on a new king cake design before the Carnival season begins.
stem_md: Which choice most effectively expresses the idea?

choices.label: collaborate with each other as a group

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Together' repeats what 'collaborate' already means — working with others (redundant_together).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — 'collaborate' alone carries the full meaning of working together.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Jointly' restates collaboration's built-in meaning, just with a fancier word (redundant_synonym).
per_choice_rationale.D: Piles on two phrases that both repeat the verb's meaning (redundant_double).

why_correct_md: **Collaborate** already means 'work together,' so any added together-type word is deadweight.
why_tempted_md: 'Collaborate together' is so common in everyday speech that the repetition slides past the ear unnoticed.
rule_md: 1) Define the key word in the span. 2) Check whether any neighboring word repeats part of that definition. 3) Delete the repeaters and reread. 4) Keep only words that add new information.

subject: act-english
context_html: The bakery switched to a local rye grower <u>due to the fact that</u> the imported flour kept arriving stale.
stem_md: Which choice most effectively expresses the idea?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Due to the fact that' is a five-word detour around a one-word causal connector (wordy_fact_that).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Owing to the fact that' swaps one bloated formula for another of the same length (wordy_swap_formula).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct — a single conjunction expresses the causal link completely.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'For the reason that' is another padded phrase that delays the cause (wordy_reason_that).

why_correct_md: One direct conjunction does everything the padded phrases do, so the **leanest** version wins.
why_tempted_md: 'Owing to the fact that' sounds more formal, and students often equate formality with correctness.
rule_md: 1) Identify the relationship the phrase expresses (here: cause). 2) List shorter ways to express that same relationship. 3) Pick the tightest version that keeps the meaning and grammar intact. 4) Reread to confirm nothing was lost.

subject: act-english
context_html: Regulars line up on the sidewalk <u>in order to be able to buy</u> the first sourdough loaves out of the oven.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most effective?

choices.label: so that they will be able to buy

per_choice_rationale.A: 'In order to be able to' spends extra words saying what a bare infinitive already says (wordy_in_order_to_able).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'So that they will be able to' restates the same purpose with a full clause of padding (wordy_purpose_clause).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'With the purpose of buying' is a heavy nominal phrase for a simple purpose (wordy_nominal_purpose).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — the plain infinitive expresses the purpose completely in two words.

why_correct_md: The bare infinitive carries the entire meaning of purpose, so every added word is **padding**.
why_tempted_md: 'In order to' appears constantly in academic-sounding prose, so it reads as properly formal rather than wordy.
rule_md: 1) State what the phrase contributes (here: purpose). 2) Try the simplest standard construction for that function. 3) If meaning and grammar survive, prefer it. 4) Only keep longer forms when they add real meaning, like contrast or emphasis.

subject: act-english
context_html: As the loaves cooled on the rack, their crusts <u>crackled</u> softly—a sound the baker's children raced downstairs to catch.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely conveys the sound described?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — 'crackled' names the small, sharp popping sounds a cooling crust actually makes.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Shattered' describes violent breaking apart, far too destructive for a cooling loaf (precision_too_extreme).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Chattered' belongs to teeth and talkers, not to baked crusts (precision_wrong_agent).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Rustled' is the soft whisper of paper or leaves, missing the crisp popping quality (precision_wrong_texture).

why_correct_md: Cooling crusts give tiny sharp pops, and **crackled** is the verb that names exactly that sound.
why_tempted_md: 'Rustled' is also a quiet sound, so its softness feels compatible with the adverb 'softly.'
rule_md: 1) Picture the literal scene. 2) Define each candidate word precisely — what sound, made by what, at what intensity? 3) Eliminate words that are too strong, too weak, or tied to the wrong source. 4) Choose the word matching the scene exactly.

subject: act-english
context_html: In its letter to the county historical society, the family wrote that the bakery <u>has hung onto a ton of</u> its original fixtures, including the marble counter installed in 1931.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the formal style appropriate to a letter to a historical society?

choices.label: has kept ahold of loads of

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Hung onto a ton of' is casual spoken idiom, mismatched with a formal letter (register_colloquial_idiom).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — measured, formal diction suited to official correspondence with a historical society.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Kept ahold of loads of' doubles down on informal idiom and a nonstandard form (register_informal_double).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Still totally rocking' is slang, wildly out of register for the context (register_slang).

why_correct_md: A formal letter calls for **standard, measured diction**, and this phrasing reports the fact without idiom or slang.
why_tempted_md: 'Hung onto a ton of' is vivid and familiar, so its informality is easy to overlook in a quick read.
rule_md: 1) Identify the document type and audience. 2) Set the register bar accordingly (official letter = formal). 3) Flag idioms, slang, and chatty intensifiers in each option. 4) Choose the option whose diction clears the bar.

subject: act-english
context_html: When inspectors examined the aging truss bridge last spring, they <u>discovered</u> hairline cracks in two of its steel joints.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Past tense 'discovered' matches the past verb 'examined' and the time marker 'last spring,' keeping the timeline consistent.
per_choice_rationale.B: Present tense ignores the explicit past-time marker 'last spring' (misconception: tense_ignores_time_marker).
per_choice_rationale.C: Future tense contradicts an event the sentence says already happened during a completed inspection (misconception: tense_future_for_past).
per_choice_rationale.D: Present progressive suggests the discovery is happening right now, clashing with the finished past inspection (misconception: progressive_for_completed).

why_correct_md: The **past** tense verb matches both 'examined' and the time marker 'last spring,' so the original is already correct.
why_tempted_md: Students often shift to present tense because the cracks presumably still exist, overlooking that the sentence narrates a past event.
rule_md: 1) Circle any time markers in the sentence (last spring, currently, by 2030). 2) Find the other verbs and note their tense. 3) Make the underlined verb match both the markers and the surrounding verbs. 4) Reread the whole sentence to confirm one consistent timeline.

subject: act-english
context_html: The system of counterweights hidden inside the bascule bridge <u>allows</u> its massive deck to swing upward in under two minutes.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: The subject's head noun 'system' is singular, so the singular verb 'allows' agrees with it.
per_choice_rationale.B: Matches the verb to the nearby plural noun 'counterweights' instead of the true subject 'system' (misconception: sv_nearest_noun).
per_choice_rationale.C: Uses a plural verb and a progressive form, doubling the error: the subject is singular and the capability is permanent, not in progress (misconception: sv_nearest_noun_progressive).
per_choice_rationale.D: Plural perfect 'have allowed' agrees with the intervening noun rather than the singular head noun 'system' (misconception: sv_nearest_noun_perfect).

why_correct_md: The verb must agree with the **head noun** of the subject — 'system,' which is singular — not with nouns inside the prepositional phrase.
why_tempted_md: The plural noun 'counterweights' sits right before students' eyes, so many match the verb to it instead of to the true subject.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb. 2) Ask 'who or what is doing this?' and locate the subject's head noun. 3) Cross out every prepositional phrase between subject and verb. 4) Match the verb's number to the head noun alone. 5) Reread the stripped-down sentence to confirm the match.

subject: act-english
context_html: Modern cable-stayed bridges are capable <u>of withstanding</u> both hurricane-force winds and constant truck traffic.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: The idiom is 'capable of' plus a gerund, so 'capable of withstanding' is standard English.
per_choice_rationale.B: Borrows the infinitive pattern of 'able to,' but 'capable' does not take an infinitive (misconception: idiom_wrong_pattern_able).
per_choice_rationale.C: Keeps the right preposition but strands a bare verb stem after it; prepositions require gerunds (misconception: bare_verb_after_preposition).
per_choice_rationale.D: Substitutes 'for' where the fixed idiom demands 'of' (misconception: idiom_wrong_preposition).

why_correct_md: The adjective 'capable' takes the fixed pairing **of + -ing form**, which the original already uses.
why_tempted_md: Because 'able to withstand' is correct English, students transfer that infinitive pattern onto 'capable,' which follows a different idiom.
rule_md: 1) Spot the adjective before the underlined portion. 2) Recall its fixed preposition partner (capable of, interested in, famous for). 3) Confirm the verb after the preposition is in its -ing form. 4) Read the full phrase aloud to verify it matches the established idiom.

subject: act-english
context_html: Cast iron is strong under compression but brittle under tension. <u>As a result,</u> nineteenth-century designers limited it to short arch spans, where the metal stayed compressed.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: The designers' caution is a direct consequence of the metal's brittleness, so the cause-effect transition 'As a result' fits.
per_choice_rationale.B: The second sentence is not an illustration of brittleness but an outcome of it (misconception: transition_example_for_effect).
per_choice_rationale.C: Signals opposition, but the second sentence follows logically from the first rather than opposing it (misconception: transition_false_contrast).
per_choice_rationale.D: Signals simultaneous events, but the sentences are linked by logic, not by timing (misconception: transition_time_for_logic).

why_correct_md: The second sentence states the **consequence** of the first — brittleness led designers to restrict cast iron — so a cause-effect transition is correct.
why_tempted_md: Students see two different ideas (a property, then a practice) and reach for a contrast word instead of tracing the cause-effect link.
rule_md: 1) Summarize sentence one in five words. 2) Summarize sentence two in five words. 3) Name the relationship: cause-effect, contrast, example, addition, or time. 4) Pick the transition that names that exact relationship. 5) Reread with the transition in place to confirm the logic.

subject: act-english
context_html: The old ferry crossing took nearly an hour even in calm weather. <u>Similarly,</u> the new bridge carries commuters over the strait in about six minutes.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most effective transition?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Similarly' claims the two crossings are alike, but an hour-long ferry ride and a six-minute drive are opposites (misconception: transition_likeness_for_opposition).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'In fact' intensifies or confirms the previous claim, but the second sentence reverses direction rather than strengthening it (misconception: transition_intensifier_misread).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Consequently' asserts that the ferry's slowness caused the bridge's speed, a causal link the passage never makes (misconception: transition_false_cause).
per_choice_rationale.D: The sentences set a slow crossing against a fast one, so an opposition transition is the logical choice.

why_correct_md: The two sentences describe **opposite** experiences — an hour versus six minutes — so the transition must signal a reversal.
why_tempted_md: Both sentences describe crossing the same strait, so students latch onto the shared topic and choose a likeness word despite the opposing details.
