rule_md: 1) Identify the key detail in each sentence (here, the two travel times). 2) Ask whether the details agree, oppose, or cause one another. 3) Reject any transition that names a different relationship. 4) Insert the surviving transition and reread both sentences to confirm the logic flows.

subject: act-english
context_html: Early builders learned that unprotected wooden trusses rotted within a decade or two of exposure to rain and snow. A roof and siding shielded the structural timbers, extending a bridge's life to a century or more.
stem_md: The writer wants to open the paragraph with a sentence that introduces its focus on the practical reason covered bridges were built with roofs. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Covered bridges owe their famous roofs to a practical concern: keeping weather away from the timbers.
Covered bridges appear on postcards and calendars all over New England.
Wood has served as a building material for thousands of years.
Several covered bridges still charge visitors a small toll.

per_choice_rationale.A: Names the paragraph's exact focus — the protective, practical purpose of the roofs — which the next two sentences develop.
per_choice_rationale.B: Introduces scenic charm, a topic the paragraph never develops (misconception: intro_offtopic_appeal).
per_choice_rationale.C: Far broader than the paragraph, which concerns one specific design decision, not all wood construction (misconception: intro_too_broad).
per_choice_rationale.D: Raises tolls, an irrelevant detail disconnected from rot and protection (misconception: intro_irrelevant_detail).

why_correct_md: An effective introduction must **preview** the paragraph's actual content — here, the practical weather-protection purpose that both following sentences explain.
why_tempted_md: The postcard sentence feels like a friendly, engaging opener, so students pick it for style even though the paragraph never returns to scenery.
rule_md: 1) Read the body sentences first and state their shared topic in one phrase. 2) Reread the stated goal in the stem. 3) Test each opener: does it forecast that exact topic? 4) Eliminate openers that are broader, narrower, or about something else. 5) Confirm the survivor flows into the first body sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Building a pier in deep water begins with a watertight enclosure called a cofferdam. [2] Crews drive interlocking steel sheets into the riverbed to form the enclosure's walls. [3] Pumps then drain the water trapped inside, exposing the riverbed. [4] With the site dry, workers pour the concrete footing. [5] Once the footing cures, the pier rises on top of it, course by course.
stem_md: The writer wants Sentence 3 placed where the construction steps remain in logical order. Which placement best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: Draining logically follows building the walls (Sentence 2) and must precede pouring on a dry site (Sentence 4), so the current position is correct.
per_choice_rationale.B: Places the draining before the enclosure exists, leaving 'the water trapped inside' with nothing to refer to (misconception: placement_ignores_reference).
per_choice_rationale.C: Puts the draining after Sentence 4, which already declares the site dry, reversing the process (misconception: placement_breaks_sequence).
per_choice_rationale.D: Delays the draining until the pier is finished, when the water would already have to be gone (misconception: placement_after_conclusion).

why_correct_md: The steps must follow the **physical sequence** — walls built, water pumped out, footing poured — and Sentence 3 already sits exactly between its prerequisite and its consequence.
why_tempted_md: Students who skim past 'With the site dry' in Sentence 4 miss that draining must already be finished, making later placements seem harmless.
rule_md: 1) Number the real-world steps the paragraph describes. 2) Find what the movable sentence depends on (its prerequisite) and what depends on it (its consequence). 3) The sentence must sit after the prerequisite and before the consequence. 4) Test the winning slot by reading the paragraph straight through.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] In the summer of 1940, the deck of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge rippled so visibly in the wind that locals nicknamed it Galloping Gertie. [2] Engineers of the era judged the rolling motion harmless. [3] On November 7, a steady forty-mile-per-hour wind twisted the deck until it tore apart. [4] Drivers had reported feeling seasick as they crossed the undulating span. [5] After the collapse, wind-tunnel testing became a standard step in long-span design.
stem_md: The writer wants Sentence 4 placed so that the paragraph's account unfolds in logical order. Which placement best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: Leaves a pre-collapse anecdote wedged between the collapse and its aftermath, forcing readers to jump backward in time (misconception: placement_ignores_flashback).
per_choice_rationale.B: The drivers' seasickness belongs with the description of the rippling deck, before engineers dismiss the motion and long before the failure.
per_choice_rationale.C: The phrase 'the undulating span' and the past-perfect 'had reported' both require the bridge and its motion to be introduced first (misconception: placement_before_referent).
per_choice_rationale.D: Ends the paragraph on a stray pre-collapse detail after the account has already reached its industry-wide conclusion (misconception: placement_after_conclusion).

why_correct_md: The **past-perfect** 'had reported' marks an event from the rippling period, so the sentence must sit with the description of the deck's motion, before the engineers' judgment and the failure.
why_tempted_md: The current position feels acceptable because 'had reported' technically signals earlier time, so students assume the flashback is intentional rather than disruptive.
rule_md: 1) Time-stamp every sentence: before the failure or after it. 2) Note pointing phrases (like 'the undulating span') that need earlier referents. 3) Place the movable sentence after its referents appear and within its own time period. 4) Reread the paragraph start to finish to confirm no backward jumps remain.

subject: act-english
context_html: To restore the stone arch, the crew ordered <u>granite blocks steel pins, and oak scaffolding</u> from suppliers across the state.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence conform to standard punctuation conventions?

choices.label: granite blocks, steel pins and, oak scaffolding
granite blocks, steel pins, and oak scaffolding
granite blocks steel pins and oak scaffolding

per_choice_rationale.A: Omits the comma between the first two items, fusing 'granite blocks steel pins' into one garbled item (misconception: series_missing_first_comma).
per_choice_rationale.B: Places a comma after 'and' instead of before it, splitting the conjunction from its item (misconception: series_comma_after_conjunction).
per_choice_rationale.C: Separates all three items with commas, with the final comma correctly before 'and.'
per_choice_rationale.D: Drops all series commas, leaving readers to guess where each material ends (misconception: series_no_commas).

why_correct_md: A series of three items needs a **comma after each item**, with the last comma placed before the conjunction.
why_tempted_md: The original looks nearly right because it has one correct comma, so students skim past the missing separator between the first two items.
rule_md: 1) Count the items in the list. 2) If there are three or more, place a comma after each item except the last. 3) Check that the final comma sits before the conjunction, never after it. 4) Read each item alone to confirm none have fused together.

subject: act-english
context_html: Suspended high above the strait, the <u>bridges main span</u> stretches nearly a mile between its twin towers.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Leaves the possessive unmarked, so 'bridges' reads as a plural noun with no grammatical role (misconception: possessive_no_apostrophe).
per_choice_rationale.B: Apostrophe after the s marks plural possession, but the passage describes only one structure (misconception: plural_possessive_for_singular).
per_choice_rationale.C: Singular noun plus apostrophe-s correctly shows that the one bridge possesses the span.
per_choice_rationale.D: Stacks apostrophe-s onto a plural form, creating a construction standard English does not allow (misconception: double_possessive_marker).

why_correct_md: One bridge owns the span, so the possessive is built from the **singular** noun plus apostrophe-s.
why_tempted_md: The apostrophe-after-s form looks sophisticated and is correct for plurals, so students apply it without counting how many owners the passage describes.
rule_md: 1) Find the owner and the thing owned. 2) Count the owners: one or more than one? 3) For one owner, write the singular noun, then apostrophe, then s. 4) For multiple owners, write the plural noun, then the apostrophe. 5) Reread to confirm the form matches the count.

subject: act-english
context_html: The main cable<u>—a bundle of thousands of pencil-thin wires,</u> was spun in place high above the water.
stem_md: Which choice best punctuates the underlined portion?

choices.label: , a bundle of thousands of pencil-thin wires—
—a bundle of thousands of pencil-thin wires
—a bundle of thousands of pencil-thin wires—

per_choice_rationale.A: Opens the appositive with a dash but closes it with a comma, mixing two styles around one interrupter (misconception: paired_punct_mismatch_open).
per_choice_rationale.B: Reverses the same mismatch, entering with a comma and exiting with a dash (misconception: paired_punct_mismatch_close).
per_choice_rationale.C: Never closes the interrupter, so the appositive runs straight into the verb and garbles the main clause (misconception: paired_punct_unclosed).
per_choice_rationale.D: Encloses the appositive in matching dashes, letting the main clause reconnect cleanly on both sides.

why_correct_md: Paired punctuation must **match**: whatever mark opens an interrupting appositive must also close it.
why_tempted_md: The unclosed version reads smoothly aloud, so students miss that the verb has been swallowed into the description of the wires.
rule_md: 1) Bracket the interrupting phrase from its first word to its last. 2) Read the sentence without it — the remainder must be complete. 3) Check the mark at the entrance and the mark at the exit. 4) If they differ or one is missing, fix them to match. 5) Reread with the interrupter restored.

subject: act-english
context_html: The engineers who designed the glass footbridge<u>, wanted</u> its deck to flex slightly underfoot.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: A lone comma between the complete subject and its verb is intrusive; nothing licenses a pause there (misconception: comma_subject_verb_split).
per_choice_rationale.B: Removes the intrusive mark, letting the subject connect directly to its verb.
per_choice_rationale.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause on each side, but 'wanted its deck to flex' has no subject (misconception: semicolon_before_predicate).
per_choice_rationale.D: A dash sets off interruptions, but the verb is the sentence's own predicate, not an aside (misconception: dash_before_predicate).

why_correct_md: A subject must connect **directly** to its verb; no single mark may stand between them.
why_tempted_md: The long subject invites a spoken pause before the verb, so students insert a comma to match their breath rather than the grammar.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb. 2) Find the complete subject, including any 'who' or 'that' clause attached to it. 3) Check what stands between subject and verb. 4) Unless a paired interrupter sits there, remove any single mark. 5) Reread to confirm the subject flows straight into the verb.

subject: act-english
context_html: At either end of the suspension bridge, a block of concrete the size of an apartment building sits buried in bedrock. Each anchorage <u>holds back the pull</u> of the main cables.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize the enormous force the anchorages must resist. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: strains against the colossal, sixty-thousand-ton pull

per_choice_rationale.A: Reports the anchorage's job in neutral terms without conveying scale (misconception: goal_neutral_wording).
per_choice_rationale.B: Swaps one plain verb for a synonym, leaving the emphasis unchanged (misconception: goal_synonym_no_emphasis).
per_choice_rationale.C: Dramatizes the force with a vivid verb and a staggering specific figure, directly serving the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.D: Abandons the idea of force entirely, describing mere attachment (misconception: goal_drops_key_idea).

why_correct_md: The stated goal is **emphasis on enormous force**, and only this wording quantifies the load and dramatizes the struggle to resist it.
why_tempted_md: The synonym swap feels like an improvement because it is a fresher verb, but changing the word without adding magnitude leaves the goal unmet.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's goal in your own words. 2) For each option, ask: does it convey that exact quality (here, sheer magnitude)? 3) Reject options that are merely grammatical, merely different, or off the goal. 4) Prefer wording with vivid, specific detail that makes the goal unmistakable. 5) Reread the sentence with the winner in place.

subject: act-english
context_html: The commission's report praised the county's rigorous maintenance program. Crews repaint the steel span every seven years, a schedule that <u>totally shuts down rust before it can mess up</u> the load-bearing plates.
stem_md: Which choice is most consistent with the tone established in the passage?

choices.label: kicks rust to the curb before it wrecks
is super effective at stopping rust on

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Totally' and 'mess up' are casual conversation, clashing with the formal report language around them (misconception: tone_casual_kept).
per_choice_rationale.B: Uses measured, technical diction that matches 'commission,' 'rigorous,' and 'maintenance program.'
per_choice_rationale.C: A street idiom is even more colloquial than the original (misconception: tone_idiom_swap).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Super' is a chatty intensifier and 'stopping rust on' is vague, so the register still fails (misconception: tone_partial_fix).

why_correct_md: Tone must stay **consistent**: a passage built on formal report language needs a precise, professional description of the rust problem.
why_tempted_md: The 'super effective' version drops the most glaring slang, so students accept it without noticing the casual intensifier that remains.
rule_md: 1) Sample the passage's diction and label its register (formal, neutral, casual). 2) Read each option and flag slang, idioms, and chatty intensifiers. 3) Eliminate every option whose register differs from the passage. 4) Confirm the survivor also keeps the sentence's exact meaning. 5) Reread the paragraph with the choice inserted.

subject: act-english
context_html: Strain gauges glued to the girders send readings to a monitoring station every fifteen minutes. When a reading drifts outside the expected range, engineers dispatch a climbing team to inspect the joint firsthand. This constant stream of data lets the county repair small problems before they grow dangerous.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence to the paragraph: "The river below the span is popular with kayakers throughout the summer." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it shows that the bridge's health matters to the local community.
Yes, because it explains why engineers monitor the span so closely.
No, because it contradicts details given earlier in the paragraph.
No, because it pulls the paragraph away from its focus on monitoring the bridge's health.

per_choice_rationale.A: Kayakers say nothing about sensors, readings, or repairs; community appeal is not the paragraph's subject (misconception: add_offtopic_justified).
per_choice_rationale.B: The sentence offers a recreational aside, not an explanation of the inspection program's purpose (misconception: add_false_explanation).
per_choice_rationale.C: Right verdict, wrong reason: nothing in the paragraph conflicts with summer kayaking (misconception: reject_wrong_reason_contradiction).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correctly rejects the sentence for irrelevance: the paragraph is a tight account of sensor-driven upkeep, and the detail develops none of it.

why_correct_md: A sentence earns its place only by developing the paragraph's **central subject** — the sensor-based inspection system — which this recreational detail does not.
why_tempted_md: The contradiction option tempts students who sense the sentence does not belong but grab the first 'no' reasoning without checking whether it is accurate.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's central subject in five words. 2) Ask whether the proposed sentence develops that subject. 3) If yes, verify the stated reason matches what the sentence actually does. 4) If no, choose the rejection whose reason names the real flaw. 5) Reread the paragraph to confirm the verdict.

subject: act-english
context_html: Every October, my grandmother and I walk the length of the harbor bridge at dawn. She points out gulls balancing on the railing and tells me stories about crossing it as a schoolgirl. By the time we reach the far tower, the sun has turned the water gold, and neither of us is in any hurry to turn back.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to explain the technical challenges of anchoring a long bridge in deep water. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it mentions the bridge's far tower, which stands in the harbor's deepest water.
Yes, because the walk shows that the bridge is safe enough for pedestrians.
No, because it describes only one bridge rather than comparing several.
No, because it is a personal reflection that never discusses how the bridge was engineered.

per_choice_rationale.A: A passing scenic mention of a tower explains nothing about construction in deep water (misconception: purpose_single_mention_suffices).
per_choice_rationale.B: Pedestrian safety is a different subject from construction challenges, and the essay proves neither (misconception: purpose_wrong_inference).
per_choice_rationale.C: Right verdict, wrong reason: an essay about a single bridge could still explain deep-water anchoring fully (misconception: reject_wrong_reason_scope).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correctly identifies the mismatch: the essay is a memory piece with no technical content at all.

why_correct_md: Judging purpose means comparing the essay's **actual content** — memories and imagery — against the stated goal of technical explanation, which it never attempts.
why_tempted_md: The single-bridge option tempts students who correctly sense failure but accept a plausible-sounding reason without testing whether it is the true cause.
rule_md: 1) Restate the supposed goal in your own words. 2) Summarize what the essay actually does in one sentence. 3) Compare the two: match or mismatch? 4) Among options with the right verdict, keep only the one whose reason describes the essay accurately. 5) Double-check that reason against specific lines.

subject: act-english
context_html: Steel expands in summer heat and contracts in winter cold. To absorb that movement, designers fit the roadway with toothed expansion joints. Without the joints, the deck would buckle or crack as the seasons changed.
stem_md: The writer wants to add a sentence that reinforces the paragraph's point about how temperature changes affect the bridge. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: The joints are manufactured by several firms in three different states.
On a hot July afternoon, the main span can grow longer by more than a foot.
Painters often use the joints as convenient boundaries between work zones.
Similar joints appear in elevated highways and parking garages.

per_choice_rationale.A: A supplier detail concerns commerce, not thermal movement, so it reinforces nothing (misconception: add_related_but_offpoint).
per_choice_rationale.B: Gives concrete, measurable proof of heat physically changing the deck, directly reinforcing the paragraph's claim.
per_choice_rationale.C: A workplace convenience that would exist even if temperature never changed (misconception: add_incidental_detail).
per_choice_rationale.D: Widens the topic to other structures without adding evidence about this bridge (misconception: add_broadens_scope).

why_correct_md: Reinforcement means **concrete evidence** for the paragraph's own claim — here, a vivid measurement of temperature physically moving the deck.
why_tempted_md: The elevated-highways option mentions the joints and sounds informative, so students accept topical overlap as support even though it proves nothing about temperature.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's claim in one sentence. 2) For each option, ask: does this give evidence for that exact claim? 3) Discard details that are merely about the same objects. 4) Prefer specific, measurable support over general association. 5) Reread the paragraph with the addition to confirm it strengthens the point.

subject: act-english
context_html: Rivets once held the girders <u>together; today,</u> high-strength bolts do the same job.
stem_md: Which choice results in a complete, correctly joined sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: The semicolon correctly joins two related independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice (misconception: comma_splice).
per_choice_rationale.C: Runs the two clauses together with no punctuation at all, producing a fused sentence (misconception: fused_sentence).
per_choice_rationale.D: Adding 'because' subordinates the second half, stranding a fragment after the semicolon (misconception: semicolon_plus_subordinator).

why_correct_md: A **semicolon** legally joins two independent clauses, and both halves here can stand alone as sentences.
why_tempted_md: The comma version sounds natural read aloud, so students accept the splice because the pause feels right even though the join is illegal.
rule_md: 1) Find the junction between the two statements. 2) Test each side: can it stand alone as a sentence? 3) If both can, they need a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus coordinating conjunction. 4) Reject any join that uses a comma alone or nothing. 5) Reread to confirm both sides keep their independence.

subject: act-english
context_html: Although the pontoon design cost half as much as a conventional span, <u>but it</u> demanded round-the-clock pumping to stay afloat.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Although' has already subordinated the first clause, so adding 'but' doubles the connector and breaks the structure (misconception: double_connector_although_but).
per_choice_rationale.B: Coordinating with 'and' leaves the subordinate clause attached to nothing (misconception: double_connector_and).
per_choice_rationale.C: After an 'although' clause and a comma, the main clause attaches directly with no added conjunction.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'So' both duplicates the existing connection and asserts a cause-effect link the sentence does not intend (misconception: double_connector_false_cause).

why_correct_md: One connector per clause pair: the subordinator **'although'** already links the clauses, so the main clause must follow the comma unadorned.
why_tempted_md: Students hear 'although...but' in casual speech and in some other languages, so the doubled connector sounds complete rather than redundant.
rule_md: 1) Circle every connecting word (although, but, and, so, because). 2) Count the clauses being linked. 3) Allow exactly one connector per pair of clauses. 4) If a subordinator opens the sentence, the main clause needs no conjunction. 5) Reread the sentence to confirm it has one backbone.

subject: act-english
context_html: Weakened by decades of salt spray, <u>engineers finally condemned the old pier</u> last October.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most logically and grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: the engineers' plan was to condemn the old pier
the old pier was condemned by engineers
it was decided by engineers that the old pier would be condemned

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening modifier attaches to 'engineers,' absurdly claiming the people were eroded by salt spray (misconception: dangling_subject).
per_choice_rationale.B: Swapping in 'plan' still dangles the modifier — an abstract plan cannot be weathered (misconception: dangling_abstract_noun).
per_choice_rationale.C: Places 'the old pier,' the thing actually weakened, immediately after the modifier.
per_choice_rationale.D: The dummy pronoun 'it' names nothing, so the modifier hangs with no logical target (misconception: dangling_expletive_it).

why_correct_md: An introductory modifier attaches to the **first noun after the comma**, so that noun must be the salt-damaged pier itself.
why_tempted_md: The 'it was decided' version sounds official and passive-formal, so students miss that 'it' gives the modifier nothing real to describe.
rule_md: 1) Read the opening modifier and ask: who or what does this describe? 2) Look at the first noun after the comma. 3) If they do not match, the modifier dangles. 4) Choose the version whose first noun is the thing described. 5) Reread to confirm the pairing makes literal sense.

subject: act-english
context_html: The suspension cables are inspected annually <u>each year</u> by a team of certified climbers.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most concise without losing information?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Each year' repeats exactly what 'annually' already states (misconception: redundant_synonym_kept).
per_choice_rationale.B: Swaps in a wordier duplicate, deepening the redundancy (misconception: redundant_intensified).
per_choice_rationale.C: Restates 'annually' with extra padding; the doubling remains (misconception: redundant_reworded).
per_choice_rationale.D: Removing the phrase leaves 'annually' to state the frequency once, cleanly.

why_correct_md: Since 'annually' already gives the frequency, **removing** the duplicate phrase is the only fix that ends the repetition.
why_tempted_md: 'On a yearly basis' sounds more polished than 'each year,' so students reword the duplicate instead of noticing it duplicates at all.
rule_md: 1) Underline every word or phrase expressing the same fact. 2) If two expressions match in meaning, keep exactly one. 3) Test the sentence with the extra expression removed — no meaning should be lost. 4) Reject any option that rewords the duplicate instead of removing it.

subject: act-english
context_html: Residents raised concerns <u>in connection with the matter of</u> whether tolls would rise after the renovation.
stem_md: Which choice expresses the idea most clearly and concisely?

per_choice_rationale.A: Five words of scaffolding convey a one-word relationship (misconception: wordy_bureaucratic_phrase).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'The question of' duplicates the job 'whether' already does (misconception: wordy_nested_filler).
per_choice_rationale.C: Formal-sounding padding that adds syllables, not substance (misconception: wordy_formal_padding).
per_choice_rationale.D: A single preposition carries the full meaning with no loss.

why_correct_md: Concision keeps the **fewest words that preserve the meaning**, and the entire underlined stretch reduces to one preposition.
why_tempted_md: 'Pertaining to the matter of' sounds elevated and official, so students mistake formality for precision.
rule_md: 1) State what the underlined portion means in plain words. 2) Cross out any words whose work is already done elsewhere (like 'the question of' before 'whether'). 3) Compare the surviving options: reject any that add words without adding meaning. 4) Reread the sentence with the leanest survivor to confirm nothing was lost.

subject: act-english
context_html: Engineers rely on sensors <u>that are attached in a permanent way</u> to the tower's base to catch even faint vibrations.
stem_md: Which choice best expresses the idea in the fewest words while keeping the meaning?

choices.label: attached in a manner that is permanent

per_choice_rationale.A: 'In a permanent way' spells out what a single adverb conveys (misconception: adverb_unpacked_to_phrase).
per_choice_rationale.B: Compresses the clause to a tight participial phrase with zero loss of meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: Stretches the padding further with a relative clause inside the prepositional phrase (misconception: wordy_relative_clause).
per_choice_rationale.D: Keeps the unneeded 'that are' and adds 'there,' which duplicates the stated location (misconception: filler_duplicate_location).

why_correct_md: The **shortest option that keeps every fact** wins: the whole clause collapses into a two-word participial phrase.
why_tempted_md: The 'attached there permanently' version is fairly short and sounds natural, so students overlook that 'there' and 'that are' do no work.
rule_md: 1) Identify the facts the underlined portion asserts. 2) For each option, delete it mentally and check which facts survive. 3) Eliminate options carrying words with no job ('that are,' 'there,' 'in a way'). 4) Among the survivors, take the most compact. 5) Reread the sentence to confirm smooth grammar.

subject: act-english
context_html: The county's iron drawbridge <u>expired</u> in 1988, when a fixed concrete span replaced it.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely describes what happened to the drawbridge?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Expired' belongs to licenses, deadlines, and perishables, not to structures taken out of service (misconception: precision_wrong_domain).
per_choice_rationale.B: The standard verb for equipment or structures withdrawn from service, precisely matching the event.
per_choice_rationale.C: A euphemism for a person's death, absurd for a machine (misconception: precision_person_euphemism).
per_choice_rationale.D: Extinction describes an entire category dying out, not one structure's end (misconception: precision_category_for_individual).

why_correct_md: Precision means matching the verb to its **domain**: structures withdrawn from use take this verb, not words for documents, people, or species.
why_tempted_md: 'Expired' feels close because the drawbridge's useful life ended, but the word's domain is dated documents and perishables, not steel structures.
rule_md: 1) Identify what literally happened (the county stopped using the structure). 2) For each verb, list its usual companions (what kinds of things do this?). 3) Reject verbs whose companions are documents, people, or species. 4) Keep the verb whose domain includes machinery and infrastructure. 5) Reread the sentence to confirm the fit.

subject: act-english
context_html: In its final report, the state commission concluded that the bearings beneath the deck were <u>pretty much shot</u> and recommended immediate replacement.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the formal register of the surrounding sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Pretty much shot' is slang, jarring inside a commission's formal findings (misconception: register_slang_kept).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Totally done for' trades one piece of slang for another (misconception: register_slang_swap).
per_choice_rationale.C: Precise, professional wording that matches 'commission,' 'concluded,' and 'recommended.'
per_choice_rationale.D: The hedge 'kind of' is casual and vague, the opposite of a formal conclusion (misconception: register_casual_hedge).

why_correct_md: A formal report demands **professional, exact diction**, and only this option names the bearings' condition in that register.
why_tempted_md: 'Kind of worn out' avoids obvious slang, so students accept it without noticing the casual hedge that softens a formal finding.
rule_md: 1) Read the surrounding sentence and label its register (formal, neutral, casual). 2) Flag slang, hedges, and conversational intensifiers in each option. 3) Eliminate every option carrying a flag. 4) Confirm the survivor states the condition precisely. 5) Reread the sentence in the report's voice.

subject: act-english
context_html: By 1964, the campus radio hour <u>features</u> two full hours of live ballads, and touring singers competed fiercely for its Friday slot.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Present tense clashes with the past time marker 'By 1964' and the past-tense verb 'competed' later in the sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: Future tense contradicts a sentence describing events already set in 1964.
per_choice_rationale.C: Present perfect ties an action to the present moment, but this sentence is anchored entirely in the past.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: simple past matches both the date marker and the past-tense 'competed.'

why_correct_md: The date marker and the later verb 'competed' anchor the sentence in the past, so the **simple past** is required.
why_tempted_md: 'Has featured' feels safely 'past' to many students, but present perfect actually links the action to right now.
rule_md: 1) Underline every time marker in the sentence (dates, 'by,' 'last year'). 2) Find the other verbs and note their tense. 3) Ask: does the underlined verb sit on the same timeline? 4) If not, shift it to match the established time frame and re-read the whole sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: Hootenannies invited everyone in the room to join the singing. The <u>appeal of these gatherings were</u> plain to anyone who attended: strangers arrived as spectators and left as collaborators.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: appeal of these gatherings have been

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Were' agrees with the nearby plural 'gatherings' instead of the true singular subject 'appeal.'
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Have been' is plural and also shifts into present perfect, doubling the error.
per_choice_rationale.C: Pluralizing 'appeal' and breaking 'these gathering' distorts the meaning and creates a new agreement error.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the singular subject 'appeal' takes the singular past verb 'was.'

why_correct_md: The subject is the singular noun **appeal** — the phrase 'of these gatherings' is only a modifier — so the verb must be singular.
why_tempted_md: 'Gatherings were' sounds natural because the plural noun sits right next to the verb, hiding the real subject.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb. 2) Cross out every prepositional phrase in front of it ('of these gatherings'). 3) Whatever noun is left is the subject. 4) Match the verb's number to that noun, then re-read the sentence with the phrases restored.

subject: act-english
context_html: Purists <u>insisted on preserving</u> the original verses, even when audiences clearly preferred the smoother modern arrangements.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the idiom is 'insist on' followed by a gerund.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Insist in' swaps in a near-sounding preposition that is not part of the fixed idiom.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Insist to preserve' forces an infinitive where the idiom requires a preposition plus gerund.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Insist for' invents a pairing that standard English does not use.

why_correct_md: Standard English pairs **insist** with the preposition 'on' plus a gerund, exactly as written.
why_tempted_md: 'Insisted to preserve' tempts students because many verbs (wanted, hoped, tried) do take infinitives.
rule_md: 1) Identify the verb and ask whether it belongs to a fixed verb-plus-preposition pair. 2) Say the pair aloud in a simple test sentence ('She insisted ___ leaving early'). 3) Reject any preposition or verb form that breaks the fixed pattern. 4) Confirm the following verb form (gerund vs. infinitive) matches the idiom.

subject: act-english
context_html: Organizers of the first Riverbend Folk Festival printed only five hundred tickets. <u>Similarly,</u> nearly four thousand people arrived at the gates.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Similarly' signals likeness, but a tiny ticket printing and an enormous turnout are opposites, not parallels.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the huge crowd defies the organizers' small expectation, so a contrast word is needed.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For example' promises an illustration of the first sentence, but the crowd is not an example of printing tickets.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'In other words' promises a restatement, but the second sentence adds a new, conflicting fact.

why_correct_md: The second sentence **contradicts** the expectation set by the first, so the transition must signal contrast.
why_tempted_md: 'In other words' tempts students because both sentences discuss the same event, masking that the second reverses the first.
rule_md: 1) Summarize the sentence before the transition in five words. 2) Summarize the sentence after it. 3) Name the relationship between them (contrast, cause, example, restatement). 4) Pick the transition that names that same relationship, then re-read the pair.

subject: act-english
context_html: Critics at the major newspapers dismissed the revival as a passing fad, and most radio programmers agreed. <u>As a result,</u> small labels kept pressing folk records, betting that an audience the critics could not see was quietly growing.
stem_md: Which choice most logically connects this sentence to the one before it?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'As a result' claims the dismissal caused the labels to keep pressing records, but their persistence happened in spite of it, not because of it.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'For instance' would make the labels' persistence an example of critics' dismissal, which it plainly is not.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In the same way' claims the labels acted like the critics, when they did the opposite.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the labels pressed on despite the critics' dismissal, a concessive relationship.

why_correct_md: The labels acted **in spite of** the critics' dismissal, so the transition must concede opposition rather than assert cause.
why_tempted_md: 'As a result' tempts students because the second sentence does follow the first in time, and sequence is easily mistaken for causation.
rule_md: 1) State what the first sentence predicts should happen next. 2) Check whether the second sentence fulfills that prediction or defies it. 3) If it defies it, you need a concession word; if it fulfills it, a cause-effect word. 4) Re-read with your choice to confirm the logic holds.

subject: act-english
context_html: In the late 1950s, college-town coffeehouses became unlikely engines of the folk revival. Their tiny stages required no amplification, so beginners could perform without renting expensive equipment. Between sets, musicians and audience members traded verses, tunings, and addresses.
stem_md: The writer wants to conclude the paragraph with a sentence that reinforces its main idea. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Many coffeehouses also served imported espresso, a novelty for audiences at the time.
Folk music itself has roots stretching back centuries in many countries.
In these cramped rooms, the revival steadily gained performers and loyal audiences.
Eventually, television would carry revival performers to far larger audiences.

per_choice_rationale.A: The espresso detail is coffeehouse trivia that ignores the paragraph's claim about the venues fueling the revival.
per_choice_rationale.B: A sweeping statement about the music's ancient roots is far broader than this paragraph's focus on one kind of venue.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: it returns to the opening claim, tying the venues directly to the movement's growth.
per_choice_rationale.D: Jumping ahead to television abandons the coffeehouse focus instead of reinforcing it.

why_correct_md: It circles back to the paragraph's **main idea** — that these venues powered the movement — and closes the loop opened by the first sentence.
why_tempted_md: The television option tempts students because it sounds like a natural 'what happened next,' but forward motion is not reinforcement.
rule_md: 1) Restate the paragraph's main idea from its opening sentence. 2) For each option, ask: does this sentence echo that idea, or drift to a side detail, a broader topic, or a new time frame? 3) Eliminate any option whose subject is not the paragraph's subject. 4) Choose the sentence that could double as a one-line summary of the paragraph.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] In 1962, a graduate student named Ellen Marsh drove through the Ozarks with a reel-to-reel recorder. [2] She stopped at churches, general stores, and kitchen tables, asking older residents to sing whatever they remembered. [3] The machine was heavy and temperamental, often jamming in humid weather. [4] Even so, by autumn she had captured more than two hundred songs. [5] Those informal settings, she believed, drew out verses that a studio would have silenced.
stem_md: For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, Sentence 5 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: At the end, 'those informal settings' points back across two sentences about the machine and the song count, leaving the pronoun phrase stranded.
per_choice_rationale.B: Opening with 'those informal settings' gives the phrase nothing at all to refer to.
per_choice_rationale.C: After Sentence 1, the only thing mentioned is the drive itself — no settings have been named yet.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: Sentence 2 lists the churches, stores, and kitchen tables that 'those informal settings' refers to.

why_correct_md: 'Those informal settings' must sit **immediately after** the sentence that names the settings — the churches, stores, and kitchen tables.
why_tempted_md: Leaving the sentence where it is tempts students because it reads as a reflective closing thought, even though its pointer word has lost its anchor.
rule_md: 1) Find the pointing words in the movable sentence ('those,' 'this,' 'these,' 'it'). 2) Ask what noun or list they must refer to. 3) Locate the sentence that supplies that referent. 4) Place the movable sentence directly after it, then re-read the paragraph for flow.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Ada Finch built her dulcimers using methods her grandfather had carried out of the mountains. [2] That patience, she often told visitors, was her true instrument. [3] She air-dried walnut boards for three years before making the first cut. [4] She shaped each soundbox by hand, discarding any curve that felt slightly wrong. [5] A single dulcimer might therefore take her four months to finish.
stem_md: For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, Sentence 2 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Directly after Sentence 1, 'that patience' has no antecedent — inherited methods have been mentioned, but no patient acts yet.
per_choice_rationale.B: After only the wood-drying detail, 'that patience' gathers just one of the three slow practices, cutting the summary short.
per_choice_rationale.C: After Sentence 4 the summary still arrives early, and it strands 'therefore' in Sentence 5 from the practices that explain it.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: placed last, the sentence gathers all three slow practices into a closing reflection, and Sentence 5's 'therefore' keeps its link to Sentences 3 and 4.

why_correct_md: The sentence is a **summary reflection** on all the slow practices, so it belongs after every practice — and after the total time they add up to — has been described.
why_tempted_md: Placing it after Sentence 4 tempts students because two patient practices have appeared by then, but it breaks the 'therefore' chain and still omits the third proof.
rule_md: 1) Decide what the movable sentence does: introduce, continue, or sum up. 2) List every sentence it depends on for meaning. 3) A summary must follow all of its evidence, so find the last sentence it draws on. 4) Check that moving it does not break any connector (like 'therefore') between neighboring sentences. 5) Re-read the paragraph in the new order.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Fiddles, banjos, and dulcimers</u> crowded the little stage before the first workshop of the weekend began.
stem_md: Which choice provides the best punctuation for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: a three-item series takes a comma after each item before the conjunction, exactly as written.
per_choice_rationale.B: Dropping the comma between the first two items fuses them into one unpunctuated pair.
per_choice_rationale.C: Sliding the comma after 'and' splits the conjunction from the item it introduces.
per_choice_rationale.D: Adding a comma after 'and' inserts punctuation where nothing needs separating.

why_correct_md: A simple **series** of three items is punctuated item-comma-item-comma-conjunction-item, which is what the original does.
why_tempted_md: 'Banjos and, dulcimers' tempts students who feel a pause near the conjunction but misplace where the comma belongs.
rule_md: 1) Count the items in the list. 2) Place a comma after each item except the last. 3) Keep the conjunction immediately before the final item with no comma after it. 4) Read the list aloud, pausing only at the commas, to confirm each item stays whole.

subject: act-english
context_html: Many of the <u>revivals leading voices</u> came out of college towns rather than the rural communities their songs described.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Revivals' has no apostrophe, so nothing marks the movement as the possessor of the voices.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Voice's' turns the plural performers into a singular possessor, though the voices own nothing here.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: one singular revival possesses ('revival's') its several leading voices, a plain plural.
per_choice_rationale.D: The plural possessive 'revivals'' implies multiple revivals, but the passage describes one movement.

why_correct_md: One movement owns the voices, so **revival's** takes a singular possessive apostrophe while 'voices' stays a plain plural.
why_tempted_md: The plural-possessive form tempts students who hear the s-sound and reach for an apostrophe without asking how many movements there are.
rule_md: 1) For each noun ending in s, ask: does it own something in this sentence? 2) If yes, ask: is the owner singular or plural? 3) Singular owner: apostrophe before the s; plural owner: apostrophe after. 4) If the noun owns nothing, leave the apostrophe out entirely. 5) Re-read to confirm each mark matches an actual owner.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>The ballads — many collected in remote mountain towns, were</u> entirely new to the city audiences who first heard them on reissued records.
stem_md: Which choice provides the best punctuation for the underlined portion?

choices.label: The ballads, many collected in remote mountain towns — were
The ballads — many collected in remote mountain towns were
The ballads — many collected in remote mountain towns — were

per_choice_rationale.A: Opening the interruption with a dash but closing it with a comma mismatches the pair.
per_choice_rationale.B: Opening with a comma and closing with a dash is the same mismatch in reverse.
per_choice_rationale.C: The dash opens the aside, but nothing ever closes it, so the interruption bleeds into the main clause.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: a parenthetical interruption opened with a dash must be closed with a matching dash.

why_correct_md: An interrupting phrase inside a sentence needs **matching punctuation** on both ends — dash with dash.
why_tempted_md: The dash-comma hybrid tempts students because each mark alone can set off an aside, and the mismatch is easy to miss mid-sentence.
rule_md: 1) Bracket the interrupting phrase with your fingers and read the sentence without it — it should still work. 2) Look at the mark before the interruption. 3) Look at the mark after it. 4) Make the two marks match (both dashes, both commas, or both parentheses). 5) Re-read with the aside included.

subject: act-english
context_html: Some of the <u>songs, dated</u> back to the eighteenth century and had crossed the Atlantic in the memories of emigrants.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: The comma splits the subject 'songs' from its own verb 'dated,' a pause with no grammatical job.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: no punctuation belongs between a subject and its verb.
per_choice_rationale.C: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but 'dated back...' cannot stand alone.
per_choice_rationale.D: A colon must follow a complete statement, and 'Some of the songs' is not one.

why_correct_md: A subject flows directly into its verb, so **no mark** belongs between 'songs' and 'dated.'
why_tempted_md: The comma tempts students who hear a breath after the subject and assume every pause earns punctuation.
rule_md: 1) Find the subject and its verb. 2) Check whether any mark stands between them. 3) Unless a complete paired interruption sits there, delete the mark. 4) For any semicolon or colon, test the words on each side against that mark's requirements. 5) Re-read the cleaned sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: When she reached the final chorus, her voice <u>went</u> through the crowded hall.
stem_md: The writer wants to convey the overwhelming power of the singer's voice. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Went' is a colorless verb of motion that conveys no force at all.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Carried' says the voice reached the room but gives no sense of its might.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Was audible' reduces the voice to the bare minimum — merely hearable.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it delivers the storm-like force the writer explicitly wants.

why_correct_md: It is the only verb whose connotation delivers **overwhelming power**, which is the writer's stated goal.
why_tempted_md: 'Carried' tempts students because it is a genuine improvement in vividness over the original — just not an improvement toward the stated goal.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's goal in one word (here: force). 2) For each verb, name the image or intensity it evokes. 3) Eliminate any verb that is merely accurate without delivering the goal's quality. 4) Choose the verb whose connotation scores highest on the stated goal, then re-read the sentence for fit.

subject: act-english
context_html: The library's folk-song archive follows strict conservation protocols. Staff members <u>routinely inspect</u> each wax cylinder for hairline cracks before it is approved for playback.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the formal tone established in the passage?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the measured, professional phrasing matches 'strict conservation protocols.'
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Poking at' is casual and even implies careless handling, clashing with the passage's precision.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Keep tabs on' is conversational idiom, too breezy for institutional prose.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Lovingly fuss over' is sentimental and fussy, trading professional distance for cuteness.

why_correct_md: The underlined phrase already matches the passage's **formal, institutional register**, so it should stand.
why_tempted_md: 'Keep tabs on' tempts students because it is common in everyday speech and feels natural, masking its casual register.
rule_md: 1) Sample the passage's register from its other sentences (formal, neutral, or casual?). 2) Read each option and label its register the same way. 3) Discard options that would sound out of place in the surrounding prose. 4) Confirm the survivor also preserves the sentence's exact meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: The Cedar Hollow Folk Festival began in 1961 with a single flatbed stage and a borrowed sound system. Within five years it filled the county fairgrounds, and by 1970 its weekend attendance rivaled the town's own population. Local motels booked out months in advance, and the festival committee hired its first full-time staff.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence to the paragraph: "The town also hosts a well-attended quilt fair each October." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it shows that the town's growth extended beyond music.
Yes, because it sharpens the paragraph's focus on community gatherings.
No, because the paragraph already includes a similar detail about the festival's early years.
No, because it introduces a detail unrelated to the paragraph's focus on the festival's growth.

per_choice_rationale.A: The paragraph never discusses the town's overall growth, so the sentence cannot extend a point that was never made.
per_choice_rationale.B: The paragraph's focus is one festival's expansion, not community gatherings in general, so the sentence blurs the focus rather than sharpening it.
per_choice_rationale.C: Rejects the sentence for a false reason — nothing in the paragraph resembles a quilt fair.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the quilt fair has no bearing on the festival's expansion, the paragraph's single subject.

why_correct_md: The paragraph documents one festival's expansion, and a quilt fair is **off-topic** — so the sentence should be rejected for exactly that reason.
why_tempted_md: The 'community gatherings' option tempts students because both events are local gatherings, inviting a topic broader than the paragraph actually has.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's focus in one phrase. 2) Ask whether the proposed sentence advances that focus. 3) Decide yes/no on that basis alone. 4) Then vet the stated reason: a right verdict with a wrong reason is still a wrong option. 5) Pick the choice whose verdict and reason both check out.

subject: act-english
context_html: The folk revival of the late 1950s and 1960s spread through many channels at once. Campus concerts introduced ballads to students, while reissued records let city listeners hear rural voices from decades earlier. Coffeehouses, festivals, and late-night radio programs each carried the music to a different audience, and by the mid-1960s dozens of performers had built national careers on songs once sung on porches.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to write a brief essay profiling a single influential figure of the folk revival. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it shows how performers built national careers during the movement.
Yes, because it follows one figure of the revival from childhood to fame.
No, because it surveys the whole movement rather than examining one figure in depth.
No, because it focuses on venues and recordings rather than on any performers.

per_choice_rationale.A: Mentioning that careers were built is not a profile of any individual, so the goal remains unmet.
per_choice_rationale.B: Misreads the essay — no individual is named, let alone traced from childhood to fame.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the essay is a panorama of channels and audiences, never narrowing to one person.
per_choice_rationale.D: The right verdict with a false reason — performers are mentioned; they simply are not profiled individually.

why_correct_md: A profile requires sustained attention to **one person**, and this essay pans across channels, audiences, and unnamed performers instead.
why_tempted_md: The other 'No' option tempts students because its verdict is right, and verifying the attached reason takes an extra reading step.
rule_md: 1) Restate the hypothetical goal precisely (here: profile one individual). 2) Ask what the essay actually does, citing its sentences. 3) Match verdict first: does the essay meet the goal? 4) Then audit each option's reason against the text. 5) Keep only the option whose verdict and reason are both true.

subject: act-english
context_html: Harbor Lantern Records, a two-room label founded in 1959, built its roster without ever placing an advertisement or holding a formal audition.
stem_md: The writer wants to add a sentence that supports the paragraph's focus on how the label found its new artists. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: The label's founder spent years collecting antique radios and old song sheets for the office.
The era's largest pressing plants often ran double shifts before the holidays.
The label's office sat above a bakery whose ovens warmed the building on winter nights.
Its founder spent weekend nights at neighborhood song contests, noting which performers drew crowds.

per_choice_rationale.A: The founder's collecting hobby decorates the office but says nothing about recruiting artists.
per_choice_rationale.B: Industry-wide manufacturing schedules have no connection to this label's talent search.
per_choice_rationale.C: The bakery is scene-setting charm, irrelevant to how the roster was built.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it describes the actual scouting method, directly supporting the stated focus.

why_correct_md: It is the only option that explains the **recruiting method** — exactly the focus the stem names.
why_tempted_md: The founder's collecting habit tempts students because it involves the same person and a musical flavor, though it never touches recruiting.
rule_md: 1) Copy the stated focus into a question ('How did the label find artists?'). 2) Test each option: does it answer that question? 3) Discard options that merely share a character, setting, or era with the paragraph. 4) Choose the one sentence that answers the focus question directly.

subject: act-english
context_html: Portable tape recorders transformed <u>song collecting collectors</u> no longer needed to transcribe melodies by hand in the field.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Two complete statements run together with no boundary at all — a fused sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: a semicolon legally joins the two related independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.C: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.D: Moving a comma after 'collectors' leaves the clauses fused and cuts a subject off from its verb.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses need a **legal boundary**, and a semicolon provides one while keeping the ideas linked.
why_tempted_md: The comma version tempts students because the pause lands in the right place — but a comma alone is too weak to hold two clauses apart.
rule_md: 1) Find every subject-verb pair and mark where each complete thought ends. 2) Check what stands at each boundary between complete thoughts. 3) If nothing or only a comma stands there, the sentence is illegal. 4) Repair with a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a conjunction. 5) Re-read each half to confirm it could stand alone.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Although the label spent almost nothing on promotion,</u> the duo's live shows steadily built a devoted following across the region.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

choices.label: Because the label spent almost nothing on promotion,
The label spent almost nothing on promotion,
Whenever the label spent almost nothing on promotion,

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the concession word sets up the logical surprise — success despite no promotion.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Because' claims the lack of promotion caused the following to grow, an illogical cause.
per_choice_rationale.C: Removing the subordinator leaves two independent clauses joined by only a comma — a splice.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Whenever' turns a standing condition into a repeated trigger, garbling the timeline and the logic.

why_correct_md: The opening clause **concedes** an obstacle that the main clause overcomes, and the original subordinator expresses exactly that relationship.
why_tempted_md: The 'because' version tempts students since both clauses feel connected, and cause is the easiest connection to assume.
rule_md: 1) Read the two clauses separately and state each one's point. 2) Name their true relationship: cause, contrast, condition, or time. 3) Check that the subordinating word matches that relationship. 4) Confirm the clauses are still legally joined (no bare comma between two independent clauses). 5) Re-read the full sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Strumming a borrowed guitar, the audience was quickly won over by the teenage singer.</u>
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: Strumming a borrowed guitar, the audience found the teenage singer impossible to resist.
The teenage singer, strumming a borrowed guitar, the audience was quickly won over.
Strumming a borrowed guitar, the teenage singer quickly won over the audience.

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening phrase attaches to 'the audience,' absurdly making the crowd the guitarist.
per_choice_rationale.B: Rewords the ending but still hands the guitar to the audience.
per_choice_rationale.C: Stacks the singer before a full clause about the audience, leaving the singer grammatically adrift.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the doer of the strumming — the singer — stands immediately after the modifier.

why_correct_md: An opening participial phrase must be followed **immediately** by its doer, and only this version puts the singer there.
why_tempted_md: The original tempts students because the intended meaning is obvious, so the grammatical misattachment slips past the ear.
rule_md: 1) Find the opening '-ing' phrase and ask: who performs this action? 2) Look at the first noun after the comma. 3) If that noun is not the performer, the modifier dangles. 4) Rearrange so the performer directly follows the comma. 5) Re-read to confirm every noun does what the sentence says it does.

subject: act-english
context_html: The archive's shellac discs are <u>fragile</u>, so librarians handle them only while wearing cotton gloves.
stem_md: Which choice best avoids redundancy while preserving the meaning of the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: one precise adjective carries the full meaning with nothing repeated.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Easily breakable' restates what 'fragile' already means, doubling the idea.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Delicate' is a synonym stacked onto 'fragile,' adding words but no information.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'In nature' is filler that adds no meaning to the adjective it trails.

why_correct_md: The single adjective already says everything, so any addition is **redundant**.
why_tempted_md: 'Fragile and easily breakable' tempts students because paired descriptions feel thorough, even when the second half repeats the first.
rule_md: 1) Define the underlined word in your own words. 2) Define each added word or phrase the same way. 3) If two definitions overlap, one of them must go. 4) Strip any phrase (like 'in nature') that could vanish without changing meaning. 5) Keep the leanest version that still says everything.

subject: act-english
context_html: The trio booked studio time after midnight <u>due to the fact that</u> the engineer charged half price once the day's paying sessions had ended.
stem_md: Which choice expresses the idea most concisely?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Due to the fact that' spends five words doing a one-word job.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Owing to the fact that' swaps the opener but keeps the same bloated construction.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a single conjunction expresses the causal link completely.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Because of the fact that' buries the right word inside four unnecessary ones.

why_correct_md: One **conjunction** expresses the entire causal relationship, so the five-word scaffolding is dead weight.
why_tempted_md: The longer phrases tempt students because they sound weighty and formal, and formality is easily mistaken for correctness.
rule_md: 1) Spot the phrase 'the fact that' — it is almost always removable. 2) Ask what relationship the phrase expresses (here: cause). 3) Try the shortest word that names that relationship. 4) If the sentence still says the same thing, the shorter version wins.

subject: act-english
context_html: The songbook printed simple tablature so that readers <u>could themselves attempt to try playing</u> the tunes at home.
stem_md: Which choice expresses the idea in the clearest, most concise way?

choices.label: could make an attempt at trying to play

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Themselves' is unnecessary and 'attempt to try' says the same thing twice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Trims one word but keeps the doubled 'attempt to try.'
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: every remaining word is doing work, and no meaning is lost.
per_choice_rationale.D: Inflates the doubling further with 'make an attempt at,' the wordiest version of all.

why_correct_md: 'Attempt' and 'try' are the **same action**, so the sentence needs only one of them — plus nothing else.
why_tempted_md: The middle-length version tempts students who trim the obvious extra word but miss that the two verbs duplicate each other.
rule_md: 1) List the verbs and verb-like words in the underlined span. 2) Ask which ones name the same action. 3) Keep exactly one word per action. 4) Delete self-evident additions (like 'themselves'). 5) Re-read: if meaning is intact, the shortest surviving version is correct.

subject: act-english
context_html: A good ballad <u>says</u> a complete story in only a handful of verses.
stem_md: Which word most precisely fits the context?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Says a story' is not idiomatic — 'say' takes words or statements, not stories.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Speaks' cannot take 'a story' as its object; one speaks a language, not a story.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Remarks' means to comment briefly in passing, the opposite of delivering a full narrative.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: stories are told; the verb pairs precisely with the object.

why_correct_md: Precision here is about **collocation** — the verb that English pairs with 'a story' as its object.
why_tempted_md: 'Says' tempts students because it is the everyday verb for speech, and the ear forgives it on a quick read.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb's object ('a story'). 2) Ask which verbs naturally take that object in everyday English. 3) Test each option in the frame 'to ___ a story.' 4) Reject any verb that breaks the pairing or changes the scale of the action. 5) Choose the verb that fits the object exactly.

subject: act-english
context_html: The historical society's handbook, written in careful and courteous prose, encourages members to <u>hang out at</u> the monthly song circle.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the formal style of the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Hang out at' is casual slang jarring against 'careful and courteous prose.'
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Swing by' is breezier still, pure conversational idiom.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Drop in on' softens the slang but remains a casual idiom, not handbook language.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: a single formal verb matching the handbook's register.

why_correct_md: The sentence itself announces its **formal register**, so the verb must match handbook prose, not hallway talk.
why_tempted_md: 'Drop in on' tempts students because it feels politer than the original, but politer slang is still slang.
rule_md: 1) Find the passage's own clues about register ('careful and courteous prose'). 2) Label each option: slang, casual idiom, neutral, or formal. 3) Eliminate every label that clashes with the passage's register. 4) Confirm the survivor preserves the sentence's meaning. 5) Re-read the sentence in the surrounding voice.

subject: act-english
context_html: During last month's dress rehearsal, the stage manager <u>calls</u> each lighting cue from the booth while the cast moved through the second act.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Present-tense 'calls' ignores the time markers 'last month's' and 'moved,' which fix the event in the past (tense_ignores_time_markers).
per_choice_rationale.B: Present perfect 'has called' ties the action to the present moment, but the rehearsal began and ended last month (perfect_for_finished_past).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: simple past 'called' matches both the time marker 'last month's' and the past-tense verb 'moved.'
per_choice_rationale.D: Future 'will call' contradicts an event the sentence says already happened (future_for_past_event).

why_correct_md: The time marker 'last month's' and the past verb 'moved' fix the sentence in the **past**, so the simple past form is required.
why_tempted_md: Students pick the present perfect because 'has called' sounds polished and complete, even though it wrongly links a finished past event to now.
rule_md: 1) Circle every time marker in the sentence (words like 'last,' 'next,' 'yesterday'). 2) Find all other verbs and note their tense. 3) Ask: is the underlined action in the same time frame? 4) Choose the verb form that matches the established frame. 5) Reread the whole sentence to confirm the timeline is consistent.

subject: act-english
context_html: By Friday, the rack of donated costumes <u>were sitting</u> untouched backstage, waiting for the designers to sort everything by era.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Plural 'were' agrees with the nearby noun 'costumes' instead of the true singular subject 'rack' (sv_nearest_noun).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Are sitting' repeats the nearest-noun agreement error and also shifts a past scene into the present (sv_nearest_noun + tense_shift).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Have been sitting' pairs a plural helping verb with a singular subject and adds an unneeded perfect construction (sv_nearest_noun + perfect_shift).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the singular subject 'rack' takes singular 'was,' and the past progressive matches the scene set by 'By Friday.'

why_correct_md: The **subject** of the verb is the singular 'rack' — not 'costumes,' which sits inside a prepositional phrase — so a singular past verb is required.
why_tempted_md: Students match the verb to 'costumes' because it sits right next to the verb, but a noun inside an 'of' phrase can never be the subject.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb. 2) Ask 'who or what is doing this?' 3) Cross out every prepositional phrase ('of donated costumes') between the subject and verb. 4) Match the verb's number to the head noun that remains. 5) Confirm the tense fits the sentence's time frame.

subject: act-english
context_html: The technical director insisted that every crew member <u>comply to</u> the safety rules posted beside the fly rail.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard written English?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Comply to' swaps in a near-sounding preposition that is not part of the fixed idiom (idiom_wrong_preposition).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Comply at' treats the rules like a location rather than something followed (idiom_location_preposition).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Comply for' wrongly signals purpose or benefit instead of adherence (idiom_purpose_preposition).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the verb 'comply' takes the fixed preposition 'with' in standard English.

why_correct_md: 'Comply' is an **idiom** with one fixed partner preposition, and only that pairing is standard written English.
why_tempted_md: Students choose 'comply to' because 'agree to' and 'adhere to' sound similar, so 'to' feels natural after a rule-following verb.
rule_md: 1) Isolate the verb and its preposition. 2) Recall or test the fixed pairing in a short, familiar sentence ('Drivers ___ the speed limit'). 3) Substitute a synonym like 'follow' to check the meaning. 4) Reject any preposition that changes the relationship to place, purpose, or direction. 5) Reread with the standard pairing.

subject: act-english
context_html: Ticket presales for the fall play stayed sluggish through September. <u>Therefore,</u> the final weekend sold out within hours.
stem_md: Which transition word or phrase is most logical in context?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Therefore' claims the slow presales caused the sellout, but the two facts oppose each other (transition_false_cause).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'For example' would make the sellout an illustration of sluggish sales, which it contradicts (transition_false_example).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In addition' stacks the sellout onto the slow sales as if they point the same way (transition_false_addition).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the sold-out weekend reverses the expectation set by sluggish presales, so a contrast transition is needed.

why_correct_md: The second sentence **contrasts** with the first — slow sales followed by a fast sellout — so a contrast transition is the only logical link.
why_tempted_md: Students pick the cause-effect transition because the two sentences describe the same ticket campaign in sequence, which feels like cause and result.
rule_md: 1) State the first sentence's idea in five words. 2) State the second sentence's idea in five words. 3) Name the relationship: cause, example, addition, or reversal. 4) Match the transition to that relationship. 5) Reread both sentences with your choice to confirm the logic holds.

subject: act-english
context_html: The improv troupe never performs from a script. <u>Similarly,</u> its members spend weeks drilling the same structured warm-up games before every show.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Similarly' claims the disciplined drilling parallels going scriptless, but the structure actually cuts against the free-form image (transition_false_similarity).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Therefore' asserts that skipping scripts causes the weeks of drills, a causal chain the sentences never establish (transition_false_cause).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In fact' should intensify the first claim, yet the drilling complicates rather than sharpens the unscripted picture (transition_false_intensifier).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: heavy structured practice is a surprising concession alongside unscripted performance, so a concessive transition fits.

why_correct_md: The second sentence **concedes** something surprising — rigid, repeated structure inside a supposedly spontaneous group — so a concession transition is required.
why_tempted_md: 'In fact' tempts students because both sentences describe the troupe's habits, making the second feel like an emphatic elaboration rather than a twist.
rule_md: 1) Summarize sentence one in your own words. 2) Summarize sentence two. 3) Ask: does the second echo, cause, intensify, or push against the first? 4) If it pushes against expectations while both remain true, choose a concessive connector. 5) Reread the pair to confirm the tension is acknowledged.

subject: act-english
context_html: ______ Apprentices begin by mending hems and replacing buttons on garments from the costume stock. By midyear, they are drafting patterns and cutting fabric for full ensembles. The most experienced seniors design an entire show on their own.
stem_md: The writer wants to open the paragraph with a sentence that introduces its main idea. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: The costume shop stores more than four hundred garments from past productions.
Many students would rather perform onstage than sew in the costume shop.
Sewing machines can be dangerous for anyone who has not been trained.
In the school's costume shop, student apprentices build skills in stages.

per_choice_rationale.A: An inventory statistic previews nothing about the progression the paragraph traces (intro_offtopic_detail).
per_choice_rationale.B: A claim about preferring performance points the paragraph toward a comparison it never makes (intro_wrong_emphasis).
per_choice_rationale.C: A safety warning promises a paragraph about hazards, which never materializes (intro_offtopic_detail).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it previews the step-by-step growth — mending, then drafting, then designing — that every following sentence develops.

why_correct_md: A strong opener **forecasts** the paragraph's throughline, and only this sentence previews the progression from simple mending to independent design.
why_tempted_md: The garment statistic tempts students because it mentions the same setting, even though no later sentence develops storage or inventory.
rule_md: 1) Read the body sentences first. 2) Name the single thread that ties them together. 3) Test each opener: does the rest of the paragraph deliver what it promises? 4) Eliminate openers whose topic never returns. 5) Choose the sentence whose promise the paragraph keeps.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] The set crew began by studying the designer's scale model. [2] Carpenters then framed each platform in the scene shop. [3] Painters followed, aging the plywood walls with sponges and tinted glaze. [4] Finally, the crew bolted the finished units to the stage floor.
stem_md: The writer wants the paragraph to present the set-building process in the order it occurred. For the sake of logic, Sentence 4 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: bolting finished units down is the last physical step, and 'Finally' confirms its closing position.
per_choice_rationale.B: Opening with installation puts the end of the process before planning even begins (sequence_end_at_start).
per_choice_rationale.C: Placing installation right after the model study makes the crew fasten units that haven't been built (sequence_before_prerequisite).
per_choice_rationale.D: Installing before painting forces painters to age walls already bolted in place, and 'Finally' contradicts a mid-paragraph slot (sequence_before_prerequisite).

why_correct_md: The sentence describes the **final** physical step — fastening completed scenery — and its signal word marks it as the close of the sequence.
why_tempted_md: Moving the sentence earlier tempts students who key on 'the crew' echoing Sentence 1 rather than tracking the physical order of the work.
rule_md: 1) List the steps each sentence describes. 2) Ask what must already exist for each step to happen. 3) Note signal words ('then,' 'followed,' 'Finally') that mark order. 4) Test the sentence in each proposed slot against the physical timeline. 5) Keep the arrangement in which every step is possible when it occurs.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Auditions for the spring musical draw students from every grade. [2] Each hopeful sings sixteen bars and reads a short scene with a partner. [3] The cast list appears on the callboard the following Friday. [4] Directors also note how quickly performers adjust when given new directions mid-scene. [5] By first bell that morning, a crowd has already gathered around the posting.
