stem_md: The writer wants Sentence 4 to appear where it will most logically support the paragraph's account of the audition process. Sentence 4 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: In its current spot the sentence rewinds from results day back to the tryout, splitting the callboard narrative (placement_interrupts_sequence).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Also' signals an added observation, so the sentence cannot lead before any first observation exists (placement_also_first).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the sentence describes what directors watch during auditions, so it belongs with the audition activities, right after the singing and scene reading.
per_choice_rationale.D: Ending with it strands an audition-day detail after the results are posted, forcing the timeline backward at the close (placement_after_resolution).

why_correct_md: The word **'also'** marks the sentence as a companion to the audition activities, so it must sit beside the singing and scene-reading it extends, before the results appear.
why_tempted_md: Leaving the sentence where it is tempts students because 'Directors' seems to follow naturally from the cast list they create, masking the backward jump in time.
rule_md: 1) Split the paragraph into phases (here: the tryout, then the posting). 2) Decide which phase the movable sentence describes. 3) Check its signal words ('also') for what must come before it. 4) Try each slot and reread for time jumps. 5) Keep the slot where the timeline never runs backward.

subject: act-english
context_html: Before the house opens, ushers <u>stack programs, check the aisle lights, and prop</u> open the lobby doors.
stem_md: Which choice provides the best punctuation for the underlined portion?

choices.label: stack programs check the aisle lights and prop
stack programs, check the aisle lights and, prop
stack programs; check the aisle lights; and prop

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: a series of three actions takes commas between the items, including one before the conjunction.
per_choice_rationale.B: Removing all commas fuses three separate tasks into one unreadable string (series_no_commas).
per_choice_rationale.C: A comma placed after 'and' splits the conjunction from the final item it introduces (comma_after_conjunction).
per_choice_rationale.D: Semicolons separate list items only when the items themselves contain commas, which these simple phrases do not (semicolon_simple_series).

why_correct_md: A **series** of three or more actions takes commas between its items, exactly as the original punctuates them.
why_tempted_md: The semicolon version tempts students who believe stronger punctuation is always more formal, even though semicolons are reserved for items with internal commas.
rule_md: 1) Count the actions or items in the list. 2) If there are three or more, place a comma after each item except the last. 3) Keep the comma before the conjunction, never after it. 4) Upgrade to semicolons only if the items themselves contain commas. 5) Reread to confirm each item stays distinct.

subject: act-english
context_html: The <u>actors's</u> entrances in the opening number are timed to a single drumbeat.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Adding 's to a plural that already ends in s creates a nonstandard double ending (possessive_double_s).
per_choice_rationale.B: The apostrophe before the s marks a single owner, but multiple performers share these entrances (possessive_singular_for_plural).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a plural noun ending in s forms its possessive with an apostrophe alone.
per_choice_rationale.D: Dropping the apostrophe removes the possession the sentence requires — the entrances belong to the performers (possessive_omitted).

why_correct_md: A **plural** noun already ending in s takes only an apostrophe after that s to show possession.
why_tempted_md: The singular possessive tempts students because the apostrophe-before-s pattern is the most familiar possessive form, regardless of how many owners there are.
rule_md: 1) Ask: does the noun own something in this sentence? 2) Decide whether the owner is singular or plural. 3) Write the plain plural first if there are multiple owners. 4) Add 's to singulars; add only an apostrophe to plurals ending in s. 5) Reread as 'the ___ of the ___' to confirm ownership survives.

subject: act-english
context_html: One backstage rule<u>—never touch another actor's prop, is</u> drilled into the crew at every rehearsal.
stem_md: Which choice provides the best punctuation for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Opening the interrupter with a dash but closing it with a comma mismatches the pair (paired_punct_mismatch).
per_choice_rationale.B: A dash cannot be closed by a parenthesis; the two marks never pair with each other (paired_punct_mixed).
per_choice_rationale.C: With no closing mark at all, the aside crashes into the main verb and the sentence loses its frame (paired_punct_unclosed).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: an interrupter opened with a dash must be closed with a matching dash.

why_correct_md: Interrupting phrases require **matching** punctuation on both ends, so a dash must be paired with a dash.
why_tempted_md: The dash-comma version tempts students because both marks can set off extra information, so mixing them feels harmless mid-sentence.
rule_md: 1) Locate where the interruption begins and where the main clause resumes. 2) Identify the opening mark. 3) Require the identical mark at the close — dashes with dashes, parentheses with parentheses. 4) Cover the interrupter and confirm the remaining sentence stands alone. 5) Reread with the matched pair in place.

subject: act-english
context_html: During the preshow check, the sound-board operator <u>tests, every wireless microphone</u> clipped to a costume.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most acceptable in standard written English?

per_choice_rationale.A: The comma needlessly separates the verb from its direct object (comma_verb_object).
per_choice_rationale.B: A colon may follow only a complete independent clause, not a bare verb mid-thought (colon_midclause).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: no punctuation belongs between a verb and its object, so the clause should flow unbroken.
per_choice_rationale.D: The dash sets off the object as if it were an aside, but the object is the essential core of the clause (dash_essential_element).

why_correct_md: No mark may **separate** a verb from its direct object, so the underlined portion needs no punctuation at all.
why_tempted_md: The colon version tempts students who see a list-like noun phrase coming and assume a colon should introduce it, forgetting the clause before a colon must be complete.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb and ask 'tests what?' to locate its object. 2) Check whether any mark falls between them. 3) Remove punctuation that splits verb from object. 4) For a colon or dash, require a complete clause before it or a true aside after it. 5) Reread the clause to confirm it flows without interruption.

subject: act-english
context_html: Waiting in the wings, Dana <u>locked her eyes on the stage manager's cue light</u> and mouthed her first line again and again.
stem_md: The writer wants to convey the intensity of Dana's concentration in the moments before her entrance. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: glanced now and then at the cue light
stood somewhere near the cue light
figured the cue light would come on soon

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the fixed, unbroken gaze dramatizes exactly the intense concentration the writer wants.
per_choice_rationale.B: Occasional glances suggest drifting, divided attention — the opposite of intensity (goal_weakened_action).
per_choice_rationale.C: A statement of physical position says nothing about her mental state (goal_no_emphasis).
per_choice_rationale.D: A casual prediction about timing conveys detachment rather than focus (goal_wrong_emphasis).

why_correct_md: The original phrase shows attention **riveted** to a single point, which is precisely the intensity the stem demands.
why_tempted_md: The glancing version tempts students because it keeps Dana watching the cue light, even though intermittent checking undercuts the required intensity.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's goal in your own words. 2) For each option, name the image or feeling its verb creates. 3) Eliminate options that merely relate to the topic without delivering the goal. 4) Compare the survivors for strength of effect. 5) Choose the one whose action itself embodies the goal.

subject: act-english
context_html: After the final bow, the cast lingered onstage beneath the dim work lights, none of them ready to leave. For the crew who had built the set piece by piece, striking it the next morning <u>was a total bummer</u>.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the tone established in the passage?

choices.label: occasioned a profound episode of lamentation

per_choice_rationale.A: Casual slang deflates the passage's subdued, wistful mood at its most reflective moment (tone_too_casual).
per_choice_rationale.B: The violent physical-impact idiom spikes the intensity far past the passage's gentle register (tone_overwrought_colloquial).
per_choice_rationale.C: The stiff, Latinate phrasing is more formal and ornate than the passage's plain reflective voice (tone_too_formal).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the understated phrasing matches the muted, lingering sadness the passage has established.

why_correct_md: Tone must stay **consistent**, and only this phrasing keeps the passage's subdued, reflective register.
why_tempted_md: The gut-punch idiom tempts students because it sounds vivid and emotional, but its jolting force clashes with the passage's gentleness.
rule_md: 1) Read the sentences around the blank and label their mood in two words. 2) Label each option's register: slangy, violent, ornate, or plain. 3) Eliminate options that miss the mood in either direction — too casual or too stiff. 4) Read the survivor back into the paragraph aloud. 5) Keep the phrasing that sounds like the same writer throughout.

subject: act-english
context_html: The greenroom's north wall carries the signature of every cast member since 1998. On each opening night, the current cast gathers there before curtain to add their names in silver ink. The writer is considering adding the following sentence after this description: "Alumni often return years later and search the wall until they find their own names among the hundreds."
stem_md: Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it demonstrates the enduring value of the signing custom for former cast members.
Yes, because it explains how the crew repaints the greenroom wall each season.
No, because it repeats details about the signing custom already given in the paragraph.
No, because it shifts the paragraph's focus to the school's fundraising efforts.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the addition extends the tradition's story into later years, showing it still matters to those who once signed.
per_choice_rationale.B: The proposed sentence never mentions repainting or maintenance, so this reason misdescribes it (reason_misreads_addition).
per_choice_rationale.C: The paragraph has said nothing about what happens years later, so the sentence adds new information rather than repeating any (reason_false_repetition).
per_choice_rationale.D: Nothing in the sentence involves money or donations, so the claimed focus-shift is invented (reason_invented_shift).

why_correct_md: The addition is **relevant** because it deepens the paragraph's account of the tradition by showing its lasting pull on those who signed long ago.
why_tempted_md: The repetition-based rejection tempts students because the new sentence revisits the same wall, making it feel like old information at a glance.
rule_md: 1) Restate the paragraph's focus in one phrase. 2) Restate what the proposed sentence literally says. 3) Decide whether it develops the focus, repeats it, or departs from it. 4) Check each reason against both the sentence's content and the paragraph's content. 5) Accept only a verdict whose reason is factually true.

subject: act-english
context_html: In the school's stagecraft course, students frame platforms, wire practical lamps, and draft budgets for each set they build. Over a semester, every student rotates through carpentry, electrics, and cost planning. By spring, most can take a set from sketch to strike without an adult stepping in.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to show how a school course builds practical, real-world abilities. Would this passage accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it praises students for winning festival awards.
Yes, because it details the hands-on training students receive in stagecraft class.
No, because it focuses on professional theaters rather than a school course.
No, because it mainly reviews a single evening's performance.

per_choice_rationale.A: The passage never mentions awards or festivals, so this reason is untrue even though its verdict is right (reason_invented_evidence).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the passage catalogs carpentry, electrics, and budgeting work that students master over a semester — exactly the practical growth the goal names.
per_choice_rationale.C: The passage explicitly describes a school course and its students, not professional venues (reason_contradicts_text).
per_choice_rationale.D: No performance is reviewed; the passage traces a semester-long process, not one evening (reason_wrong_scope).

why_correct_md: The passage **fulfills** the goal by documenting concrete, escalating tasks students learn to do independently over a semester.
why_tempted_md: The single-performance rejection tempts students because theater passages often review shows, so they assume this one does without checking its actual scope.
rule_md: 1) Restate the proposed goal in your own words. 2) List what the passage actually contains. 3) Decide yes or no by comparing the two lists. 4) Then vet the reason: is its claim about the passage factually true? 5) Accept only the verdict-reason pair where both parts check out.

subject: act-english
context_html: By final dress rehearsal, the lighting crew has programmed more than two hundred cues into the board. ______ Operators then run the entire show twice using only the stage manager's calls, never glancing at the script.
stem_md: The writer wants to add a sentence that will keep the paragraph focused on the lighting crew's preparation for opening night. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Each cue is checked against the designer's paperwork and rehearsed until the timing is automatic.
The auditorium's seats were reupholstered in a deep blue fabric last spring.
Several well-known lighting designers began their careers at small high schools.
Ticket prices this year include a small fee that helps maintain the building.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: verifying and drilling the cues develops exactly what the paragraph tracks — the crew's run-up to opening night.
per_choice_rationale.B: Upholstery describes the building, not the crew's preparation (detail_offtopic).
per_choice_rationale.C: Famous designers' origins are lighting-related but say nothing about this crew's readiness (detail_ontopic_offfocus).
per_choice_rationale.D: A budgeting fee answers a question the paragraph never asks (detail_offtopic).

why_correct_md: The added sentence must **develop** the paragraph's focus — the crew's preparation — and only the cue-verification detail does that work.
why_tempted_md: The famous-designers option tempts students because it stays inside the world of lighting, masking that it abandons this crew's preparation story.
rule_md: 1) Name the paragraph's focus in one phrase. 2) For each option, ask: does this advance that focus or a different topic? 3) Watch for details that share the theme but not the focus. 4) Eliminate anything the surrounding sentences never pick up. 5) Choose the sentence that pushes the paragraph's own story forward.

subject: act-english
context_html: The fog machine hissed to <u>life the audience</u> gasped as mist spilled over the edge of the stage.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Two independent clauses run together with nothing joining them — a fused sentence (fused_sentence).
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma alone cannot hold two independent clauses together (comma_splice).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a comma plus a coordinating conjunction legally joins the two independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.D: The comma lands after the conjunction, severing it from the clause it introduces (comma_after_conjunction).

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses need a **comma plus coordinating conjunction** (or stronger punctuation) between them, and only this option supplies that legal join.
why_tempted_md: The comma splice tempts students because the pause sounds natural when reading aloud, masking that a comma alone is too weak to join full sentences.
rule_md: 1) Find each subject-verb pair and count the complete clauses. 2) If there are two, locate what joins them. 3) Require a comma plus coordinating conjunction, a semicolon, or a period. 4) Reject a bare comma or nothing at all. 5) Confirm any comma sits before the conjunction, not after it.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Although the understudy had rehearsed the role for weeks, but she</u> still asked to run her scenes one more time before the house opened.
stem_md: Which choice results in the most logical and grammatically sound sentence?

choices.label: Although the understudy had rehearsed the role for weeks, she
The understudy had rehearsed the role for weeks, she
Although the understudy had rehearsed the role for weeks, and she

per_choice_rationale.A: Pairing the subordinator 'Although' with the coordinator 'but' doubles the connector and leaves no independent clause (double_conjunction).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the single subordinator marks the contrast, and the main clause follows cleanly after the comma.
per_choice_rationale.C: Dropping the subordinator leaves two independent clauses joined by only a comma (comma_splice).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Although' plus 'and' still stacks two connectors, so no clause is left to stand as the main statement (double_conjunction).

why_correct_md: One clause relationship gets **one** connector: the subordinating opener alone handles the contrast, leaving a clean main clause.
why_tempted_md: The original tempts students because 'although... but' mirrors how people talk, and each connector sounds correct in isolation.
rule_md: 1) Underline every connecting word in the sentence. 2) Count the clauses being related. 3) Allow exactly one connector per relationship. 4) If two connectors compete, delete one and check that a full main clause remains. 5) Reread to confirm the sentence has one subordinate clause attached to one independent clause.

subject: act-english
context_html: Balancing carefully on the top rung of the ladder, <u>the technician angled the spotlight</u> toward center stage.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: the spotlight was angled by the technician
it was angled by the technician

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the person doing the balancing — the technician — immediately follows the introductory modifier.
per_choice_rationale.B: Placing the equipment after the comma makes the modifier claim the fixture is balancing on the ladder (dangling_subject).
per_choice_rationale.C: With only an angle being adjusted, nothing in the sentence can be the balancer, and the doer vanishes (dangling_subject + agent_deleted).
per_choice_rationale.D: The vague pronoun gives the modifier nothing concrete to attach to and hides what was angled (dangling_pronoun).

why_correct_md: An introductory **modifier** must be followed immediately by the person or thing it describes, and only the original places the balancer there.
why_tempted_md: The passive version tempts students because it still names the technician later in the sentence, obscuring that the opening phrase now describes the equipment.
rule_md: 1) Find the introductory phrase and ask who or what it describes. 2) Look at the first noun after the comma. 3) Require those two to match. 4) If they don't, the modifier dangles — reject the option. 5) Also confirm the doer of the main action survives in the sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: The two leads practiced their duet <u>together with each other</u> until every harmony locked into place.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most concise without losing information?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Together with each other' states three times what 'duet' by two leads already guarantees (redundant_synonym).
per_choice_rationale.B: Commas dress up the redundancy but add no new information (redundant_repunctuated).
per_choice_rationale.C: Reordering the redundant phrases leaves them just as repetitive, in a clumsier sequence (redundant_reordered).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: a duet practiced by the two leads is by definition a joint effort, so the phrase can be dropped with no loss.

why_correct_md: The word 'duet' already **implies** joint performance by the two leads, so the underlined phrase adds words without meaning.
why_tempted_md: Keeping the original tempts students because the phrase sounds natural in speech, where such doubling is common and goes unnoticed.
rule_md: 1) Ask what each underlined word adds beyond the rest of the sentence. 2) Check whether another word in the sentence already carries that meaning. 3) Test the sentence without the phrase. 4) If nothing is lost, the phrase is redundant. 5) Prefer the version where every remaining word earns its place.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each Monday morning, the stage manager <u>posts the rehearsal schedule</u> outside the choir room.
stem_md: Which choice expresses the idea most effectively?

choices.label: engages in the posting of the rehearsal schedule
posts, in a timely manner, the rehearsal schedule
makes it a point to post the rehearsal schedule

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the direct verb states the action completely, with no padding.
per_choice_rationale.B: Nominalizing the verb into 'the posting of' inflates one action into a ceremony (wordy_nominalization).
per_choice_rationale.C: The inserted phrase duplicates the timing already fixed by 'Each Monday morning' while interrupting the verb (wordy_redundant_insert).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Makes it a point to' is an empty frame that delays the verb without informing the reader (wordy_filler_frame).

why_correct_md: The original is already **direct** — one verb, one object — and every alternative adds words that carry no new information.
why_tempted_md: The 'makes it a point to' version tempts students because it seems to add earnestness, though it tells the reader nothing the plain verb doesn't.
rule_md: 1) Identify the core action and its object. 2) For each option, list any words beyond that core. 3) Ask what new information each extra word supplies. 4) Strike phrases that duplicate the sentence or merely wrap the verb. 5) Keep the version where nothing can be cut without losing meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: Crew volunteers who <u>are the kind of people that show up</u> early usually get first choice of painting assignments.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence clearest and most concise?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'The kind of people that' wraps the action in empty classification that restates nothing new (wordy_classification_frame).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the bare verb phrase delivers the full meaning in the fewest words.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Happen to' pads the phrase and miscolors habitual early arrival as accidental (filler_meaning_shift).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Known for' swaps the act itself for a reputation about it, changing the meaning while adding words (concision_meaning_shift).

why_correct_md: The **shortest** version that preserves the exact meaning wins, and the plain verb phrase loses nothing the frame provided.
why_tempted_md: The 'known for' version tempts students because it sounds polished, hiding that a reputation is not the same as actually being there early.
rule_md: 1) State the sentence's core claim in your own words. 2) Strip each option to what it literally asserts. 3) Reject options that add scaffolding with no new content. 4) Reject options that quietly change the claim. 5) Keep the briefest version whose meaning matches the original claim exactly.

subject: act-english
context_html: A single follow spot <u>looked at</u> the soloist as she wove between the darkened set pieces.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely describes the action of the follow spot?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Looked at' vaguely personifies the fixture and misses the continuous following of a moving performer (imprecise_vague_verb).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Witnessed' carries courtroom-observer connotations and suggests passive watching, not active following (imprecise_connotation).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the verb precisely captures a light continuously following a performer in motion.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Stared down' injects hostility into a neutral technical action (imprecise_hostile_connotation).

why_correct_md: Precision means matching the verb to the **action** — a light continuously following a moving performer — and only this verb conveys that motion.
why_tempted_md: 'Witnessed' tempts students because it sounds elevated and formal, though its bystander connotation contradicts the light's active role.
rule_md: 1) Picture the literal action the sentence describes. 2) For each verb, name its core image and its connotation. 3) Eliminate verbs whose image misses the motion or mechanism. 4) Eliminate verbs whose connotation adds attitude the scene lacks. 5) Choose the verb that matches both the action and the mood.

subject: act-english
context_html: In the printed program, the director wrote that the ensemble had <u>totally crushed</u> the show's most demanding choreography.
stem_md: Which choice is most consistent with the formal style of the director's note?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Totally crushed' is conversational slang out of place in a printed program note (register_slang).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Pretty much' hedges vaguely and 'nailed' is casual idiom — doubly informal (register_hedge_plus_slang).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Been awesome at' is empty conversational praise that neither fits the register nor names the achievement (register_colloquial_vague).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the single formal verb suits a printed note and states the accomplishment precisely.

why_correct_md: A printed program note demands **formal** register, and only this verb matches that setting while naming the achievement exactly.
why_tempted_md: 'Pretty much nailed' tempts students because it feels vivid and confident, masking that both the hedge and the idiom are conversational.
rule_md: 1) Identify where the sentence will be read and by whom. 2) Set the expected register for that setting. 3) Flag slang, hedges, and empty praise words in each option. 4) Eliminate options that miss the register in either direction. 5) Choose the wording that a careful writer would publish in that document.

subject: act-english
context_html: Last July, the survey team snowmobiled to the glacier's upper basin, drilled a shallow core, and <u>labels</u> each segment before the weather turned.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Present-tense 'labels' breaks the past-tense sequence established by 'snowmobiled' and 'drilled' (tense shift within a series).
per_choice_rationale.B: Future 'will label' contradicts a narrative of events already completed last July (future_in_past_narrative).
per_choice_rationale.C: The past-tense verb matches the other verbs in the series and the time marker 'Last July.'
per_choice_rationale.D: The present progressive describes an ongoing action, clashing with the completed past events (progressive_shift).

why_correct_md: The series began in the past ('snowmobiled... drilled'), so the third verb must stay in the **past tense**.
why_tempted_md: 'Labels' sounds fine in isolation, so students who read only the underlined words miss the past-tense verbs earlier in the sentence.
rule_md: 1) Find every verb in the sentence. 2) Circle the time marker (here, 'Last July'). 3) Make all verbs in the same series match that time frame. 4) Reject any option that jumps to a different time without a reason.

subject: act-english
context_html: The array of solar-powered sensors bolted along the ridge <u>transmit</u> hourly readings to a laboratory in Ottawa.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Plural 'transmit' wrongly agrees with the nearest noun 'sensors' instead of the singular subject 'array' (sv_nearest_noun).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Are transmitting' repeats the same agreement error with a plural helping verb (sv_nearest_noun in progressive form).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Have transmitted' is plural and also shifts to a completed time frame that clashes with 'hourly' (agreement plus aspect error).
per_choice_rationale.D: The subject is the singular 'array,' so the verb correctly takes the singular form.

why_correct_md: The true subject is **array**, a singular noun, so the verb must be singular despite the plural nouns crowded in between.
why_tempted_md: 'Sensors' sits right next to the verb, so students match the verb to the nearest noun instead of the real subject.
rule_md: 1) Ask: what is doing the action? 2) Cross out the prepositional phrase and description between subject and verb ('of solar-powered sensors bolted along the ridge'). 3) Match the verb to the noun that remains. 4) Ignore any noun that sits inside a crossed-out phrase.

subject: act-english
context_html: Even veteran glaciologists marvel <u>on</u> the speed with which a crevasse field can rearrange itself.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Marvel on' borrows the preposition from phrases like 'comment on'; English idiom does not pair 'marvel' with 'on' (preposition borrowed from a different verb).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Marvel about' imports the preposition from 'think about' or 'wonder about,' which is not the fixed pairing (synonym-analogy error).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Marvel for' is not an English idiom in any register (invented pairing).
per_choice_rationale.D: The fixed idiom is 'marvel at' something, so this preposition is correct.

why_correct_md: **Marvel** takes one fixed preposition, and only this pairing is idiomatic in standard English.
why_tempted_md: 'Marvel about' feels natural because near-synonyms like 'wonder' do take 'about.'
rule_md: 1) Isolate the verb and its preposition. 2) Test the pair in a simple sentence you trust ('We marveled ___ the view'). 3) Swap in each option and trust the fixed pairing, not the preposition a similar verb takes. 4) Reject any pairing you have never seen in edited prose.

subject: act-english
context_html: After a record-breaking winter of snowfall, the team expected the glacier to gain mass. <u>Accordingly,</u> the spring laser survey showed that the ice had thinned by nearly a meter.
stem_md: Which transition word creates the most logical connection between these sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Accordingly' signals that the second sentence follows naturally from the first, but the survey result defied the expectation (transition_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Consequently' makes the thinning a result of the team's expectation, which reverses the logic (false cause-effect).
per_choice_rationale.C: The survey contradicted what the team expected, so a contrast transition is the logical link.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'For example' wrongly presents the thinning as an illustration of the expectation (illustration misread).

why_correct_md: The second sentence **contradicts** the expectation set up in the first, so the transition must signal contrast.
why_tempted_md: 'Consequently' tempts readers who see 'expected... showed' as a cause-and-effect chain rather than a reversal.
rule_md: 1) State sentence one's idea in five words. 2) State sentence two's idea in five words. 3) Name the relationship: same direction, opposite direction, cause, or illustration. 4) Pick the transition that names that exact relationship. 5) Reread with your pick to confirm.

subject: act-english
context_html: Fieldwork on the ice demands relentless upkeep of equipment. <u>Nevertheless,</u> the GPS beacons must be dug out of drifting snow every few weeks, and the weather stations need fresh batteries even in midwinter.
stem_md: Which transition best fits the relationship between these two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Nevertheless' signals concession, but the second sentence supports rather than resists the first (transition_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'In contrast' requires opposing ideas, and both sentences point the same way (false contrast).
per_choice_rationale.C: The beacons and batteries are specific cases of the 'relentless upkeep' the first sentence asserts, so an illustrating transition fits.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'In other words' promises a restatement, but the second sentence adds new, specific detail instead of rephrasing (restatement misread).

why_correct_md: The second sentence gives **specific cases** of the general claim about upkeep, so an illustrating transition is required.
why_tempted_md: 'In other words' attracts readers who notice the sentences share a subject and mistake support for restatement.
rule_md: 1) Label sentence one as general or specific. 2) Label sentence two the same way. 3) If a general claim is followed by concrete cases, use an illustrating transition; if it is reworded, use a restating one; if it is opposed, use a contrasting one. 4) Reread with your pick.

subject: act-english
context_html: For eleven years, Dr. Imai has returned to the same stretch of ice to remeasure a line of bamboo stakes. Each visit yields only a few numbers in a waterproof notebook. No single measurement says much on its own; the value grows with the column of figures.
stem_md: The writer wants to conclude the paragraph with a sentence that reinforces its main point about the slow accumulation of evidence in glacier research. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Bamboo is favored for stakes because it flexes without snapping in high winds.
Dr. Imai also collaborates with colleagues who study permafrost in Alaska.
Someday, satellites may make such repeated visits unnecessary.
Only after a decade of these small entries does the glacier's story become legible.

per_choice_rationale.A: Explains an equipment choice, shifting the closing focus from accumulating evidence to materials (add_offtopic).
per_choice_rationale.B: Introduces an unrelated collaboration instead of closing on the paragraph's point (topic drift).
per_choice_rationale.C: Undercuts the paragraph by suggesting the patient method may soon be obsolete (goal_wrong_emphasis).
per_choice_rationale.D: Ties the years of tiny measurements to their payoff, restating the main point as a closing thought.

why_correct_md: It **circles back** to the paragraph's central idea — that meaning emerges only from years of accumulated measurements.
why_tempted_md: The satellite option feels forward-looking and sophisticated, but it changes the subject rather than reinforcing the point.
rule_md: 1) Write the paragraph's main point in one short clause. 2) Test each closing sentence: does it restate or extend that point? 3) Eliminate any that add new topics, equipment trivia, or doubts about the method. 4) Keep the one that sends the reader off with the main idea.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] The camp's routine begins before sunrise. [2] Technicians check the overnight radar files while the coffee brews. [3] Any anomalies are flagged for the morning briefing. [4] By the time the sun clears the ridge, the day's drilling targets have already been chosen.
stem_md: For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, Sentence 4 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: The paragraph moves chronologically from pre-dawn to sunrise, and Sentence 4 completes that arc in its current position.
per_choice_rationale.B: Opening with the sun clearing the ridge would put the latest moment first and strand 'already been chosen' without prior steps (time-order violation).
per_choice_rationale.C: Placing it right after the opener interrupts the sequence before the radar check that produces the targets (breaks the workflow chain).
per_choice_rationale.D: Inserting it before the flagging step reverses cause and effect: targets are chosen from flagged anomalies (cause-effect reversal).

why_correct_md: The paragraph follows **time order**, and this sentence marks the latest moment of the morning, so it belongs at the end.
why_tempted_md: 'Before Sentence 3' tempts readers who link 'targets' to 'anomalies' without noticing that the choosing must follow the flagging.
rule_md: 1) Underline every time cue ('before sunrise,' 'while the coffee brews,' 'by the time the sun clears'). 2) Order the events on a mental clock. 3) Check cause-effect links between neighboring sentences. 4) Place the sentence where its time stamp and its logic both fit.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Ice cores are only as trustworthy as their storage. [2] There, technicians catalog each cylinder under red light that keeps the labels from fading. [3] Cores pulled from the drill are sleeved in plastic within minutes. [4] They then ride in freezer trucks to an archive kept at minus thirty-six degrees. [5] A single afternoon of warmth can erase ten thousand years of chemistry.
stem_md: For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, Sentence 2 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: In its current spot, 'There' has nothing to refer to, since Sentence 1 names no location (unanchored pronoun).
per_choice_rationale.B: Opening the paragraph with 'There' leaves the locator with no referent at all (referent before mention).
per_choice_rationale.C: After the sleeving step, 'There' would point to the drill site, where no cataloging archive exists (wrong referent).
per_choice_rationale.D: Placed after the archive is introduced, 'There' clearly refers to it, and the cataloging logically follows arrival.

why_correct_md: The locator **'There'** needs an immediately preceding place — the archive — to point to, and cataloging happens once the cores arrive.
why_tempted_md: Readers who loosely connect 'catalog' with 'storage' in Sentence 1 leave the sentence where it is without testing what 'There' refers to.
rule_md: 1) Find the pointing word in the movable sentence ('There'). 2) Ask what place it must refer to. 3) Locate the sentence that names that place. 4) Put the movable sentence immediately behind it. 5) Reread the paragraph to confirm smooth time order.

subject: act-english
context_html: Our field manager<u>, a climber from Chamonix,</u> plans every route across the icefall.
stem_md: Which choice provides the best punctuation for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: The appositive is nonessential, so it is correctly set off by a comma on both sides.
per_choice_rationale.B: Dropping the closing comma leaves the aside unfinished and fuses it with the verb (missing second comma).
per_choice_rationale.C: Dropping the opening comma makes the appositive crash into 'manager' while still closing with one (missing first comma).
per_choice_rationale.D: With no commas, the extra description reads as if it were essential to identifying the manager (unmarked nonessential).

why_correct_md: A nonessential appositive must be **fenced off by a pair of commas**, and the original already does exactly that.
why_tempted_md: Students often think one comma is enough for an interrupting phrase and delete the second.
rule_md: 1) Find the interrupting description. 2) Test deletion: if the sentence survives without it, it is nonessential. 3) Nonessential interrupters take punctuation on BOTH sides. 4) Check that the marks match — two commas, not one.

subject: act-english
context_html: The two <u>glaciers's</u> shared meltwater basin feeds a chain of turquoise lakes.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Glaciers's' double-marks possession; a plural ending in -s never adds another -s after the apostrophe (double-marked possessive).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Glacier's' is a singular possessive, but the sentence specifies two glaciers (singular_possessive_for_plural).
per_choice_rationale.C: A plural noun ending in -s shows possession with the apostrophe alone, matching 'the two.'
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Glaciers' shows no possession at all, though the basin belongs to them (missing possessive).

why_correct_md: A **plural ending in -s** takes only an apostrophe after the s to show possession.
why_tempted_md: The singular possessive looks tidy and familiar, so students forget the word must stay plural to match 'the two.'
rule_md: 1) Ask: who owns it? 2) Write the owner as a plain noun first (two of them → plural). 3) If the plural ends in -s, add the apostrophe after the s and stop. 4) If it does not end in -s, add apostrophe + s. 5) Reread to confirm both number and ownership survive.

subject: act-english
context_html: The thermal drill<u>—a two-ton rig flown in by helicopter,</u> melted its way toward the bedrock at four meters an hour.
stem_md: Which choice provides the best punctuation for the underlined portion?

choices.label: , a two-ton rig flown in by helicopter—
—a two-ton rig flown in by helicopter—
, a two-ton rig flown in by helicopter

per_choice_rationale.A: The aside opens with a dash but closes with a comma; paired punctuation must match (mismatched pair).
per_choice_rationale.B: This version reverses the mismatch, opening with a comma and closing with a dash (mismatched pair, mirrored).
per_choice_rationale.C: The interrupter opens and closes with the same mark — a matched pair of dashes — so it is correctly fenced.
per_choice_rationale.D: A comma opens the aside, but nothing closes it before the verb, leaving the interrupter unfenced (missing closing mark).

why_correct_md: An interrupting appositive must be enclosed by a **matched pair** — dash with dash or comma with comma, never mixed.
why_tempted_md: Readers register that some punctuation frames the aside and overlook that the opening and closing marks disagree.
rule_md: 1) Bracket the interrupter with your fingers. 2) Identify the mark at its entrance. 3) Identify the mark at its exit. 4) If they differ, the pair is broken: make both the same mark. 5) Confirm the sentence reads cleanly with the aside deleted.

subject: act-english
context_html: The stakes <u>planted along the centerline reveal</u> how unevenly the glacier is thinning.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Planted along the centerline' is an essential identifying phrase, and no punctuation should separate the subject from its verb.
per_choice_rationale.B: The comma splits the subject 'stakes planted along the centerline' from its verb (subject-verb comma).
per_choice_rationale.C: The comma cuts into the middle of the identifying phrase itself (intrusive comma inside a unit).
per_choice_rationale.D: A colon may appear only after a complete statement, not between a subject and its verb (colon_midclause).

why_correct_md: Nothing here is nonessential, so **no internal punctuation** belongs between the subject and its verb.
why_tempted_md: The long subject makes readers want a breathing comma before the verb, a pause the rules do not permit.
rule_md: 1) Find the subject and its verb. 2) Ask whether anything between them could be lifted out without changing which stakes are meant. 3) If the phrase is essential, use no commas. 4) Never let a single comma or a colon stand between subject and verb. 5) Reread the bare sentence to confirm it flows.

subject: act-english
context_html: When the ice face finally gave way, a slab the size of a cathedral <u>dropped</u> into the fjord.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize the overwhelming sound of the calving event. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Dropped' reports the motion neutrally and says nothing about sound (goal ignored).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Plunged' adds speed and drama but appeals to the eye, not the ear (goal_wrong_emphasis).
per_choice_rationale.C: This verb makes the slab's descent audible, directly serving the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Tumbled' suggests chaotic motion yet stays silent about the noise (wrong sense).

why_correct_md: Only this verb carries an **auditory** charge, matching the writer's stated goal of emphasizing sound.
why_tempted_md: 'Plunged' feels vivid and forceful, so students choose drama in general instead of the specific sense the stem demands.
rule_md: 1) Underline the goal word in the stem (here, sound). 2) For each verb, name the sense it appeals to: sight, sound, or motion. 3) Eliminate every option serving a different sense, however vivid. 4) Choose the one aimed at the stated goal. 5) Reread the stem to confirm the match.

subject: act-english
context_html: In its annual report, the advisory panel reviewed the projected costs of relocating the field station and <u>was seriously bummed out by</u> the figures.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the formal style established in the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Bummed out' is slang, jarring against 'annual report' and 'projected costs' (register clash).
per_choice_rationale.B: A measured, formal verb phrase that matches the report's register.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Sort of down about' is casual hedging that deflates the formal context (colloquial hedge).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Could not even deal with' imports conversational exaggeration into a formal report (spoken-register idiom).

why_correct_md: The sentence's **formal register** ('annual report,' 'advisory panel') requires equally formal diction.
why_tempted_md: 'Bummed out' conveys the right meaning, so students who check meaning but not register keep it.
rule_md: 1) Scan the sentence for register clues (titles, documents, technical terms). 2) Label the passage formal or casual. 3) Label each option the same way. 4) Eliminate every mismatch, even if the meaning fits. 5) Choose the option whose register matches the clues.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each morning at the drill site follows the same sequence. The crew flushes the borehole, lowers the barrel, and brings up a meter of ice before noon. Every core is measured, sleeved, and logged within an hour of surfacing.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the second sentence: "The camp cook, meanwhile, is famous for his sourdough pancakes." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it shows that camp life involves more than drilling.
Yes, because it adds a vivid detail about the drilling camp.
No, because it interrupts the focused description of the drilling procedure.
No, because it repeats information about the camp cook given earlier.

per_choice_rationale.A: Broadening the picture of camp life is not this paragraph's job, which is to trace one work sequence (add_offtopic justification).
per_choice_rationale.B: Vividness alone cannot justify a detail that pulls away from the paragraph's single subject (color over relevance).
per_choice_rationale.C: The paragraph traces one tightly ordered work routine, and the pancake sentence breaks that thread.
per_choice_rationale.D: The reason is factually wrong — the cook has not been mentioned anywhere (false-premise reason).

why_correct_md: The paragraph has a **single focus** — the morning drilling routine — and the proposed sentence departs from it.
why_tempted_md: 'A vivid detail' sounds like good writing advice, so students accept color without checking relevance.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's focus in one clause. 2) Ask whether the proposed sentence advances that focus. 3) If yes, add it; if no, keep it out. 4) Then check the stated reason: it must be both true of the passage and about relevance. 5) Reject reasons that are factually false, even when the yes/no feels right.

subject: act-english
context_html: The essay recounts the narrator's first season at a high-altitude drill camp: learning to sleep through wind, budgeting fuel for the stove, and celebrating a birthday with canned peaches. Ice cores appear mainly as heavy boxes the narrator hauls to the weighing tent.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to explain to general readers what ice cores reveal about past climates. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it explains what the cores reveal about ancient climates.
Yes, because the narrator's descriptions of the field season show scientific work.
No, because it dwells on the narrator's experience rather than on what the cores reveal.
No, because the essay is too short to accomplish any scientific goal.

per_choice_rationale.A: The reason misstates the essay, which treats cores as luggage, not as climate evidence (false-premise yes).
per_choice_rationale.B: Scenes of camp life show the setting of science without explaining any findings (setting mistaken for substance).
per_choice_rationale.C: The essay is a personal narrative and never explains what cores tell us about climate, so it fails the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.D: Length is not the test; a short essay could still explain core science, and this one simply does not try (wrong criterion).

why_correct_md: Judge purpose questions by **what the essay actually does**, and this one narrates camp life without explaining core science.
why_tempted_md: Because the narrator is clearly doing science, students credit the essay with explaining science it only gestures at.
rule_md: 1) Restate the proposed goal precisely. 2) List what the essay actually spends its sentences on. 3) Compare: does the content deliver the goal, not merely touch its topic? 4) Pick the yes/no that matches, then verify the reason is true of the essay. 5) Discard options with false or irrelevant reasons.

subject: act-english
context_html: A blanket of rockfall debris does strange things to the ice beneath it. A thin dusting of grit darkens the surface and speeds melting. A thick rubble layer, by contrast, works like insulation and shields the ice from the sun.
stem_md: The writer wants to add a sentence that develops the paragraph's focus on how debris depth changes the way glaciers melt. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Debris-covered glaciers are especially common in the Himalaya, where trekkers often cross them.
Between those extremes lies a critical thickness at which the debris neither hastens nor slows the loss of ice.
Rockfall has also been known to crush monitoring gear anchored to the ice.
Some debris layers contain pollen that helps scientists date past avalanches.

per_choice_rationale.A: Geographic trivia about where such glaciers occur ignores the depth-and-melt relationship (shared topic, wrong question).
per_choice_rationale.B: It completes the spectrum the paragraph sets up, adding the pivot point where the thin and thick effects cancel.
per_choice_rationale.C: Damaged equipment is a hazard story, not a point about how depth changes melting (add_offtopic).
per_choice_rationale.D: Pollen dating serves a different scientific question and drops the melt thread entirely (interesting but irrelevant).

why_correct_md: It **extends the paragraph's own contrast** — thin speeds melt, thick shields it — by supplying the pivot point in the middle.
why_tempted_md: The Himalaya sentence stays on the topic of debris-covered glaciers, so it feels relevant even though it abandons the melt question.
rule_md: 1) Name the paragraph's focus as a question it is answering (how does debris depth change melting?). 2) For each option, ask: does it answer that same question? 3) Strike options that merely share vocabulary or setting. 4) Keep the one that pushes the paragraph's specific line of thought forward.

subject: act-english
context_html: New crevasses opened across the route <u>overnight the team rerouted</u> its supply line before dawn.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Two complete statements run together with no punctuation or connector — a fused sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma alone cannot join two complete statements; this is a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Therefore' is an adverb, not a conjunction, so a comma before it still splices the clauses (conjunctive-adverb splice).
per_choice_rationale.D: A comma plus the coordinating conjunction properly joins the two independent clauses.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses need a **comma plus a coordinating conjunction** (or stronger punctuation) to join legally.
why_tempted_md: The comma in the splice version supplies a pause that sounds right aloud, hiding the missing conjunction.
rule_md: 1) Find each subject-verb pair. 2) Ask whether each clause could stand alone. 3) If both can, the junction needs a period, a semicolon, or comma + FANBOYS. 4) Remember conjunctive adverbs (therefore, however) are not FANBOYS. 5) Apply the weakest legal fix that keeps the meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Because</u> the forecast promised three days of clear weather, the crew postponed the traverse until the following week.
stem_md: Which choice makes the relationship between the two parts of the sentence most logical?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Because' claims good weather caused the delay, which reverses common sense (cause where concession is needed).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Since' makes the same causal claim in different clothing (synonym of the same error).
per_choice_rationale.C: The crew postponed despite favorable conditions — the concession this sentence needs.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Whenever' turns a single decision into a recurring habit triggered by forecasts (time-trigger distortion).

why_correct_md: The main clause acts **against** what the opening clause would predict, so the joint needs a concession word.
why_tempted_md: 'Because' and 'since' sound natural at the start of a clause, and readers accept the cause without testing its direction.
rule_md: 1) Read the subordinate clause and predict what should follow. 2) Read the main clause and check: does it fulfill or defy the prediction? 3) Fulfilled → cause word; defied → concession word; repeated → time word. 4) Reread with your connector to verify the logic.

subject: act-english
context_html: Skiing back from the terminus, <u>the storm caught the surveyors</u> two kilometers from camp.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: the surveyors were caught by the storm
the storm's fury caught the surveyors
it was the storm that caught the surveyors

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening phrase attaches to 'the storm,' absurdly putting the storm on skis (dangling_subject).
per_choice_rationale.B: The skiers — the surveyors — now stand next to the phrase that describes them.
per_choice_rationale.C: Swapping in 'the storm's fury' still leaves a non-skier right after the modifier (cosmetic fix, same dangle).
per_choice_rationale.D: The cleft 'it' construction places a dummy pronoun where the skiing party must go (dummy-subject dangle).

why_correct_md: An opening participial phrase must be followed **immediately** by the noun it describes — the people on skis.
why_tempted_md: The original sounds dramatic and natural aloud, so the dangling modifier hides in plain hearing.
rule_md: 1) Find the opening -ing phrase. 2) Ask: who performs that action? 3) Check the first noun after the comma. 4) If they do not match, rearrange so the doer sits right after the comma. 5) Reread to confirm the image makes sense.

subject: act-english
context_html: The monitoring flights are repeated <u>each year on an annual basis</u> so that thinning rates can be compared.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Each year' and 'on an annual basis' say the same thing twice (redundant_synonym).
per_choice_rationale.B: One time expression carries the full meaning without repetition.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Annually' and 'every single year' stack the same idea into a bigger pile (double redundancy).
per_choice_rationale.D: The added 'annually,' restates 'each year' and litters the sentence with commas (redundant appositive).

why_correct_md: One time phrase suffices; the other versions repeat the **same meaning** in different words.
why_tempted_md: 'On an annual basis' sounds official and technical, so the doubling masquerades as precision.
rule_md: 1) Circle every word or phrase that expresses time. 2) Ask whether any two circles mean the same thing. 3) Delete duplicates, keeping the simplest. 4) Reread: has any information been lost? If not, the cut was right.

subject: act-english
context_html: The expedition was delayed for a week <u>due to the fact that</u> the helicopter needed a replacement rotor.
stem_md: Which choice most effectively expresses this idea?

choices.label: in light of the fact that it was the case that

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Due to the fact that' spends five words on a job one word can do (empty formula).
per_choice_rationale.B: A single subordinating word delivers the causal link cleanly.
per_choice_rationale.C: This version keeps the empty 'the fact that' scaffolding around the useful word (partial trim).
per_choice_rationale.D: Two nested filler formulas make this the wordiest option of all (compounded padding).

why_correct_md: The **shortest construction that preserves the meaning** wins, and one word states the cause completely.
why_tempted_md: 'Due to the fact that' appears constantly in official-sounding prose, so it reads as formal rather than inflated.
rule_md: 1) Bracket the connector phrase. 2) Ask what work it does (here: signal cause). 3) Try the shortest expression of that work. 4) If nothing is lost, adopt the shorter form. 5) Beware phrases containing 'the fact that' — they almost always deflate.

subject: act-english
context_html: Researchers rely on <u>data that has been gathered and collected by automated sensors</u> to track winter snowfall.
stem_md: Which choice most effectively expresses this idea?

choices.label: data gathered and also collected by automated sensors
the gathered data collected via automated sensor readings

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Gathered' and 'collected' duplicate each other inside a padded 'that has been' clause (doubled verb plus clause bulk).
per_choice_rationale.B: Trimming the clause but keeping 'and also collected' preserves the doubling (incomplete cut).
per_choice_rationale.C: One participle and the essential agent, with nothing repeated and no fact lost.
per_choice_rationale.D: Rearranging the pile-up still says the collecting twice and adds 'via... readings' clutter (reshuffled redundancy).

why_correct_md: The best version keeps every fact — the data and its source — while cutting the **duplicate verb** and the clause padding.
why_tempted_md: The full clause 'that has been gathered and collected' sounds thorough and precise, hiding its redundancy.
rule_md: 1) List the facts the phrase must keep (what, obtained by what). 2) Strike words that repeat a fact already stated. 3) Prefer a participle to a full 'that has been' clause when meaning survives. 4) Choose the shortest option that still lists every fact.

subject: act-english
context_html: On warm afternoons, meltwater <u>goes</u> down through the porous upper layers of the snowpack.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely describes the movement of the meltwater?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Goes' is the vaguest possible motion verb and specifies nothing about how the water descends (maximum vagueness).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Moves' is scarcely more specific than 'goes' (generic swap).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Travels' suggests distance covered but not the manner of passing through pores (near-precise but wrong emphasis).
per_choice_rationale.D: This verb names precisely the slow filtering of liquid down through a porous material.

why_correct_md: Precision means naming the **specific manner** of motion — a slow filtering through tiny pores — not motion in general.
why_tempted_md: 'Travels' sounds more writerly than 'goes,' so students upgrade the vagueness slightly instead of choosing the exact term.
rule_md: 1) Ask what the sentence's own details demand (porous layers → passage through pores). 2) For each verb, state exactly what picture it draws. 3) Eliminate verbs that could describe almost any motion. 4) Choose the verb whose picture matches the sentence's details.

subject: act-english
context_html: In its final report, the review board <u>commended</u> the team for its meticulous record keeping.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the formal style of the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Commended' matches the formal register of 'final report' and 'review board.'
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Shout-out' is social-media slang, clashing with an official report (slang intrusion).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Totally impressed' is conversational intensifier talk, not report language (casual intensifier).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Thought the world of' is a cozy idiom too informal for the context (folksy idiom).

why_correct_md: The original verb already matches the sentence's **formal register**, so it should stand.
why_tempted_md: 'Was totally impressed with' feels vivid and clear, so students trade formality for punch without noticing the register clash.
rule_md: 1) Identify the context clues for register ('final report,' 'review board'). 2) Label the required register: formal. 3) Grade each option against that label. 4) If the original already matches, keep it; revise only what is broken.

subject: act-english
context_html: Last October, the honey vendor <u>arrived before dawn and stacked</u> her jars of wildflower honey into neat pyramids before the first customers wandered in.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: had arrived before dawn and had stacked

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — 'Last October' and the later verb 'wandered' set a simple-past frame, and both underlined verbs stay inside it.
per_choice_rationale.B: Shifts the first verb to present tense while the rest of the sentence describes a finished past morning (tense_shift_present).
per_choice_rationale.C: Shifts the second verb to present tense, splitting two simultaneous past actions across time frames (tense_shift_present).
per_choice_rationale.D: Uses past perfect although the sentence sets up no earlier-than-past sequence (unneeded_past_perfect).

why_correct_md: The opening time marker **Last October** anchors the sentence in the simple past, and both underlined verbs already match that frame.
why_tempted_md: The 'had' forms sound formal and cautious, so students assume they make past events extra correct even without an earlier-past sequence.
rule_md: 1) Circle the time markers (e.g., 'Last October'). 2) List every verb in the sentence and its tense. 3) Decide whether the events occupy one time frame or two. 4) One frame → keep every verb in the same simple tense; reserve 'had + verb' for an action completed before another past action. 5) Re-test each option against that frame.

subject: act-english
context_html: The <u>lineup of food trucks parked along the market's south fence changes</u> every Saturday, depending on which owners reserve a spot.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: lineup of food trucks parked along the market's south fence change
lineup of food trucks parked along the market's south fence are changing
lineups of food trucks parked along the market's south fence changes

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — the singular subject 'lineup' takes the singular verb 'changes'; the intervening phrases don't affect agreement.
per_choice_rationale.B: Matches the verb to the nearby plural nouns 'trucks' and 'fence' instead of the true subject (sv_nearest_noun).
per_choice_rationale.C: Pairs the singular head noun 'lineup' with the plural auxiliary 'are' (sv_plural_aux).
per_choice_rationale.D: Pluralizes the subject but keeps the singular verb, creating a new mismatch (sv_forced_plural).

why_correct_md: The head noun **lineup** is singular, and prepositional phrases between subject and verb never change agreement.
why_tempted_md: The plural nouns 'trucks' and 'fence' sit right before the verb, so the plural form sounds natural to the ear.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb. 2) Ask who or what performs it. 3) Cross out every prepositional and participial phrase between subject and verb. 4) Match the verb's number to the bare subject that remains. 5) Re-test each option against that bare pairing.

subject: act-english
context_html: County health codes <u>prohibit vendors to sell</u> samples that have sat unrefrigerated for more than two hours.
stem_md: Which choice conforms to the conventions of standard written English?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Prohibit' does not take a to-infinitive; this borrows the pattern of 'forbid' (idiom_wrong_pattern).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — 'prohibit' idiomatically takes an object plus 'from' with an -ing form.
per_choice_rationale.C: Hypercorrects with a 'that' clause, a structure 'prohibit' does not allow (idiom_that_clause).
per_choice_rationale.D: Drops the required preposition, leaving a nonstandard shortcut (idiom_dropped_prep).

why_correct_md: The verb **prohibit** takes the fixed pattern 'prohibit someone from doing something.'
why_tempted_md: 'Forbid vendors to sell' is standard English, so students transfer the infinitive pattern onto 'prohibit.'
rule_md: 1) Identify the verb that controls the underlined pattern. 2) Recall its fixed companion pattern by testing a familiar example ('the sign prohibits visitors ___ feeding the ducks'). 3) Eliminate any option that borrows a different verb's pattern. 4) Eliminate any option missing the required connector. 5) Confirm the survivor reads naturally in the sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: The forecast promised heavy rain through the morning. <u>Similarly,</u> the market manager moved every stall under the covered pavilion before opening.
stem_md: Which transition is most logical here?

per_choice_rationale.A: Signals similarity between two like things, but the second sentence responds to the first rather than resembling it (transition_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.B: Promises an example of the previous statement, but no example follows (transition_false_example).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct — moving the stalls indoors is a direct effect of the rainy forecast.
per_choice_rationale.D: Signals contrast where the two sentences actually align as cause and consequence (transition_false_contrast).

why_correct_md: Moving the stalls indoors is a direct **effect** of the rainy forecast, so a cause-and-effect transition fits.
why_tempted_md: Both sentences concern the same rainy morning, so a similarity word feels loosely connected enough to keep.
rule_md: 1) State sentence 1 in five words. 2) State sentence 2 in five words. 3) Name the logical relationship (cause→effect, contrast, example, addition, time). 4) Match the transition to that relationship. 5) Reread the pair with your candidate inserted to confirm.

subject: act-english
context_html: Shoppers often assume that produce at the farmers' market costs more than it does at the supermarket. <u>Therefore,</u> a July comparison of twelve stalls found that seasonal fruit at the market was frequently cheaper.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: Treats the finding as a conclusion drawn from the assumption, but the finding contradicts the assumption (transition_false_cause).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — it signals that reality counters the common assumption stated first.
per_choice_rationale.C: Claims similarity between an assumption and a finding that undercuts it (transition_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.D: Imposes a time-based, simultaneous relationship that the sentences don't have (transition_false_time).

why_correct_md: The survey's finding **contradicts** the shoppers' assumption, so the transition must signal a correcting turn from belief to reality.
why_tempted_md: 'Therefore' feels safe because the second sentence presents data that seems to follow from investigating the first sentence's topic.
rule_md: 1) Summarize sentence 1 (a common belief). 2) Summarize sentence 2 (what was found). 3) Ask: does the second confirm, contradict, exemplify, or merely follow the first in time? 4) Choose the transition matching that relationship. 5) Reread the pair with the candidate installed.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] ______ [2] By six each Saturday, Marisol has already pulled forty sourdough loaves from her portable oven. [3] Customers begin lining up for her caraway rye before she finishes unloading. [4] By ten, only crumbs remain on the wooden boards.
stem_md: The writer wants to open the paragraph with a sentence that introduces its main subject and prepares readers for the details that follow. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: A visit to Marisol's bread stand rewards the market's earliest risers.
Farmers' markets in this country date back to the colonial era.
Sourdough bread rises with a starter made of fermented flour and water.
Marisol also sells peach jam produced by a neighboring farm.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — it names the paragraph's subject, Marisol's stand, and its early-riser angle forecasts the timeline of details that follow.
per_choice_rationale.B: Opens with a scope far wider than one baker's Saturday morning (broad_opener).
per_choice_rationale.C: Zooms in on a technical baking detail the paragraph never develops (narrow_offfocus).
per_choice_rationale.D: Introduces a side product that no later sentence mentions (add_offtopic).

why_correct_md: It names the paragraph's subject and **forecasts** the early-morning urgency that every following sentence develops.
why_tempted_md: The historical opener sounds authoritative and market-related, so students accept a scope far wider than one baker's Saturday.
rule_md: 1) Read the body sentences and list what they share (one baker, early hours, fast sellout). 2) Draft a one-line topic from that list. 3) Test each option: does it name that subject and match that scope? 4) Reject options that are broader, narrower, or about a different detail. 5) Confirm the survivor flows smoothly into the second sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Tomás arranges his cut flowers in the dark, a full hour before the market opens. [2] Dahlias and zinnias, his most delicate stems, fill the tall buckets at the front of the stand. [3] Sturdier flowers, such as sunflowers, need far less attention once they are set out. [4] Whatever remains at closing time is bundled and sold at half price.
stem_md: The writer wants to add the following sentence to the paragraph: "Their petals must be misted every hour to survive the afternoon heat." To make the paragraph most logical and cohesive, the sentence should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Opens the paragraph with the pronoun 'Their,' which would have no antecedent (pronoun_no_antecedent).
per_choice_rationale.B: Attaches the misting to all of Tomás's flowers, contradicting Sentence 3's claim that sturdier ones need little care (placement_wrong_referent).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct — 'Their' points to the delicate dahlias and zinnias, and the misting detail sets up Sentence 3's contrast.
per_choice_rationale.D: Delivers care instructions after the flowers have already been bundled and sold (placement_bad_timeline).

why_correct_md: 'Their' must point to the **delicate** dahlias and zinnias, and the misting detail sets up the very next sentence's contrast with lower-maintenance flowers.
why_tempted_md: The first sentence also mentions flowers, so students park the addition at the earliest available antecedent without testing the later contrast.
rule_md: 1) Circle the added sentence's pronouns and pointing words ('Their'). 2) Find the noun each must refer to. 3) Slot the sentence right after the sentence containing that noun. 4) Read the whole paragraph through, checking that contrasts and time order still work. 5) Confirm no other slot passes both tests.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Five years ago, the market began accepting SNAP benefits through a token system. [2] Shoppers swipe a card at the information booth and receive wooden tokens to spend at any stall. [3] Vendors turn in the tokens for cash at the close of each market day. [4] At first, only a handful of farmers agreed to participate. [5] Today, every produce stand at the market accepts the tokens.
stem_md: The writer wants to add the following sentence: "That hesitation faded once the first season's sales figures were shared at a vendors' meeting." To make the paragraph most logical, the sentence should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: 'That hesitation' has nothing to refer to right after the program's launch is announced (pointer_no_referent).
per_choice_rationale.B: Sentence 2 describes shoppers' mechanics, not any reluctance the pointer phrase could name (placement_wrong_section).
per_choice_rationale.C: Tempting because it mentions vendors and money, but Sentence 3 describes routine redemption, not doubt (placement_word_match).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — 'That hesitation' points to the handful of reluctant farmers, and its fading explains the final sentence's turnaround.

why_correct_md: 'That hesitation' needs a just-named reluctance — the **handful** of reluctant farmers — and its fading bridges directly to the paragraph's final turnaround.
why_tempted_md: The redemption sentence mentions vendors and cash, which looks like a vocabulary match for a sentence about vendors' sales figures.
rule_md: 1) Circle the added sentence's backward-pointing phrase ('That hesitation'). 2) Find the sentence that names a hesitation. 3) Place the addition immediately after it. 4) Check the forward link: does the next sentence continue the change? 5) Reject slots where the pointer has no referent, even if vocabulary overlaps.

subject: act-english
context_html: By eight in the morning, shoppers were filling their baskets with <u>peaches, plums, and early apples</u> from the orchard stands.
stem_md: Which choice is correctly punctuated?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — the three items are separated by commas, with the conjunction attached to the final item.
per_choice_rationale.B: Shifts a comma to follow the conjunction, splitting 'and' from the item it introduces (comma_after_conjunction).
per_choice_rationale.C: Omits the comma between the first two items, fusing them together (series_missing_comma).
per_choice_rationale.D: Adds an extra comma after the conjunction where no boundary exists (series_extra_comma).

why_correct_md: Items in a **series** take a comma after each item, with the conjunction staying attached to the final item.
why_tempted_md: Keeping a comma near 'and' looks balanced, so students accept the version that pauses just after the conjunction.
rule_md: 1) Count the items in the list. 2) Mark the boundary between each pair of items. 3) Put one comma at each boundary, before the conjunction. 4) Never put a comma directly after the conjunction. 5) Reread to confirm each item stands cleanly apart.

subject: act-english
context_html: Founded by thirty area farms, the <u>growers' cooperative</u> votes on booth fees each spring.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — the cooperative belongs to many growers (thirty farms), so the plural possessive puts the apostrophe after the s.
per_choice_rationale.B: The singular possessive implies one grower owns the cooperative, contradicting 'thirty area farms' (possessive_wrong_number).
per_choice_rationale.C: Drops the apostrophe entirely, erasing the ownership relationship (possessive_missing_apostrophe).
per_choice_rationale.D: Adds a nonstandard extra s to a plural that already ends in s (possessive_double_s).

why_correct_md: Thirty farms own the cooperative, so the **plural possessive** — s followed by an apostrophe — is required.
why_tempted_md: The apostrophe-before-s form is the possessive students write most often, so it looks right by habit.
rule_md: 1) Ask: who owns it, and how many of them are there? 2) Look for a number clue elsewhere in the sentence. 3) One owner → apostrophe + s. 4) Multiple owners whose plural ends in s → s + apostrophe only. 5) Confirm some apostrophe appears whenever ownership is meant.

subject: act-english
context_html: The market's oldest vendor<u>—a fourth-generation orchardist,</u> still climbs the ladders in his orchard at eighty-two.
stem_md: Which choice is correctly punctuated?

per_choice_rationale.A: Opens the interrupter with a dash but closes it with a comma — a mismatched pair (dash_comma_mismatch).
per_choice_rationale.B: Never closes the interrupter, so the aside collides with the main verb (interrupter_unclosed).
per_choice_rationale.C: Opens with a parenthesis but closes with a comma, another mismatched frame (paren_comma_mismatch).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — the interrupter opens and closes with the same mark, and the frame sentence reads whole without it.

why_correct_md: A mid-sentence interrupter must be **enclosed** by a matched pair of marks — here, a dash on each side.
why_tempted_md: The comma after 'orchardist' supplies a pause, so the mismatched dash-and-comma frame sounds fine when read aloud.
rule_md: 1) Bracket the phrase you could lift out of the sentence. 2) Note the mark that opens it. 3) Require the identical mark to close it. 4) Delete the interrupter mentally and confirm the remaining sentence still reads whole. 5) Eliminate any option whose opening and closing marks differ.

subject: act-english
context_html: The jam vendor's best-selling <u>flavor, is</u> a strawberry rhubarb that usually sells out by nine.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: A lone comma illegally splits the subject from its verb (comma_subject_verb).
per_choice_rationale.B: A semicolon must join two independent clauses; the words before it are only a subject (semicolon_fragment).
per_choice_rationale.C: A colon must follow a complete statement, not interrupt a clause midway (colon_midclause).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — no punctuation belongs between a subject and its verb.

why_correct_md: A subject and its verb form one unit, so **no punctuation** may divide them.
why_tempted_md: The long, modified subject invites a spoken pause before the verb, and students translate that pause into a comma.
