rule_md: 1) Find the subject and its verb. 2) Ask whether any complete grammatical structure (a clause, an interrupter needing two marks) sits between them. 3) If not, remove every mark between subject and verb. 4) Test semicolons by requiring full clauses on both sides. 5) Test colons by requiring a complete statement before them.

subject: act-english
context_html: At the cheese maker's stand, wheels of aged gouda <u>perfume the aisle with a nutty, caramel-like sweetness</u> that stops shoppers mid-stride.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize the sensory experience of walking past the cheese maker's stand. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: are offered for purchase in several convenient sizes
have been aged in the shop's cellar for at least twelve months
tend to be quite popular with regular customers

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — smell-and-taste imagery delivers exactly the sensory emphasis the writer wants.
per_choice_rationale.B: Supplies retail logistics with no appeal to any sense (goal_wrong_emphasis).
per_choice_rationale.C: Gives specific production background, but facts about aging inform rather than immerse (goal_factual_not_sensory).
per_choice_rationale.D: Offers vague general approval with no perceivable detail (goal_vague_praise).

why_correct_md: Only this version puts a **sense impression** — an aroma a passerby can experience — on the page.
why_tempted_md: The cellar-aging detail sounds atmospheric and specific, so students mistake concrete information for sensory description.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's goal in your own words (make the reader smell, taste, hear, see, or feel). 2) For each option, name the sense it engages, if any. 3) Strike options that inform, evaluate, or advertise without engaging a sense. 4) Choose the option with genuine sensory detail. 5) Confirm it still fits the sentence grammatically.

subject: act-english
context_html: The market commission's annual report praised vendors for their professionalism and cleanliness; it noted, however, that weekend parking <u>was a total mess</u> and recommended hiring a lot attendant.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the tone established elsewhere in the sentence?

choices.label: had gotten seriously out of hand
was, frankly, a headache for everybody

per_choice_rationale.A: The slangy intensifier 'total mess' clashes with the report's formal register (tone_slang).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Out of hand' is a conversational idiom that undercuts official prose (tone_colloquial_idiom).
per_choice_rationale.C: The chatty aside 'frankly' and informal 'headache' address readers personally, unlike a formal report (tone_chatty_interjection).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — measured, formal diction consistent with an official commission report.

why_correct_md: An official report calls for **measured**, formal diction, which this even-toned phrasing supplies.
why_tempted_md: 'A total mess' states the problem vividly and briefly, so it feels efficient rather than slangy.
rule_md: 1) Identify the document type and its register from surrounding wording ('annual report,' 'recommended'). 2) Label each option's register: formal, neutral, conversational, slang. 3) Strike options with idioms, slang, or chatty asides. 4) Choose the option matching the established register. 5) Reread the full sentence to confirm one consistent voice.

subject: act-english
context_html: The forager's stand draws one of the market's most curious crowds. Each week she sets out whatever the woods have offered: golden chanterelles, shaggy manes, and blue-gray oyster mushrooms. A laminated card beside each basket explains where the species grows and how to cook it.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence at the end of the paragraph: "She also fields questions about telling edible mushrooms apart from their toxic look-alikes." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it explains why shoppers find the mushrooms difficult to identify.
Yes, because it extends the paragraph's description of how the stand informs shoppers.
No, because it repeats the description of the laminated cards.
No, because it shifts attention away from the mushrooms the stand sells.

per_choice_rationale.A: Right verdict, wrong reason — the sentence shows the forager helping with identification, not explaining why it is hard (reason_misdescribes).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — the cards already educate visitors, and answering safety questions continues that educational thread.
per_choice_rationale.C: Answering live questions about toxic look-alikes is new information, not a repeat of the cards' habitat and cooking notes (false_redundancy).
per_choice_rationale.D: The sentence stays squarely on the stand and its mushrooms, so no shift occurs (false_offtopic).

why_correct_md: The paragraph already shows the stand teaching visitors through the cards, and the new sentence **continues** that educational thread.
why_tempted_md: The laminated cards and the safety questions both involve mushroom information, so the new sentence can look like a repeat of what the cards do.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's focus in one line. 2) Ask whether the proposed sentence develops that focus, repeats it, or derails it. 3) Decide add or don't add. 4) Then vet the stated reason: it must match what the sentence actually does. 5) Reject right-verdict options whose reasons misdescribe the sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: When the city tore up Main Street last spring, the Riverbend farmers' market seemed doomed. Instead, its manager negotiated a temporary lease on a school parking lot two blocks away, printed detour maps for regular customers, and persuaded a local radio station to announce the new location every Friday. Attendance dipped for a month and then rebounded past the previous year's numbers.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to show how one farmers' market adapted to a disruptive construction season. Would this passage accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it lists every vendor who agreed to move to the school parking lot.
Yes, because it recounts the manager's responses to the disruption and the outcome.
No, because it dwells on the radio station's schedule rather than on the market.
No, because it never identifies the reason the city planned the construction.

per_choice_rationale.A: Right verdict, wrong reason — the passage names no individual vendors, so this justification misdescribes the text (reason_misdescribes).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — the passage narrates specific adaptive steps and their result, exactly matching the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.C: The radio station appears in a single supporting detail; the market's adjustment stays the focus (false_focus_shift).
per_choice_rationale.D: The construction's cause is irrelevant to whether the passage shows adaptation (irrelevant_criterion).

why_correct_md: The passage narrates the specific adaptive moves — new site, detour maps, radio announcements — and their **result**, which is precisely what the supposed goal requires.
why_tempted_md: Because the passage never explains the construction project itself, students conclude it fails a goal that never demanded that background.
rule_md: 1) Restate the supposed goal in your own words. 2) Ask: does the passage as written do that? Fix your verdict. 3) Discard options whose verdict disagrees with yours. 4) Among matching verdicts, verify the reason against the text line by line. 5) Choose the option whose reason describes what the passage actually contains.

subject: act-english
context_html: Every Saturday, a small stage near the market's entrance hosts local musicians. The market pays each act a modest stipend funded by vendor dues. Regulars say the live music is what separates a morning at the market from an errand at the grocery store.
stem_md: The writer wants to add a sentence that maintains the paragraph's focus on the market's live-music program. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: A chalkboard near the entrance lists each day's produce prices.
Stipends are also common in industries such as publishing.
One of the musicians recently moved to the area from out of state.
This season, student musicians will join the Saturday lineup for a second afternoon set.

per_choice_rationale.A: Shares a location with the stage but concerns prices, not music (add_shared_scenery).
per_choice_rationale.B: Chases the word 'stipend' into unrelated industries, abandoning the topic (add_word_association).
per_choice_rationale.C: Mentions a musician but offers personal biography rather than the program (add_biographical_drift).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — it develops the music program itself with a planned expansion of its performances.

why_correct_md: Only this sentence **develops** the music program itself — its performers and its schedule — rather than a nearby object, a stray word, or a personal story.
why_tempted_md: The musician's relocation mentions a performer, so students accept biography as if it were information about the program.
rule_md: 1) Name the paragraph's declared focus in a short phrase. 2) For each option, ask: does this sentence give new information about that focus? 3) Reject options linked only by location, by a repeated word, or by a person's unrelated life details. 4) Choose the option that advances the focus. 5) Reread the paragraph with it inserted to confirm cohesion.

subject: act-english
context_html: The cider press draws the market's biggest crowd every <u>October families line up</u> to watch bushels of apples tumble into the hopper.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Fuses two independent clauses with no mark at all (fused_sentence).
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses (comma_splice).
per_choice_rationale.C: Places the comma after the conjunction instead of before it, leaving the junction unmarked (comma_after_conjunction).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — a semicolon legally joins two related independent clauses.

why_correct_md: **Semicolons** can join two complete, closely related sentences on their own.
why_tempted_md: The comma-only version supplies a pause where readers hear one, and many students believe a pause is all that's required between clauses.
rule_md: 1) Find each subject–verb pair. 2) Ask whether each could stand alone as a sentence. 3) Two independent clauses need a legal joint: a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus coordinating conjunction (or subordinate one clause). 4) Reject bare commas and bare adjacency. 5) If a conjunction is used, put the comma before it, never after.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Because the health inspector arrives unannounced,</u> vendors keep their coolers stocked with ice from the market's first hour to its last.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable and logical?

choices.label: Because the health inspector arrives unannounced, so
Although the health inspector arrives unannounced,

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — 'Because' subordinates the reason to the main clause, tying cause to effect in one grammatical sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: Removes the connector, leaving two independent clauses spliced by a comma (comma_splice).
per_choice_rationale.C: Doubles the connector: the subordinator already links the clauses, so adding 'so' breaks the grammar (double_connector).
per_choice_rationale.D: Signals contrast, but the ice-stocking happens because of the inspections, not despite them (subordinator_wrong_logic).

why_correct_md: Subordinating the reason with **Because** ties cause to effect in a single grammatical sentence.
why_tempted_md: Students hear 'because..., so...' as a natural spoken pattern and don't notice it doubles the connection.
rule_md: 1) Identify the two clauses and their logical relationship (cause, contrast, condition, time). 2) Choose one connector whose meaning matches that relationship. 3) Use exactly one connector per clause pair — a subordinator or a coordinator, never both. 4) Confirm no comma splice remains. 5) Reread to verify the logic sounds right.

subject: act-english
context_html: Stacked in wobbly towers beside the register, <u>shoppers eyed the egg cartons</u> at the poultry farmer's stand.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: shoppers' eyes fell on the egg cartons
the egg cartons caught shoppers' attention
there were egg cartons that shoppers eyed

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening phrase attaches to 'shoppers,' absurdly claiming the people were stacked in towers (dangling_subject).
per_choice_rationale.B: Swaps in 'shoppers' eyes,' which still aren't the stacked things (dangling_new_noun).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct — it places 'the egg cartons' immediately after the modifier that describes them.
per_choice_rationale.D: Opens the clause with the empty subject 'there,' giving the modifier nothing sensible to describe (dangling_expletive).

why_correct_md: An introductory modifier must describe the noun that **immediately follows** it, and only this option puts the stacked items in that spot.
why_tempted_md: Changing the words after the comma feels like a fix, even when the new noun still isn't the stacked thing.
rule_md: 1) Bracket the opening modifier. 2) Ask: who or what does it describe? 3) Check the noun right after the comma. 4) If they don't match, choose the version whose first noun is the described thing. 5) Reread the whole sentence for sense.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each vendor must <u>submit an annual application</u> to keep a reserved booth at the market.
stem_md: Which choice avoids redundancy while preserving the sentence's meaning?

choices.label: submit an annual application every year

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — 'annual' already carries the once-a-year meaning, so nothing repeats.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Every year' restates what 'annual' already says (redundant_time_phrase).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Yearly' is a direct synonym of 'annual,' stacked beside it (redundant_synonym).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Annually' repeats the same idea in adverb form (redundant_adverb).

why_correct_md: The adjective **annual** already states the once-a-year timing, so any added time expression repeats it.
why_tempted_md: Adding 'every year' feels like helpful clarification rather than repetition, since the phrase is so common in speech.
rule_md: 1) Underline every word or phrase that expresses timing. 2) Ask what each one adds that the others don't. 3) If two expressions encode the same fact, cut until one remains. 4) Reread to confirm the meaning survived. 5) Prefer the version stating each idea exactly once.

subject: act-english
context_html: After months of debate, the committee <u>made the decision to give its approval to</u> a second market day on Wednesdays.
stem_md: Which choice expresses the idea most concisely?

choices.label: made a decision to approve of
decided it would go about approving

per_choice_rationale.A: Buries the action inside two padded noun phrases, 'made the decision' and 'give its approval' (nominalization_stack).
per_choice_rationale.B: Trims one layer but keeps the padded 'made a decision' and adds unidiomatic 'approve of' for formal authorization (partial_trim_wrong_idiom).
per_choice_rationale.C: The filler 'go about' adds motion without meaning (empty_filler).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — a single strong verb conveys the entire action.

why_correct_md: One **strong verb** replaces two padded noun phrases with no loss of meaning.
why_tempted_md: Students equate longer, noun-heavy phrasing with formality, so the original's official sound feels appropriate for a committee.
rule_md: 1) Find the real action hiding inside the noun phrases. 2) Convert it to a single verb. 3) Compare each option's meaning to the original. 4) Prefer the shortest option that keeps the meaning and stays idiomatic. 5) Confirm nothing essential disappeared.

subject: act-english
context_html: Volunteers tally attendance <u>by means of the use of a handheld clicker</u> at each of the market's three gates.
stem_md: Which choice expresses the idea most clearly and concisely?

choices.label: through the use of a handheld clicker
by utilizing a handheld clicker for the count

per_choice_rationale.A: Chains two prepositional formulas — 'by means of' and 'the use of' — around one simple tool (double_formula).
per_choice_rationale.B: Keeps the padded 'the use of' construction after a partial trim (partial_trim).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct — a single small preposition expresses the instrument cleanly and completely.
per_choice_rationale.D: Swaps in the inflated 'utilizing' and repeats the counting idea already present in 'tally' (inflated_verb_plus_echo).

why_correct_md: An instrument needs only one small preposition, making this the **shortest** option that keeps the full meaning.
why_tempted_md: Cutting 'by means of' feels like enough trimming, so students stop before removing the equally empty 'the use of.'
rule_md: 1) Identify the core fact (tool used to tally). 2) Strip every formula that can vanish without losing that fact. 3) Compare the surviving candidates for idiomatic fit. 4) Check the longest options for repeated ideas already in the sentence. 5) Pick the shortest version that still says everything.

subject: act-english
context_html: Years of Saturday foot traffic had <u>demolished</u> shallow ruts into the grassy field where the market sets up.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely conveys how the ruts formed?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Demolished' means destroyed outright and cannot describe gradually forming ruts (overstated_intensity).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Punctured' means pierced a hole through — the wrong physical action for slow, repeated footsteps (wrong_physical_action).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Erased' means removed, the opposite of creating ruts (reversed_direction).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — 'worn' captures gradual shaping by repeated contact and fits the idiom of ruts formed into a field.

why_correct_md: Only this verb captures **gradual** shaping by repeated contact and fits the idiom of ruts formed into a surface.
why_tempted_md: 'Demolished' sounds forceful and vivid, so students reward its drama instead of testing its literal meaning.
rule_md: 1) Picture the literal physical event the sentence describes. 2) For each verb, state its literal action and intensity. 3) Check the direction: does the verb create or remove the named thing? 4) Check intensity: sudden force or gradual repetition? 5) Choose the verb matching both the direction and the pace.

subject: act-english
context_html: In its grant application, the market described its central mission: <u>to increase residents' access to</u> fresh, affordable produce.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the formal style established in the sentence?

choices.label: to boost folks' chances of grabbing

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — precise, formal diction suited to a grant application.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Hook up with' is a slang idiom out of place in official prose (register_slang_idiom).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Snag' is casual, grab-bag diction that deflates a mission statement (register_casual_verb).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Folks' and 'grabbing' are conversational words unsuited to a document for funders (register_conversational).

why_correct_md: A grant application demands **formal**, precise diction, and this phrasing alone maintains it.
why_tempted_md: 'Hook residents up with' sounds friendly and energetic, so students mistake warmth for effective style.
rule_md: 1) Identify the document type named in the sentence. 2) Set the expected register from that document (formal, neutral, casual). 3) Flag any option containing slang, idioms, or conversational words. 4) Keep only options a reader of that document would expect. 5) Reread the sentence to confirm one consistent voice.

subject: act-english
context_html: Audiences in 1914 gasped as Gertie the Dinosaur lumbered across the screen; Winsor McCay <u>stands</u> beside the projection each night and pretended to command his hand-drawn creature.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: The present-tense 'stands' clashes with the past-tense narrative ('gasped,' 'pretended') and the 1914 setting.
per_choice_rationale.B: The simple past 'stood' matches 'gasped' and 'pretended,' keeping the sentence in one consistent past time frame.
per_choice_rationale.C: Past perfect 'had stood' wrongly signals the standing was completed before another past event, but no such later reference event exists.
per_choice_rationale.D: The present progressive 'is standing' places the action in the present moment, contradicting the past-tense verbs around it.

why_correct_md: Simple past **matches the time frame** established by 'gasped' and 'pretended.'
why_tempted_md: 'Had stood' sounds appropriately 'past,' so students reach for it even though no second, later past event requires past perfect.
rule_md: 1) List every verb in the sentence and its tense. 2) Identify the controlling time frame from dates and the other verbs. 3) Make the underlined verb match that frame. 4) Use past perfect only if the action must be shown finished before another past action.

subject: act-english
context_html: The archive of nitrate cels and pencil tests, stacked for decades in vaults beneath the old ink-and-paint building, <u>were finally digitized</u> last spring.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Were' agrees with the nearby plurals 'cels,' 'tests,' and 'vaults' instead of the singular head noun 'archive.'
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Was' correctly agrees with the singular subject 'archive,' the head noun of the long subject phrase, and fits the past cue 'last spring.'
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Are' is both plural and present tense, failing the singular subject and the 'last spring' time cue.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Have been' is plural; the singular 'archive' would require 'has been,' and the simple past better fits a completed event 'last spring.'

why_correct_md: The verb must agree with the **head noun** 'archive,' which is singular, and match the past time cue 'last spring.'
why_tempted_md: The plural nouns stacked between subject and verb ('cels,' 'tests,' 'vaults') pull students toward a plural verb.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb. 2) Ask 'who or what does this?' to find the subject. 3) Cross out every prepositional phrase and modifier between subject and verb. 4) Match the verb to the head noun in number. 5) Check time cues in the sentence for tense.

subject: act-english
context_html: Early studio animators <u>prided themselves in</u> completing thousands of drawings a week without a single traced frame.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Prided themselves in' borrows the preposition from 'take pride in,' but the reflexive verb 'pride oneself' does not take 'in.'
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Prided themselves for' imports the pattern of 'praised for'; 'for' is not idiomatic with 'pride oneself.'
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Prided themselves on' uses the fixed preposition that the idiom 'pride oneself on' requires.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Prided themselves about' follows verbs like 'bragged about,' but 'about' is not the preposition this idiom takes.

why_correct_md: The reflexive idiom is **pride oneself on** — a fixed pairing that cannot be swapped.
why_tempted_md: Because 'take pride in' is correct English, 'prided themselves in' sounds right by association.
rule_md: 1) Spot the verb + preposition combination. 2) Ask whether the verb belongs to a fixed idiom. 3) Recall the idiom in its own dictionary form, not a related phrase's form. 4) Test each option in that frame and keep the conventional pairing.

subject: act-english
context_html: Cel animation dominated commercial studios for most of the twentieth century. <u>Therefore,</u> by the early 2000s, computer-generated imagery had replaced it almost entirely.
stem_md: Which transition word or phrase is most logical in context?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Therefore' claims the replacement of cel animation follows logically from its dominance, but the second sentence reverses the first.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Similarly' promises a parallel idea, yet the second sentence contradicts rather than echoes the first.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For example' would introduce an instance of cel animation's dominance, not its downfall.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'However' correctly signals the contrast between decades of dominance and near-total replacement.

why_correct_md: The second sentence **reverses** the first, so a contrast transition is required.
why_tempted_md: The time gap ('for most of the century... by the early 2000s') feels like a natural progression, luring students to a cause-and-effect word.
rule_md: 1) Cover the transition. 2) Read both sentences and state their relationship in your own words (contrast, cause, example, addition, time). 3) Match that relationship to each option's category. 4) Reject any transition whose category differs, no matter how smooth it sounds.

subject: act-english
context_html: Rotoscoping allowed animators to trace live-action footage one frame at a time. <u>As a result,</u> their characters moved with an eerily lifelike fluidity that hand-timed drawings rarely achieved.
stem_md: Which transition word or phrase is most logical in context?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'As a result' correctly presents the lifelike movement as the consequence of tracing real footage.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'In contrast' asserts opposition, but the fluid motion follows from the tracing rather than opposing it.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For instance' would make the second sentence an example of the first, yet it is an effect, not an illustration.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Meanwhile' implies two separate simultaneous events, but the sentences describe a cause producing its effect.

why_correct_md: Tracing real footage **causes** the lifelike fluidity, so the cause-and-effect transition already in place is right.
why_tempted_md: 'Eerily' feels faintly negative, tempting students to read the second sentence as a contrast with the technique's promise.
rule_md: 1) Cover the transition and read the two sentences bare. 2) Name their logical link in your own words. 3) Sort each option by category (contrast, example, time, result). 4) Keep the option whose category matches your named link — even if that means keeping what is already there.

subject: act-english
context_html: Walt Disney's studio unveiled the multiplane camera in 1937, mounting layers of painted glass at different distances from the lens. As the camera pushed forward, foreground trees slid past faster than distant hills, mimicking real parallax. Scenes gained a sense of dimension that flat cel setups had never achieved.
stem_md: The writer wants to conclude the paragraph with a sentence that emphasizes the multiplane camera's lasting influence on animation. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: The camera itself weighed nearly a ton and required several technicians to operate its layered glass setups.
Decades later, digital compositing programs would still imitate its parallax effects to convey depth.
Disney also invested heavily in Technicolor processes during the same period.
Audiences at the 1937 premiere applauded the effects and the sense of depth in the backgrounds.

per_choice_rationale.A: The camera's weight and crew are production trivia; they say nothing about influence on later animation.
per_choice_rationale.B: It projects the camera's technique forward in time, showing later tools copying it — exactly the lasting influence the goal demands.
per_choice_rationale.C: Technicolor is a different technology; this sentence changes the subject instead of concluding it.
per_choice_rationale.D: Premiere-night applause is an immediate reaction, not evidence of lasting influence.

why_correct_md: Only this sentence extends the camera's technique **beyond its own era**, which is what 'lasting influence' requires.
why_tempted_md: The applause detail stays on topic and feels like a satisfying ending, but it measures one night, not a legacy.
rule_md: 1) Restate the stem's goal in your own words. 2) For each option, ask: does it address the goal's key idea (here, influence that persists)? 3) Eliminate options that are on-topic but answer a different question. 4) Pick the one that most directly performs the stated goal.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Lotte Reiniger cut intricate silhouette figures from black cardboard and thin sheets of lead. [2] She jointed each limb with fine wire so the figures could gesture expressively. [3] The result, The Adventures of Prince Achmed, premiered in 1926 and still enchants audiences. [4] Working frame by frame on a backlit table, she animated these delicate puppets for a feature-length fairy tale. [5] The production consumed three years and roughly 250,000 separate exposures.
stem_md: For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, Sentence 3 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: In its current spot, 'The result' appears before the animating and the three-year effort have been described, so the phrase has too little to refer to.
per_choice_rationale.B: Opening with 'The result' would give the summary phrase nothing at all to point back to.
per_choice_rationale.C: After Sentence 5, 'The result' caps the complete account — cutting, jointing, animating, and three years of exposures — so the premiere lands as the paragraph's payoff.
per_choice_rationale.D: Placing the premiere before Sentence 5 makes the production-cost detail trail anticlimactically after the film's debut.

why_correct_md: 'The result' must **follow the full process** it summarizes, and Sentence 5 is the last piece of that process.
why_tempted_md: After Sentence 4 the film has been animated, so the result seems ready to announce — but the effort tally in Sentence 5 still belongs to the making.
rule_md: 1) Find pointing phrases in the movable sentence ('The result,' 'these,' 'that'). 2) Identify everything those phrases must refer back to. 3) Place the sentence after the last required referent. 4) Reread the paragraph in the new order to confirm nothing later is orphaned.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] In 1963, Astro Boy became Japan's first weekly animated television series. [2] These shortcuts, born of necessity, hardened into an aesthetic that later directors deliberately embraced. [3] To survive the brutal weekly schedule, the studio reused walk cycles and held single poses on screen for several frames. [4] Critics dismissed the look as jerky, but viewers embraced its bold graphic rhythm. [5] That rhythm of stillness and sudden motion still echoes through anime today.
stem_md: For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, Sentence 2 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Where it stands, 'These shortcuts' follows a sentence about a premiere date that mentions no shortcuts.
per_choice_rationale.B: Right after Sentence 3 the referent works, but the long-term canonization then arrives before the initial critical reaction, scrambling the timeline.
per_choice_rationale.C: After Sentence 5 the paragraph has already reached the present day, so rewinding to the hardening of the aesthetic weakens the close.
per_choice_rationale.D: After Sentence 4 the sentence follows both the shortcuts and their first reception, completing the chronology: techniques, immediate reaction, later canonization, present-day echo.

why_correct_md: The sentence needs its referent **and** its place in the timeline: after the shortcuts are described and first judged, before the present-day close.
why_tempted_md: Because 'These shortcuts' points at Sentence 3, putting it immediately after Sentence 3 feels safest — but that breaks the order of reactions.
rule_md: 1) Find the referent of any pointing phrase. 2) List the paragraph's events in time order (creation, first reception, later status, today). 3) Place the sentence where both the referent and the chronology are satisfied. 4) Reread to check every pointer still lands.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>After the storyboard was approved animators</u> began timing each scene to the prerecorded soundtrack.
stem_md: Which choice most effectively punctuates the sentence?

choices.label: After, the storyboard was approved animators
After the storyboard was approved animators,
After the storyboard was approved, animators

per_choice_rationale.A: With no comma, the introductory clause runs into the main clause, inviting the misreading 'approved animators.'
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma directly after 'After' severs the subordinator from the clause it introduces.
per_choice_rationale.C: This comma falls between the subject 'animators' and its verb 'began' while leaving the clause boundary unmarked.
per_choice_rationale.D: The comma after 'approved' correctly closes the introductory dependent clause before the main clause begins.

why_correct_md: An **introductory clause** is set off with a comma at its end, just before the main clause's subject.
why_tempted_md: Students who place commas by pause often stop after 'animators,' hearing the whole opening chunk as one breath.
rule_md: 1) Find where the sentence's main subject-verb pair begins. 2) Everything before it that starts with a subordinator is the introduction. 3) Put one comma at the introduction's end. 4) Confirm no comma splits the subject from its verb.

subject: act-english
context_html: The <u>films's success</u> at the box office convinced the bank to fund a second animated feature.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Films's' doubles the possessive marker; no English form stacks an extra 's' that way.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Films success' drops the apostrophe entirely, leaving two stacked nouns with no possessive relationship.
per_choice_rationale.C: The apostrophe-after-s form is a plural possessive, but the studio has completed only one feature at this point.
per_choice_rationale.D: The singular possessive matches the single completed film whose success persuaded the bank.

why_correct_md: One film owns the success, so the **singular possessive** — base noun + apostrophe + s — is required.
why_tempted_md: The apostrophe-after-s form looks polished and 'possessive enough,' but it silently asserts multiple films.
rule_md: 1) Decide how many owners there are from context clues. 2) Write the owner noun in that number. 3) Add apostrophe + s for a singular owner, or an apostrophe alone after a plural ending in s. 4) Reject any form that doubles the marker.

subject: act-english
context_html: The <u>zoetrope—a spinning drum lined with sequential drawings,</u> delighted parlor audiences decades before cinema existed.
stem_md: Which choice most effectively punctuates the sentence?

choices.label: zoetrope, a spinning drum lined with sequential drawings—
zoetrope—a spinning drum lined with sequential drawings—
zoetrope a spinning drum lined with sequential drawings,

per_choice_rationale.A: The appositive opens with a dash but closes with a comma — mismatched bookends.
per_choice_rationale.B: Opening with a comma and closing with a dash mixes the two systems in the other direction.
per_choice_rationale.C: Matching dashes set off the appositive on both sides, and the remaining sentence reads cleanly without it.
per_choice_rationale.D: The appositive's start is unmarked, so readers get no signal that the main sentence has been interrupted.

why_correct_md: Paired interrupters must use **matching punctuation** on both ends — dash with dash.
why_tempted_md: The dash-then-comma original sounds fine aloud because both marks create pauses, hiding the mismatch on the page.
rule_md: 1) Bracket the insertable phrase and remove it; the sentence must still work. 2) Look at the mark before it and the mark after it. 3) Make both marks the same kind (two commas, two dashes, or parentheses). 4) Reject any mixed pair or missing side.

subject: act-english
context_html: Animators who mastered the new <u>xerographic process found</u> steady work at studios scrambling to cut inking costs.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: No punctuation is needed: the long subject flows directly into its verb 'found.'
per_choice_rationale.B: This comma splits the subject from its verb, a pause-based error common after long subjects.
per_choice_rationale.C: A colon may follow only a complete independent clause; here it interrupts mid-clause before the verb.
per_choice_rationale.D: This comma severs the adjective 'xerographic' from the noun 'process' it modifies.

why_correct_md: No mark belongs between a subject and its verb, **however long the subject is**.
why_tempted_md: After the lengthy 'Animators who mastered the new xerographic process,' students hear a breath and insert a comma.
rule_md: 1) Identify the subject (with all its modifiers) and its verb. 2) Check that nothing but a full paired interrupter stands between them. 3) Test any colon: could the words before it end with a period? 4) If every mark fails a rule, the span may need none at all.

subject: act-english
context_html: For its first full-length feature, the studio's artists <u>produced</u> well over a million preliminary sketches before a single cel was painted.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize the painstaking care the artists invested in the drawings. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Produced' is accurate but neutral; it records output without conveying any care.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Meticulously refined' dramatizes deliberate, careful craftsmanship, directly serving the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Cranked out' implies fast, mechanical output — the opposite of painstaking care.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Eventually completed' stresses elapsed time, not the quality of attention.

why_correct_md: The goal asks for **care**, and only this wording builds carefulness into the verb phrase itself.
why_tempted_md: 'Eventually completed' hints at a long effort, which students mistake for an image of careful work.
rule_md: 1) Underline the key quality in the stated goal. 2) For each option, name the connotation its verb carries. 3) Eliminate options whose connotation is neutral, opposite, or about a different quality. 4) Choose the one that embodies the goal's exact quality.

subject: act-english
context_html: Film scholars once treated cartoons as disposable entertainment; today, most <u>think animation is a pretty big deal</u> and analyze it alongside live-action classics.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the tone established in the rest of the sentence?

choices.label: regard animation as a serious subject of study
figure animation is worth a look

per_choice_rationale.A: 'A pretty big deal' is conversational slang that clashes with the sentence's academic diction.
per_choice_rationale.B: This phrasing matches the formal, scholarly register of 'disposable entertainment' and 'analyze ... classics.'
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Totally obsessed' is hyperbolic fan-speak, not a description of scholars' professional stance.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Figure' and 'worth a look' are breezy colloquialisms that deflate the sentence's formality.

why_correct_md: The sentence's scholarly frame demands **formal register**, which only this option sustains.
why_tempted_md: 'A pretty big deal' states the right idea, so students keep it despite the register clash.
rule_md: 1) Sample the passage's diction: list two or three of its formal (or informal) words. 2) Label each option's register. 3) Discard options whose register differs from the sample, even if the meaning fits. 4) Confirm the survivor also preserves the intended meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: Fleischer Studios built its reputation on surreal, rubber-limbed gags that turned city streets into dreamscapes. Cabs sprouted legs, tenement buildings danced, and household objects burst into song. The brothers Max and Dave supervised the work from a studio on Broadway. The building had previously housed a garment business.
stem_md: The writer is considering deleting the final sentence of the paragraph. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?

choices.label: Kept, because the garment business shaped the studio's surreal animation style.
Kept, because the note about the building's previous life adds a memorable detail.
Deleted, because the paragraph's earlier sentences focus too heavily on visual gags.
Deleted, because the building's previous tenant is unrelated to the paragraph's focus on the studio's animation style.

per_choice_rationale.A: The paragraph never links the garment trade to the studio's style; this keep-reason invents a connection.
per_choice_rationale.B: Memorability alone does not justify a detail that serves no point the paragraph is making.
per_choice_rationale.C: The verdict is right but the reason misfires: the problem is this sentence's irrelevance, not the other sentences' emphasis.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct on both counts: delete it, because the building's past has nothing to do with the paragraph's portrait of the studio's style.

why_correct_md: Both the **verdict and the reason** must be right: the detail strays from the paragraph's focus on the studio's surreal style.
why_tempted_md: The garment-business fact is genuinely interesting, so the 'memorable detail' justification feels persuasive.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's focus in one phrase. 2) Ask whether the sentence advances that focus. 3) Decide keep or delete on that basis alone. 4) Then vet the stated reason: it must accurately describe both the sentence and the paragraph.

subject: act-english
context_html: In this essay, the writer recounts attending a weekend retrospective of stop-motion films, describing the handcrafted puppets displayed in the lobby and her conversations with a restoration archivist about the challenges of preserving fragile, decades-old sets.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to explain the technical steps involved in producing a stop-motion film. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because the essay describes the handcrafted puppets and sets from a personal visit.
Yes, because preservation efforts require step-by-step production knowledge.
No, because the essay focuses on early features rather than on recent methods.
No, because the essay centers on a personal visit and preservation efforts rather than on production methods.

per_choice_rationale.A: Describing puppets and sets shows the essay's subject matter, not a step-by-step production process.
per_choice_rationale.B: Whatever the archivist knows offstage, the essay itself never conveys production steps to the reader.
per_choice_rationale.C: The verdict is right, but era is irrelevant: the goal never demanded recent methods.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct verdict and reason: the essay is a personal account of a retrospective and preservation work, not an explanation of production technique.

why_correct_md: Purpose questions test what the essay **actually delivers**, and this one delivers a visit narrative, not a how-to.
why_tempted_md: Because puppets and sets are production equipment, mentioning them feels like technical coverage.
rule_md: 1) Restate the hypothetical goal precisely. 2) Summarize what the essay actually does in one sentence. 3) Compare: does the essay's content match the goal's requirement? 4) Pick the verdict whose reason accurately describes both the essay and the goal.

subject: act-english
context_html: At a mid-century animation studio, no scene belonged to a single artist. Story artists pitched gags, layout crews staged the action, and animators passed rough scenes to assistants for cleanup. A finished shot might carry the fingerprints of forty people.
stem_md: The writer wants to add a sentence that further emphasizes the paragraph's focus on teamwork across the studio's departments. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Some directors kept private sketchbooks that no colleague ever saw.
The cafeteria, even at peak production, served lunch in three daily shifts.
Even the music staff joined early story meetings, matching tunes to unfinished scenes.
One animator skipped story meetings and drew his most famous scenes alone over a single weekend.

per_choice_rationale.A: Private sketchbooks illustrate secrecy, undercutting the teamwork theme.
per_choice_rationale.B: Cafeteria logistics show the studio's size, not collaboration on the work itself.
per_choice_rationale.C: Another department pitching in on story work is one more instance of cross-department teamwork — exactly what the goal asks for.
per_choice_rationale.D: A solo triumph contradicts the paragraph's claim that no scene belonged to one artist.

why_correct_md: The addition must supply **more evidence of the stated focus** — cooperation across departments — and only this detail does.
why_tempted_md: The cafeteria detail is set inside the studio, so it feels on-topic even though it says nothing about shared work.
rule_md: 1) Name the paragraph's focus in a phrase. 2) For each candidate, ask: does it add another example of that focus? 3) Strike details that are merely nearby in setting or that cut against the focus. 4) Choose the remaining example.

subject: act-english
context_html: In the 1950s, Norman McLaren scratched and painted images directly onto clear film <u>stock he bypassed</u> the camera entirely.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Two independent clauses stand fused with no punctuation or connector between them.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Therefore' is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction; after a mere comma it still leaves a splice.
per_choice_rationale.D: Turning the second clause into the participial phrase 'bypassing ...' attaches it grammatically to the main clause.

why_correct_md: Reducing the second clause to a **participial phrase** removes the second independent clause — and the boundary problem with it.
why_tempted_md: The comma-plus-'therefore' version sounds formal and connected, masking that a comma still cannot hold two clauses together.
rule_md: 1) Count the independent clauses. 2) If there are two, check the joint: it needs a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus coordinating conjunction. 3) Conjunctive adverbs like 'therefore' need a semicolon before them. 4) Alternatively, demote one clause to a phrase or dependent clause. 5) Pick the option that satisfies one of these fixes.

subject: act-english
context_html: Because television networks paid a fraction of what theaters once had, <u>so even prestigious studios</u> trimmed their animation budgets to the bone.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Because ... so ...' doubles the causal connector and leaves the sentence with no independent clause.
per_choice_rationale.B: With 'Because' already subordinating the cause, the main clause simply begins with its subject — one connector, one link.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'And' tries to coordinate a subordinate clause with a main clause, which are not equal units.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'So that' asserts purpose — as if networks paid less in order to force cuts — and still strands the sentence without a main clause.

why_correct_md: A fronted 'Because' clause needs a **bare main clause** after the comma; one connector carries the whole logic.
why_tempted_md: 'Because ... so' mirrors speech patterns and some other languages' paired connectors, so it sounds naturally emphatic.
rule_md: 1) Find the subordinator that opens the sentence. 2) Locate the comma ending its clause. 3) Verify the words after the comma form an independent clause with no second connector. 4) If a connector duplicates the logic, delete it mentally and retest the sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Working frame by frame for nearly three months, the mural of galloping horses slowly took shape under the animator's brush.</u>
stem_md: Which choice best corrects the underlined sentence?

choices.label: Working frame by frame for nearly three months, the mural of galloping horses was slowly painted by the animator.
Working frame by frame for nearly three months, the animator slowly painted the mural of galloping horses.
The mural of galloping horses, working frame by frame for nearly three months, slowly took shape under the animator's brush.

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening phrase dangles: the mural, not a person, ends up doing the 'working.'
per_choice_rationale.B: The passive rewrite still parks 'the mural' next to the modifier, so the dangler survives.
per_choice_rationale.C: The doer — the animator — now directly follows the introductory phrase, which finally modifies the right noun.
per_choice_rationale.D: Relocating the phrase beside 'the mural' still attaches the working to the artwork rather than the artist.

why_correct_md: An opening participial phrase must be followed **immediately by its doer**, and only here is that the animator.
why_tempted_md: Adding 'by the animator' names the artist, so the passive version feels fixed even though the modifier still grabs the mural.
rule_md: 1) Find the opening (or movable) modifier. 2) Ask who or what performs its action. 3) Check the noun right next to the modifier. 4) If they do not match, choose the version that puts the true doer beside the modifier.

subject: act-english
context_html: When a sequence tested poorly with preview audiences, the director would <u>revert back to</u> an earlier version of the storyboard.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most concise without losing meaning?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Revert' already means to go back, so 'back' repeats the idea.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Back' and 'again' both duplicate the return built into 'revert.'
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Revert to' expresses the complete idea once, with no repetition.
per_choice_rationale.D: Nominalizing into 'make a reversion' adds bulk, and 'back' still doubles the direction.

why_correct_md: **Redundancy** check: the direction is already inside 'revert,' so nothing may repeat it.
why_tempted_md: 'Revert back' is so common in speech that the doubling is invisible to the ear.
rule_md: 1) Define the key verb precisely. 2) Ask whether any nearby word repeats part of that definition. 3) Delete the repeaters and reread. 4) Keep the version that preserves the full meaning with no duplicated idea.

subject: act-english
context_html: The arrival of synchronized sound in 1928 <u>transformed</u> the animation industry almost overnight.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most concise without losing meaning?

choices.label: brought about a state of transformation in

per_choice_rationale.A: The single direct verb delivers the action with no wasted words.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Was something that' is an empty frame adding words but no meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Had the effect of transforming' restates the verb's own meaning in five words.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Brought about a state of transformation in' buries the action in an abstract noun phrase.

why_correct_md: The original verb is already **concise and direct**; every alternative pads it.
why_tempted_md: 'Had the effect of' sounds analytically precise, as if it were describing causation more carefully.
rule_md: 1) Identify the core action. 2) For each option, ask what each added word contributes. 3) Strike phrases that restate the verb ('had the effect of,' 'was something that'). 4) Select the version in which every word earns its place.

subject: act-english
context_html: Theater owners booked cartoon shorts <u>due to the fact that</u> audiences expected one before every feature.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most concise without losing meaning?

choices.label: in light of the fact that

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Due to the fact that' spends five words on a link one word can make.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'In light of the fact that' adds formality but no meaning — six words of filler.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Because' states the causal link completely in one word.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Because of the fact that' wraps the working word in pure padding.

why_correct_md: 'The fact that' constructions are classic **filler**; the bare conjunction does the whole job.
why_tempted_md: The longer connectors sound more formal and essay-like, so students equate length with sophistication.
rule_md: 1) Spot any phrase containing 'the fact that.' 2) Ask what single connector the phrase reduces to. 3) Substitute the one-word version and reread. 4) If the meaning is unchanged, the shorter form wins.

subject: act-english
context_html: By reusing background paintings across dozens of episodes, the producers <u>conserved</u> both money and time.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most precise word in context?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Conserved' precisely names careful, planned economy of resources.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Hoarded' implies secretive, excessive stockpiling the passage never suggests.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Salvaged' presupposes rescue from loss or wreckage, not planned reuse.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Withheld' means refusing to give something owed, importing a recipient the sentence lacks.

why_correct_md: Precision questions hinge on **connotation and scenario**: only the original names prudent resource management.
why_tempted_md: 'Salvaged' shares the sense of making the most of materials, so its rescue scenario slips past many readers.
rule_md: 1) State the sentence's literal situation. 2) For each verb, name the scenario it presupposes (rescue, greed, denial, economy). 3) Match scenario to situation. 4) Reject any verb that imports facts the passage does not support.

subject: act-english
context_html: The 1941 animators' strike, which halted production for five weeks, <u>got super ugly</u> before federal mediators stepped in.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the style and tone of the passage?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Got super ugly' is casual slang out of step with the sentence's formal, historical register.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'A real train wreck' is colloquial hyperbole that clashes with 'federal mediators' and 'halted production.'
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Kind of spiraled' hedges vaguely, in chatty diction unsuited to a serious labor dispute.
per_choice_rationale.D: This choice describes the escalation in measured, formal language matching the passage.

why_correct_md: The passage's **formal register** requires precise, measured diction for the strike's escalation.
why_tempted_md: 'Got super ugly' is vivid and roughly accurate, so its energy tempts students despite the register clash.
rule_md: 1) Identify the passage's register from surrounding word choices. 2) Label each option formal, neutral, or colloquial. 3) Eliminate register mismatches. 4) Among matches, keep the most precise description of events.

subject: act-english
context_html: Last October, my grandmother and I drove to the hawk lookout before sunrise. While we waited on the ridge, she <u>scanned the horizon and pointed out</u> a kestrel hovering over the frosty field.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: scans the horizon and points out
scanned the horizon and had pointed out
was scanning the horizon and points out

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: both verbs stay in simple past, matching the narrative frame set by 'drove' and 'waited.'
per_choice_rationale.B: Shifts into the present tense mid-story, breaking consistency with the past-tense frame verbs.
per_choice_rationale.C: Past perfect 'had pointed out' falsely signals that the pointing happened before the scanning, though the actions are simultaneous.
per_choice_rationale.D: Mixes a past progressive with a present-tense verb, splitting one moment into two conflicting time frames.

why_correct_md: The surrounding narrative is anchored in the **simple past** ('drove,' 'waited'), so both underlined verbs must remain in that tense.
why_tempted_md: The vivid scene lures students into the historical present, making 'scans' and 'points out' feel immediate even though the frame is past.
rule_md: 1) Find the un-underlined verbs that set the passage's time frame. 2) Name their tense. 3) Make every underlined verb match that tense. 4) Allow a shift only if the meaning clearly requires a different time. 5) Reject options that mix time frames within one action.

subject: act-english
context_html: The chorus of chickadees and nuthatches at the feeding station <u>grows</u> louder whenever fresh suet appears.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the head noun 'chorus' is singular, so the singular verb 'grows' agrees with it.
per_choice_rationale.B: Matches the nearby plural nouns 'chickadees and nuthatches' instead of the true subject, 'chorus.'
per_choice_rationale.C: Uses the plural 'are' for a singular subject and adds a progressive form where 'whenever' calls for a habitual simple verb.
per_choice_rationale.D: Uses plural 'have' for the singular 'chorus' and imposes a completed-action tense on a repeated habit.

why_correct_md: Strip away the prepositional phrases and the subject is **chorus** — singular — so it takes a singular verb.
why_tempted_md: The plural nouns 'chickadees and nuthatches' sit right beside the verb, tempting students to match the nearest noun rather than the head noun.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb. 2) Ask 'who or what does this?' 3) Cross out every prepositional phrase ('of...', 'at...') between subject and verb. 4) Match the verb to the head noun that remains. 5) Ignore any noun inside the crossed-out phrases, no matter how close it sits to the verb.

subject: act-english
context_html: Serious birders comply <u>to</u> a strict code of ethics that discourages playing recorded calls near active nests.
stem_md: Which choice is most acceptable in standard written English?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Comply to' borrows the preposition from look-alike verbs such as 'conform to'; it is not the standard pairing.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Comply on' is not an established idiom in English and adds no coherent meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Against' signals opposition, reversing the sentence's meaning that birders follow the code.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the verb 'comply' idiomatically takes 'with' as its fixed preposition.

why_correct_md: The verb *comply* takes **with** as its fixed idiomatic partner.
why_tempted_md: 'Comply to' sounds plausible because related verbs like *conform to* and *adhere to* legitimately take *to*.
rule_md: 1) Spot the verb-plus-preposition pair. 2) Ask whether this is the fixed partner the verb always takes or one borrowed from a similar verb. 3) Test the pairing in a short sentence you trust. 4) Reject any preposition that changes or muddies the verb's meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: Common loons need a long stretch of open water to get airborne. <u>Similarly,</u> they seldom touch down on small ponds.
stem_md: Which transition word or phrase is most logical in context?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Similarly' claims the second sentence is a parallel fact, but it actually follows from the first as its effect.
per_choice_rationale.B: The second sentence is not an example of the takeoff requirement; it is what that requirement causes.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: needing a long watery runway is the cause, and avoiding small ponds is its effect.
per_choice_rationale.D: There is no opposition between the two statements; the second flows directly from the first.

why_correct_md: The second sentence states the **consequence** of the first, so a cause-and-effect transition fits.
why_tempted_md: Both sentences describe loon behavior, so 'Similarly' feels superficially right even though the logic is causal, not parallel.
rule_md: 1) Read the sentence before and the sentence after the transition. 2) State their relationship in your own words: cause, contrast, example, or addition. 3) Match the transition to that relationship. 4) Re-read with your choice inserted to confirm the logic clicks.

subject: act-english
context_html: The refuge closes its main trail during nesting season. <u>Even so,</u> visitors can still watch the herons from the observation deck across the channel.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the second sentence offers what remains possible despite the closure — a concessive relationship.
per_choice_rationale.B: The closure does not cause the deck viewing; the viewing persists in spite of the closure, so a causal word misstates the logic.
per_choice_rationale.C: The second sentence adds new, contrasting information rather than restating the closure in different words.
per_choice_rationale.D: The sentences are not parallel similar facts; the second pushes back against the limitation in the first.

why_correct_md: The second sentence tells what is still possible **despite** the closure, so a concessive transition is the logical link.
why_tempted_md: 'Therefore' attracts students who assume any two connected facts must be cause and effect.
rule_md: 1) Summarize each sentence in five words or fewer. 2) Ask: does the second sentence result from the first, restate it, resemble it, or push against it? 3) Select the transition class that matches. 4) Reinsert your choice and confirm the paragraph's logic survives.

subject: act-english
context_html: Every December, dozens of volunteers fan out across our county for the annual winter bird count. Working in teams from dawn to dusk, they tally every cardinal, crow, and kinglet they can find. Scientists then compare the totals with decades of earlier tallies to detect population shifts.
stem_md: The writer wants to conclude the paragraph with a sentence that emphasizes the lasting scientific value of the volunteers' work. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Some volunteers bring thermoses of hot cocoa to share during the long day.
Birds are also tallied during springtime surveys held throughout North America.
The county's first winter count was organized more than fifty years ago.
In this way, a single Saturday of counting by amateurs becomes part of a scientific record spanning generations.

per_choice_rationale.A: A cozy sidelight about snacks ignores the stated goal of emphasizing lasting scientific value.
per_choice_rationale.B: Broadening to other surveys elsewhere drifts away from this count and these volunteers.
per_choice_rationale.C: A founding date supplies history but never connects the volunteers' effort to ongoing science.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it explicitly ties one day of volunteer effort to the long-term data scientists depend on.

why_correct_md: Only this sentence links the volunteers' one-day effort to the **long-term scientific value** the stem demands.
why_tempted_md: The founding-date option feels weighty and historical, so students mistake age for scientific importance.
rule_md: 1) Underline the goal stated in the stem. 2) For each option, ask: does it address that exact goal, or something merely related? 3) Eliminate options that are on-topic but off-goal. 4) Pick the sentence that names the goal's key idea most directly.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] A spotting scope changes what a mudflat can reveal. [2] Through binoculars, distant shorebirds blur into gray specks against the shine. [3] At thirty-power magnification, however, those specks resolve into dowitchers stitching the mud like sewing machines. [4] Most birders eventually save up for a scope for exactly this reason.
stem_md: For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, the best placement for Sentence 1 is:

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: as the opening, it announces the claim that Sentences 2-4 then demonstrate and conclude.
per_choice_rationale.B: Inserted between the binocular problem and the scope payoff, it breaks the contrast that 'however' completes.
per_choice_rationale.C: After the demonstration, it merely repeats what readers just saw and leaves the paragraph without an opening claim.
per_choice_rationale.D: Placed after the wrap-up, it trails the conclusion and strands the paragraph with a detail-first start.

why_correct_md: The sentence is a **topic claim** that the binoculars-versus-scope demonstration then proves, so it belongs at the paragraph's head.
why_tempted_md: Because Sentence 1 seems to summarize the demonstration, students are tempted to move it after the dowitcher payoff as a wrap-up.
rule_md: 1) Identify the sentence's job: claim, evidence, or conclusion. 2) Find the sentences it must connect to (pointing words, contrast words). 3) Test each slot by reading the paragraph with the sentence there. 4) Keep the slot where every connector still points at its target.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Urban peregrine falcons treat skyscrapers as substitute cliffs. [2] A window ledge forty stories up mimics the rocky shelf where the species has always nested. [3] Pigeons, abundant in every downtown, supply the hunters with a steady food source. [4] City biologists, delighted by the arrangement, band dozens of falcon chicks on office towers each spring.
stem_md: The writer wants to add the following sentence to the paragraph: 'These city menus differ little from the pigeon-heavy diets of wild falcons on remote cliffs.' For the sake of logic and cohesion, the sentence should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: 'These city menus' has nothing to point back to — no food has been mentioned after the opening claim.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it directly follows the pigeon sentence, so 'these city menus' clearly refers to the food source just named.
per_choice_rationale.C: After the ledge sentence, the diet comparison interrupts the nesting discussion and precedes any mention of food.
per_choice_rationale.D: Parked after the banding sentence, the comparison trails the paragraph's shift to fieldwork and sits far from the food idea it develops.

why_correct_md: The pointer phrase **'these city menus'** must immediately follow the sentence that introduces the pigeons as food.
why_tempted_md: The added sentence also mentions cliffs, tempting students to attach it to the cliff-and-ledge sentences early in the paragraph.
rule_md: 1) Circle pointing words in the added sentence ('these,' 'this,' 'such'). 2) Find what they must refer back to. 3) Place the sentence immediately after that referent. 4) Re-read the paragraph to confirm no other idea is interrupted.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>After the rain stopped birders, gathered</u> at the marsh boardwalk to look for rails.
stem_md: Which choice correctly punctuates the underlined portion?

choices.label: After the rain, stopped birders gathered
After the rain stopped, birders, gathered
After the rain stopped, birders gathered

per_choice_rationale.A: Omits the comma after the introductory clause and inserts an intrusive one between subject and verb.
per_choice_rationale.B: Cuts the introductory clause short, turning 'stopped' into a strange adjective describing the birders.
per_choice_rationale.C: Adds the needed boundary comma but keeps the intruder splitting 'birders' from 'gathered.'
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: one comma closes the introductory clause, and nothing separates the subject from its verb.

why_correct_md: An **introductory dependent clause** takes a comma at its end, and no comma may split a subject from its verb.
why_tempted_md: Students who fix the missing boundary comma often overlook the second error — the stray comma after 'birders.'
rule_md: 1) Find where the introductory clause truly ends. 2) Place one comma there. 3) Locate the main subject and verb. 4) Confirm no comma stands between them. 5) Reject options that fix one error but keep the other.

subject: act-english
context_html: A pair of bald eagles has rebuilt the same nest each winter for a decade. By late March of this year, the <u>eagles nest</u> on the river bluff had grown to nearly a ton of stacked branches.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: With no apostrophe, 'eagles nest' reads as a plural noun plus a verb rather than as ownership.
per_choice_rationale.B: Places the apostrophe for a single owner and wrongly pluralizes the nest, though the passage describes two birds sharing one nest.
per_choice_rationale.C: Plural nouns already ending in s take only an apostrophe, not an added apostrophe-s.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the plural owners (the pair) take an apostrophe after the s, and the single nest stays singular.

why_correct_md: Two owners and one owned thing call for the **plural possessive** — apostrophe after the s, singular noun following.
why_tempted_md: The apostrophe-before-s habit is so automatic that students apply the singular pattern even when the passage clearly names a pair.
rule_md: 1) Rephrase as 'the ___ of the ___' to confirm possession. 2) Count the owners. 3) One owner: apostrophe before s. 4) Plural owners ending in s: apostrophe after s, nothing added. 5) Check that the owned noun keeps its true number.

subject: act-english
context_html: The trail <u>that loops past the beaver pond</u> offers the best chance of seeing wood ducks at first light.
stem_md: Which choice is most acceptable in standard written English?

choices.label: , that loops past the beaver pond,
, which loops past the beaver pond,
that loops past the beaver pond,

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the clause identifies which trail is meant, so it is restrictive — 'that' with no commas.
per_choice_rationale.B: That-clauses are restrictive by definition and are never set off with commas as asides.
per_choice_rationale.C: The comma-wrapped 'which' clause signals removable information, but this clause is essential to identifying the trail.
per_choice_rationale.D: A lone comma after the essential clause splits the subject from its verb.

why_correct_md: The clause is **restrictive** — it tells which trail — so it takes 'that' and no commas.
why_tempted_md: Comma-wrapped 'which' looks polished and formal, so students choose it without testing whether the clause is removable.
rule_md: 1) Cover the clause and read the sentence. 2) If the meaning loses its identity ('which trail?'), the clause is essential. 3) Essential: no commas. 4) Nonessential: commas plus 'which.' 5) Never split a subject from its verb with a single comma.

subject: act-english
context_html: Refuge biologists <u>estimate, that nearly</u> half of the mallard ducklings hatched along the dike survive their first summer.
stem_md: Which choice correctly punctuates the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: The comma intrudes between the verb and the clause that serves as its object.
per_choice_rationale.B: A colon may only follow a complete statement; 'Refuge biologists estimate' is an unfinished thought.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the reporting verb flows straight into its object clause with no punctuation.
per_choice_rationale.D: Doubles the intrusion, wrapping the essential connector in commas as if it were an aside.

why_correct_md: A verb runs **directly** into the clause that acts as its object; no punctuation belongs at that seam.
why_tempted_md: Students hear a spoken pause after 'estimate' and translate it into a comma, though grammar allows nothing there.
rule_md: 1) Ask what the verb needs to feel complete. 2) If the following clause answers 'estimate what?', it is the object. 3) Remove any punctuation between verb and object clause. 4) Reserve colons for after statements that could stand alone.

subject: act-english
context_html: As the fog thinned, a bittern <u>stood</u> at the edge of the reeds, bill tilted skyward, until it seemed to dissolve among the pale stems.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize how completely motionless the bittern remained. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Stood' states the bird's position but places no special stress on stillness.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Waited' stresses passing time and expectation rather than absolute stillness.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: it pictures the bird locked mid-motion — the strongest possible image of immobility.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Appeared' describes becoming visible, saying nothing about holding still and even implying movement into view.

why_correct_md: The goal is maximum **immobility**, and only this verb depicts the bird halted utterly in place.
why_tempted_md: 'Waited' tempts students because waiting implies standing in one spot for a long time, which feels close to stillness.
rule_md: 1) Restate the stem's goal in one word. 2) For each verb, ask what it emphasizes most: position, time, visibility, or stillness. 3) Cut every option whose core meaning misses the goal. 4) Choose the verb whose image delivers the goal hardest.

subject: act-english
context_html: In the hour before dawn, the marsh holds its breath. Then a lone sedge wren begins to sing, and one by one the reeds <u>get noisy with</u> answering voices.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the tone established in the passage?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Get noisy with' is flat and faintly negative, clashing with the hushed, lyrical mood.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Crank up with' is slangy and mechanical, breaking the quiet reverence of the scene.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: it extends the passage's gentle personification, matching 'the marsh holds its breath.'
per_choice_rationale.D: Stiff, clinical phrasing trades the passage's lyricism for lab-report language.

why_correct_md: The passage personifies the marsh tenderly, so the phrase must carry the same **lyrical** warmth.
why_tempted_md: 'Commence vocalization with' sounds elevated, and students often equate formality with good style even when it clashes with a poetic voice.
rule_md: 1) Name the passage's tone from its strongest image. 2) Test each option's register: slang, neutral, clinical, or lyrical. 3) Eliminate anything that breaks the spell in either direction — too casual or too technical. 4) Keep the phrase that sounds like the same writer throughout.

subject: act-english
context_html: All July, a single male rufous hummingbird ruled our back garden. He perched on the same bare twig between patrols, swooping at any rival that dared approach the bee balm. Watching his dives became the highlight of my mornings.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the second sentence: 'Hummingbird feeders should be rinsed with a vinegar solution every few days in hot weather.' Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it explains why the hummingbird returned to the garden each day.
Yes, because it gives readers practical advice they can apply at home.
No, because it interrupts a descriptive account with unrelated how-to instructions.
No, because it repeats details stated earlier in the paragraph.

per_choice_rationale.A: The maintenance tip says nothing about the bird's motivation — the bee balm explains the visits.
per_choice_rationale.B: Usefulness elsewhere cannot justify a sentence that abandons this paragraph's descriptive purpose.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the paragraph paints one bird's behavior, and a care tip derails that portrait.
per_choice_rationale.D: Feeder cleaning appears nowhere else in the paragraph, so the sentence cannot be repetitive.

why_correct_md: The paragraph is a **portrait of one bird's behavior**, and a maintenance tip breaks that focus entirely.
why_tempted_md: The advice is genuinely useful, so students reason that helpful information must be worth adding regardless of the paragraph's purpose.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's purpose in one phrase. 2) Ask whether the proposed sentence serves that purpose. 3) Check each option's reason for factual accuracy against the passage. 4) Choose the verdict whose reason is both true and decisive.

subject: act-english
context_html: When my uncle began birding in the 1970s, he carried a dog-eared field guide and a pocket notebook. Today, an app on my phone identifies a song in seconds and uploads each sighting to a global database. Researchers mine millions of these records to map migration in real time. What was once a solitary pastime has become a worldwide collaboration.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to show how new technology has transformed a long-standing pastime. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because the essay contrasts earlier birding tools with the digital methods that reshaped the hobby.
Yes, because the essay demonstrates that smartphone apps identify birds more accurately than human experts can.
No, because the essay focuses on one family's memories rather than on any form of technology.
No, because the essay argues that printed field guides remain superior to newer alternatives.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the essay moves from 1970s gear to app-and-database practice, directly showing the transformation.
per_choice_rationale.B: Right verdict, unsupported reason — the essay never compares app accuracy with expert accuracy.
per_choice_rationale.C: The family anecdote frames the essay, but technology's effect on the pastime is its through line.
per_choice_rationale.D: The essay celebrates the change; it never defends the old guides as superior.

why_correct_md: The essay's **then-versus-now structure** — notebook era to database era — is exactly the transformation the goal describes.
why_tempted_md: The accuracy claim sounds plausible because the app is praised, so students accept a 'yes' whose reason the essay never actually supports.
rule_md: 1) Restate the proposed goal. 2) Ask whether the essay as a whole pursues it. 3) Then verify each option's reason against specific sentences. 4) Reject any option whose verdict is right but whose reason misstates the passage.

subject: act-english
context_html: Our night hike began at the edge of the pine plantation, where the leader played a recording of a saw-whet owl. Within minutes, a real saw-whet answered from the dark canopy, its toots drawing closer with each exchange. The leader, a retired mail carrier, has guided these walks for nine years. When the tiny owl finally landed on a branch overhead, twenty flashlights stayed politely dark.
stem_md: The writer is considering deleting the sentence 'The leader, a retired mail carrier, has guided these walks for nine years.' Should the sentence be kept or deleted?

choices.label: Kept, because it explains how the leader first learned to attract owls.
Kept, because it adds a personal touch that makes the leader more relatable.
Deleted, because it breaks the mounting suspense of the owl's approach with a biographical aside.
Deleted, because the leader is not mentioned anywhere else in the paragraph.

per_choice_rationale.A: The sentence states tenure and a former job; it never explains how the leader learned to attract owls.
