per_choice_rationale.B: The relatable detail is real but minor, and it cannot outweigh stalling the narrative at its tensest point.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the encounter tightens sentence by sentence, and the career note halts that momentum mid-scene.
per_choice_rationale.D: Factually false — the paragraph's first sentence shows the leader playing the recording.

why_correct_md: The paragraph's power is its **narrative momentum**, and the biographical detour stalls the scene just as the bird closes in.
why_tempted_md: The 'personal touch' reason is genuinely true, so students keep the sentence without weighing what the interruption costs the scene.
rule_md: 1) Identify what the paragraph is building toward. 2) Ask what the candidate sentence contributes to that build. 3) Verify each option's reason against the passage's actual words. 4) Prefer the verdict whose reason is both accurate and decisive for this paragraph.

subject: act-english
context_html: The tide was falling <u>fast the godwits</u> followed the retreating waterline, probing each fresh strip of mud.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Fuses two independent clauses with no punctuation or conjunction at the seam.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses — that creates a splice.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a comma plus a coordinating conjunction legally joins the two independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.D: The semicolon joins the clauses correctly, but the added comma then splits the second subject from its verb.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses need a **comma plus a coordinating conjunction** (or a full stop) at the seam.
why_tempted_md: The semicolon version looks sophisticated, so students accept it without noticing the stray comma it plants after the subject.
rule_md: 1) Find every subject-verb pair. 2) Mark where one complete thought ends and the next begins. 3) At that seam, require a period, a semicolon, or comma-plus-conjunction. 4) Then proofread inside each clause for stray punctuation.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Although the refuge protects ten thousand acres, and its</u> wetlands still depend on water released from dams far upstream.
stem_md: Which choice results in the clearest, most effective sentence?

choices.label: Although the refuge protects ten thousand acres, its
The refuge protects ten thousand acres, its
Although the refuge protects ten thousand acres, so its

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Although' plus 'and' double-marks the link, leaving no clause free to stand as the main one — a fragment.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: one subordinator sets up the concession, and the second clause stands independent to complete the sentence.
per_choice_rationale.C: Dropping the subordinator leaves two independent clauses joined by a bare comma — a splice — and loses the concessive logic.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Although' and 'so' both mark the relationship, contradicting each other and again leaving no clean main clause.

why_correct_md: One relationship gets **one connector**: subordinate the first clause and let the second stand as the main clause.
why_tempted_md: The double-connector versions sound complete when read quickly, because each clause individually flows smoothly.
rule_md: 1) Count the clauses. 2) Count the connectors joining them. 3) Two clauses need exactly one link — a subordinator or a coordinator, never both. 4) Confirm one clause remains fully independent. 5) Re-read to check the logical relationship survives.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Crouching behind a driftwood log, the photographer</u> waited for the snowy plover to lead its chicks across the open sand.
stem_md: Which choice results in the clearest, most logical sentence?

choices.label: Crouching behind a driftwood log, the photographer's camera
Crouching behind a driftwood log, there was a photographer who
A driftwood log, which the photographer crouched behind,

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the doer of the crouching — the photographer — sits immediately after the modifier.
per_choice_rationale.B: Makes the camera the croucher; the possessive pushes the true doer out of the subject slot.
per_choice_rationale.C: Parks the empty placeholder 'there' where the doer belongs, leaving the modifier dangling.
per_choice_rationale.D: Hands the main verb to the log, so a piece of driftwood ends up waiting for the plover.

why_correct_md: An opening participial phrase must be followed **immediately** by the noun performing it — here, the photographer.
why_tempted_md: The possessive version keeps the word 'photographer' visible, so students miss that the grammatical subject has become the camera.
rule_md: 1) Find the opening action phrase. 2) Ask who or what performs that action. 3) Check the first noun after the comma. 4) If they do not match, the modifier dangles. 5) Also confirm the main clause's subject can logically do the main verb.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each April the same pair of tree swallows returns <u>back again</u> to claim the nest box beside the garden gate.
stem_md: Which choice is most acceptable in standard written English?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Returns back again' says the same thing three times — 'returns' already contains both the direction and the repetition.
per_choice_rationale.B: Swaps in more words but keeps the same double redundancy.
per_choice_rationale.C: Trims one echo yet still repeats the recurrence already established by 'Each April' and 'returns.'
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the sentence is complete and cleanest with nothing added.

why_correct_md: 'Each April' and 'returns' already express **direction and recurrence**, so any addition merely repeats them.
why_tempted_md: 'Once again' sounds idiomatic and shorter than the original, so students take it as the fix without testing it against the rest of the sentence.
rule_md: 1) List each idea inside the underlined span. 2) Scan the whole sentence for another word carrying the same idea. 3) Cross out every duplicated idea. 4) If nothing unique remains, the span itself is expendable — keep only words that add new meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: The festival's keynote speaker <u>made reference to the fact that</u> shorebird numbers have fallen sharply since the 1980s.
stem_md: Which choice results in the clearest, most effective sentence?

choices.label: made a notation of the fact that

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Made reference to the fact that' buries one verb's worth of meaning under five extra words.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: one precise reporting verb does the entire job.
per_choice_rationale.C: Even wordier, piling a noun phrase on top of the same padding.
per_choice_rationale.D: Keeps the empty 'the fact' padding and adds the unidiomatic 'of how.'

why_correct_md: **Concision** wins: a single direct verb replaces the five-word scaffold without losing any meaning.
why_tempted_md: The longer constructions sound official and speech-like, so students equate their bulk with formality.
rule_md: 1) Ask what action the phrase performs. 2) Try to say it in one verb. 3) If the one-verb version keeps the full meaning, the extra words are padding. 4) Watch especially for 'made ___ to' and 'the fact that' constructions — they usually hide a strong verb.

subject: act-english
context_html: The dawn chorus began <u>at that point in time</u> when the first robin sang from the top of the maple.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: at that particular point in time
at the point of the time

per_choice_rationale.A: 'At that point in time' is filler — the 'when' clause already fixes the moment.
per_choice_rationale.B: Adds 'particular,' stretching the filler even longer without adding meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: Reshuffles the same empty phrase into something clumsier and unidiomatic.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: 'began when the first robin sang' says everything with no padding.

why_correct_md: The **'when' clause** already pins down the moment, so the time phrase adds nothing but bulk.
why_tempted_md: 'At that point in time' is so common in speech that it sounds like normal, harmless phrasing rather than filler.
rule_md: 1) Read the sentence without the underlined phrase. 2) Ask whether any meaning disappeared. 3) If nothing was lost, the phrase is empty filler. 4) Prefer the version that keeps every unit of meaning in the fewest words.

subject: act-english
context_html: With its wings folded tight, the falcon <u>fell</u> toward the flock of starlings, reaching nearly two hundred miles an hour.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most precise word in context?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Fell' implies gravity acting on a passive object, not a hunter's deliberate attack.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Descended' is accurate but bland, suggesting a gentle, gradual drop rather than a strike.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Tumbled' means falling out of control — the opposite of a falcon's precision.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it names the swift, purposeful plunge of a hunting bird.

why_correct_md: Precision demands a verb of **deliberate, high-speed attack**, matching the folded wings and the two-hundred-mile-an-hour figure.
why_tempted_md: 'Descended' feels safe because it is formal and technically true, but it drains the speed and intent from the action.
rule_md: 1) List what the context tells you: speed, posture, purpose. 2) For each verb, ask whether it matches all three. 3) Cut verbs that add wrong ideas (accident, chaos, slowness). 4) Choose the verb whose core image fits the scene exactly.

subject: act-english
context_html: According to the refuge's annual report, volunteer participation <u>shot up like crazy</u> after the new boardwalk opened.
stem_md: Which choice is most consistent with the formal style of the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Shot up like crazy' is casual slang inside a sentence citing an official report.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: plain, precise wording matched to the report's formal register.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'To the max' is even more slangy than the original phrase.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Went through the roof' is an informal idiom that clashes with the documentary tone.

why_correct_md: A sentence attributing data to an official report needs **measured, formal** wording, not slang or idiom.
why_tempted_md: The colloquial idioms are vivid and familiar, so students mistake their energy for effective style.
rule_md: 1) Identify the sentence's register from its cues (here, a citation of an annual report). 2) Label each option: slang, idiom, neutral, or formal. 3) Eliminate anything the source document itself would never print. 4) Choose the option matching the established register.

subject: act-english
context_html: By the time the first network feed reached the valley in 1927, the Cole family <u>already owns</u> a six-tube console radio.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Present tense 'owns' clashes with the past-time frame set by 'By the time the first network feed reached the valley in 1927.'
per_choice_rationale.B: The bare participle 'owning' leaves the clause with no finite verb at all.
per_choice_rationale.C: Present perfect 'has owned' anchors the action to the present moment, but the sentence needs an action completed before another past event.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: past perfect places the family's ownership before the 1927 arrival of the network feed, the earlier of two past events.

why_correct_md: When one past event precedes another past event, the earlier one takes the **past perfect** (had + past participle).
why_tempted_md: The present perfect in 'has already owned' feels safely 'past,' so students miss that it ties the action to now instead of to 1927.
rule_md: 1) Circle every time marker (here: 'By the time... in 1927'). 2) List the two events and decide which happened first. 3) Put the earlier past event in past perfect (had + past participle) and the later one in simple past. 4) Reread the sentence to confirm the sequence sounds finished before 1927.

subject: act-english
context_html: Neither the faded schematics nor the original service manual <u>were</u> much help until Priya located the factory parts list.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Were' treats the neither/nor pair as a plural unit, but with neither/nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject, the singular 'manual.'
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Have been' is doubly wrong: plural agreement plus a perfect aspect that clashes with the past-tense narrative anchored by 'located.'
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'manual' (singular) and stays in the simple past to match 'located.'
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Are' breaks both the past time frame of the narrative and the nearer-subject agreement rule.

why_correct_md: With **neither/nor**, the verb agrees with the subject *nearer* to it — here the singular 'manual' — and must match the sentence's past time frame.
why_tempted_md: Two items joined by 'neither...nor' feel like a plural pair, so students default to a plural verb.
rule_md: 1) Spot the pair marker (neither/nor, either/or). 2) Underline the noun closer to the verb. 3) Match the verb's number to that noun alone. 4) Check the rest of the sentence for tense anchors and match them. 5) Reread with only the nearer subject: 'the manual ___ much help.'

subject: act-english
context_html: The station manager <u>insisted for the announcers to memorize</u> the sponsor's script before every broadcast.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard written English?

choices.label: insisted on the announcers to memorize

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Insisted for...to' forces an unidiomatic for...to construction onto a verb that never takes it.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Insisted on' is a real idiom, but it must be followed by a noun or gerund, never by a noun plus infinitive.
per_choice_rationale.C: Dropping the connective leaves a bare noun-plus-infinitive pattern that 'insist' does not allow.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: 'insist' reports a demand as a that-clause with the base-form (subjunctive) verb.

why_correct_md: 'Insist' takes its demand as a **that-clause** with a base-form verb, not a for...to or noun-plus-infinitive construction.
why_tempted_md: 'Insisted on' sounds familiar because it is a genuine idiom, so students accept it without noticing the infinitive stuck onto its object.
rule_md: 1) Identify the reporting verb ('insisted'). 2) Recall the patterns it allows: insist on + noun/gerund, or insist + that-clause with a base verb. 3) Test the sentence against each allowed pattern. 4) Reject any option that mixes patterns or invents a for...to frame. 5) Reread the survivor aloud to confirm it sounds like edited prose.

subject: act-english
context_html: Crystal sets needed no batteries and cost almost nothing to operate. <u>Therefore,</u> they were too weak to drive a loudspeaker, so the whole family shared one pair of headphones.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Therefore' claims the weakness follows logically from being cheap and battery-free, but the second sentence is a drawback, not a conclusion.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the second sentence cuts against the first sentence's advantages, so a contrast transition is needed.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Likewise' claims the second sentence parallels the first, but it actually opposes it.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'For example' promises an illustration of the first claim, but a limitation is not an example of low cost.

why_correct_md: The second sentence introduces a **drawback** that pushes against the first sentence's praise, so the transition must signal contrast.
why_tempted_md: 'Therefore' tempts students because the second sentence feels like it continues the description, but continuation is not the same as consequence.
rule_md: 1) Summarize sentence one in five words. 2) Summarize sentence two in five words. 3) Name the relationship: cause, contrast, example, or addition. 4) Pick the transition that names that same relationship. 5) Reread both sentences with your pick to confirm the logic clicks.

subject: act-english
context_html: In 1942, wartime production orders halted the manufacture of consumer radios, and replacement tubes all but vanished from store shelves. <u>Even so,</u> repair shops across the country began rebuilding burned-out tubes by hand.
stem_md: Which transition best expresses the relationship between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Even so' concedes an obstacle overcome despite the first sentence, but the shortage is the very cause of the hand-rebuilding, not an obstacle to it.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'In other words' signals restatement, but the second sentence reports a new development, not a paraphrase.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'By comparison' requires two items weighed against each other, and no second term of comparison exists here.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the tube shortage directly caused shops to start rebuilding tubes by hand, a cause-and-effect link.

why_correct_md: The second sentence is the direct **consequence** of the shortage described in the first, so a cause-and-effect transition is required.
why_tempted_md: 'Even so' is tempting because rebuilding tubes sounds like defying the shortage, when in fact the shortage is what forced the practice into being.
rule_md: 1) State sentence one as a plain fact. 2) Ask: did that fact cause, contradict, resemble, or get restated by sentence two? 3) Match your answer to a transition family (consequence, concession, comparison, restatement). 4) Substitute one transition from that family and reread. 5) Confirm no other family fits better.

subject: act-english
context_html: Live radio drama depended on improvised sound effects. A sheet of cellophane, crumpled near the microphone, became a crackling campfire; coconut shells clopped like horses on cobblestones; a knife driven into a cabbage stood in for grim business offstage. Technicians rehearsed these tricks as carefully as the actors rehearsed their lines.
stem_md: The writer wants to conclude the paragraph with a sentence that reinforces its main idea about the resourcefulness of sound-effects technicians. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Radio dramas eventually gave way to television in the 1950s.
Many radio actors later found steady work in film and television.
With nothing but everyday odds and ends, these artists could conjure a storm, a stampede, or a murder.
Cellophane, patented years earlier, had dozens of uses outside the studio.

per_choice_rationale.A: Pivots to the medium's later decline, abandoning the paragraph's subject of ingenious effects work.
per_choice_rationale.B: Spotlights the actors' future careers instead of the technicians the paragraph has been praising.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: it gathers the paragraph's examples into a closing statement about what the technicians could create from humble materials.
per_choice_rationale.D: Burrows into trivia about one prop rather than widening back to the technicians' inventiveness.

why_correct_md: A strong conclusion **circles back** to the paragraph's governing idea — here, the technicians' inventiveness with humble props — and generalizes it.
why_tempted_md: The historical note about television feels like a natural 'ending' because it closes the era, but it abandons the paragraph's actual subject.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's main idea in one clause. 2) Check each option: does it restate or extend that idea, or introduce a new subject? 3) Eliminate options about different people, later eras, or single details. 4) Pick the sentence that widens the examples back into the main idea. 5) Reread the paragraph with it in place.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Restorers begin by photographing the chassis from every angle before touching a single wire. [2] These photographs become the map they will follow during reassembly. [3] Only then do they pull the tubes, labeling each socket as they go. [4] Wax capacitors, the most frequent casualties of age, are replaced next. [5] Finally, the cabinet is cleaned and waxed with conservator-grade polish.
stem_md: For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, Sentence 2 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: 'These photographs' must directly follow Sentence 1, which introduces the photographing, and the map idea sets up the ordered steps that follow.
per_choice_rationale.B: Moving the sentence after the tube-pulling step separates 'These photographs' from its antecedent.
per_choice_rationale.C: Placing the purpose of the photographs after the capacitor stage strands the reference and interrupts the repair sequence.
per_choice_rationale.D: Putting a setup sentence after the job is finished leaves 'These' with nothing nearby to point to and previews a step already completed.

why_correct_md: The pointer phrase **'These photographs'** must sit immediately after the sentence that creates the photographs, and its map idea frames the steps that follow.
why_tempted_md: Because reassembly happens late in a restoration, students are tempted to push the map sentence toward the end, forgetting that 'These' needs its antecedent next door.
rule_md: 1) Find pointer words in the movable sentence ('These,' 'this,' 'such'). 2) Locate the sentence that introduces what they point to. 3) Keep the pointer sentence immediately after that antecedent. 4) Check that the paragraph's step order still reads first-to-last. 5) Reread the full paragraph to confirm cohesion.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] In the hobby known as DXing, listeners chase the faintest and most distant stations they can find. [2] A verified reception report, mailed back to the listener by the station itself, is the hobby's most coveted trophy. [3] The ionosphere settles after dark, letting weak signals skip for thousands of miles. [4] Veteran listeners therefore wait until well past midnight, in the depths of winter, to begin scanning the dial. [5] When a far-off station finally surfaces, they log its call sign and frequency and mail the station a detailed account of what they heard.
stem_md: For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, Sentence 2 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: As written, the station's mailed reply appears before the paragraph has described the listener's own letter, and it interrupts the definition-to-science flow.
per_choice_rationale.B: Between the ionosphere explanation and the 'therefore' that depends on it, the trophy sentence severs a welded cause-and-effect pair.
per_choice_rationale.C: At this point no station has been caught and no report mailed, so the station's reply is still premature.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: only after Sentence 5, where the listener mails the station an account, does a report 'mailed back by the station' logically follow as the payoff.

why_correct_md: The trophy sentence describes the station's **reply**, so it must follow the sentence in which the listener's own letter is written and mailed.
why_tempted_md: Leaving the sentence where it is feels fine because trophies sound like introductory color, but its 'mailed back' detail answers a letter the paragraph hasn't sent yet.
rule_md: 1) Identify what the movable sentence responds to (here: a letter being answered). 2) Find the sentence that supplies that prerequisite. 3) Place the movable sentence after the prerequisite, never before. 4) Check that no welded pairs (like a 'therefore' leaning on its cause) get split. 5) Reread the paragraph start to finish.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>After the last chime faded the</u> engineer cued the national anthem and signed off for the night.
stem_md: Which choice provides the best punctuation for the underlined portion?

choices.label: After the last chime faded, the
After the last chime, faded the
After, the last chime faded the

per_choice_rationale.A: With no comma, the introductory clause crashes into the main clause and readers momentarily parse 'faded the engineer.'
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: an introductory dependent clause is set off with a comma before the main clause begins.
per_choice_rationale.C: The comma lands inside the introductory clause, cutting it off from its own verb.
per_choice_rationale.D: A comma directly after 'After' severs the subordinating word from the clause it introduces.

why_correct_md: An **introductory dependent clause** takes a comma at its end, right before the main clause begins.
why_tempted_md: The original reads smoothly at a glance, so students skip the misreading trap where 'faded' momentarily grabs 'the engineer.'
rule_md: 1) Find the opening subordinating word. 2) Read forward to where that clause's own subject and verb end. 3) Place one comma there. 4) Confirm the main clause after the comma can stand alone. 5) Reread to check no comma sits inside either clause.

subject: act-english
context_html: Every August the Harris family hosts a swap meet for collectors, and folding tables of Bakelite sets crowd <u>the Harris' lawn</u> from dawn until dusk.
stem_md: Which choice correctly punctuates the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Harris'' marks possession on the singular name with a bare apostrophe, but the owners are the whole family, so the name must be pluralized first.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Harris's' is a correct singular possessive, but the sentence credits the entire family, not one person.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Harrises' pluralizes the family but includes no apostrophe, so it never shows ownership of the lawn.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: pluralize the name to 'Harrises,' then add the apostrophe after the s to mark plural possession.

why_correct_md: For a family name, **pluralize first, then mark possession**: Harris → Harrises → Harrises'.
why_tempted_md: The bare-apostrophe form looks like the familiar rule for words ending in s, so students apply it to the singular name without ever pluralizing.
rule_md: 1) Ask who owns the thing: one person or the whole family? 2) Write the correct plural of the name if the family owns it (add -es to names ending in s). 3) Add the possessive mark to that form (apostrophe after the plural s). 4) Reread to confirm both number and ownership are visible.

subject: act-english
context_html: Collectors especially prize radios<u>, which</u> still wear their original station-logo dials.
stem_md: Which choice is most acceptable for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: The comma-plus-'which' marks the clause as removable, but the clause defines which radios are prized, so it is essential.
per_choice_rationale.B: Even without the comma, standard test usage reserves 'which' for nonessential clauses; a defining clause takes the other relative.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the clause restricts the radios to those with original dials, so it takes 'that' with no comma.
per_choice_rationale.D: A comma never precedes 'that' introducing a restrictive clause; the two signals contradict each other.

why_correct_md: A clause that **defines** which items are meant is restrictive: it takes 'that' and no comma.
why_tempted_md: The comma-plus-'which' version sounds polished and formal, so students accept it without testing whether the clause can really be lifted out.
rule_md: 1) Drop the clause and reread. 2) If the sentence's meaning narrows or changes, the clause is essential. 3) Essential clause → 'that,' no comma. 4) Removable aside → comma + 'which.' 5) Never allow a comma directly before 'that.'

subject: act-english
context_html: Engineers soon discovered <u>that, shielding the power supply,</u> quieted the hum listeners had complained about for years.
stem_md: Which choice best punctuates the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: The paired commas fence off the gerund phrase as if it were an aside, but it is the subject of the embedded clause.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the gerund phrase flows straight from the connective to its verb 'quieted' with no intrusive punctuation.
per_choice_rationale.C: The single comma after the connective splits it from the very clause it introduces.
per_choice_rationale.D: The comma divides the embedded clause's subject from its own verb, a seam no lone comma may cross.

why_correct_md: No punctuation belongs around an **essential subject phrase**: the gerund is the subject of 'quieted' and must run unbroken from connective to verb.
why_tempted_md: The paired commas look like a tidy interrupter frame, so students never test whether the fenced material can actually be removed.
rule_md: 1) Find the embedded clause's verb ('quieted'). 2) Ask what performs that verb — that phrase is the subject. 3) Try lifting any comma-fenced material out; if the clause collapses, the fencing is illegal. 4) Remove commas that separate connective from clause or subject from verb. 5) Reread the clean version.

subject: act-english
context_html: When the red light blinked on, the announcer leaned toward the microphone and <u>let each syllable land like a struck bell</u>.
stem_md: The writer wants to convey the announcer's vocal precision through a vivid, concrete image. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: spoke with a great deal of clarity and self-control
pronounced his words in an impressively professional manner
made sure everything he said could be clearly understood by all

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the simile gives a concrete, audible image of each syllable's precision.
per_choice_rationale.B: Abstract nouns name the announcer's virtues without letting the reader see or hear anything.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Impressively professional' is an evaluation that tells rather than shows.
per_choice_rationale.D: This wordy option shifts to the audience's comprehension and carries no image of the delivery itself.

why_correct_md: The original simile is the only option that renders precision as a **sensory image** rather than a label or a judgment.
why_tempted_md: 'Clarity and self-control' sounds accurate and mature, so students mistake naming the quality for depicting it.
rule_md: 1) Restate the stem's goal in your own words (a vivid, concrete picture of precision). 2) For each option, ask: can I see or hear something specific? 3) Strike options that only evaluate, summarize, or describe effects on others. 4) Keep the option that plants a sensory image. 5) Reread it in context to confirm fit.

subject: act-english
context_html: Restoring the console became my grandfather's winter meditation. Replacing the brittle wax capacitors <u>was a real pain in the neck</u>, yet he never rushed a single joint of solder.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the tone established in the passage?

choices.label: was seriously the most annoying part of the whole deal
constituted an endeavor of considerable magnitude

per_choice_rationale.A: The breezy body-part idiom snaps the passage's quiet, reflective register.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: measured and specific, it matches the contemplative voice of 'winter meditation' and 'never rushed.'
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Seriously' and 'the whole deal' push even further into conversational slang.
per_choice_rationale.D: The inflated, bureaucratic diction overshoots the passage's modest register as badly as slang undershoots it.

why_correct_md: Tone must match the frame: the passage's **reflective, measured register** calls for plain but dignified wording, neither slangy nor pompous.
why_tempted_md: The grand-sounding 'constituted an endeavor of considerable magnitude' tempts students who equate formality with quality, but overshooting register is a tone error too.
rule_md: 1) Collect two or three tone-setting words from the surrounding sentences. 2) Name the register they establish (casual, conversational, measured, formal). 3) Test each option against that register in both directions — too loose and too grand both fail. 4) Choose the option that could have been written by the same voice. 5) Reread the paragraph with it in place.

subject: act-english
context_html: Sponsors' jingles in the 1940s went out over the air in real time, sung in the studio at the moment of broadcast. A small combo — piano, clarinet, and two singers — gathered around a single microphone. Their arrangement was rehearsed to fill exactly twenty seconds. The clarinetist, a former vaudeville player, had once toured with a circus band. When the second hand swept past twelve, the pianist counted off, and the jingle sailed out across the country.
stem_md: The writer is considering deleting the sentence 'The clarinetist, a former vaudeville player, had once toured with a circus band.' Should that sentence be kept or deleted?

choices.label: Kept, because it explains how the combo fit the jingles into exactly twenty seconds.
Kept, because it gives the musicians a vivid backstory that enlivens the scene.
Deleted, because the reader has already been told where the clarinetist trained.
Deleted, because it drifts from the paragraph's focus on how the jingles were performed live.

per_choice_rationale.A: The touring detail says nothing about timing, so this keep-reason claims a connection the sentence never makes.
per_choice_rationale.B: Vividness alone cannot justify a biographical detour in a paragraph tracing a studio routine.
per_choice_rationale.C: Right action, false premise: no earlier sentence mentions the clarinetist's training or background.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the sentence is an off-topic biographical aside in a paragraph devoted to the real-time studio routine.

why_correct_md: A sentence earns its place only by serving the paragraph's **controlling idea**, and this biographical aside serves a different subject entirely.
why_tempted_md: The backstory is genuinely charming, so students choose to keep it for color even though color is not the test.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's controlling idea in one clause. 2) Ask what job the target sentence does for that idea. 3) If it does none, it goes — then check each 'deleted' reason against the facts of the paragraph. 4) Reject reasons with false premises, even when their verdict is right. 5) Pick the reason that names the actual problem.

subject: act-english
context_html: The essay recounts Saturday mornings in the author's childhood kitchen, where a green enamel radio sat above the stove. The author describes her grandmother humming along to border-station ballads, the smell of toast, and the static that arrived with every thunderstorm. The essay closes with the author finding the same model radio at an estate sale decades later and carrying it home.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to trace how radio receiver design advanced from the 1920s through the 1950s. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it mentions a radio manufactured decades before the author found it.
Yes, because it shows the radio remained useful across two generations.
No, because it centers on personal memories rather than on changes in receiver design.
No, because it never gives the radio's model year or other design details.

per_choice_rationale.A: A single old radio appearing in an essay is a passing mention, not sustained coverage of design history.
per_choice_rationale.B: Durability across generations is a different claim from tracing how designs evolved.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the essay is a family reminiscence, so its subject matter never engages the stated technical goal.
per_choice_rationale.D: Right verdict, wrong reason: adding a model year would not turn a reminiscence into a survey of design history.

why_correct_md: Judging a purpose question means matching the essay's **actual subject** to the stated goal, and this essay's subject is family life, not engineering.
why_tempted_md: The no-verdict about missing product details tempts students because it is factually true of the essay, even though it misdiagnoses why the goal fails.
rule_md: 1) Restate the hypothetical goal in your own words. 2) Summarize what the essay actually spends its space on. 3) Decide yes/no by comparing the two subjects. 4) Then audit the reason: it must name the real match or mismatch, not an incidental fact. 5) Reject true-but-irrelevant reasons.

subject: act-english
context_html: Collectors often find hairline cracks spidering across the once-glossy cabinets of 1930s table radios. The damage rarely comes from rough handling; even sets stored carefully in closets for decades develop the same fine fractures. The explanation lies in the material itself.
stem_md: The writer wants to add a sentence here that explains why Bakelite cabinets crack even when carefully stored. Which choice provides information most relevant to that purpose?

choices.label: Bakelite was named for Leo Baekeland, the Belgian-born chemist who patented it in 1909.
Some collectors prefer wooden cabinets, which can be refinished with ordinary tools.
As Bakelite ages, it keeps curing, and the slow shrinkage stresses its molded corners.
Bakelite also turned up in telephone housings, costume jewelry, and billiard balls.

per_choice_rationale.A: Origin trivia about the inventor answers a history question, not the promised why.
per_choice_rationale.B: A preference for wooden cabinets swaps the subject and explains nothing about the plastic's behavior.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: it supplies the internal mechanism that produces cracks even in carefully stored sets.
per_choice_rationale.D: A catalog of other products shows versatility but gives no cause for the fractures.

why_correct_md: The paragraph promises a cause inside the material, so the relevant addition is the one that supplies that **mechanism**.
why_tempted_md: The inventor fact feels authoritative and on-brand, so students mistake background information for explanation.
rule_md: 1) Read the sentence before the insertion point and name the question it raises. 2) Demand that the added sentence answer exactly that question. 3) Eliminate options that give history, comparisons, or lists of uses. 4) Keep the option describing what physically happens. 5) Reread the paragraph to confirm the promise is paid off.

subject: act-english
context_html: The clear-channel signal faded within an hour of sunset<u>; the operators</u> switched the evening feed to a relay tower in the foothills.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: a semicolon legally joins the two independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.B: A bare comma between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.C: With no punctuation at all, the two independent clauses fuse into a run-on.
per_choice_rationale.D: A transitional phrase after a comma does not repair the splice; the joint is still just a comma.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses may be joined by a **semicolon**; a comma alone — with or without a transitional phrase — cannot carry that load.
why_tempted_md: The version with 'as a result' tempts students because adding logic words feels like adding grammatical glue, but the underlying comma splice survives.
rule_md: 1) Test each half: can it stand alone as a sentence? 2) If both can, list the legal joints: period, semicolon, or comma + coordinating conjunction. 3) Check the option's actual punctuation against that list, ignoring any logic words. 4) Reject bare commas and missing punctuation. 5) Reread the survivor.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Although the station's tower stood barely sixty feet tall, its signal carried</u> across the valley on clear winter nights.
stem_md: Which choice is most logical and grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: Although the station's tower stood barely sixty feet tall, but its signal carried
The station's tower stood barely sixty feet tall, its signal carried
Because the station's tower stood barely sixty feet tall, its signal carried

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: one subordinator sets up the concession, and the main clause delivers the surprising reach.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Although... but' doubles the connectors, leaving the sentence with two dependent-feeling halves and no main clause.
per_choice_rationale.C: Dropping the connector leaves two independent clauses spliced by a comma and erases the logical relationship.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Because' claims the tower's small size caused the long reach, reversing the sentence's logic of surprising contrast.

why_correct_md: One **concessive subordinator** plus one main clause expresses the intended surprise: a small tower whose signal nonetheless traveled far.
why_tempted_md: 'Although... but' tempts students because both words feel like they reinforce the contrast, when in fact each pair of clauses allows only one connector.
rule_md: 1) Count the clauses. 2) Count the connecting words — a clause pair gets exactly one. 3) Name the logical relationship the sentence intends (cause, contrast, concession). 4) Confirm the surviving connector expresses that relationship. 5) Verify one clause remains fully independent.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Hoping to hear the championship broadcast, the radio was tuned by Marta</u> a full hour before airtime.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: Hoping to hear the championship broadcast, the dial was set by Marta
Hoping to hear the championship broadcast, Marta tuned the radio
Hoping to hear the championship broadcast, Marta's radio was tuned

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening modifier attaches to 'the radio,' which cannot hope — a classic dangler.
per_choice_rationale.B: Swapping in 'the dial' changes the noun but not the problem; a dial cannot hope either.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the hoper, Marta, stands immediately after the modifier as the clause's subject.
per_choice_rationale.D: A noun buried in a possessive cannot anchor the modifier; the subject is still the radio.

why_correct_md: An opening participial phrase must attach to the **very next noun**, so the person doing the hoping must be the subject of the main clause.
why_tempted_md: The possessive version tempts students because Marta's name appears right after the comma, hiding that the true subject is still the radio.
rule_md: 1) Read the opening phrase and ask who performs its action. 2) Look at the first noun after the comma. 3) If they don't match, the modifier dangles. 4) Beware possessives: an owner inside another noun doesn't count as the subject. 5) Choose the version whose after-the-comma noun is the true performer.

subject: act-english
context_html: By June the chassis work was <u>completely finished in its entirety</u>, and only the cabinet still needed attention.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most concise without losing information?

per_choice_rationale.A: Both 'completely' and 'in its entirety' restate what 'finished' already guarantees — a double redundancy.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the verb alone carries the full meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Completely' repeats the completion already built into 'finished.'
per_choice_rationale.D: 'In its entirety' is the same redundancy as 'completely,' dressed as a prepositional phrase.

why_correct_md: 'Finished' is an **absolute**: modifiers that restate its built-in completion add words but no information.
why_tempted_md: Keeping 'completely' feels like added emphasis, so students treat the intensifier as meaningful rather than redundant.
rule_md: 1) Ask what the verb already guarantees by definition. 2) Test each modifier: does it add information or repeat the verb's meaning? 3) Delete every repeater, one at a time. 4) Reread to confirm nothing factual was lost. 5) Keep the leanest version that still says everything.

subject: act-english
context_html: Replacement tubes, <u>owing to the fact that they had become scarce</u>, often cost more than the radios they were meant to revive.
stem_md: Which choice best eliminates wordiness while preserving the meaning?

choices.label: because of their having become scarce
being that they are now scarce

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Owing to the fact that' is a six-word runway carrying no information of its own.
per_choice_rationale.B: The possessive-gerund construction rearranges the baggage without lightening it.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a two-word appositive delivers the scarcity and its cause-flavor with no scaffolding.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Being that' is nonstandard, and the clause it drags in restates what a bare description shows.

why_correct_md: Concision keeps only the **idea itself**: a compact appositive conveys the scarcity without connective scaffolding.
why_tempted_md: 'Because of their having become scarce' feels like a real revision since the wording changed, but the word count and machinery barely did.
rule_md: 1) Isolate the single idea the phrase must express. 2) Count the words each option spends on it. 3) Strike options using scaffolding formulas ('the fact that,' 'being that'). 4) Check the shortest survivor still preserves the meaning and fits grammatically. 5) Reread the sentence with it in place.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>As a matter of fact, the</u> first commercial broadcasting license in the United States was issued in 1920.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence clearest and most direct?

choices.label: It is actually a fact that the

per_choice_rationale.A: 'As a matter of fact' is throat-clearing that adds nothing to the sentence's content.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'In point of fact' is the same filler formula in different clothes.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the sentence states its fact plainly with no empty preamble.
per_choice_rationale.D: The expletive frame 'It is actually a fact that' certifies its own sentence — the emptiest kind of filler.

why_correct_md: **Empty openers** that announce a fact before stating it can be deleted with zero loss of meaning.
why_tempted_md: Filler openers sound conversational and confident, so students read them as emphasis instead of padding.
rule_md: 1) Cover the opening phrase and reread the sentence. 2) Ask: did any information disappear? 3) If nothing disappeared, the opener is filler — cut it. 4) Repeat for any candidate replacement. 5) Keep the version that starts with the real subject.

subject: act-english
context_html: Static <u>crackled</u> through the speaker grille whenever lightning flashed over the ridge.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most precise word for the context?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the onomatopoeic verb captures the abrupt, spitting character of storm interference.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Occurred' is an all-purpose event verb that erases the sound entirely.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Emerged' implies gradual coming-into-view, the wrong sense for sudden bursts.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Was heard' is a flat passive that reports reception, not the noise's texture.

why_correct_md: Precision means the verb carries the **specific character** of the action — here, the abrupt texture of storm static.
why_tempted_md: 'Was heard' tempts students because it is unimpeachably grammatical, but grammatical safety is not the same as exactness.
rule_md: 1) Picture the action the sentence describes. 2) For each verb, ask what specific manner it conveys. 3) Eliminate all-purpose verbs that could describe anything. 4) Eliminate verbs whose manner contradicts the scene. 5) Keep the verb whose sense matches the event exactly.

subject: act-english
context_html: In his 1901 reports to investors, Marconi maintained that transatlantic signaling <u>was going to be a pretty big deal</u> for shipping companies.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the formal register of the sentence?

choices.label: would represent a majorly significant development

per_choice_rationale.A: 'A pretty big deal' is a casual idiom badly out of place in formal reports to investors.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: measured, businesslike diction that fits the investor-report frame.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Bound to be huge' stays at conversational pitch, trading one casual idiom for another.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Majorly' is a colloquial intensifier that contaminates an otherwise formal phrase — a register mix.

why_correct_md: Register must match the frame: **formal business context** demands measured diction with no colloquial intruders.
why_tempted_md: The 'majorly significant development' option sounds elevated at a glance, so students miss the single slang intensifier buried inside it.
rule_md: 1) Identify the sentence's frame and its formality level ('reports to investors' = formal). 2) Test each option word by word against that level. 3) Reject any option containing even one colloquial word, however formal its wrapper. 4) Reject options that are entirely casual. 5) Keep the option whose every word fits the frame.

subject: act-english
context_html: By the time the final round began, the young challenger <u>studies</u> hundreds of her opponent's earlier games.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Present tense ignores the past time marker 'By the time the final round began,' which sets the whole sentence in the past.
per_choice_rationale.B: Past perfect correctly places the studying before another completed past event, the start of the final round.
per_choice_rationale.C: Present perfect anchors an action to the present moment, but the sentence's reference point is a past event.
per_choice_rationale.D: Future perfect points the action forward toward a coming deadline, the opposite of the backward-looking sequence the sentence needs.

why_correct_md: The **past perfect** places the studying before another completed past event ('began').
why_tempted_md: 'has studied' sounds finished, so students miss that present perfect ties an action to now rather than to a moment in the past.
rule_md: 1) Find the time marker ('By the time X began'). 2) Decide when the underlined action happened relative to that marker. 3) If the action finished before a past event, use had + past participle. 4) Reread the sentence with the marker to confirm the sequence of events.

subject: act-english
context_html: The lineup of challengers seeking the three qualifying spots <u>have narrowed</u> steadily since the opening weekend.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: The plural verb agrees with the nearby nouns 'challengers' and 'spots' instead of the true singular subject 'lineup.'
per_choice_rationale.B: The head subject is the singular 'lineup,' so the singular verb is required despite the plural nouns packed in between.
per_choice_rationale.C: Switching to a progressive form does not fix the agreement error: the verb is still plural while the subject is singular.
per_choice_rationale.D: The passive construction misreads the sentence's gradual, active shrinking and still pairs a plural verb with a singular subject.

why_correct_md: The subject is the singular **lineup**, so the verb must be singular.
why_tempted_md: 'challengers' and 'spots' sit right before the verb, luring the ear into plural agreement with the wrong noun.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb. 2) Ask 'who or what does this?' and cross out prepositional and participial phrases ('of challengers,' 'seeking the three qualifying spots'). 3) Match the verb to that bare subject's number. 4) Reread subject and verb alone to confirm they agree.

subject: act-english
context_html: Federation rules prohibit players <u>to consult</u> engines or printed notes during adjourned games.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: The infinitive borrows the pattern of the near-synonym 'forbid'; 'prohibit' never takes 'to' plus a base verb.
per_choice_rationale.B: Standard idiom pairs 'prohibit' with 'from' plus a gerund: prohibit someone from doing something.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Against' belongs to verbs like 'warn' and 'advise'; it is not the fixed partner of 'prohibit.'
per_choice_rationale.D: Stretching the infinitive into a progressive keeps the wrong pattern and adds needless words.

why_correct_md: Standard idiom pairs **prohibit** with 'from' plus an -ing form.
why_tempted_md: 'forbid players to consult' is standard English, so the infinitive sounds fine after the near-synonym 'prohibit.'
rule_md: 1) Circle the verb that controls the idiom ('prohibit'). 2) Recall its fixed pattern: prohibit + object + from + -ing verb. 3) Swap the pattern in and reread. 4) If unsure, test it in a simple sentence: 'The law prohibits me from parking here.'

subject: act-english
context_html: Blitz chess rewards instinct and nerve. <u>Therefore,</u> classical time controls give players hours to verify every idea.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Therefore' claims the second sentence results from the first, but no cause-and-effect chain connects them.
per_choice_rationale.B: The second sentence is not an example of blitz rewarding instinct; it introduces an opposing format.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Likewise' asserts similarity, but the two sentences describe opposite approaches to time and thought.
per_choice_rationale.D: The sentences oppose each other — speed and instinct versus hours of verification — so a contrast word is needed.

why_correct_md: The sentences **oppose** each other — instinct and speed versus hours of verification — so a contrast transition is required.
why_tempted_md: 'Likewise' tempts because both sentences describe chess formats, and that surface similarity masks the reversal in meaning.
rule_md: 1) Read the sentence before and the sentence after the transition. 2) State their relationship in your own words: cause, contrast, example, or restatement. 3) Match the transition word to that relationship. 4) Reread with your pick to confirm the logic clicks.

subject: act-english
context_html: Arbiters rarely rule on a touch-move dispute without first hearing both players. <u>In addition,</u> at last spring's open, the chief arbiter questioned four witnesses before deciding the fate of a single knight.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'In addition' treats the anecdote as a brand-new coordinate point, but it actually illustrates the general claim just made.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Nevertheless' signals contradiction, yet the arbiter's careful questioning confirms, rather than opposes, the first sentence.
per_choice_rationale.C: The second sentence gives one specific case of the general habit described in the first, so an illustration transition fits.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'In other words' promises a restatement, but the anecdote adds a concrete new scene rather than paraphrasing the claim.

why_correct_md: The second sentence offers a **specific case** that illustrates the general claim in the first.
why_tempted_md: 'In addition' tempts because the anecdote does feel like more information, masking that it illustrates rather than adds a new point.
rule_md: 1) Label the first sentence: general claim or specific detail? 2) Label the second sentence the same way. 3) General followed by specific calls for an illustration transition; general followed by a new general point calls for an addition word. 4) Reread with your choice and check the logic.

subject: act-english
context_html: Ten years ago, our district had two school chess clubs; today it has fourteen. Streaming broadcasts have introduced thousands of students to the game, and teachers report waiting lists for after-school boards. Local shops have even begun stocking tournament sets.
stem_md: The writer wants to conclude the paragraph with a sentence that reinforces its main idea. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: The district also plans to renovate several gymnasiums this year.
Checkers clubs, by contrast, have not grown at all.
In this district, chess has clearly moved from the margins to the mainstream.
Chess pieces were once carved from bone and ivory.

per_choice_rationale.A: Renovated gymnasiums introduce an unrelated facilities topic instead of closing the paragraph's account of the game's growth.
per_choice_rationale.B: A pivot to a different game shifts the emphasis away from the paragraph's subject, which never mentions other games.
per_choice_rationale.C: It restates the paragraph's central point — the game's rapid local growth — as a closing generalization.
per_choice_rationale.D: Historical trivia about antique pieces points backward in time and ignores the paragraph's present-day claim.

why_correct_md: It restates the paragraph's central point — the game's rapid local **growth** — in a closing generalization.
why_tempted_md: The checkers comparison tempts because contrast can feel like a punchy ending, yet the paragraph never discusses other games.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's main idea in one phrase. 2) Test each candidate closer: does it restate or reinforce that idea? 3) Reject closers that open new topics, pivot to other subjects, or shrink to trivia. 4) Confirm the survivor echoes the paragraph's opening claim.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Simultaneous exhibitions test a master's stamina as much as her skill. [2] The master walks a ring of boards, pausing at each one just long enough to move. [3] Her opponents, meanwhile, enjoy the length of a full lap to plan a reply. [4] Some exhibitions stretch past six hours and cover more than forty boards. [5] At every stop, she has only seconds to read the position before circling on.
stem_md: For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, Sentence 5 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Stranded after the statistics about hours and board counts, 'At every stop' loses the walking scene it depends on.
per_choice_rationale.B: Placed before the paragraph describes the master walking a ring of boards, the phrase 'every stop' has no referent.
per_choice_rationale.C: The sentence elaborates Sentence 2's board-to-board pausing and sets up the contrast with the opponents' full lap in Sentence 3.
per_choice_rationale.D: Placing it after the opponents' full lap reverses the contrast that 'meanwhile' is built on, forcing the reader backward.

why_correct_md: The sentence expands on the master's **board-to-board pace** and must precede the contrasting note about her opponents' full lap.
why_tempted_md: Leaving it where it is tempts because the sentence still makes literal sense at the end, hiding the broken link to the walking scene.
rule_md: 1) Find the words in the movable sentence that depend on other sentences ('every stop,' 'she,' 'circling on'). 2) Locate the sentence that introduces those ideas. 3) Place the movable sentence immediately after its anchor. 4) Reread the paragraph to confirm each contrast lands in order.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] The Riverbend Chess Society began in 1987 with six members and a borrowed classroom. [2] Its founder, a retired mail carrier, bought the club's first clocks himself. [3] Meetings moved twice before the society settled into the old firehouse on Grant Street. [4] For years, the group's only trophy was a hand-painted pawn. [5] Last season, Riverbend entered the state league for the first time. [6] Its top board won nine straight matches against far larger clubs. [7] The society now hosts the very qualifier it once only dreamed of attending.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide this paragraph into two, with the first paragraph focusing on the society's humble early years and the second on its recent rise. The most logical place to begin the second paragraph is at:

per_choice_rationale.A: Splitting after the opening line severs the founder's clock purchase from the founding story it belongs to.
per_choice_rationale.B: The move into the old firehouse is still part of the club's scrappy early history, not its recent success.
per_choice_rationale.C: The hand-painted pawn is the clearest image of the humble era; breaking before it strands that detail in the wrong paragraph.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Last season' pivots both the time frame and the topic, launching the account of the club's recent breakthrough.

why_correct_md: 'Last season' marks the spot where **time frame and topic shift together**, from humble origins to recent success.
why_tempted_md: The trophy sentence tempts as a break point because a trophy suggests success, but a hand-painted pawn actually epitomizes the modest years.
rule_md: 1) Label each sentence by era and topic. 2) Find the seam where both the time frame and the subject change at once. 3) Begin the new paragraph at the first sentence of the new era. 4) Reread both halves to confirm each is unified.

subject: act-english
context_html: Priya <u>Raman, the club's newest arbiter,</u> settled the dispute over the fallen king in under a minute.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: The appositive 'the club's newest arbiter' is extra, removable information, so it is correctly enclosed by a pair of commas.
per_choice_rationale.B: Dropping the opening comma leaves the aside fenced on only one end, so the description crashes into the name.
per_choice_rationale.C: Dropping the closing comma lets the aside run into the main verb, obscuring where the sentence resumes.
per_choice_rationale.D: Removing both commas treats a removable description as essential identification, which the named subject does not need.

why_correct_md: A **nonrestrictive appositive** must be enclosed by a matched pair of commas.
why_tempted_md: Dropping the second comma tempts because the voice barely pauses there when the sentence is read quickly.
rule_md: 1) Find the descriptive phrase and try deleting it. 2) If the sentence still identifies its subject, the phrase is extra. 3) Fence extra phrases with commas on both ends, like brackets. 4) Reread, lifting the phrase out, to confirm the frame is complete.

subject: act-english
context_html: When the rapid tiebreak finally ended, the arbiter collected both <u>grandmaster's scoresheets</u> for the federation archive.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: The apostrophe before the s marks a single owner, but 'both' tells us two players own the scoresheets.
per_choice_rationale.B: With no apostrophe at all, nothing signals that the scoresheets belong to the players.
per_choice_rationale.C: Two owners require the plural possessive: the apostrophe follows the plural -s of the owners, and the owned noun stays a plain plural.
per_choice_rationale.D: The owned noun 'scoresheets' possesses nothing, so it takes no apostrophe of its own.

why_correct_md: With two owners, the **plural possessive** places the apostrophe after the plural -s.
why_tempted_md: The singular possessive tempts because 'grandmaster's' looks routine and the word 'both' sits far enough away to be overlooked.
rule_md: 1) Count the owners (the word 'both' says two). 2) Write the owners' plural form first. 3) Add the apostrophe after the plural -s. 4) Check the owned noun: if it owns nothing, leave it a plain plural.

subject: act-english
context_html: The rule <u>which</u> lets a pawn capture in passing confuses many beginners.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: The clause is essential to identifying the rule, and standard written English reserves the comma-free 'that' for essential clauses.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma turns the clause into a droppable aside, but without it the sentence cannot say which rule confuses beginners.
per_choice_rationale.C: The essential relative pronoun never follows a comma in standard English.
per_choice_rationale.D: The clause is essential identification, so it takes 'that' with no comma.

why_correct_md: An **essential** clause identifying the noun takes 'that' with no comma.
why_tempted_md: Keeping the original pronoun tempts because 'which' often sounds more formal, masking the essential-versus-extra distinction.
rule_md: 1) Delete the clause mentally and reread. 2) If the sentence no longer identifies its subject, the clause is essential. 3) Essential clauses take 'that' and no commas; extra clauses take a comma plus 'which.' 4) Reread with your choice to confirm the meaning survives.

subject: act-english
context_html: The trophy that the state <u>federation awards, goes</u> to the highest scorer under eighteen.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: The comma severs the subject 'The trophy that the state federation awards' from its verb 'goes,' a break no single comma may make.
per_choice_rationale.B: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and 'goes to the highest scorer under eighteen' cannot stand alone.
per_choice_rationale.C: This comma slices the inner clause's subject from its verb, mangling the identifying clause.
per_choice_rationale.D: No punctuation belongs anywhere in this stretch: the subject flows directly into its verb.

why_correct_md: No punctuation may separate a subject from its verb, so the stretch must run **unbroken**.
why_tempted_md: The original comma tempts because the long identifying clause creates a natural spoken pause right before the verb.
rule_md: 1) Find the main verb. 2) Trace back to the full subject, including any identifying clause attached to it. 3) Confirm no comma or semicolon stands between subject and verb. 4) Reread the sentence without pausing to verify it flows as one clause.

subject: act-english
context_html: Down to her final five minutes, Anaya <u>watched</u> the tangled position, hunting for the one move that might save her.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize how intensely Anaya searched the position for a saving idea. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'watched' is emotionally flat, reporting mere looking rather than the strained, effortful search the goal demands.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'examined' is studious but temperate — a calm, clinical word that misses the intensity the writer wants.
per_choice_rationale.C: It conveys close, critical, effortful inspection, matching the stated goal of emphasizing intensity.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'observed' casts Anaya as a detached bystander, the opposite of a player straining for a save.

why_correct_md: The goal demands the verb conveying the most **intense**, effortful inspection of the position.
why_tempted_md: 'examined' tempts because it sounds appropriately studious, yet it stays clinical and calm rather than intense.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's goal in one word (here: intensity). 2) Rank each verb by how strongly it conveys that quality. 3) Eliminate verbs that are neutral, detached, or merely accurate. 4) Pick the survivor and reread the sentence to confirm the emphasis lands.

subject: act-english
context_html: In his memoir, the former champion recounts each defeat with measured candor, examining <u>the miscalculations that cost him decisive games</u>.
stem_md: Given that all the choices are accurate, which one best maintains the essay's measured, formal tone?

choices.label: the bonehead moves that totally tanked his biggest games
the harrowing blunders that forever shattered his fragile spirit
the suboptimal decision outcomes occurring in high-stakes contest scenarios

per_choice_rationale.A: The plain, precise phrasing matches the essay's measured candor: formal without inflation, direct without drama.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'bonehead' and 'tanked' are slang, snapping the essay's calm, formal register.
per_choice_rationale.C: Melodramatic language ('forever shattered his fragile spirit') overheats a passage defined by restraint.
per_choice_rationale.D: Bureaucratic jargon ('decision outcomes,' 'contest scenarios') inflates the diction, trading candor for stiffness.

why_correct_md: The original phrasing already matches the essay's **measured**, formal register — precise, calm, and direct.
why_tempted_md: The jargon-heavy version tempts because piled-up formal-sounding nouns can masquerade as sophistication.
rule_md: 1) Find the passage's tone cues ('measured candor'). 2) Sort each option by register: slang, melodrama, jargon, or plain formal. 3) Eliminate anything more casual, more emotional, or more inflated than the cues. 4) Keep the phrasing that matches the passage's own temperature.

subject: act-english
context_html: For decades, tournament games ended in frantic scrambles, players slamming pieces and punching clocks as their final seconds drained away. Digital clocks changed that by granting a small time bonus after every completed move. At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence: "Even a player down to two seconds can survive indefinitely by moving quickly enough."
stem_md: Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it clarifies how the bonus eliminates the scrambles described earlier.
Yes, because it proves digital clocks cost less than the analog clocks they replaced.
No, because it repeats a point already made earlier in the paragraph.
No, because it shifts the paragraph's focus to the etiquette of casual games.

per_choice_rationale.A: The sentence shows concretely how the time bonus ends the frantic scrambles, directly extending the paragraph's point.
per_choice_rationale.B: The verdict is right, but the reason invents a price comparison the paragraph never makes.
per_choice_rationale.C: The two-second scenario is new information; nothing earlier explains what happens to a player almost out of time.
per_choice_rationale.D: The sentence stays squarely on tournament timekeeping; it mentions nothing about etiquette or casual play.

why_correct_md: The sentence **clarifies the mechanism** — how the bonus ends the scrambles — so both the verdict and the reason fit the paragraph.
why_tempted_md: The repetition claim tempts because the sentence circles back to the scramble idea, disguising that its two-second detail is entirely new.
rule_md: 1) Decide independently whether the proposed sentence helps the paragraph's point. 2) Check each option's verdict against your decision. 3) Then check each reason against the passage: is it factually true, and does it describe what the sentence actually does? 4) Keep only the option where verdict and reason are both accurate.

subject: act-english
context_html: Sixteen-year-old Mira Adeyemi wakes at five to review endgame flashcards before school. Afternoons belong to her coach, who drills one opening line until Mira can recite its traps blindfolded. In the final month before the national championship, she plays practice matches against partners chosen to mimic her likely opponents. By the eve of the event, she says, the work is done; all that remains is to sleep well.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to outline how a single young competitor prepares for a major tournament. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because the essay describes the training habits of several rival champions.
Yes, because the essay concentrates on a single competitor's training methods.
No, because the essay never explains how chess ratings are calculated.
No, because the essay focuses on a single player rather than covering many.

per_choice_rationale.A: The verdict is right, but the reason misdescribes the essay, which follows only Mira, not several rivals.
per_choice_rationale.B: The essay tracks one young player's preparation step by step, exactly matching the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.C: Rating math is a side topic the goal never asks for; its absence is irrelevant to whether the goal is met.
per_choice_rationale.D: This reason faults the essay for doing precisely what the goal requests: profiling one player's preparation.

why_correct_md: The essay does exactly what the goal asks: it **profiles one player's preparation** from dawn drills to the eve of the event.
why_tempted_md: The single-player objection tempts because narrow scope often sounds like a flaw, even when the goal explicitly asks for that narrow scope.
rule_md: 1) Restate the hypothetical goal in your own words, noting its scope. 2) Summarize what the essay actually does. 3) Compare the two: match means yes, mismatch means no. 4) Then verify the winning option's reason accurately describes the essay itself.

subject: act-english
context_html: Weeknight traffic on the largest chess servers now peaks just as American high schools let out. In a survey of one large district, half the varsity roster reported playing at least ten online blitz games a day.
stem_md: The writer wants to add a sentence that supports the paragraph's focus on why online blitz appeals to teenagers. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: A full game fits into the gap between homework assignments, and a rematch is always one tap away.
Several veteran grandmasters have publicly refused to play blitz online.
The same servers also offer correspondence games that unfold over several weeks.
Blitz thrived in city parks and coffeehouses long before the internet existed.

per_choice_rationale.A: It supplies concrete reasons for the appeal — speed and instant rematches — directly supporting the paragraph's focus.
per_choice_rationale.B: Grandmasters opting out says nothing about teenagers and, if anything, points away from the appeal.
per_choice_rationale.C: A slower format on the same servers is a catalog detail that never explains why fast games attract teens.
per_choice_rationale.D: Pre-internet history is on-topic but answers no question about what draws today's students.

why_correct_md: It gives a concrete **reason for the appeal** — games that fit teenagers' pockets of free time — which is exactly what the focus needs.
why_tempted_md: The historical note tempts because it is genuinely about blitz, hiding that it explains nothing about modern teenagers' attraction to it.
rule_md: 1) Write the paragraph's focus as a question ('Why does online blitz appeal to teens?'). 2) Test each option: does it answer that exact question? 3) Reject details that are merely on the same topic without answering the question. 4) Confirm the survivor adds a reason, not just a fact.

subject: act-english
context_html: The final position looked dead <u>drawn, but neither player would offer</u> the customary handshake.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: drawn, however, neither player would offer

per_choice_rationale.A: A comma plus the coordinating conjunction correctly joins the two independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.B: A lone comma between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.C: Removing all punctuation and connectors fuses the two independent clauses together.
per_choice_rationale.D: A conjunctive adverb set off by commas cannot join independent clauses; it leaves a splice behind.

why_correct_md: A comma plus a **coordinating conjunction** is a legal weld between two independent clauses.
why_tempted_md: The conjunctive-adverb version tempts because the interrupter sounds formal and the commas look busy enough to be doing the joining.
rule_md: 1) Count the independent clauses (find each subject-verb pair that could stand alone). 2) Inspect the seam between them. 3) Accept only: comma + coordinating conjunction, semicolon, or period. 4) Reject a bare comma, no punctuation, or comma-wrapped adverbs at the seam.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Because it was the oldest trophy in the federation's vault, the silver rook was</u> left out of an exhibit meant to celebrate the federation's proudest history.
stem_md: Which choice most effectively expresses the logical relationship between the ideas in the sentence?

choices.label: Although it was the oldest trophy in the federation's vault, the silver rook was
The silver rook was the oldest trophy in the federation's vault, it was
Because of it being the oldest trophy in the federation's vault, the silver rook was

per_choice_rationale.A: The causal connector claims the trophy's age explains its exclusion, but a history exhibit would be expected to feature its oldest treasure.
per_choice_rationale.B: A concession connector correctly signals that the exclusion defies what the trophy's status leads us to expect.
per_choice_rationale.C: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses, and dropping the connector erases the relationship entirely.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Because of it being' is nonstandard in formal prose and still asserts cause where the sentence implies contradiction.

why_correct_md: A **concession** connector signals that the exclusion runs against what the trophy's status would lead us to expect.
why_tempted_md: The causal opener tempts because age could plausibly explain many things, hiding that a history exhibit should prize its oldest piece.
rule_md: 1) Read the two ideas and predict: given the first, what outcome would you expect? 2) If the actual outcome matches the expectation, a cause connector fits. 3) If the outcome defies the expectation, use a concession connector. 4) Check the join is also grammatical: a subordinate clause attached to a full main clause.

subject: act-english
context_html: Arriving an hour before the first round, <u>the veteran claimed her favorite table</u> beside the tall windows.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: her favorite table was claimed by the veteran
the veteran's favorite table was claimed
it was the veteran who claimed her favorite table

per_choice_rationale.A: The person who arrived — the veteran — stands immediately after the opening modifier, exactly where the doer belongs.
per_choice_rationale.B: The passive makes the table the subject, so the opening phrase absurdly describes furniture arriving early.
per_choice_rationale.C: A possessive cannot serve as the doer; this version leaves no one performing the arrival.
per_choice_rationale.D: The placeholder 'it' sits where the doer belongs, leaving the opening modifier dangling.

why_correct_md: The **doer of the opening modifier** — the veteran — correctly stands right after the comma.
why_tempted_md: The passive version tempts because every word is still present, obscuring that the subject slot now holds furniture instead of the person who arrived.
rule_md: 1) Find the opening modifier and ask who performs its action. 2) Look at the noun immediately after the comma. 3) If that noun is not the performer, the modifier dangles. 4) Choose the version that puts the performer in the subject slot, then reread.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each spring, the lakeside invitational <u>returns again for another year</u> to the same resort where it began.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most concise without changing its meaning?

choices.label: returns once more for another year

per_choice_rationale.A: 'again' and 'for another year' both restate the yearly repetition that 'Each spring' already establishes.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'once more for another year' is the same doubled repetition in different clothes.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'back' is built into the verb itself, so the pair says one thing twice.
