per_choice_rationale.D: The bare verb carries the full meaning once 'Each spring' has established the repetition.

why_correct_md: 'Each spring' already establishes the repetition, so the bare verb is the only **non-redundant** option.
why_tempted_md: The two-word version tempts because it trims most of the phrase while quietly keeping a duplicated direction inside it.
rule_md: 1) Circle every word in the underlined portion. 2) For each, ask: is this idea already stated elsewhere in the sentence or inside the verb itself? 3) Delete every duplicate. 4) Reread to confirm no meaning was lost.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>In light of the fact that</u> engines can evaluate any position instantly, commentators now spend broadcasts explaining ideas rather than reporting moves.
stem_md: Which choice best avoids wordiness while preserving the meaning of the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: Five words of packaging perform the job of a single causal connector.
per_choice_rationale.B: This merely swaps one 'the fact that' scaffold for its twin, keeping the padding.
per_choice_rationale.C: The single-purpose connector states the cause relationship with no padding.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'In consideration of how' is both inflated and off-meaning, turning a cause into a manner.

why_correct_md: A single **causal connector** does the entire job of the five-word scaffold.
why_tempted_md: 'Owing to the fact that' tempts because it sounds elevated, so students mistake its formality for concision.
rule_md: 1) Ask what relationship the underlined phrase expresses (here: cause). 2) Flag scaffolds built on 'the fact that' as padding. 3) Substitute the plainest connector that expresses the same relationship. 4) Reread to confirm the meaning is untouched.

subject: act-english
context_html: The chess club <u>meets on Thursdays</u> in the library annex.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most effective wording?

choices.label: meets, as a rule, on Thursdays
basically meets on Thursdays, for all intents and purposes,
meets, as it happens, on Thursdays

per_choice_rationale.A: The wording is already lean and exact; every word carries information.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'as a rule' hedges a plain fact without qualifying anything real.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'basically' and 'for all intents and purposes' are empty intensifiers stacked on a simple statement.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'as it happens' is a filler aside that interrupts the sentence while adding nothing.

why_correct_md: Every word in the original carries **information**; each alternative inserts empty filler.
why_tempted_md: 'as a rule' tempts because schedules do have exceptions, so a hedge feels responsibly cautious even though it adds no facts.
rule_md: 1) Read each option and underline any word not stating a fact. 2) Delete the underlined words mentally and reread. 3) If the meaning is identical, those words were filler. 4) Keep the version where nothing can be deleted without losing meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: Her queen sacrifice <u>lured</u> White's rook onto a square from which it could never escape.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely conveys how the sacrifice affected the rook?

per_choice_rationale.A: The original verb means enticing a target into danger with bait — exactly what a sacrifice does to an enemy piece.
per_choice_rationale.B: Persuasion implies convincing a mind with reasons; a wooden rook cannot weigh an argument.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'placed' hands her direct control of an opponent's piece, which the rules of the game forbid.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'sent' implies dispatching something under one's own command; no player commands the opponent's rook.

why_correct_md: The original verb precisely captures the **bait-and-trap** mechanism: the rook is tempted into danger, not moved by her hand.
why_tempted_md: 'persuaded' tempts because it preserves the sense of influence, hiding that persuasion requires a mind capable of being reasoned with.
rule_md: 1) Identify who controls each piece in the sentence. 2) Ask what the subject literally did: move the object, command it, or tempt it? 3) Match the verb to that exact mechanism. 4) Reread and check the verb's literal meaning against the scene.

subject: act-english
context_html: Analysts agreed that, after five hours of precise defense, the defending champion <u>totally botched</u> a drawn endgame in one careless moment.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the formal style of the essay?

per_choice_rationale.A: The casual intensifier 'totally' and the slangy verb clash with the sentence's analytic voice.
per_choice_rationale.B: A single restrained verb reports the error in the same formal register as 'analysts agreed' and 'precise defense.'
per_choice_rationale.C: 'goofed up' is schoolyard slang, even further from the essay's register.
per_choice_rationale.D: The kitchen idiom is breezy and conversational, mismatched with a measured match report.

why_correct_md: The formal context calls for **restrained diction**, and this verb reports the error without slang or idiom.
why_tempted_md: Keeping the original tempts because 'totally botched' is vivid and clear, so its casual register slips past the ear.
rule_md: 1) Identify the passage's register from its surrounding vocabulary. 2) Label each option: slang, idiom, casual intensifier, or formal diction. 3) Eliminate every option below the passage's register. 4) Reread the sentence with the survivor to confirm the voice stays even.

subject: act-english
context_html: In 1981, marine biologists on the Great Barrier Reef documented mass coral spawning for the first time; until that night, most researchers <u>have assumed</u> that corals released their eggs quietly throughout the year.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Present perfect claims the assumption continues into the present, but 'until that night' seals the belief in the past (misconception: present_perfect_for_completed_past).
per_choice_rationale.B: Past perfect correctly places the outdated belief before the 1981 documentation, matching the 'until that night' cutoff.
per_choice_rationale.C: Present tense contradicts the passage's past time frame set by the 1981 date (misconception: general_truth_present).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Would have' injects a hypothetical condition the sentence never states; the belief really existed (misconception: would_have_for_real_past).

why_correct_md: Past perfect marks a belief that ended **before** another past event — the 1981 documentation.
why_tempted_md: 'Have assumed' sounds natural read aloud, but present perfect quietly claims the assumption still holds today.
rule_md: 1) Find the time anchors in the sentence (here, a dated past event). 2) Ask whether the underlined action ended before, during, or after that anchor. 3) If it ended before another past event, use past perfect (had + past participle). 4) Reject any tense that drags the action into the present or adds a hypothetical the sentence never states.

subject: act-english
context_html: The dense network of symbiotic algae packed inside a coral's translucent tissues <u>supply</u> the animal with up to ninety percent of its energy.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: The plural verb agrees with the nearby nouns 'algae' and 'tissues' instead of the true singular subject 'network' (misconception: sv_nearest_noun).
per_choice_rationale.B: Still plural, and the progressive aspect is wrong for a standing biological fact (misconception: sv_nearest_noun plus needless progressive).
per_choice_rationale.C: The singular verb agrees with the head noun of the subject, 'network,' once the prepositional phrases are stripped away.
per_choice_rationale.D: Plural again, and the perfect aspect wrongly treats an ongoing general truth as a completed past action (misconception: sv_nearest_noun plus tense shift).

why_correct_md: The verb must agree with the **head noun** of the subject — the singular 'network' — not with nouns inside prepositional phrases.
why_tempted_md: The plural nouns 'algae' and 'tissues' sit directly before the verb, luring the ear toward a plural form.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb. 2) Cross out every prepositional phrase between the start of the subject and the verb. 3) The noun left standing is the true subject — mark it singular or plural. 4) Match the verb's number to that noun. 5) Separately confirm the tense fits a general fact (simple present) rather than a finished or ongoing event.

subject: act-english
context_html: New harbor regulations prohibit charter captains <u>to anchor</u> anywhere along the shallow reef flat, where a single dragged chain can shear off decades of growth.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: The infinitive follows the pattern of 'forbid,' but 'prohibit' never takes an infinitive (misconception: idiom_pattern_transfer_forbid).
per_choice_rationale.B: Standard English fixes the idiom as 'prohibit someone from doing something.'
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In' belongs to verbs like 'succeed' and 'persist,' not 'prohibit' (misconception: wrong_fixed_preposition).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Against' transfers from warning verbs like 'warn' and 'advise'; a legal ban uses a different fixed preposition (misconception: idiom_pattern_transfer_warn).

why_correct_md: The verb 'prohibit' is **idiomatically fixed**: it takes its own required preposition plus an '-ing' form, never an infinitive.
why_tempted_md: 'Forbid captains to anchor' is standard, so students transfer that infinitive pattern onto the near-synonym 'prohibit.'
rule_md: 1) Circle the verb and the word(s) that follow it. 2) Recall the verb's fixed pattern by testing it in a simple sentence you trust. 3) Check whether near-synonyms ('forbid,' 'warn') use a different pattern — do not borrow theirs. 4) Choose the option matching the verb's own idiom, not one built from logic.

subject: act-english
context_html: Parrotfish grind mouthfuls of coral skeleton with fused, beak-like teeth, digesting the algae and excreting the leftover minerals as fine white grains. <u>However,</u> a single large parrotfish can generate hundreds of pounds of sand in a year.
stem_md: Which transition word best expresses the relationship between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'However' signals contrast, but the second sentence follows from the first rather than opposing it (misconception: transition_wrong_logic_contrast).
per_choice_rationale.B: The sand production is the direct outcome of the grinding and excreting described first — a cause-and-effect link.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For example' requires a general claim followed by an illustration; the first sentence makes no broad claim being illustrated (misconception: transition_false_example).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Meanwhile' marks two events unfolding at the same time in different places, not a causal chain (misconception: transition_time_for_logic).

why_correct_md: The second sentence states the **effect** of the grinding described in the first, so a cause-and-effect transition is required.
why_tempted_md: The surprising statistic feels contrast-worthy, so 'However' seems to fit even though nothing is being opposed.
rule_md: 1) Read the sentence before and the sentence after the transition. 2) Label the relationship in your own words: opposes, illustrates, follows from, or happens alongside. 3) Match that label to the transition's job. 4) Reject any connector whose job doesn't match your label, no matter how smooth it sounds.

subject: act-english
context_html: Shallow-water corals starve without sunlight, since the algae in their tissues must photosynthesize to feed their hosts. <u>Likewise,</u> the cold-water corals of the deep North Atlantic build sprawling mounds in total darkness, snaring drifting plankton with their tentacles.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Likewise' claims the second sentence parallels the first, but sunlight-dependence and life in total darkness are opposing conditions (misconception: transition_false_similarity).
per_choice_rationale.B: The two sentences set opposite feeding strategies against each other, so an opposition transition is correct.
per_choice_rationale.C: Nothing about shallow corals' need for light causes deep corals to trap plankton; there is no causal chain (misconception: transition_false_cause).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'In other words' promises a restatement, but the second sentence introduces new, opposing information about a different group (misconception: transition_false_restatement).

why_correct_md: The sentences **oppose** each other — light-dependent feeding versus feeding in total darkness — so the connector must flag a difference.
why_tempted_md: Both sentences describe corals feeding, so the surface similarity of topic makes a likeness transition feel right even though the two strategies clash.
rule_md: 1) Summarize each sentence in five words or fewer. 2) Ask: does the second echo, oppose, follow from, or restate the first? 3) Ignore shared topic words — judge the logic, not the vocabulary. 4) Pick the transition whose job matches the logic you identified.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] The bleaching begins invisibly, with stressed corals expelling the colorful algae that both feed and tint them. [2] Within weeks the reef fades to a ghostly white, and if warm water lingers, the starved animals die. [3] Scientists once thought such events were rare, but severe bleaching now strikes many reefs several times a decade.
stem_md: The writer wants an opening sentence that introduces the paragraph's focus on coral bleaching as a gradual, escalating process. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Coral reefs are among the most biologically diverse ecosystems on the planet.
Warm water is only one of many threats that reefs face today.
Divers often describe the eerie beauty of a freshly bleached reef.
Coral bleaching unfolds in stages, each one pushing a reef closer to collapse.

per_choice_rationale.A: A generic praise of reef diversity ignores the paragraph's specific focus on the stages of bleaching (misconception: intro_too_broad).
per_choice_rationale.B: It shifts attention to the range of threats rather than the single escalating process the paragraph traces (misconception: intro_wrong_focus).
per_choice_rationale.C: It fixes on divers' aesthetic reactions, a side detail absent from the paragraph's body (misconception: intro_offtopic_detail).
per_choice_rationale.D: It names bleaching as a staged, worsening process, framing the step-by-step description that follows.

why_correct_md: The paragraph traces bleaching **stage by stage**, so the opener must announce a gradual, escalating process.
why_tempted_md: The diversity sentence sounds like a natural reef-topic opener, but it never mentions bleaching or its progression.
rule_md: 1) Read the whole paragraph and state its single controlling idea in one phrase. 2) List what the body sentences actually cover. 3) Choose the opener that both names that idea and sets up the body. 4) Reject openers that are broader than the paragraph, shift its focus, or fixate on a side detail.

subject: act-english
context_html:
[1] Restoring a damaged reef often begins in an underwater nursery. [2] Technicians clip finger-sized fragments from healthy colonies and fasten them to floating frames. [3] After months of sheltered growth, the hardened fragments are cemented onto the degraded reef. [4] There they fuse and spread, slowly rebuilding the living structure.

Divers monitor each transplant for signs of disease.
stem_md: The writer wants to place the sentence 'Divers monitor each transplant for signs of disease' where it best supports the paragraph's chronological account of reef restoration. The sentence should most logically be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Placing it first introduces monitoring transplants before any transplant has been described, stranding the reference (misconception: order_reference_before_referent).
per_choice_rationale.B: After Sentence 1 the nursery process hasn't started, so 'each transplant' still has no antecedent (misconception: order_premature_detail).
per_choice_rationale.C: After Sentence 2 the fragments are only on nursery frames, not yet transplanted, so monitoring transplants is premature (misconception: order_step_out_of_sequence).
per_choice_rationale.D: After Sentence 4 the fragments have been cemented and are spreading, so monitoring the finished transplants is the logical final step.

why_correct_md: The sentence refers to 'each transplant,' which only exists **after** the fragments are cemented onto the reef in Sentence 4.
why_tempted_md: The monitoring sentence mentions transplants and disease, so it feels at home early beside the hands-on nursery work in Sentence 2.
rule_md: 1) Identify the sequence the paragraph follows (here, chronological steps). 2) Note the key referring words in the movable sentence ('each transplant'). 3) Find where in the sequence that referent first exists. 4) Place the sentence right after that point, never before its referent appears.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Coral polyps look deceptively simple, resembling tiny upside-down jellyfish anchored to a stony cup. [2] Each polyp secretes calcium carbonate around its base, and generation after generation cements new layers onto the old. [3] Over centuries these layers accumulate into the massive limestone ridges we call reefs. [4] A whole reef, then, is really the collective skeleton of billions of these minuscule builders. [5] Tourism built on reefs generates billions of dollars for coastal economies each year. [6] Dive operators, hotels, and restaurants all depend on the reefs staying healthy and vivid.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide this text into two paragraphs so that each has a single clear focus. The second paragraph should begin at:

per_choice_rationale.A: Sentences 1 and 2 both describe the polyp's structure and secretion, so splitting between them cuts one idea in half (misconception: divide_mid_topic).
per_choice_rationale.B: Sentence 3 continues the same reef-building process begun in Sentence 2, so the topic hasn't shifted yet (misconception: divide_too_early).
per_choice_rationale.C: The focus turns from how reefs are built (1–4) to their economic value (5–6) exactly at Sentence 5.
per_choice_rationale.D: Sentences 5 and 6 both concern reef tourism, so dividing between them splits the new topic (misconception: divide_too_late).

why_correct_md: The text shifts from the **biology of reef-building** (Sentences 1–4) to **reef economics** (Sentences 5–6) at Sentence 5.
why_tempted_md: Sentence 6 lists specific businesses, so it feels like a fresh start even though it merely extends the tourism idea introduced in Sentence 5.
rule_md: 1) Give each sentence a one-word topic tag. 2) Scan the tags for the point where the topic clearly changes. 3) Start the new paragraph at the first sentence of the new topic. 4) Do not divide within a run of sentences sharing one topic, whether early or late.

subject: act-english
context_html: The reef's night shift includes hunting moray eels, tentacled feather stars, and <u>brittle stars, which</u> unfurl their arms to sift the current for food.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English punctuation?

per_choice_rationale.A: The comma correctly closes the series and sets off the nonrestrictive 'which' clause describing brittle stars.
per_choice_rationale.B: Dropping the comma before a nonrestrictive 'which' clause fuses the description onto the noun (misconception: missing_nonrestrictive_comma).
per_choice_rationale.C: The extra comma after 'which' wrongly separates the relative pronoun from its own verb (misconception: comma_splits_subject_verb).
per_choice_rationale.D: The comma after 'which' interrupts the clause while omitting the needed comma before it (misconception: comma_misplaced_in_clause).

why_correct_md: A nonrestrictive 'which' clause takes a comma **before** it and no comma splitting the pronoun from its verb.
why_tempted_md: The clause feels like a natural pause point, tempting an extra comma after 'which' that actually severs subject from verb.
rule_md: 1) Confirm the 'which' clause adds extra, nonessential information — if so, it needs a comma before it. 2) Read from 'which' to its verb; never drop a comma between them. 3) Check that the comma sits before 'which,' not after it. 4) Keep the series comma that separates the final list item.

subject: act-english
context_html: The survey team compared several <u>species' recovery rates</u> after the storm, noting that the fastest-growing corals had also suffered the heaviest breakage.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Species' is both singular and plural; here it is the plural possessor, so a plural possessive apostrophe after the final 's' is correct.
per_choice_rationale.B: Omitting the apostrophe drops the possession the sentence needs — the rates belong to the species (misconception: missing_possessive_apostrophe).
per_choice_rationale.C: Adding 's after a word already ending in 's' overworks the possessive for this plural form (misconception: double_s_possessive).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Specie' means coined money, not an organism; the singular of the biological term is still 'species' (misconception: false_singular_backformation).

why_correct_md: 'Species' spelled the same in singular and plural takes a **plural possessive** apostrophe after its final 's' when several species possess the rates.
why_tempted_md: Because 'species' looks singular, students reach for 's or invent 'specie,' not realizing the word is already plural here.
rule_md: 1) Decide whether the possessor is singular or plural in meaning. 2) Note that 'species' keeps the same spelling for both. 3) For a plural possessor ending in 's,' add only an apostrophe after that 's.' 4) Never invent a new singular ('specie') or double the 's' for a word already ending in one.

subject: act-english
context_html: Among the thousands of anemones scattered across the reef, a clownfish will settle only in the one <u>which</u> matches the chemical scent it memorized as a drifting larva.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Which' introduces the clause here, but standard usage reserves 'which' for nonrestrictive, extra-information clauses (misconception: which_for_restrictive).
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma after the relative pronoun severs it from its verb 'matches' (misconception: comma_splits_pronoun_verb).
per_choice_rationale.C: The comma wrongly sets off a clause that is essential to identify which anemone (misconception: comma_before_restrictive).
per_choice_rationale.D: The essential clause pins down which single anemone the clownfish chooses, so it is restrictive and takes 'that' with no comma.

why_correct_md: An essential clause that identifies **which** anemone is restrictive, so it uses 'that' and no comma.
why_tempted_md: 'Which' feels interchangeable with 'that,' so students keep it even when the clause is essential.
rule_md: 1) Decide whether the clause is needed to identify the noun. 2) If removing it would blur which thing is meant, the clause is restrictive. 3) Restrictive clauses take 'that' and no comma. 4) Reserve 'which' — and its comma — for clauses that merely add extra detail.

subject: act-english
context_html: The bold stripes of a reef fish may <u>serve as camouflage because</u> they break up its outline against the dappled coral, confusing a predator's aim.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English punctuation?

per_choice_rationale.A: No punctuation is needed: 'because' introduces a tightly bound reason clause with no pause before it.
per_choice_rationale.B: The comma before 'because' wrongly separates an essential reason clause from the main clause (misconception: comma_before_because).
per_choice_rationale.C: The paired commas box off 'as camouflage,' which is an integral part of the verb phrase (misconception: intrusive_appositive_commas).
per_choice_rationale.D: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but 'because they break up its outline' is subordinate (misconception: semicolon_before_subordinate).

why_correct_md: A 'because' clause that gives an essential reason attaches **without** any punctuation before it.
why_tempted_md: A long sentence invites a breath-mark, so a comma before 'because' feels natural even though it splits bound elements.
rule_md: 1) Read the underlined stretch and ask whether any pause is grammatically required. 2) Remember that a 'because' clause giving an essential cause attaches directly, with no comma. 3) Reserve semicolons for two complete sentences. 4) Do not box off words the verb phrase needs. 5) If every mark you add merely interrupts bound elements, use none.

subject: act-english
context_html: During a population explosion, a swarm of crown-of-thorns starfish can <u>eat</u> a healthy reef faster than it can regrow, leaving bleached skeletons where vivid coral stood only weeks before.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize how voraciously and destructively the starfish consume the reef. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Eat' is accurate but flat, conveying none of the destructive intensity the writer wants to stress (misconception: neutral_word_misses_goal).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Consume' is precise but clinical, adding no sense of ferocity or speed (misconception: formal_but_flat).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Devour' carries the greedy, rapid destruction the writer wants to emphasize.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Nibble' suggests dainty, harmless eating — the opposite of the intended emphasis (misconception: opposite_connotation).

why_correct_md: The chosen verb must carry a connotation of **greedy, rapid** eating that matches the goal of stressing destruction.
why_tempted_md: 'Eat' is the plain, safe verb, so students keep it without weighing the emphasis the stem asks for.
rule_md: 1) Reread the stated goal and name the exact impression the word must create. 2) For each option, describe its connotation, not just its dictionary meaning. 3) Discard words that are neutral, clinical, or opposite in feeling. 4) Keep the word whose connotation matches the goal most vividly.

subject: act-english
context_html: A thriving reef is startlingly noisy, alive with the crackle of snapping shrimp and the low drumming of fish; researchers now believe that drifting coral larvae <u>home in on this racket</u> to choose where they will settle and grow.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the passage's tone, which is scientific yet richly descriptive?

choices.label: vibe out to these sick beats
navigate toward this chorus of sound

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Racket' carries a negative, unpleasant connotation that clashes with the passage's admiring, vivid description (misconception: tone_negative_word).
per_choice_rationale.B: The slang is far too casual for the passage's scientific register (misconception: register_too_colloquial).
per_choice_rationale.C: The phrase is both precise and vivid, matching the passage's blended tone.
per_choice_rationale.D: The stiff, bureaucratic 'utilize said' is too clinical for the passage's lively description (misconception: register_too_stilted).

why_correct_md: The phrase must keep the passage's balance of **scientific accuracy and vivid imagery**.
why_tempted_md: 'Racket' fits the loud-reef idea, so its casual negativity slips past students focused only on meaning.
rule_md: 1) Characterize the passage's tone in two words (here, precise and vivid). 2) For each option, judge its register and connotation against that tone. 3) Reject wording that is slangy, coldly technical, or negatively colored. 4) Keep the phrasing that is both accurate and evocative.

subject: act-english
context_html: As the ocean absorbs more of the carbon dioxide humans release, its surface water grows slightly more acidic. That shift makes the carbonate minerals corals need for their skeletons harder to pull from the water, so corals must burn extra energy just to grow at their normal pace. With less energy to spare, they reproduce and heal more slowly.
stem_md: At this point the writer is considering adding the following sentence: 'Carbon dioxide is also the gas people breathe out with every exhale.' Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it reminds readers where the ocean's carbon dioxide originally came from.
Yes, because relating the gas to the reader's own breathing makes the science feel more personal.
No, because the sentence introduces an off-topic fact that strays from the paragraph's focus on acidification.
No, because the paragraph has already told readers how carbon dioxide enters the ocean.

per_choice_rationale.A: The added sentence doesn't actually explain where the ocean's carbon comes from; it just states a biological trivium, so this justification misreads it (misconception: add_false_justification).
per_choice_rationale.B: A personal connection can't rescue a detail that derails the paragraph's scientific argument (misconception: add_relevance_overridden_by_interest).
per_choice_rationale.C: The exhale detail is a tangent that pulls attention from the paragraph's explanation of how acidification harms corals, so it should be left out.
per_choice_rationale.D: The paragraph never explains how carbon dioxide enters the ocean, so this reason is factually wrong (misconception: add_misreads_passage).

why_correct_md: A sentence belongs only if it serves the paragraph's point; this tangent **distracts** from the acidification argument.
why_tempted_md: The exhale fact is true and vaguely on-theme, so it feels like a friendly way to hook the reader.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's single controlling point. 2) Ask whether the candidate sentence advances that point or merely relates to the topic loosely. 3) If it pulls attention elsewhere, keep it out — interest alone is not relevance. 4) Reject any justification that misdescribes what the sentence or paragraph actually says.

subject: act-english
context_html: A living reef is more than a tourist attraction; it is a wall. As swells roll in from the open sea, the reef's rough, branching structure absorbs and scatters their energy, so that only gentle water reaches the shore behind it. Scientists estimate that healthy reefs can cut incoming wave energy by up to ninety-seven percent, sparing shorelines from erosion and flooding. Where reefs have died, the beaches behind them have begun to wash away.
stem_md: Which of the following best describes the primary purpose of the passage?

choices.label: To contrast the recreational value of reefs with their scientific value.
To trace the biological steps by which a coral reef is built.
To explain how reefs shield coastlines from the force of ocean waves.
To urge coastal communities to abandon low-lying beaches.

per_choice_rationale.A: The passage mentions tourism only in passing and never contrasts two kinds of value (misconception: purpose_minor_detail_as_main).
per_choice_rationale.B: The passage covers what reefs do for the coast, not how they grow (misconception: purpose_wrong_topic).
per_choice_rationale.C: Every sentence builds one point: reefs blunt wave energy and protect the land behind them.
per_choice_rationale.D: The passage never calls for abandoning beaches; it describes their protection (misconception: purpose_unstated_argument).

why_correct_md: The whole passage develops a single idea — reefs **protect** the coast by breaking wave energy.
why_tempted_md: The opening line names tourism, so a purpose about recreation-versus-science feels grounded even though the passage drops that thread immediately.
rule_md: 1) Read the whole passage and note what every sentence has in common. 2) State that shared idea as the passage's job in one phrase. 3) Match each option to that job, not to a single sentence. 4) Reject purposes that seize on a minor detail, name the wrong topic, or invent an argument the passage never makes.

subject: act-english
context_html: Charles Darwin proposed that a ring-shaped atoll begins as a reef fringing a volcanic island. As the island slowly subsides beneath the sea, the coral keeps building upward toward the sunlight, until the drowned peak leaves only a circle of reef around a central lagoon. For decades the idea remained an elegant guess.
stem_md: The writer wants to add a sentence that best supports the paragraph's point that Darwin's idea was eventually put to the test. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Darwin first developed the theory during his voyage aboard the Beagle.
In the twentieth century, geologists bored deep into a Pacific atoll and struck volcanic rock beneath thick layers of coral, exactly as the theory required.
Atolls are among the most photographed formations in tropical seas.
Coral polyps can survive only within a narrow range of water temperatures.

per_choice_rationale.A: Where the theory came from doesn't show it was tested; it only gives background (misconception: relevance_background_not_support).
per_choice_rationale.B: This physical evidence directly confirms the prediction, supporting the paragraph's point that the idea was tested.
per_choice_rationale.C: How photogenic atolls are is irrelevant to whether the theory was verified (misconception: relevance_offtopic_appeal).
per_choice_rationale.D: A fact about temperature tolerance is true but does nothing to test the subsidence theory (misconception: relevance_true_but_irrelevant).

why_correct_md: Only the boring evidence **confirms** the prediction, which is exactly the point the paragraph is building toward.
why_tempted_md: The Beagle detail is famous and on-subject about Darwin, so it feels supportive even though it never tests the theory.
rule_md: 1) Pin down the paragraph's point (here, that the theory was finally tested). 2) For each candidate, ask whether it advances that specific point or merely touches the general topic. 3) Keep the detail that provides evidence for the point. 4) Discard details that are background, decorative, or true-but-unrelated.

subject: act-english
context_html: Aquarium scientists have finally learned to spawn coral in the <u>lab, they</u> now ship hardy fragments to reef-restoration projects around the world.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this is a comma splice (misconception: comma_splice).
per_choice_rationale.B: Adding the coordinating conjunction 'and' properly joins the two independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.C: Removing all punctuation fuses the two clauses into a run-on (misconception: fused_sentence).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Thus' is a conjunctive adverb, so a comma before it still leaves a splice; it would need a semicolon (misconception: conjunctive_adverb_splice).

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses can be joined by a comma **plus** a coordinating conjunction.
why_tempted_md: The comma marks a natural pause, so it feels like enough to hold the two statements together.
rule_md: 1) Check whether the words on each side of the join could stand alone. 2) If both are complete sentences, a lone comma is illegal. 3) Fix it with a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, or a semicolon, or a period. 4) Remember a conjunctive adverb after a comma does not repair a splice.

subject: act-english
context_html: Mangrove roots and seagrass meadows act as nurseries for the <u>reef. Providing</u> shelter and food for young fish until they are large enough for open water.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: The period leaves 'Providing shelter and food...' as a fragment with no subject or main verb (misconception: participial_fragment).
per_choice_rationale.B: The comma attaches the participial phrase to the main clause, forming one complete sentence.
per_choice_rationale.C: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but the participial phrase cannot stand alone (misconception: semicolon_before_fragment).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'They providing' is not a grammatical clause; the -ing form needs a helping verb to be a predicate (misconception: missing_auxiliary).

why_correct_md: A comma links the **participial phrase** to the clause it modifies, curing the fragment.
why_tempted_md: The fragment is long and detailed, so it looks sentence-like enough to end with a period.
rule_md: 1) Check whether each capital-to-period stretch is a complete sentence. 2) A group built on an -ing word with no subject and helping verb is a fragment. 3) Attach such a phrase to the neighboring clause with a comma. 4) Don't use a period or semicolon to set off something that can't stand alone.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Drifting weightlessly above the reef, the camera recorded</u> a hawksbill turtle sliding gracefully between the branching corals.
stem_md: Which choice most clearly and correctly expresses the intended meaning?

choices.label: Drifting weightlessly above the reef, the diver recorded
Drifting weightlessly above the reef, there was a recording made by the camera of
The camera, drifting weightlessly above the reef, recorded

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening modifier illogically attaches to 'the camera,' as if the camera were drifting on its own (misconception: dangling_modifier).
per_choice_rationale.B: Naming the person as the subject gives the introductory phrase a logical thing to modify.
per_choice_rationale.C: The passive construction still leaves the modifier without a sensible subject and adds wordiness (misconception: passive_evades_subject).
per_choice_rationale.D: Moving the phrase mid-sentence still says the camera is doing the drifting (misconception: relocated_but_still_dangling).

why_correct_md: The introductory modifier must sit beside the **person** actually drifting, not the equipment.
why_tempted_md: The camera does the recording, so making it the subject feels natural even though it isn't what drifts.
rule_md: 1) Find the introductory -ing phrase and ask who or what performs its action. 2) Locate the subject right after the comma. 3) Make sure that subject is the doer of the introductory action. 4) If it isn't, rewrite so the true doer becomes the subject — don't just move the phrase or hide the subject in a passive.

subject: act-english
context_html: By steadily grazing on fast-growing seagrass and algae, green sea turtles keep the beds <u>trimmed</u> so that sunlight can still reach the coral below.
stem_md: Which choice is the most concise version of the underlined portion?

choices.label: trimmed and thereby reduced in length

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Trimmed' says everything needed; the single verb is complete and non-redundant.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Cut back' merely repeats the meaning of 'trimmed,' a redundant pair (misconception: redundant_synonym).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Down' and 'shortened' pile on meanings 'trimmed' already carries (misconception: redundant_particle_and_synonym).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Thereby reduced in length' restates 'trimmed' in wordier form (misconception: redundant_restatement).

why_correct_md: One precise verb conveys the idea; adding synonyms only **repeats** it.
why_tempted_md: Pairing verbs sounds thorough, so a doubled phrase feels more complete than the lone word.
rule_md: 1) Identify the core meaning of the underlined verb. 2) Check whether the added words say anything the verb doesn't already say. 3) If they only restate it, they are redundant. 4) Prefer the shortest wording that keeps the full meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: Marine pathologists are still trying to pin down <u>the specific underlying cause that is responsible for producing</u> stony coral tissue loss, a disease that can kill a colony within weeks.
stem_md: Which choice best expresses the idea most concisely?

choices.label: the causal factor that lies behind and produces
what it is that actually causes

per_choice_rationale.A: The phrase stacks 'specific,' 'underlying,' 'responsible for,' and 'producing' to say what a short phrase says (misconception: wordiness_pileup).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'The cause of' expresses the full idea with no wasted words.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Lies behind and produces' doubles the same idea and stays bloated (misconception: wordy_redundant_pair).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'What it is that actually' is an empty filler frame around a simple idea (misconception: empty_expletive_frame).

why_correct_md: The **shortest** phrasing that keeps the meaning is best; the long version adds no information.
why_tempted_md: Extra qualifiers sound more scientific, so the padded phrase feels more precise than it is.
rule_md: 1) Find the core idea of the underlined phrase. 2) Cross out any word that doesn't change the meaning. 3) Rebuild the phrase from what's left. 4) Choose the option that matches that lean version, not the one that sounds most elaborate.

subject: act-english
context_html: Researchers now fly small camera drones over the shallows <u>in order to</u> photograph an entire reef in a single low pass.
stem_md: Which choice is the most concise?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'In order to' is a padded way of saying 'to' (misconception: filler_purpose_phrase).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'So as to' is another wordy substitute for the plain 'to' (misconception: wordy_purpose_variant).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'To' expresses the purpose in a single word — nothing is lost.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'In an effort to' adds an unneeded sense of striving and extra words (misconception: filler_with_extra_connotation).

why_correct_md: A simple 'to' states purpose completely; the longer versions are just **filler**.
why_tempted_md: 'In order to' sounds formal and complete, so it seems more correct than the bare 'to.'
rule_md: 1) Spot phrases whose whole job is to signal purpose. 2) Test whether replacing them with 'to' changes the meaning. 3) If not, the longer phrase is filler. 4) Choose the shortest form that still reads smoothly.

subject: act-english
context_html: Under blue light, some corals blaze in neon greens and reds, a glow created by special proteins that <u>give off</u> light at a color different from the light they absorb.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely conveys the intended meaning?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Give off' is loose and informal for a precise optical process (misconception: vague_phrasal_verb).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Emit' precisely names the act of sending out light.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Release' suggests letting go of a stored substance, not producing light (misconception: imprecise_near_synonym).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Reflect' means bouncing back existing light, which misstates how fluorescence works (misconception: wrong_technical_meaning).

why_correct_md: The **exact** term for giving out light fits the scientific context.
why_tempted_md: 'Give off' is common and roughly right, so it slips by when a sharper term is available.
rule_md: 1) Name the precise action the sentence describes. 2) For each option, ask whether it means exactly that or only approximately. 3) Rule out words that imply a different process. 4) Keep the word whose technical meaning fits perfectly.

subject: act-english
context_html: By uploading their dive photos to a shared database, volunteers give marine biologists <u>a ton of</u> observations that a small research team could never collect alone.
stem_md: Which choice best fits the formal style of the passage?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'A ton of' is casual, conversational register unsuited to formal scientific writing (misconception: colloquial_quantifier).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Loads of' is equally informal slang for a large amount (misconception: colloquial_quantifier).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'A whole bunch of' is chatty and imprecise for this register (misconception: colloquial_quantifier).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'A wealth of' conveys a large, valuable quantity in appropriately formal language.

why_correct_md: The formal context calls for an elevated quantifier rather than **conversational** phrasing.
why_tempted_md: 'A ton of' is vivid and familiar, so it feels expressive even though it clashes with the formal tone.
rule_md: 1) Judge the passage's register — formal, neutral, or casual. 2) Rate each quantifier's formality. 3) Rule out slangy or conversational phrasings in formal contexts. 4) Choose the option whose register matches the surrounding prose.

subject: act-english
context_html: Before 1869, news from California crawled east by stagecoach and steamer; when the two track crews met at Promontory Summit that May, telegraph operators <u>will flash</u> word of the final spike to both coasts within minutes.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: The future 'will flash' clashes with the past-time frame fixed by 'Before 1869' and the dated meeting of the crews.
per_choice_rationale.B: The present perfect 'have flashed' cannot attach to a completed event pinned to a definite past date.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Flashes' is present tense and also fails to agree with the plural subject 'operators.'
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the simple past 'flashed' matches the past-tense narrative established by 'crawled' and 'met.'

why_correct_md: The clause reports a completed, dated 1869 event, so the verb must stay in the **simple past** to match 'met.'
why_tempted_md: 'Have flashed' tempts students who hear a finished action and reach for the perfect without checking the definite past date.
rule_md: 1) Circle every time marker (dates, 'before,' 'when'). 2) Find the tense of the other verbs in the same time frame. 3) Ask: is the action finished at a definite past time? If yes, use simple past. 4) Reject any tense that points to the future or to an unfinished span reaching the present.

subject: act-english
context_html: The network of branch lines that once linked these mining villages to the coastal ports <u>was</u> abandoned in the 1960s, though hikers still trace its overgrown embankments today.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the subject is the singular 'network,' so 'was' agrees despite the plural nouns stacked between subject and verb.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Were' wrongly agrees with the nearby plurals 'lines,' 'villages,' and 'ports' instead of the true subject.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Have been' is both plural and present perfect, mismatching the singular subject and the dated past event.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Are' is present tense and plural, failing both the time frame and the singular subject 'network.'

why_correct_md: The head of the subject is the singular noun **network**, so the singular past 'was' is required.
why_tempted_md: 'Were' attracts anyone who matches the verb to 'ports,' the plural noun sitting right beside it.
rule_md: 1) Find the verb. 2) Ask 'who or what does this?' and trace back to the head noun of the subject. 3) Cross out every prepositional phrase and relative clause between subject and verb. 4) Match the verb to the head noun's number, then confirm the tense fits the time markers.

subject: act-english
context_html: Early brakemen learned to couple cars, to set the hand brakes, and <u>signaling the engineer</u> with a swinging lantern.
stem_md: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Signaling' breaks the pattern set by the infinitives 'to couple' and 'to set.'
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: 'to signal' completes the series in the same infinitive form as the first two items.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'They signaled' inserts a full clause into a list of phrases, derailing the parallel series.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'The signaling of' switches to a noun phrase that cannot follow 'learned' alongside the other items.

why_correct_md: Items in a series must share one grammatical form, and the first two items are **infinitives**.
why_tempted_md: The -ing form sounds natural read alone, so students who don't scan back to the start of the list accept it.
rule_md: 1) Find the list and mark each item's first word. 2) Identify the form of item one (to + verb, -ing, noun). 3) Force every later item into that same form. 4) Reread the whole series to confirm each item hooks onto the lead-in verb.

subject: act-english
context_html: Early steam locomotives terrified many onlookers, who feared the boilers would burst without warning. <u>Similarly,</u> crowds still gathered along the route to cheer the engines at every trial run.
stem_md: Which transition word is most logical in context?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Similarly' promises a parallel idea, but fear and cheering pull in opposite directions.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'As a result' claims the cheering was caused by the fear, which reverses the sentence's logic.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In other words' signals a restatement, yet the second sentence adds a contrasting fact, not a paraphrase.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the crowds cheered despite the fear, so a concession transition fits the logic.

why_correct_md: The second sentence pushes **against** the first — fear, yet cheering — so the transition must concede a contrast.
why_tempted_md: 'As a result' lures readers who see any two linked events as cause and effect.
rule_md: 1) Cover the transition. 2) State each sentence's idea in five words. 3) Name the true relationship: same-direction, contrast, cause, example, or restatement. 4) Pick the transition that names that relationship, then reread both sentences with it.

subject: act-english
context_html: For decades, packers shipped live cattle east in slatted cars, absorbing the weight the animals lost along the way. <u>For example,</u> the refrigerated car let them ship only dressed beef, and freight bills fell by nearly half.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition from the preceding sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'For example' would make the refrigerated car an instance of shipping live cattle, which it is not.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Likewise' treats the new method as more of the same, but it replaced the old practice.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In short' announces a summary, yet the second sentence introduces new information rather than condensing the first.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the refrigerated car supplanted the live-cattle system, so a replacement transition captures the logic.

why_correct_md: Sentence two describes what packers did **in place of** the old practice, so the transition must mark a substitution.
why_tempted_md: 'Likewise' tempts readers who notice both sentences discuss shipping and miss that the second method displaced the first.
rule_md: 1) Restate sentence one and sentence two in plain words. 2) Ask: does idea two continue, illustrate, summarize, or replace idea one? 3) Match the transition to that exact function. 4) Reread the pair; if the connector implies the old practice continued, reject it.

subject: act-english
context_html: ______ Crews laid track across permafrost that heaved the rails each spring, ferried supplies over Lake Baikal when ice closed the shoreline route, and blasted tunnels through cliffs with hand drills. By the time the line opened end to end in 1916, the project had consumed more than two decades of labor.
stem_md: The writer wants to open the paragraph with a sentence that introduces its focus on the physical obstacles the builders faced. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Building the Trans-Siberian Railway meant defeating some of the harshest terrain engineers had ever confronted.
The Trans-Siberian Railway remains the longest single rail line in the world.
Russian officials argued for years over which route the new railway should follow.
Travelers today can cross the whole of Russia in about a week by rail.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: it names the railway and frames the paragraph's list of terrain-related obstacles.
per_choice_rationale.B: A superlative about length previews nothing about construction hardships.
per_choice_rationale.C: Political debates over the route concern planning, not the physical obstacles the paragraph details.
per_choice_rationale.D: A fact about modern travel times looks past the construction story entirely.

why_correct_md: Only this opener points directly at the **obstacles** — terrain and hardship — that every following sentence illustrates.
why_tempted_md: The record-length fact feels impressively relevant because it is true and famous, though it sets up no sentence that follows.
rule_md: 1) List what every body sentence has in common. 2) Write a one-line label for that common thread. 3) Test each opener: does it promise exactly that thread? 4) Reject openers that are merely true, interesting, or on the same general subject.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] The Pullman Company hired formerly enslaved men as sleeping-car porters soon after the Civil War. [2] Porters greeted passengers, converted seats into berths, and answered call bells at every hour of the night. [3] Despite that grueling load, the job offered steady wages and a rare chance to travel. [4] In 1925, porters organized the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, which became the first Black-led union to win a contract with a major American corporation.
stem_md: The writer wants to add the following sentence: "A porter's shifts could stretch to four hundred hours a month, with only brief naps snatched between stations." To preserve the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, where should the sentence be placed?

per_choice_rationale.A: Opening with shift lengths would dangle a detail before readers even know who porters were.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the hours extend the list of duties in Sentence 2 and set up 'that grueling load' in Sentence 3.
per_choice_rationale.C: After Sentence 3, the detail trails the phrase that summarizes it, weakening the 'despite' contrast.
per_choice_rationale.D: Tacked on after the union milestone, the sentence yanks readers back in time and buries the paragraph's climax.

why_correct_md: The sentence supplies the workload that Sentence 3's phrase 'that grueling load' points **back** to.
why_tempted_md: Placing it after Sentence 3 tempts readers because both discuss hardship, but the pointer phrase must follow its evidence, not precede it.
rule_md: 1) Find pointer words in the paragraph ('that,' 'this,' 'despite'). 2) Ask what each pointer refers to. 3) Place the new sentence so every pointer still has its referent behind it. 4) Reread the paragraph start to finish to confirm the flow.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] London opened the world's first underground railway in 1863, running steam trains beneath the city's streets. [2] Riders coughed through smoke-filled tunnels, yet the line carried nine million passengers in its first year. [3] Electric traction soon replaced steam, and Londoners embraced the deep-level lines they nicknamed the Tube. [4] By 1900, the network reached suburbs that had been open fields a generation earlier. [5] Across the Atlantic, Boston opened the first American subway in 1897, and New York soon followed with a far larger system.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide the paragraph into two paragraphs, the first about London's underground and the second about American subways. The best place to begin the new paragraph is at:

per_choice_rationale.A: Sentence 2 continues London's opening story, so a break here splits that account mid-thought.
per_choice_rationale.B: Sentence 3 still develops London's system as it modernizes; the topic has not shifted.
per_choice_rationale.C: Sentence 4 tracks the London network's suburban growth, keeping the first topic alive.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: 'Across the Atlantic' announces the shift to American cities, exactly where the second topic begins.

why_correct_md: The paragraph's subject changes at the phrase **'Across the Atlantic,'** the first sentence about America.
why_tempted_md: Sentence 3 fools readers who treat the switch from steam to electric power as a change of topic rather than a development within it.
rule_md: 1) Label each sentence's subject in two or three words. 2) Find where consecutive labels stop matching. 3) Check for signpost phrases ('across,' 'meanwhile,' place names) confirming the shift. 4) Start the new paragraph at the first sentence of the new subject.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>When the evening express arrived</u> the platform filled with porters, trunks, and shouted greetings.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: With no comma, the introductory clause crashes into the main clause and momentarily misreads.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: a comma must close an introductory dependent clause before the main clause begins.
per_choice_rationale.C: A comma after 'When' splits the subordinating word from its own clause.
per_choice_rationale.D: A comma between the subject 'express' and its verb 'arrived' interrupts the clause's core.

why_correct_md: An **introductory clause** takes a comma at its end, right before the main clause starts.
why_tempted_md: The missing comma is easy to accept because the sentence is short enough to parse without one on a fast read.
rule_md: 1) Ask whether the sentence opens with a dependent chunk ('When…,' 'After…,' 'Because…'). 2) Find where that chunk ends and the main subject begins. 3) Place one comma exactly at that seam. 4) Confirm no comma splits a subject from its verb inside either clause.

subject: act-english
context_html: By 1900, the <u>companys</u> flagship express was covering the run from London to Edinburgh in under nine hours.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Companys' is not a word; a possessive requires an apostrophe.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: one company owns the flagship express, so the singular possessive with the apostrophe before the s is right.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Companies' is a simple plural and shows no ownership of the express.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Companies'' marks possession by several companies, but the sentence describes a single owner's flagship.

why_correct_md: One owner plus ownership demands the **singular possessive**: apostrophe before the s.
why_tempted_md: The plural possessive lures students who see an s and assume more than one owner without checking the sentence's logic.
rule_md: 1) Ask: does the noun own the thing that follows? 2) If yes, count the owners. 3) One owner: add apostrophe + s to the singular. 4) Multiple owners: form the plural first, then add the apostrophe. 5) Reread to confirm the number matches the sentence's meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: Engineers tested three gauges on the switchback grade before choosing one; the gauge <u>that handled the sharpest curves</u> won the contract.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the clause identifies which of the three gauges won, so restrictive 'that' with no commas is right.
per_choice_rationale.B: Paired commas with 'which' mark the clause as removable extra detail, leaving 'the gauge' unable to specify which of the three is meant.
per_choice_rationale.C: A comma after the clause cuts the complete subject off from its verb 'won.'
per_choice_rationale.D: 'That' never follows a comma, and the stray comma leaves the clause half-punctuated.

why_correct_md: Because three gauges were tested, the clause is **essential** identification and takes 'that' with no commas.
why_tempted_md: The comma-wrapped 'which' version sounds polished and formal, so students who never run the removal test accept it.
rule_md: 1) Ask: does the clause identify which one, or add extra detail? 2) Try lifting the clause out; if the sentence no longer says which one, the clause is essential. 3) Essential clauses take 'that' with no commas. 4) Extra-detail clauses take 'which' inside a pair of commas. 5) Never place a comma directly before 'that.'

subject: act-english
context_html: At noon on November 18, 1883, dispatchers across the country <u>reset their clocks to the new standard time</u> that the railroads had agreed upon.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: reset their clocks, to the new standard time
reset, their clocks to the new standard time
reset their clocks to the new, standard time

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the verb, its object, and the completing phrase form one unbroken unit that needs no internal punctuation.
per_choice_rationale.B: The comma severs the verb phrase from the prepositional phrase that completes its meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: A comma between the verb 'reset' and its object 'their clocks' interrupts the sentence's core.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Standard time' is a fixed unit that 'new' modifies as a whole, so no comma can split the adjectives.

why_correct_md: No punctuation belongs anywhere in this span, because verb, object, and completing phrase form **one continuous unit**.
why_tempted_md: The comma before 'to the new standard time' mimics a natural breath pause, which many students mistake for a required comma.
rule_md: 1) Locate the verb, its object, and any phrase completing the verb's meaning. 2) For each comma a choice adds, name the two parts it separates. 3) If it splits verb from object, verb from complement, or an adjective from a fixed noun unit, reject it. 4) Keep punctuation only where a true grammatical boundary exists.

subject: act-english
context_html: In 1934, the new stainless-steel streamliner <u>hurtled</u> across the prairie, holding a pace no steam-hauled schedule had ever sustained.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize the startling speed of the streamliner as vividly as possible. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the verb delivers force and velocity, giving the reader a vivid sense of startling speed.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Moved' is grammatical but generic, conveying no particular speed at all.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Proceeded' sounds procedural and unhurried, working against the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Made its way' suggests slow, careful progress — the opposite of startling speed.

why_correct_md: Only the original verb carries the **vivid, forceful motion** the writer's goal demands.
why_tempted_md: 'Proceeded' feels appropriately formal for historical writing, so students choose polish over the stated goal.
rule_md: 1) Underline the goal words in the stem. 2) For each option, name the mental picture the verb paints. 3) Eliminate any verb that is neutral, slower, or calmer than the goal requires. 4) Choose the option whose connotation matches the goal exactly.

subject: act-english
context_html: Historians describe the signal box as a place of quiet method: levers polished by decades of hands, timetables known to the minute. The signalman's ledger, in which every passing train was entered, <u>stands as a soul-stirring monument to humanity's eternal wrestle with time itself</u>.
stem_md: Which choice best matches the tone of the surrounding passage?

choices.label: is a totally awesome window into the signalman's work
constitutes documentation of considerable operational significance
records the steady rhythm of that work

per_choice_rationale.A: The grand, emotional flourish clashes with the passage's quiet, observational voice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Chatty slang like 'totally awesome' falls far below the passage's measured register.
per_choice_rationale.C: Stiff bureaucratic phrasing overshoots the passage's plain, human vocabulary.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: calm, concrete wording continues the passage's quiet, factual tone.

why_correct_md: The passage speaks in a **quiet, measured** voice, and only this choice stays inside it.
why_tempted_md: The sweeping original feels like fine writing, so students reward its drama instead of testing it against the passage.
rule_md: 1) Read the sentences around the span and label their tone in two words. 2) Label each option's tone the same way. 3) Reject options that are more casual, more grandiose, or more technical than the passage. 4) Keep the option whose label matches the passage's.

subject: act-english
context_html: Railway Post Office clerks sorted letters in a swaying car while the train ran, pigeonholing mail for towns the line would not reach for hours. Each clerk memorized hundreds of local routes and passed a yearly sorting exam at better than ninety percent accuracy. At small stations the train never even slowed; a steel catcher arm snatched the waiting mail pouch at forty miles an hour.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the first sentence: "The first adhesive postage stamp had been issued in Britain in 1840." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it explains why so much mail traveled by train.
Yes, because it establishes when the clerks' profession began.
No, because it shifts attention from the clerks' work aboard the train to the broader history of postage.
No, because it repeats information given earlier in the paragraph.

per_choice_rationale.A: The stamp's debut explains nothing about mail volume on trains, so the offered reason fails.
per_choice_rationale.B: The 1840 stamp dates postal prehistory, not the founding of the sorting clerks' profession.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the paragraph profiles the clerks' onboard duties, and a British stamp fact pulls readers away from that focus.
per_choice_rationale.D: The rejection is right but the reason is false: no earlier sentence mentions stamps or 1840.

why_correct_md: The detail is **off-focus**: every sentence serves the clerks' onboard routine, and the stamp fact serves none of it.
why_tempted_md: The 'repeats information' option tempts students who sense the sentence doesn't belong but grab the first 'No' reason without checking it.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's focus in one line. 2) Ask whether the proposed sentence advances that focus. 3) If not, lean 'No' — then verify the stated reason describes what the sentence actually does. 4) Reject any option whose reason is factually wrong, even when its verdict is right.

subject: act-english
context_html: Hired by a major eastern railroad in 1920 as its first female engineer, Olive Dennis rode thousands of miles in ordinary coaches to study what passengers endured. She designed reclining seats, dimmable ceiling lights, and window vents that let travelers draw fresh air without a blast of cinders. Features she sketched for one railroad spread through the industry, quietly resetting what a coach ticket promised.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to show how one engineer's work changed the experience of ordinary train passengers. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it lists the official titles Dennis held during her long career.
Yes, because it connects specific innovations Dennis designed to the comfort of everyday riders.
No, because it concentrates on freight operations rather than on passenger service.
No, because it describes the reactions of railroad executives instead of those of travelers.

per_choice_rationale.A: The essay succeeds, but not by listing titles — it names only one position.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the essay ties Dennis's seat, lighting, and ventilation designs directly to what passengers experienced.
per_choice_rationale.C: Freight never appears in the passage, so this reason misdescribes the essay.
per_choice_rationale.D: No executive reactions are given; the essay follows what travelers gained.

why_correct_md: The essay pairs each of Dennis's **designs** with a passenger benefit, exactly matching the stated goal.
why_tempted_md: The titles option tempts readers who remember the impressive opening about her hiring and mistake it for the essay's method.
rule_md: 1) Restate the proposed goal in your own words. 2) Decide from the passage alone whether it achieves that goal — verdict first. 3) Audit each option's reason against specific sentences. 4) Eliminate any option whose reason describes content the passage does not contain.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] On logging railroads, geared locomotives crept up grades twice as steep as any main line would allow. [2] Instead of driving the wheels directly, their pistons spun a shaft that geared the power down, trading speed for grip. [3] Lumber camps of that era also kept teams of oxen, which dragged felled trunks to the loading decks. [4] Because every axle was powered, a geared engine could crawl over rough temporary track that would have derailed an ordinary locomotive.
stem_md: The writer wants the paragraph to stay focused on how geared locomotives mastered steep, rough track. Which sentence should be deleted because it strays from that focus?

per_choice_rationale.A: Sentence 1 announces the exact focus — geared engines on steep grades — so it must stay.
per_choice_rationale.B: Sentence 2 explains the gearing that makes the climbing possible, directly serving the focus.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: oxen dragging trunks concern camp logistics, not how the locomotives handled difficult track.
per_choice_rationale.D: Sentence 4 shows the engines conquering rough track, the second half of the stated focus.

why_correct_md: Only the oxen sentence abandons the **locomotives** for an unrelated camp activity.
why_tempted_md: Sentence 4 tempts readers who feel the paragraph is complete once the mechanism is explained, though it extends the stated focus.
rule_md: 1) Write the stated focus at the top. 2) For each sentence, note its subject in three words. 3) Mark any sentence whose subject is not the focus. 4) Confirm the paragraph still flows once the marked sentence is removed.

subject: act-english
context_html: The hundred-foot turntable balanced perfectly on its center <u>pivot, a single worker could spin</u> a locomotive weighing eighty tons.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: pivot, however, a single worker could spin
pivot a single worker could spin
pivot, so a single worker could spin

per_choice_rationale.A: A comma alone links two independent clauses, creating a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'However' is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction, so the splice remains — and its contrast is illogical here.
per_choice_rationale.C: Removing the comma fuses the two clauses with no boundary at all.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the comma plus the coordinating conjunction 'so' legally joins the clauses and captures the cause-effect logic.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses need a **comma plus a coordinating conjunction** (or a stronger stop), and the conjunction chosen matches the cause-effect meaning.
why_tempted_md: The 'however' version tempts students who believe any transition word can glue two clauses together.
rule_md: 1) Find each subject-verb pair and confirm both clauses stand alone. 2) Inspect the joint: comma alone = splice; nothing = fused. 3) Legal joints are a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. 4) Pick the legal joint whose logic — cause, contrast, addition — fits the sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: Every August the excursion special left the mill town at <u>dawn its coaches</u> were packed with families bound for the shore.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: With no mark at all, two complete statements run together as a fused sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Because' makes the second clause dependent, which a semicolon cannot introduce — and it asserts a cause the sentence never intends.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: a semicolon legally joins the two closely related independent clauses.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses may be joined by a **semicolon**, which supplies the boundary the fused original lacks.
why_tempted_md: The comma version tempts students who hear a short pause and assume a comma is boundary enough.
rule_md: 1) Read to where the first complete statement ends. 2) Confirm the second part is also a complete statement. 3) Between two such statements, allow only a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. 4) Reject a semicolon if a subordinating word has made the second part dependent.

subject: act-english
context_html: Restored plank by plank by volunteers over ten summers, <u>visitors can now tour the depot</u> and its telegraph office free of charge.
stem_md: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.label: touring the depot is now possible for visitors
the depot now invites visitors to tour it
there are now tours of the depot for visitors

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening modifier grabs 'visitors,' absurdly claiming the visitors were restored.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Touring' becomes the subject, but an activity cannot be restored plank by plank.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: 'the depot' — the thing actually restored — immediately follows the modifier.
per_choice_rationale.D: The placeholder 'there' gives the modifier nothing real to describe, so it still dangles.

why_correct_md: An introductory modifier must be followed **immediately** by the noun it describes — here, the restored depot.
why_tempted_md: The 'there are' version tempts students because it sounds neutral and inoffensive, hiding the fact that the modifier still has no owner.
rule_md: 1) Bracket the opening modifier. 2) Ask: who or what does it describe? 3) Check the first noun after the comma — it must be that very thing. 4) If it is not, choose the option that moves the true owner into the subject slot.

subject: act-english
context_html: The dining-car crew iced the lockers at Albany while the chef planned each <u>evening menu in advance before</u> the train left the yard.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most concise while preserving its meaning?

choices.label: evening menu ahead of time before
evening menu in advance, well before

per_choice_rationale.A: 'In advance' and 'before' make the same time claim, so the phrase says 'early' twice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: one time expression carries the full meaning with nothing repeated.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Ahead of time' merely swaps in a third synonym while keeping the doubled time idea.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'In advance, well before' still tells the reader twice that the planning came early.

why_correct_md: A single time expression does the job; stacking synonyms for *earlier* is **redundancy**.
why_tempted_md: 'Ahead of time before' tempts students who sense the problem but repair redundancy by rewording it instead of cutting it.
rule_md: 1) Underline every word or phrase in the span that expresses time. 2) Ask whether any two of them answer the same question. 3) Keep exactly one and delete its twins. 4) Reread to confirm no meaning was lost.

subject: act-english
context_html: The stationmaster's log <u>shows</u> that freight tonnage doubled during the war years, straining every siding on the division.
stem_md: Which choice most effectively expresses the writer's point?

choices.label: provides an indication of the fact

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the single verb states the log's action directly with no padding.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Serves to' adds an empty helper that delays the verb without adding meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Is capable of showing' shifts from what the log does to what it could do, inflating the phrase and weakening the claim.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Provides an indication of the fact' buries the action under a chain of nouns and filler.

why_correct_md: The bare verb states the log's action directly, and **concise** wording that loses no meaning is always preferred.
why_tempted_md: 'Serves to show' attracts students who equate longer, more ceremonial phrasing with stronger academic style.
rule_md: 1) Find the core action of the clause. 2) Delete candidate words one at a time; if the meaning survives, the words were padding. 3) Reject any option that adds helpers, hedges, or noun chains around the action. 4) Keep the version in which every remaining word changes the meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: For eighty years, the narrow-gauge line <u>carried</u> slate from the mountain quarries down to the harbor.
stem_md: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.label: carried, for all intents and purposes,
in a very real sense carried

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the plain verb states the fact; nothing about it needs qualifying.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Basically' hedges a claim that is not approximate, adding filler.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For all intents and purposes' is a stock idiom that delays the object without adding meaning.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'In a very real sense' insists the claim is real without supplying any information.

why_correct_md: The verb needs no hedge: **filler** phrases that can be deleted without changing meaning must be deleted.
why_tempted_md: 'For all intents and purposes' sounds like polished adult prose, so students mistake the familiar idiom for substance.
rule_md: 1) Bracket any phrase you could delete without altering the sentence's claim. 2) If deletion changes nothing, the phrase is filler. 3) Reject options that insert hedges, intensifiers, or stock idioms. 4) Reread the surviving sentence to confirm it says everything the original did.

subject: act-english
context_html: Before recommending a route through the pass, the survey team <u>looked at</u> the valley floor for an entire season, measuring snowmelt and charting every flood channel.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely describes the survey team's work?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Looked at' is too vague to convey a season of systematic measurement.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it conveys sustained, careful examination, matching the measuring and charting the sentence describes.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Glimpsed' means a brief, often accidental look — the opposite of a season's deliberate work.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Regarded' suggests a manner of viewing or an opinion, not methodical investigation.

why_correct_md: Only one option matches the **sustained, systematic** examination the sentence goes on to describe.
why_tempted_md: 'Regarded' tempts students who reach for a formal-sounding synonym without checking whether its meaning fits the described work.
rule_md: 1) List what the sentence says the actor actually did. 2) For each verb option, state its core meaning — duration, intent, and method. 3) Eliminate verbs that are too vague, too brief, or about attitude rather than action. 4) Choose the verb whose meaning covers all the described work.

subject: act-english
context_html: Completed in 1848 and still carrying its original boiler plate, the museum's oldest locomotive <u>is a pretty big deal for</u> visiting historians, who often travel hundreds of miles to examine it.
