stem_md: Which choice best maintains the register of the sentence as a whole?

choices.label: is an object of ineffable, transcendent wonder to

per_choice_rationale.A: 'A pretty big deal' is conversational slang, well below the sentence's formal, historical register.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Seriously cool' is even more casual, clashing with the measured description around it.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Ineffable, transcendent wonder' overshoots into ornate prose the plain passage never uses.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: measured, formal phrasing matches the sentence's historical voice.

why_correct_md: Measured, formal phrasing keeps the **register** consistent with the sentence's historical voice.
why_tempted_md: The ornate option lures students who assume the most elevated vocabulary must be the most appropriately formal.
rule_md: 1) Label the passage's register in two words (e.g., formal-historical). 2) Label each option the same way. 3) Reject anything more casual than the passage and anything more ornate. 4) Read the survivor in place to confirm one consistent voice.

subject: act-english
context_html: By the time the 1900 hurricane reached the Texas coast, forecasters at the national office <u>have dismissed</u> the warnings that Cuban meteorologists had cabled days earlier.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Present perfect 'have dismissed' ties the action to the present moment, but the sentence is anchored to a past event in 1900 (misconception: present perfect for remote past).
per_choice_rationale.B: Future perfect 'will have dismissed' points to completion before a future moment, yet every event here is past (misconception: any perfect form fits 'by the time').
per_choice_rationale.C: Past progressive 'were dismissing' portrays the action as ongoing at landfall, but 'days earlier' shows it was already complete (misconception: progressive equals past-sounding vividness).
per_choice_rationale.D: Past perfect 'had dismissed' correctly marks an action completed before another past event, the landfall.

why_correct_md: **Past perfect** places the dismissal before the landfall, the sentence's other past event.
why_tempted_md: 'Were dismissing' sounds convincingly past, so students accept it without checking whether the action was already finished before landfall.
rule_md: 1) Find the time anchor ('By the time X happened...'). 2) Ask: was the underlined action finished before that anchor? 3) If yes, use past perfect (had + past participle). 4) If it was ongoing at the anchor, use past progressive; if simultaneous, simple past. 5) Re-read the sentence to confirm the sequence.

subject: act-english
context_html: The array of sensors that ring the airfield, along with the ceilometer and the two anemometers installed last spring, <u>report</u> current conditions to the tower every sixty seconds.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Report' is plural, but the subject 'array' is singular; the writer matched the verb to the nearby plural nouns (misconception: agree with the nearest noun).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Have reported' is both plural and present perfect, clashing with the singular subject and the recurring 'every sixty seconds' routine (misconception: perfect form for habitual action).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the singular subject 'array' takes the singular present 'reports,' regardless of the plural nouns in the intervening phrases.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Are reporting' is plural and progressive; the subject is singular and the action is a repeated routine, not one in progress (misconception: plural pulled from attached phrases).

why_correct_md: The verb must agree with the **singular subject** 'array,' not the plural nouns stacked between subject and verb.
why_tempted_md: 'Sensors' and 'anemometers' sit right before the verb, luring students into nearest-noun agreement.
rule_md: 1) Find the main verb. 2) Cross out prepositional phrases and relative clauses between the subject and the verb. 3) Identify the bare subject that remains. 4) Match the verb's number to that subject. 5) Confirm the tense fits time cues like 'every sixty seconds.'

subject: act-english
context_html: Before going on air, the meteorologist checks the radar loop, updates the temperature graphic, and <u>is reviewing</u> the script one final time.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Is reviewing' breaks the series of simple present verbs 'checks' and 'updates' (misconception: any present-time form counts as parallel).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: 'reviews' matches the simple present form of the other verbs in the series.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'To review' switches the third item to an infinitive, snapping the parallel pattern (misconception: an infinitive reads as an upcoming action).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Reviewing' is a bare participle that cannot stand as the third verb in a series of conjugated verbs (misconception: -ing forms are interchangeable with finite verbs).

why_correct_md: Items in a series must share one grammatical form, so the third verb must be **simple present** like 'checks' and 'updates.'
why_tempted_md: 'Is reviewing' still sounds present-time, so students miss that the helping verb breaks the series' matching form.
rule_md: 1) Find the list and mark each item. 2) Label the grammatical form of item one. 3) Check every later item against that label. 4) Rewrite any item that wears a different form. 5) Read the full series aloud to confirm the rhythm matches.

subject: act-english
context_html: Satellite imagery shows forecasters where clouds are gathering. <u>However,</u> it cannot reveal how much rain those clouds will actually release.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the second sentence limits what satellite imagery can do, so the contrast word fits.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Therefore' claims the limitation follows logically from the strength, but the two ideas oppose each other (misconception: any connector between related sentences reads as cause-effect).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For example' promises an instance of clouds being shown, but the second sentence is a limitation, not an example (misconception: example word for any elaboration).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Likewise' asserts the two sentences run parallel, yet one states an ability and the other an inability (misconception: same topic means same direction).

why_correct_md: The second sentence **contrasts** with the first — an ability set against a limitation — so the original connector is logical.
why_tempted_md: Because both sentences discuss what imagery does, 'Therefore' feels like a natural continuation until the opposing direction is checked.
rule_md: 1) Read the sentence before and after the transition. 2) State each sentence's point in five words. 3) Name the relationship: contrast, cause, example, addition, or similarity. 4) Match the connector to that relationship. 5) Re-read with the connector in place to verify.

subject: act-english
context_html: The two most trusted models now disagree sharply about the storm's likely track. <u>In other words,</u> the hurricane center has widened its cone of uncertainty on the latest advisory.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'In other words' promises a restatement, but widening the cone is a new action caused by the disagreement (misconception: restatement word for any follow-up).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Nevertheless' signals the second sentence happens despite the first, yet the widening happens because of it (misconception: formal-sounding contrast fits anywhere).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For instance' would introduce an example of models disagreeing, but the sentence reports the center's response instead (misconception: example word for consequences).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the widened cone is the direct consequence of the models' disagreement, which this connector signals.

why_correct_md: The second sentence is the **consequence** of the first, so a cause-and-effect connector is required.
why_tempted_md: The second sentence does re-describe the situation in new terms, making a restatement connector feel plausible until the action-versus-rephrasing distinction is checked.
rule_md: 1) Summarize the first sentence and the second sentence separately. 2) Ask: does sentence two repeat, oppose, illustrate, or follow from sentence one? 3) Pick the connector class matching that answer. 4) Test by reading the pair with a plain word like 'so' or 'but.' 5) Choose the option in that class.

subject: act-english
context_html: Twice a day, at hundreds of stations around the world, technicians release weather balloons that climb until they burst high in the stratosphere. Each balloon carries a radiosonde, an instrument package that measures temperature, humidity, and pressure as it rises. The readings stream back to forecast centers within minutes.
stem_md: The writer wants to conclude the paragraph with a sentence that emphasizes the global coordination of the balloon launches. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Radiosondes were first developed in the 1930s and have changed little since then.
Some launches send balloons drifting a hundred miles before the instruments parachute back to earth.
Forecasters also rely on satellites, radar, and surface stations to monitor the atmosphere.
Together, these simultaneous launches give forecasters a snapshot of the entire atmosphere at the same instant.

per_choice_rationale.A: Shifts to the instrument's design history, which says nothing about worldwide coordination (misconception: any related fact can close a paragraph).
per_choice_rationale.B: Follows a single balloon's drift, a local detail that narrows the scope when the goal demands scale (misconception: vivid detail equals strong conclusion).
per_choice_rationale.C: Broadens to other observing tools, diluting the paragraph's focus on balloon launches (misconception: a wider survey feels suitably 'global').
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it names the shared timing of the launches and their worldwide payoff, exactly the coordination the goal requires.

why_correct_md: Only this choice states that the launches happen **worldwide on a shared schedule**, which is the coordination the goal names.
why_tempted_md: The option adding satellites and radar feels appropriately global, but it drifts from balloon launches to other tools entirely.
rule_md: 1) Restate the stated goal in your own words. 2) Strike any option that changes the subject. 3) Strike any option that zooms in on a single case when the goal is scale. 4) Of what remains, pick the sentence whose main clause states the goal's idea directly. 5) Re-read the paragraph with it in place to confirm the emphasis.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] When rotation appears on radar, the local forecast office weighs the signature against reports from trained spotters on the ground. [2] If the evidence is convincing, a warning goes out to phones, sirens, and broadcasters within minutes. [3] Residents in the storm's path are urged to move to interior rooms on the lowest floor. [4] After the storm passes, survey teams examine the damage to confirm whether a tornado actually touched down.
stem_md:
The writer wants to add the following sentence to the paragraph:

*Spotters are especially valuable because radar cannot show what is happening at ground level.*

For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, the sentence should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Placed first, the sentence praises spotters before either spotters or radar has been introduced (misconception: explanatory sentences belong up front).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: Sentence 1 introduces both radar and spotters, so the explanation of why spotters matter follows it naturally.
per_choice_rationale.C: Wedged after the safety instructions, the sentence interrupts the sequence from warning to sheltering (misconception: extra facts can go wherever space remains).
per_choice_rationale.D: At the end, the sentence trails the damage-survey step, which it has nothing to do with (misconception: added material defaults to the end).

why_correct_md: The sentence explains ideas introduced in Sentence 1, so **cohesion** demands it sit immediately after that introduction.
why_tempted_md: Adding new material at the very end feels safe because nothing after it can be disrupted — but the sentence then dangles far from the ideas it explains.
rule_md: 1) Circle the key nouns in the sentence to be added. 2) Find where those nouns first appear in the paragraph. 3) Place the new sentence just after the sentence that introduces them. 4) Re-read the paragraph to check no sequence is interrupted. 5) Confirm every pronoun and reference still points backward, never forward.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] For most of the nineteenth century, farmers judged the coming season by folklore: red skies, aching joints, and the thickness of caterpillars' coats. [2] Almanacs bundled such signs into confident yearly predictions. [3] Tested against actual records, those predictions performed no better than chance. [4] Even so, the booklets sold briskly, offering a certainty nothing else claimed to provide. [5] The first government forecasts, issued by telegraph in the 1870s, took the opposite approach. [6] They predicted only a day ahead, drew on observations wired in from dozens of cities, and admitted their limits plainly.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide this paragraph into two paragraphs in order to separate the discussion of folklore-based prediction from the discussion of early government forecasting. The best place to begin the second paragraph is at:

per_choice_rationale.A: Sentence 2 still describes folklore prediction — almanacs packaging the signs — so the break splits the first topic in half (misconception: break right after the opening sentence).
per_choice_rationale.B: Sentence 3 evaluates the almanac predictions and belongs with them (misconception: a negative turn signals a new topic).
per_choice_rationale.C: Sentence 4 opens with 'Even so,' which reaches back to the failed predictions, chaining it to the almanac discussion (misconception: ignoring a backward-pointing transition).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: Sentence 5 introduces a new actor and era — government forecasts of the 1870s — which is where the topic actually shifts.

why_correct_md: The paragraph's subject changes only when the **new actor** — government forecasting — first appears, so the break belongs there.
why_tempted_md: The verdict that almanac predictions failed feels like a turning point, so students mistake a shift in tone for a shift in topic.
rule_md: 1) Label each sentence with its subject in two or three words. 2) Find where the label changes for good. 3) Check that the proposed first sentence of paragraph two stands alone, with no backward-pointing opener. 4) Check that everything before the break belongs to topic one. 5) Re-read both halves as separate paragraphs.

subject: act-english
context_html: The station's chief meteorologist<u>, a veteran of twenty storm seasons</u> rarely raises her voice on air, even when the radar map turns solid red.
stem_md: Which choice correctly punctuates the underlined portion?

choices.label: a veteran of twenty storm seasons
, a veteran of twenty storm seasons,
a veteran of twenty storm seasons,

per_choice_rationale.A: Opens the aside with a comma but never closes it, leaving the interrupter half-fenced (misconception: one comma is enough for an aside).
per_choice_rationale.B: Removes both commas, welding the appositive onto the main clause as if 'meteorologist a veteran' were one noun (misconception: short asides need no commas).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the appositive is extra, droppable information, so it takes a comma on each side.
per_choice_rationale.D: Fences only the back end of the aside (misconception: commas placed by pause rather than by structure).

why_correct_md: A nonrestrictive appositive needs **paired commas** — one before it and one after it.
why_tempted_md: The single opening comma matches where readers naturally pause, so the missing closing comma slips past unnoticed.
rule_md: 1) Find the phrase that renames the noun. 2) Test: can you lift it out and still have a full sentence? 3) If yes, it is extra information. 4) Fence extra information with a comma on both sides — never just one. 5) Re-read the sentence without the phrase to confirm it still works.

subject: act-english
context_html: Buoys anchored far offshore record wave heights every hour<u>; the</u> readings reach forecasters ashore by satellite link.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English punctuation?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: complete statements sit on either side, and a semicolon may join two independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma alone between two complete statements creates a comma splice (misconception: a comma can join independent clauses).
per_choice_rationale.C: The semicolon does the joining by itself, so adding 'and' after it doubles the connector (misconception: a semicolon works like a comma before a conjunction).
per_choice_rationale.D: With no punctuation, the two statements fuse into a run-on (misconception: closely related ideas may run together).

why_correct_md: A **semicolon** legally joins the two independent clauses on either side of the break.
why_tempted_md: The comma feels natural because the second clause continues the same topic so smoothly.
rule_md: 1) Cover the punctuation and read each side alone. 2) Ask: could each side stand as its own sentence? 3) If both could, join them with a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction — never a comma alone or nothing. 4) Reject doubled connectors. 5) Re-read the joined sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each autumn, forecast offices issue frost advisories for valleys <u>that trap cold air</u> after sunset, because growers on those low fields face the season's first freezes.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the clause pinpoints which valleys get advisories — essential information — so restrictive 'that' with no comma is right.
per_choice_rationale.B: The comma plus 'which' makes the clause an aside, implying advisories cover all valleys rather than only the cold-trapping ones (misconception: 'which' with a comma is interchangeable with 'that').
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Traps' breaks agreement with the plural 'valleys' the clause describes (misconception: verb drawn to the singular feel of 'air').
per_choice_rationale.D: A comma never precedes restrictive 'that' (misconception: a spoken pause before the clause earns a comma).

why_correct_md: The clause is **restrictive** — it tells which valleys are meant — so 'that' with no comma is correct.
why_tempted_md: 'Which' sounds more formal, so the comma-plus-'which' version feels like an upgrade even though it changes the meaning.
rule_md: 1) Ask: does the clause narrow down which noun you mean, or add bonus detail? 2) If it narrows, use 'that' with no comma. 3) If it adds bonus detail, use a comma with 'which.' 4) Never put a comma directly before 'that.' 5) Check the clause's verb against the noun it describes.

subject: act-english
context_html: As the derecho crossed the county line, a wall of dust <u>moved</u> across the dry fields toward town.
stem_md: The writer wants to convey the storm's speed and force as vividly as possible. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Moved' is grammatical but generic, conveying no speed or force (misconception: the original stands if nothing is wrong with it).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it depicts fast, heavy, unstoppable motion, delivering both speed and force.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Traveled' is as neutral as 'moved,' adding distance but no violence (misconception: any synonym counts as a revision).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Appeared' removes motion altogether, freezing the image (misconception: a dramatic-sounding word equals dramatic meaning).

why_correct_md: The key verb packs **speed and force** into the image itself, exactly what the goal demands.
why_tempted_md: 'Traveled' feels slightly more specific than 'moved,' so it masquerades as the vivid upgrade.
rule_md: 1) Underline the goal words in the stem. 2) For each option, ask: does this verb by itself show that quality? 3) Cut options that are merely grammatical. 4) Cut options that add a different quality than the goal names. 5) Pick the one that shows the goal's quality without extra help.

subject: act-english
context_html: In her morning forecast discussion, the meteorologist <u>conceded</u> that the overnight model runs had diverged, then laid out why she still favored the colder solution.
stem_md: The writer wants to show that the meteorologist honestly acknowledged a point that weakened her own forecast. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the original verb means admitting something reluctantly true that cuts against one's own position — precisely the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Announced' is a neutral public statement, carrying no sense that the point works against her (misconception: formal tone equals the right nuance).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Noted' records the fact without any admission against interest (misconception: any verb of saying will do).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Lamented' adds grief, overshooting honesty into mourning (misconception: stronger emotion means stronger writing).

why_correct_md: The original verb uniquely carries **admission against one's own position**, matching every part of the goal.
why_tempted_md: 'Noted' sounds appropriately calm and professional, hiding that it drops the crucial sense of admitting a weakness.
rule_md: 1) Turn the goal into a checklist (here: honest + acknowledges + hurts her own case). 2) Test each verb against every box, not just one. 3) Reject verbs that are neutral reports. 4) Reject verbs that add feelings the goal never mentioned. 5) Keep the verb that checks every box with nothing extra.

subject: act-english
context_html: Predicting snowfall totals for a single town is among the hardest jobs in forecasting. A thirty-mile shift in a storm's track can turn a dusting into a foot of snow. Temperature differences too small for most instruments to flag can decide whether roads stay merely wet or glaze over with ice.
stem_md:
The writer is considering adding the following sentence:

*Because school superintendents must often decide on closings by 5 a.m., they depend on these hair-thin margins hours before the first flake falls.*

Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it illustrates a real-world stake that depends on the fine distinctions the paragraph describes.
Yes, because it explains why storm tracks shift as storms approach a town.
No, because it repeats information given earlier in the paragraph.
No, because it shifts the paragraph's focus to debates over school policy.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the sentence shows who must act on the paragraph's tiny margins, adding a concrete stake without changing the subject.
per_choice_rationale.B: The sentence says nothing about why tracks shift, so this reason misdescribes what the addition does (misconception: right verdict paired with an unexamined reason).
per_choice_rationale.C: Nothing earlier mentions superintendents or deadlines, so the sentence repeats nothing (misconception: same general topic equals repetition).
per_choice_rationale.D: One sentence about a decision deadline does not open a policy debate; the emphasis stays on forecasting's fine margins (misconception: any new actor equals a new focus).

why_correct_md: The addition supplies a **concrete consequence** of the forecasting difficulty the paragraph details, and the reason accurately says so.
why_tempted_md: The 'No' option about shifting focus tempts readers who see a new character — a superintendent — and assume the topic changed with it.
rule_md: 1) Decide the verdict first: does the sentence serve the paragraph's purpose? 2) Then audit the reason: does it accurately describe what the sentence does? 3) Reject right verdicts with wrong reasons. 4) Reject wrong verdicts however plausible the reason sounds. 5) Keep the pairing where verdict and reason are both true.

subject: act-english
context_html: Hurricane hunter crews fly directly into a storm's eyewall to collect measurements no satellite can supply. Dropsondes released from the aircraft fall through the storm, radioing back pressure and wind readings every few seconds. Those readings often revise the official intensity estimate within the hour. The plane itself is heavily reinforced, with instruments bolted to nearly every exterior surface.
stem_md: The writer is considering deleting the final sentence of the paragraph. Should the sentence be deleted?

choices.label: No, because it explains how the plane's reinforced frame lets crews survive the eyewall.
No, because it is the only sentence that describes the instruments used on the flights.
Yes, because it shifts attention from the data the flights gather to the plane's construction.
Yes, because it contradicts the earlier claim that satellites cannot supply such data.

per_choice_rationale.A: The sentence never connects reinforcement to crew survival, and the paragraph's purpose is the measurements, not the airframe (misconception: invented relevance rescues a detail).
per_choice_rationale.B: Being the only sentence on a side topic is a reason to cut it, not keep it, when the paragraph is about what the readings accomplish (misconception: unique information is automatically valuable).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the paragraph tracks how the flights' measurements improve intensity estimates, and a closing description of the airframe strays from that thread.
per_choice_rationale.D: Nothing in the sentence contradicts the satellite claim; the deletion verdict is right but this reason is false (misconception: right verdict, wrong reason).

why_correct_md: The paragraph's through-line is the **measurements** and their effect on forecasts, and the final sentence departs from it to describe hardware.
why_tempted_md: The survival explanation feels reasonable — reinforcement must be for safety — but the sentence itself never says so, and safety is not the paragraph's point.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's main job in one clause. 2) Ask what the candidate sentence contributes to that job. 3) If it serves a different job, lean toward deletion. 4) Then vet each option's reason: is it factually true of the sentence? 5) Choose the option whose verdict and reason are both accurate.

subject: act-english
context_html: Until the 1980s, a forecaster tracking a thunderstorm could see where rain was falling but not what the wind inside the storm was doing. Doppler radar changed that by measuring whether raindrops were moving toward or away from the antenna. With that upgrade, rotation inside a supercell became visible many minutes before any funnel dropped. Tornado warning lead times, once close to zero, stretched past ten minutes within a decade.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to write a brief essay showing how one technological advance improved severe-weather warnings. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it recounts the full history of radar from its invention to the present day.
Yes, because it identifies a single advance and traces its specific effect on warning capability.
No, because it addresses only the tornado warning process rather than the full range of severe weather.
No, because it never identifies a single measurable effect of the advance it describes.

per_choice_rationale.A: The essay covers one upgrade and its aftermath, not radar's full history, so the verdict is right but the description is false (misconception: a generous misreading of scope).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the essay names one advance and follows its measurable effect on lead times, which is exactly the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.C: The stated goal asks for one advance's effect on warnings, so a tight focus is fulfillment, not failure (misconception: narrow scope reads as falling short).
per_choice_rationale.D: The essay cites lead times stretching from near zero past ten minutes — a measurable effect (misconception: skimming past the data sentence).

why_correct_md: The essay does precisely what the goal specifies: **one advance, one traced effect** on warnings, with numbers to prove it.
why_tempted_md: Readers who expect coverage of severe weather generally may judge the tornado-only focus too narrow, forgetting the goal asked for a single advance.
rule_md: 1) Restate the hypothetical goal in your own words. 2) Summarize what the essay actually does in one sentence. 3) Compare the two: match or mismatch? 4) Discard options whose reasons misdescribe the essay, even if their verdict matches yours. 5) Choose the option where verdict and description are both accurate.

subject: act-english
context_html: The county's tornado sirens date from the 1950s. <u>Although the sirens are tested on the first Wednesday of every month.</u> Few residents have ever heard them in a real emergency.
stem_md: Which choice results in a complete sentence?

choices.label: Although the sirens being tested on the first Wednesday of every month.
The sirens are tested on the first Wednesday of every month.
While the sirens are tested on the first Wednesday of every month.

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Although' turns the statement into a dependent clause that never attaches to a main clause — a fragment (misconception: length plus a period equals a sentence).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Being tested' supplies no finite verb, so the word group still cannot stand alone (misconception: an -ing form works as a main verb).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: removing the subordinator leaves a complete statement with a subject and a finite verb.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'While' subordinates the clause just as 'Although' did, leaving the fragment intact (misconception: swapping subordinators fixes the structure).

why_correct_md: Deleting the **subordinating word** lets the clause stand alone as a complete sentence.
why_tempted_md: The original is long and information-rich, so it feels sentence-like despite opening with a word that demands a follow-up clause.
rule_md: 1) Read the word group alone. 2) Find a subject and a finite verb. 3) Check the first word: does it make the clause lean on another sentence ('although,' 'while,' 'because')? 4) If it leans and nothing follows, delete the leaning word or attach the clause. 5) Re-read to confirm it stands alone.

subject: act-english
context_html: The morning forecast promised unbroken <u>sunshine, the</u> picnic committee left every tent and tarp at home.
stem_md: Which choice most effectively joins the two statements?

per_choice_rationale.A: A comma alone joins two complete statements — a comma splice (misconception: short clauses may share a comma).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'However' is an adverb, not a conjunction, so the splice remains — and the logic even turns contrastive (misconception: a transition word equals a connector).
per_choice_rationale.C: Deleting the comma fuses the clauses into a run-on (misconception: removing the flagged comma fixes the join).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: a comma plus the coordinating conjunction links the clauses and states the cause-effect logic.

why_correct_md: A comma plus a **coordinating conjunction** legally joins two independent clauses — and this one supplies the cause-and-effect link.
why_tempted_md: 'However' looks like a strong connector, so the splice hides behind its formality.
rule_md: 1) Confirm both sides could stand as sentences. 2) List the legal joins: period, semicolon, comma + coordinating conjunction, or subordinating one clause. 3) Match the join to the logic between the clauses. 4) Reject comma-alone and adverb-with-commas joins. 5) Re-read the repaired sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: The regional lightning network locates each strike within <u>seconds, this</u> speed lets utility crews reroute power before damaged lines fail.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: The comma tries to join two complete statements by itself — a splice (misconception: a backward-pointing opener like 'this speed' feels connected enough).
per_choice_rationale.B: No punctuation at all fuses the two statements (misconception: removing the comma removes the problem).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a period ends the first complete statement, and the next begins cleanly.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Because' makes the second statement a dependent clause stranded alone after the period — a fragment (misconception: subordinators can be sprinkled on for flow).

why_correct_md: A **period** is a clean, legal boundary between these two independent statements.
why_tempted_md: 'This speed' refers back so tightly to the previous clause that the comma join feels cohesive.
rule_md: 1) Find where the first complete thought ends. 2) Verify the second word group is also complete. 3) Choose a legal boundary: period, semicolon, or comma with a coordinating conjunction. 4) If you add a subordinating word, make sure a main clause still follows. 5) Re-read both halves separately.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Hoping to verify the hail reports, the flattened cornfield was photographed by the survey team</u> before insurance adjusters arrived.
stem_md: Which of the following provides the most logical version of the sentence?

choices.label: Hoping to verify the hail reports, the survey team photographed the flattened cornfield
Hoping to verify the hail reports, the cornfield's flattened rows were photographed by the survey team
The flattened cornfield, hoping to verify the hail reports, was photographed by the survey team

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening modifier grabs the nearest subject, making the cornfield do the hoping (misconception: the doer can arrive later in the sentence).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the survey team — the only party capable of hoping — sits immediately after the modifier.
per_choice_rationale.C: Swapping in 'rows' still leaves a non-hoping subject beside the modifier (misconception: rewording the subject phrase fixes the dangle).
per_choice_rationale.D: Moving the modifier inside the clause attaches it even more firmly to the cornfield (misconception: modifier placement is flexible if commas fence it).

why_correct_md: An opening participial modifier must be followed **immediately by its doer** — here, the survey team.
why_tempted_md: The passive rewrite with 'rows' keeps the original's rhythm, so its unchanged subject slips past inspection.
rule_md: 1) Find the opening -ing phrase. 2) Ask: who performs that action? 3) Check the very next noun after the comma. 4) If doer and next noun differ, rewrite so the doer follows the comma. 5) Re-read to confirm the action pairs with a capable subject.

subject: act-english
context_html: Emergency managers urge coastal residents to make <u>advance preparations ahead of time</u> whenever a tropical system organizes offshore.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most concise without losing information?

choices.label: preparations in advance ahead of the storm

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Advance' and 'ahead of time' say the same thing twice (misconception: reinforcing a point strengthens it).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the noun already implies action taken before the event, so no time-stamp is needed.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Beforehand' merely swaps one duplicate for another (misconception: changing the redundant word cures the redundancy).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'In advance' plus 'ahead of the storm' doubles the time idea yet again (misconception: extra phrasing adds precision).

why_correct_md: The bare noun already contains the **before-the-event** idea, so every added time phrase is redundant.
why_tempted_md: 'Advance preparations beforehand' rearranges the words enough to feel edited while keeping the doubled meaning.
rule_md: 1) Define the head word (preparing = getting ready before something happens). 2) Check each modifier: does it add new information or repeat the definition? 3) Delete the repeaters. 4) Prefer the shortest version that keeps the full meaning. 5) Re-read for anything lost — if nothing, the cut stands.

subject: act-english
context_html: The station finally rebuilt its on-air graphics <u>due to the fact that viewers were of the opinion that</u> the old maps looked cluttered and dated.
stem_md: Which choice expresses the idea most concisely?

choices.label: owing to the fact that viewers held the opinion that
because of the reason that viewers thought that

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Due to the fact that' and 'were of the opinion that' are inflated stand-ins for two short words (misconception: longer phrasing sounds more professional).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it delivers the same cause and the same belief in three words.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Owing to the fact that' trades one padded formula for another (misconception: swapping formal phrases counts as trimming).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Because of the reason that' states the cause idea twice — the connector already means 'for the reason that' (misconception: piling on connectors adds clarity).

why_correct_md: The tightest version keeps every fact — the cause and the belief — while cutting the **empty formula phrases**.
why_tempted_md: The original's roundabout formality reads like news-report style, so the padding masquerades as professionalism.
rule_md: 1) Bracket each multi-word formula ('due to the fact that,' 'of the opinion that'). 2) Ask what single word does the same job. 3) Substitute the single word. 4) Confirm no meaning was lost. 5) Keep the shortest version that survives steps 1 through 4.

subject: act-english
context_html: Frost can whiten low-lying fields <u>even when official thermometer readings stay</u> a few degrees above freezing.
stem_md: Which choice expresses the idea most effectively and concisely?

choices.label: even when, as a matter of fact, official thermometer readings stay
even in the event that it so happens that official thermometer readings stay
even when official thermometer readings, for all intents and purposes, stay

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the original states the condition directly, with no filler.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'As a matter of fact' asserts nothing the sentence does not already assert (misconception: filler phrases add emphasis).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In the event that it so happens that' buries the simple time word under empty machinery (misconception: elaborate phrasing sounds precise).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'For all intents and purposes' hedges a plain factual claim for no reason (misconception: stock phrases add authority).

why_correct_md: The original is already **filler-free**; every candidate revision adds words that assert nothing.
why_tempted_md: 'For all intents and purposes' is common in serious-sounding prose, so it passes as a scholarly touch.
rule_md: 1) Read the sentence and mark any phrase you could delete without losing a fact. 2) Delete it mentally and re-read. 3) If the meaning is untouched, the phrase is filler. 4) Prefer the version with zero deletable phrases. 5) Confirm the survivor still reads smoothly.

subject: act-english
context_html: Meteorologists warn that a single failed buoy can <u>injure</u> the accuracy of wave forecasts along an entire stretch of coastline.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most precise word for the context?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Injure' applies to living things; accuracy cannot be injured (misconception: any harm word fits any harmed thing).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Wound' has the same living-victim problem, only more vividly (misconception: vivid equals precise).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: it names the gradual lowering of quality that data loss actually causes.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Shrink' means to get smaller in size or amount; accuracy worsens rather than gets smaller (misconception: any lessening verb fits any decline).

why_correct_md: The key verb pairs correctly with **quality nouns** like accuracy, naming a lowering of quality rather than a bodily harm or a size change.
why_tempted_md: 'Shrink' correctly signals reduction, so it feels compatible with accuracy going down.
rule_md: 1) Identify the object of the verb ('accuracy'). 2) Ask what kind of noun it is: living thing, quantity, or quality. 3) Test each verb against that kind — can this verb act on a quality? 4) Reject verbs built for bodies or sizes. 5) Choose the verb whose natural partners include the object.

subject: act-english
context_html: In its annual summary, the state climate office reported that the summer's rainfall totals were <u>totally out of whack with</u> the fifty-year average.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the tone and register of the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Out of whack' is slangy conversation, jarring inside an official annual summary (misconception: familiar idioms are universally acceptable).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Way off' is casual intensifier-speak, mismatched with a formal report (misconception: shorter always sounds cleaner).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Crazily' keeps the chatty register even though 'different from' is standard (misconception: fixing half the phrase fixes the register).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: measured, precise wording that matches the document's formal register.

why_correct_md: A formal report requires **register-matched** wording — measured and precise rather than conversational.
why_tempted_md: 'Crazily different from' upgrades part of the phrase, so it can pass a quick scan as the formal fix.
rule_md: 1) Identify the document and audience named in the sentence. 2) Set the register bar: official report = formal. 3) Test every word of each option against that bar, not just the obvious slang. 4) Reject any option with even one word below the bar. 5) Choose the option whose every word a careful report writer would sign.

subject: act-english
context_html: By the time the salt kiln finally reached cone ten last June, the studio's resident potters <u>have monitored</u> its flame color for nearly eighteen hours, adjusting the dampers whenever the atmosphere inside shifted.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: The present perfect 'have monitored' ties the action to the present moment, clashing with the past-time frame set by 'reached' and 'last June' (present-perfect-for-past confusion).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the eighteen hours of monitoring were completed before another past event ('reached cone ten'), so the past perfect is required.
per_choice_rationale.C: Simple past 'monitored' treats the monitoring and the kiln's arrival at cone ten as an undifferentiated past, failing to mark which happened first (ignores tense sequence).
per_choice_rationale.D: Future perfect 'will have monitored' places completion at a future moment, contradicting 'last June' (mistakes any perfect form for future time).

why_correct_md: With **by the time** plus a past event, the earlier of the two past actions must take the past perfect.
why_tempted_md: The bare simple past sounds natural read aloud, so students never ask which of the two past events finished first.
rule_md: 1) List every action in the sentence and note when each happens. 2) If two actions are both past, ask which one finished first. 3) Give the earlier action 'had' + past participle. 4) Confirm with time cues like 'by the time' and 'last June'. 5) Reread the sentence to check the sequence now reads clearly.

subject: act-english
context_html: Every apprentice at Riverbend Clayworks must sign <u>his or her</u> name on the kiln log before loading a single shelf.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: 'every apprentice' is grammatically singular, so the singular pair 'his or her' agrees with it.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Their' is plural, but 'every apprentice' is singular on this test — the classic plural-pronoun-for-singular-antecedent error.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'There' is the place word, a homophone confusion; it cannot show possession of 'name'.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Its' refers to objects and animals, not to a person such as an apprentice.

why_correct_md: **Every** makes its noun singular, and a singular antecedent needs a singular pronoun.
why_tempted_md: Everyday speech uses 'their' for one person, so students trust their ear instead of checking the antecedent's number.
rule_md: 1) Find the pronoun and draw an arrow back to its antecedent. 2) Decide whether that antecedent is singular or plural — words like 'every' and 'each' force singular. 3) Confirm the pronoun matches in number. 4) Confirm it also matches in kind (person vs. thing). 5) Reread the sentence with your check in place.

subject: act-english
context_html: New members spend their first month learning <u>to wedge the clay, to center it on the wheel, and to pull</u> an even cylinder.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: to wedge the clay, centering it on the wheel, and to pull
to wedge the clay, to center it on the wheel, and pulling
wedging the clay, to center it on the wheel, and to pull

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: all three items in the series share the same to + verb form.
per_choice_rationale.B: Swaps the middle item to an -ing form, breaking the pattern set by the first and third items (mixed forms mid-series).
per_choice_rationale.C: Lets the final item drift into an -ing form after two matching items (last-item drift).
per_choice_rationale.D: Opens the series with an -ing form that the second and third items then abandon (mismatched first item).

why_correct_md: Items in a series must be **parallel** — here, three matching to + verb phrases.
why_tempted_md: The -ing swap in the middle is easy to miss because each item still sounds fine read in isolation.
rule_md: 1) Spot the list — look for commas plus 'and'. 2) Write the items in a column. 3) Check that each item begins with the same grammatical shape. 4) If one item breaks the pattern, reject that version. 5) Choose the version whose items all match.

subject: act-english
context_html: Stoneware can survive the hottest chamber of the wood kiln without warping. <u>Similarly,</u> earthenware slumps and blisters if it is fired even slightly past its low maturing point.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Similarly' claims the two clays behave alike, but one endures high heat and the other fails in it (likeness transition on opposing ideas).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the sentences set the two clays' behaviors against each other, so an opposition transition fits.
per_choice_rationale.C: The second sentence is not an instance of the first, so an example transition misfires (false-example).
per_choice_rationale.D: Stoneware's toughness does not cause earthenware's slumping, so a cause-effect transition is illogical (false-cause).

why_correct_md: The two sentences describe **opposite** behaviors, so the transition must signal opposition.
why_tempted_md: Both sentences discuss firing clay, so the surface similarity of topic lures students toward a likeness transition.
rule_md: 1) Restate each sentence in your own words. 2) Name the relationship between them: alike, opposed, example, cause, or sequence. 3) Match the transition to that named relationship. 4) Reread the pair with your choice inserted. 5) Confirm no other option names the relationship better.

subject: act-english
context_html: Nearly every glaze recipe at the Ashfield co-op circulates freely, photocopied and traded like family recipes. <u>For instance,</u> a few signature formulas remain locked in the private notebooks of the potters who perfected them.
stem_md: Which transition word or phrase is most logical here?

per_choice_rationale.A: The second sentence is an exception to the sharing culture, not an example of it (false-example transition).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'In fact' promises an even stronger restatement of the first claim, but this sentence pulls back from it (false-intensifier).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the guarded formulas persist despite the open-sharing norm, so a concession transition fits.
per_choice_rationale.D: Free sharing does not cause the secrecy, so a cause-effect transition misstates the logic (false-cause).

why_correct_md: The second sentence is a **concession** — an exception that stands despite the general rule just described.
why_tempted_md: 'In fact' tempts students because the second sentence also discusses recipes, masking that it limits rather than intensifies the first claim.
rule_md: 1) Summarize sentence one's claim. 2) Ask what sentence two does to that claim: extend it, illustrate it, limit it, or result from it. 3) If sentence two limits or surprises, choose a concession connector. 4) Insert your choice and reread. 5) Verify no other option names the move more precisely.

subject: act-english
context_html: [NEW OPENING SENTENCE] Twice a month, members haul buckets of bone-dry scraps to the reclaim station, where the shards soak overnight in water. The softened slurry is then spread across plaster slabs until it stiffens. Finally, volunteers wedge the reclaimed clay into neat blocks and return it to the communal shelves. Last year the program put more than a ton of clay back into members' hands.
stem_md: The writer wants to open the paragraph with a sentence that introduces its main focus. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Rather than discarding unusable clay, Millbrook Pottery runs a reclaim program that turns studio scraps back into fresh working material.
Plaster slabs wear down over time and must be resurfaced every few years.
People have shaped vessels from clay for more than twenty thousand years.
Millbrook Pottery also hosts a popular series of weekend glaze-chemistry workshops.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: it names the reclaim program and previews the scrap-to-fresh-clay process the paragraph then details.
per_choice_rationale.B: Spotlights one minor prop from the middle of the paragraph, far too narrow to frame the whole process (too-narrow opener).
per_choice_rationale.C: Sweeps across twenty thousand years of history the paragraph never discusses (too-broad opener).
per_choice_rationale.D: Introduces a different program entirely, which nothing in the paragraph develops (off-topic opener).

why_correct_md: A strong opener **previews the paragraph's whole focus** — here, the studio's process for turning scraps back into usable clay.
why_tempted_md: The broad history of ceramics sounds impressively essay-like, so students pick grandeur over fit.
rule_md: 1) Read the paragraph and state its main focus in one phrase. 2) Test each opener: does it announce that exact focus? 3) Reject openers wider than the paragraph. 4) Reject openers that enlarge one small detail. 5) Reject openers about topics the paragraph never returns to.

subject: act-english
context_html:
[1] Every August, Kilnhouse Collective throws open its gates for the unbricking of its enormous wood-fired kiln. [2] Visitors begin lining up before dawn to watch the crew dismantle the kiln door brick by brick. [3] As each shelf emerges, volunteers ferry the still-warm pots to long tables on the lawn. [4] By noon, nearly every piece has been claimed by a collector or a curious first-timer.

The writer wants to add the following sentence to the paragraph:

The tradition began twelve years ago as a modest potluck for a dozen members.
stem_md: To make the paragraph most logical, the sentence should be placed after:

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the origin backstory belongs right after the event is introduced, before the dawn-to-noon account begins.
per_choice_rationale.B: Interrupts the chronological account just as the crowd gathers and the door comes down (breaks the timeline).
per_choice_rationale.C: Wedges a twelve-year flashback between two tightly linked actions in the unloading sequence (severs linked actions).
per_choice_rationale.D: Dangles history after the paragraph's closing image, leaving the story to trail off (backstory after the ending).

why_correct_md: Background about an event belongs **where the event is introduced**, before the chronological narration starts.
why_tempted_md: Placing history at the very end feels like a graceful coda, but it strands the origin story after the day has already concluded.
rule_md: 1) Identify what the added sentence does — here, it gives origin background. 2) Find where the paragraph introduces its subject in general terms. 3) Find where minute-by-minute narration begins. 4) Slot background between those two zones. 5) Reread to confirm the timeline flows unbroken.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Coil building, among the oldest of ceramic techniques, requires no wheel at all. [2] The artist rolls long ropes of clay and stacks them in rings, blending each new layer into the one below. [3] With patience, a coiled vessel can rise taller than the potter who shapes it. [4] This spring, Harborview Clay Center devoted its entire gallery to such handbuilt work. [5] Twenty-eight artists contributed pieces ranging from thimble-sized bowls to a chimney-like urn that nearly grazed the ceiling. [6] By closing weekend, attendance had broken the gallery's ten-year record.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide this paragraph into two in order to separate its two main ideas. The most logical place to begin the second paragraph is at:

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the paragraph pivots from explaining the technique to reporting the exhibition exactly here.
per_choice_rationale.B: Starts the split one sentence late, stranding the exhibition's introduction with the technique material (break placed after the shift).
per_choice_rationale.C: Cuts the technique explanation in half, separating the stacking description from its payoff (break inside a topic).
per_choice_rationale.D: Orphans the opening definition from the explanation that depends on it (break inside a topic).

why_correct_md: A paragraph break belongs at the **first sentence of the new topic** — the pivot from craft explanation to exhibition report.
why_tempted_md: The sentence naming twenty-eight artists feels like a fresh start, but the exhibition topic actually begins one sentence earlier.
rule_md: 1) Label each sentence with its topic in one or two words. 2) Find where the labels change. 3) Place the break at the first sentence carrying the new label. 4) Check that each resulting paragraph reads as one complete idea. 5) Reject any split that leaves a topic's opening sentence behind.

subject: act-english
context_html: Marisol's first <u>teapot a lopsided vessel with a drippy spout still</u> greets visitors from the studio's welcome shelf.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: teapot, a lopsided vessel, with a drippy spout still
teapot a lopsided vessel with a drippy spout, still
teapot, a lopsided vessel with a drippy spout, still

per_choice_rationale.A: With no punctuation, the nonessential appositive crashes into the sentence's subject and verb (missing both commas).
per_choice_rationale.B: Slices the appositive apart, fencing off its own prepositional phrase and leaving part of the aside unmarked (comma dropped inside the unit).
per_choice_rationale.C: Closes an interruption that was never opened, so readers cannot tell where the aside began (missing the opening comma).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the nonessential appositive describing the teapot is framed by a comma on each side.

why_correct_md: A **nonessential appositive** must be enclosed by a matched pair of commas.
why_tempted_md: The single closing comma sounds right aloud because the voice drops there, so students forget the interruption also needs an entrance marker.
rule_md: 1) Cover the descriptive phrase and confirm the sentence still stands. 2) If it does, the phrase is nonessential. 3) Mark where the phrase begins and where it ends. 4) Place one comma at each boundary — never just one, never inside the phrase. 5) Reread to confirm subject meets verb cleanly.

subject: act-english
context_html: The gas kiln finally hit cone ten just before <u>midnight; the</u> bleary-eyed crew celebrated with cocoa while the burners hissed down to silence.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: a semicolon legally joins these two independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.C: Stacking a semicolon with a coordinating conjunction doubles the connector at one seam (redundant joining).
per_choice_rationale.D: No punctuation at all fuses the two clauses into a run-on.

why_correct_md: A **semicolon** is a full-strength weld between two independent clauses.
why_tempted_md: The comma feels natural because the clauses are short and closely related, which is exactly how splices sneak past the ear.
rule_md: 1) Test each half: could it stand alone as a sentence? 2) If both halves pass, the seam needs a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. 3) Reject a lone comma. 4) Reject a bare gap. 5) Reject doubled connectors doing the same job twice.

subject: act-english
context_html: Dario's signature crackle glaze<u>, that he mixes in five-gallon batches,</u> gives each raku pot its spiderweb finish.
stem_md: Which choice best punctuates the underlined portion?

choices.label: that he mixes in five-gallon batches
, which he mixes in five-gallon batches
, which he mixes in five-gallon batches,

per_choice_rationale.A: 'That' cannot introduce a clause set off by commas; comma-marked asides require a different relative pronoun (that-with-commas).
per_choice_rationale.B: Dropping the commas treats the clause as essential, but 'signature' already identifies the glaze uniquely (restrictive misread).
per_choice_rationale.C: Opens the aside with a comma but never closes it, leaving the interruption half-fenced (missing closing comma).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: a nonessential clause takes 'which' and a comma at each of its two boundaries.

why_correct_md: A **nonessential** clause is introduced by 'which' and enclosed in a matched pair of commas.
why_tempted_md: The commas create a natural spoken pause, so students accept 'that' with commas without checking that 'that' clauses must run unpunctuated.
rule_md: 1) Cover the clause and check whether the noun is still fully identified. 2) If it is, the clause is nonessential. 3) Nonessential clauses take 'which' — never 'that'. 4) Fence the clause with a comma at each end. 5) Reread to confirm both boundaries are marked.

subject: act-english
context_html: Porcelain is unforgiving at the trimming stage: one heavy-handed pass of the tool can <u>slice through a wall the potter has spent hours thinning</u>.
stem_md: The writer wants to stress how quickly a single mistake can undo hours of careful work. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: have an unfortunate effect on the piece
make the pot slightly less even than before
mess the whole thing up big-time

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: slicing through a wall thinned over hours makes both the speed of the error and the scale of the loss vivid.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'An unfortunate effect' is so vague it conveys neither speed nor loss (goal-vague wording).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Slightly less even' shrinks a catastrophe to a cosmetic flaw, muting the stakes (understates the goal).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Big-time' injects slang that clashes with the passage's register even as it gestures at severity (tone violation).

why_correct_md: The goal needs wording that makes the **sudden destruction of long labor** visible, not vague or minimized.
why_tempted_md: The mild phrasing about evenness sounds appropriately modest and technical, so students miss that it erases the drama the goal demands.
rule_md: 1) Underline the key words of the stated goal. 2) Test each option against those exact words. 3) Reject options too vague to show the goal's idea. 4) Reject options that shrink or exaggerate the stakes. 5) Reject options whose tone clashes with the passage, then pick what remains.

subject: act-english
context_html: To raise the studio's tallest planters, Imani <u>works with</u> nearly twenty pounds of clay at a time, coaxing the walls upward through a dozen slow pulls.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize the physical effort that throwing large forms demands. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Works with' is neutral about exertion, fitting light tasks as easily as heavy ones (goal-neutral verb).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Shapes' emphasizes artistry and skill rather than the muscle the goal demands (wrong emphasis).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: 'wrestles' turns the clay into a physical opponent, foregrounding strenuous bodily effort.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Manages' suggests calm competence at a distance, understating physical labor (weak emphasis).

why_correct_md: Only a verb that conveys **strenuous bodily struggle** fulfills the stated goal of emphasizing physical effort.
why_tempted_md: 'Shapes' feels apt because the sentence is about pottery, but it spotlights craftsmanship instead of the exertion the goal names.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's goal in one word (here: effort). 2) Ask of each verb: what does it emphasize? 3) Eliminate verbs that are neutral about the goal's idea. 4) Eliminate verbs that emphasize a different quality. 5) Keep the verb whose core meaning is the goal itself.

subject: act-english
context_html:
Each November, Glazed Harvest Pottery hosts an Empty Bowls dinner to fight hunger in its county. Members spend October throwing hundreds of simple soup bowls, and local restaurants donate pots of soup and fresh bread. Guests choose a handmade bowl, share a modest meal, and take the bowl home as a reminder that someone's bowl is often empty.

The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the final sentence of the paragraph:

Last year the dinner raised more than four thousand dollars for the county food pantry.
stem_md: Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it explains how the members make the bowls.
Yes, because it gives concrete evidence of the dinner's impact.
No, because it repeats information stated earlier in the paragraph.
No, because it shifts attention away from the dinner itself.

per_choice_rationale.A: The sentence says nothing about bowl-making, so this 'yes' rests on a misdescription of the sentence (right verdict, wrong reason).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: a dollar total for the food pantry documents what the event achieves, strengthening the paragraph's close.
per_choice_rationale.C: No earlier sentence mentions money or the pantry, so nothing is repeated (phantom repetition).
per_choice_rationale.D: The total is the outcome of the dinner itself, so attention stays exactly where the paragraph put it (false off-topic call).

why_correct_md: The addition supplies a **specific, verifiable result** that supports the paragraph's account of the event.
why_tempted_md: Students often accept a correct verdict paired with a reason that misdescribes what the sentence actually contains.
rule_md: 1) Read the proposed sentence and state what it contains. 2) Decide whether that content serves the paragraph's purpose. 3) Pick the verdict (add or not). 4) Then test each stated reason against the sentence's actual content. 5) Accept only the verdict whose reason accurately describes the sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html:
Slip trailing turns liquid clay into raised lines of surface ornament. Nadia fills a rubber bulb with slip about the consistency of cake batter, then squeezes steady beads of it across a leather-hard platter. Because the trailed lines sit above the surface, they catch the glaze during firing and emerge a shade darker than the ground beneath them.

The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the second sentence of the paragraph:

Nadia also teaches a beginners' wheel class on Tuesday evenings.
stem_md: Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it establishes that Nadia is an experienced teacher.
Yes, because it adds another example of Nadia's skill with clay.
No, because the paragraph's description of the process is already detailed enough.
No, because it strays from the paragraph's focus on a single decorating process.

per_choice_rationale.A: Nadia's teaching credentials are beside the point in a walkthrough of one technique (irrelevant-but-true lure).
per_choice_rationale.B: A wheel class involves a different skill entirely, not an example of slip trailing (false-example).
per_choice_rationale.C: Length is not the issue; the sentence fails on relevance, not on the explanation's completeness (right verdict, wrong reason).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the sentence veers away from the paragraph's one subject, the slip-trailing technique.

why_correct_md: Every sentence in a paragraph must serve its **one controlling subject**; the proposed sentence belongs to a different topic.
why_tempted_md: The near-miss 'no' tempts students because its verdict is right, and only its stated reason fails to match why the sentence doesn't belong.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's subject in a short phrase. 2) State what the proposed sentence is about. 3) If the two don't match, the verdict is no. 4) Among matching verdicts, test each reason against the sentence's actual flaw. 5) Choose the verdict-plus-reason pair that is accurate on both counts.

subject: act-english
context_html: At Foxglove Pottery, apprentices spend their first season mixing glazes and loading kilns before they ever sit at a wheel. In their second season, they throw the studio's standard forms — mugs, bowls, plates — until each piece matches the house template within a few grams. Only in the third season do apprentices design work of their own, which the studio sells alongside its established line. By the time they leave, most can run every station in the building.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to describe how one pottery studio trains its apprentices. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it explains why handmade pottery costs more than factory ware.
Yes, because it traces the stages of training an apprentice completes at one studio.
No, because it does not compare that training with programs at other studios.
No, because it follows one apprentice through a single day rather than describing the training.

per_choice_rationale.A: The passage never mentions cost or factory production, so this reason has no textual basis (yes-with-fabricated-reason).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the essay moves season by season through Foxglove's training, exactly matching the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.C: The goal never asks for comparison with other programs, so their absence is no failure (demands-unrequested-content).
per_choice_rationale.D: The essay covers years of training for apprentices in general, not one person's day (misreads the passage's scope).

why_correct_md: The essay's season-by-season structure **matches the stated goal** of describing one studio's apprentice training.
why_tempted_md: Students often reject a passage for lacking comparisons or context the stated goal never demanded.
rule_md: 1) Restate the supposed goal in your own words. 2) Summarize what the passage actually does. 3) Judge only whether the two match — nothing more. 4) Reject reasons that describe content the passage doesn't contain. 5) Reject reasons that demand content the goal never required.

subject: act-english
context_html: Whenever the afternoon class ends, <u>the aprons hang</u> on numbered hooks beside the sink.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: 'the aprons hang' supplies the subject and finite verb the main clause needs.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Hanging' alone is a participle with no helping verb, so no complete predicate remains (bare -ing fragment).
per_choice_rationale.C: An infinitive cannot act as a main verb, leaving the thought unfinished (infinitive fragment).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'That' folds the verb into a description of the aprons, stranding the sentence without a predicate (relative-clause fragment).

why_correct_md: A complete sentence needs a subject paired with a **finite verb** in its main clause.
why_tempted_md: The -ing version sounds fluid read aloud, so students don't notice the main clause has lost its working verb.
rule_md: 1) Cross out the introductory clause. 2) Find the subject of what remains. 3) Find a finite verb — one that changes with tense and subject. 4) If the only verb candidate is an -ing form, a to-form, or trapped after 'that,' it's a fragment. 5) Keep the version with a free-standing verb.

subject: act-english
context_html: The pug mill jammed on Friday, <u>so the</u> handbuilding class switched to slab rollers for the week.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: a comma plus the coordinating conjunction 'so' legally joins the clauses and states the right cause-effect logic.
per_choice_rationale.B: Deleting the conjunction leaves two independent clauses spliced by a lone comma.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'However' reverses the logic and, as a conjunctive adverb after a mere comma, still splices the clauses.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Consequently' fits the logic but is a conjunctive adverb; after only a comma it creates a splice.

why_correct_md: A comma can join two independent clauses only when a **coordinating conjunction** rides along with it.
why_tempted_md: 'Consequently' names the cause-effect relationship correctly, so students overlook that it lacks the punctuation power of a true conjunction.
rule_md: 1) Confirm both halves are independent clauses. 2) List what sits at the seam. 3) A comma alone fails; a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) passes. 4) Conjunctive adverbs like 'however' or 'consequently' need a semicolon instead. 5) Finally, check that the connector's meaning fits the logic.

subject: act-english
context_html: Glaze buckets must be stirred before every <u>use, sediment</u> settles to the bottom within hours.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: A lone comma between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: a period gives each independent clause its own complete sentence.
per_choice_rationale.C: No punctuation at all fuses the clauses and momentarily misreads as 'use sediment' (run-on).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Although' concedes what is actually the reason for stirring, reversing the logic (wrong subordinator).

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses need a **full-strength boundary** — here, a period ending the first statement.
why_tempted_md: The comma feels sufficient because the clauses are short and closely related, which is exactly how splices slip past the ear.
rule_md: 1) Test each half: can it stand alone as a sentence? 2) If both pass, the seam needs a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. 3) Reject a lone comma. 4) Reject a bare gap. 5) If a subordinator is offered, check that its logic matches the meaning before accepting it.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Balanced on a narrow bat, Tomas carried the still-wet vase across the studio</u> while classmates cleared a path.
stem_md: Which of the following provides the clearest, most logical version of the sentence?

choices.label: Balanced on a narrow bat, the studio watched Tomas carry the still-wet vase
Tomas carried the still-wet vase, balanced on a narrow bat, across the studio
Being balanced on a narrow bat, Tomas carried the still-wet vase across the studio

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening modifier grabs the first noun after it — Tomas — absurdly claiming the potter is balanced on the bat (dangling modifier).
per_choice_rationale.B: Recasting the subject as 'the studio' hands the modifier an even less plausible owner (wrong noun promoted).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the participial phrase now sits beside 'vase,' the thing actually balanced on the bat.
per_choice_rationale.D: Adding 'being' is cosmetic; the phrase still attaches to Tomas (surface fix, same dangler).

why_correct_md: A modifier must sit **next to the noun it describes** — the vase, not the person carrying it.
why_tempted_md: Adding 'being' makes the phrase sound more deliberate, so students believe the attachment problem has been repaired when it hasn't.
rule_md: 1) Find the modifying phrase. 2) Ask: who or what does it really describe? 3) Find the noun the phrase currently touches. 4) If the two don't match, rearrange so the phrase sits beside its true owner. 5) Reread each option running the same touch test.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each spring the members <u>collaborate together on</u> a single monumental sculpture for the courthouse lawn.
stem_md: Which choice is most effective for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Collaborate' already means work together, so adding 'together' repeats the idea (unnoticed redundancy).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the bare verb carries the whole idea without repetition.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Jointly' is a synonym for the idea already inside the verb, so the redundancy survives (synonym swap).
per_choice_rationale.D: Reordering the words leaves the doubled meaning fully intact (order-not-meaning fix).

why_correct_md: **Redundancy** is cut by deleting the word whose meaning the verb already contains.
why_tempted_md: Swapping 'together' for the more formal 'jointly' feels like an improvement, but the meaning is still stated twice.
rule_md: 1) Define the verb in your own words. 2) Check every nearby modifier: does any repeat part of that definition? 3) If so, the modifier is redundant no matter what synonym or position it takes. 4) Keep the version that states the idea exactly once. 5) Reread to confirm no meaning was lost.

subject: act-english
context_html: After weighing three bids, the co-op <u>made the decision to go forward with purchasing</u> a second slab roller.
stem_md: Which choice expresses the idea most concisely?

choices.label: decided that they would go forward with purchasing

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Made the decision to go forward with purchasing' buries one action under three layers of padding (noun-heavy inflation).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: 'decided to purchase' states the entire idea in three words.
per_choice_rationale.C: Trimming 'go forward with' still leaves the buried-verb opener 'made the decision to' (half-trim).
per_choice_rationale.D: Opens with a strong verb but re-inflates the sentence with an empty trailing clause (relocated wordiness).

why_correct_md: Concision means converting **buried actions** back into direct verbs and dropping every phrase that adds no meaning.
why_tempted_md: The half-trimmed version feels reformed because it is shorter than the original, so students stop auditing before the padding is gone.
rule_md: 1) Find the real action hiding in the phrase. 2) Convert noun constructions like 'made the decision' into their verb. 3) Delete connector padding such as 'go forward with.' 4) Reread: is any remaining word free of a job? 5) Keep the version where every word earns its place and no meaning is lost.

subject: act-english
context_html: The wax resist must dry completely<u>, as a matter of fact,</u> before any glaze touches the pot.
stem_md: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'As a matter of fact' adds no facts; it only delays the instruction (retained filler).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'In point of fact' is the same empty formula in different clothes (filler swap).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For all intents and purposes' hedges an absolute requirement while adding no information (hedging filler).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: with the filler gone, the instruction is direct and loses nothing.

why_correct_md: A phrase that can vanish with **zero loss of meaning** is filler and should go.
why_tempted_md: Fact-flavored interrupters sound authoritative, so students assume they add emphasis rather than empty bulk.
rule_md: 1) Read the sentence without the underlined phrase. 2) List what meaning, if any, disappeared. 3) If nothing disappeared, the phrase is filler. 4) Test each replacement the same way — a swapped filler is still filler. 5) Prefer the version that keeps only working words.

subject: act-english
context_html: A fine mist from the spray bottle <u>soaks</u> the leather-hard tiles just enough to keep them workable overnight.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely describes the action?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Soaks' claims heavy saturation that a fine mist cannot deliver (degree overshoot).
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Sprinkles' pictures scattered separate drops rather than an even, gentle wetting (wrong image).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Coats' suggests a layer resting on the surface instead of moisture absorbed by the clay (wrong mechanism).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: 'moistens' matches the light, even dampening that 'fine mist' and 'just enough' describe.

why_correct_md: Precise word choice means matching the verb's **degree and mechanism** to the context clues 'fine mist' and 'just enough.'
why_tempted_md: 'Soaks' feels natural because water is involved, so students miss that its intensity contradicts the delicate action described.
rule_md: 1) Collect the sentence's context clues about scale and manner. 2) Define each verb option precisely. 3) Reject verbs whose degree overshoots or undershoots the clues. 4) Reject verbs that describe the wrong kind of action. 5) Keep the verb whose exact meaning the clues confirm.

subject: act-english
context_html: When an entire glaze batch fired to a dull gray, the workshop's founder <u>didn't freak out</u>; she quartered the batch and retested one variable at a time.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the tone of the passage?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Freak out' is slang at odds with the passage's formal, technical register (colloquial retention).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: 'remained composed' states the idea in the same measured register as the rest of the sentence.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Kept her cool' trades one informal idiom for another (idiom swap).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Exhibited an imperturbable equanimity' overshoots into stilted, showy diction (hypercorrection).

why_correct_md: Register repair means landing in the passage's **plain formal middle** — neither slang nor ornate excess.
