why_tempted_md: The ornate version sounds impressively academic, so students overcorrect the slang instead of matching the passage's plain style.
rule_md: 1) Sample the passage's diction from nearby words. 2) Classify the underlined phrase: slang, plain formal, or ornate. 3) Reject anything more casual than the passage. 4) Reject anything more inflated than the passage. 5) Keep the phrase that sits in the same register as its neighbors.

subject: act-english
context_html: By the time the council approved the greenway plan in 2019, volunteers, working weekends with borrowed mowers, <u>will have cleared</u> nearly three miles of the abandoned rail corridor.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Future perfect points forward from the present, but the reference point ('approved... in 2019') is past — the misconception that 'by the time' always triggers 'will have.'
per_choice_rationale.B: Present perfect ties a past action to right now, but the clearing must be anchored before a specific past event, not before the present.
per_choice_rationale.C: Simple future contradicts the past-tense reference point established in the opening clause.
per_choice_rationale.D: Past perfect correctly marks the clearing as completed before another past event, the 2019 approval.

why_correct_md: **Past perfect** signals an action finished before another past event — here, before the 2019 approval.
why_tempted_md: 'By the time' so often pairs with 'will have' in speech that students apply future perfect without checking the anchor event's tense.
rule_md: 1) Find the time anchor ('by the time X happened'). 2) Note the anchor's tense. 3) If the anchor is past, the earlier action takes past perfect; if the anchor is future or present, use future perfect. 4) Re-read with both events placed on a timeline.

subject: act-english
context_html: When a resident applies for a curb-cut permit, <u>they must submit</u> two copies of the site drawing.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'They' is plural, but the antecedent 'a resident' is singular — the misconception of defaulting to a plural pronoun for one generic person.
per_choice_rationale.B: This keeps the plural pronoun and adds an unneeded progressive verb form on top of it.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'It' matches in number but wrongly refers to a person as if the resident were a thing.
per_choice_rationale.D: The paired singular personal pronouns agree with the singular human antecedent 'a resident.'

why_correct_md: The singular antecedent **'a resident'** requires singular personal pronouns.
why_tempted_md: Everyday speech uses 'they' for one unnamed person, so the plural sounds perfectly natural.
rule_md: 1) Find the pronoun. 2) Trace it back to its antecedent. 3) Ask: singular or plural? person or thing? 4) Match the pronoun on both number and personhood. 5) Re-read the sentence with the match in place.

subject: act-english
context_html: The revised zoning code rewards developers for planting street trees, widening sidewalks, and <u>to include ground-floor retail</u>.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: The infinitive 'to include' breaks the pattern set by the gerunds 'planting' and 'widening.'
per_choice_rationale.B: The gerund matches the two earlier '-ing' items, keeping the series parallel.
per_choice_rationale.C: A 'the ___ of' noun phrase disrupts the '-ing' pattern — the misconception that any noun-like form counts as parallel.
per_choice_rationale.D: A full clause with its own subject cannot sit in a series of gerund phrases after the preposition 'for.'

why_correct_md: Items in a series must share the same grammatical form — here, **gerunds**.
why_tempted_md: The infinitive sounds fine in isolation, so students miss that the series already established an '-ing' pattern.
rule_md: 1) Find the list. 2) Label the form of each item (gerund, infinitive, noun phrase, clause). 3) Identify the pattern set by the first items. 4) Convert the odd one out to match. 5) Re-read the whole series.

subject: act-english
context_html: The pilot bike lane came in well under budget. <u>Similarly,</u> merchants along the route reported stronger weekend sales.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Similarly' claims the two facts resemble each other, but low cost and strong sales are different kinds of good news, not parallels.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'However' signals contrast, yet the second sentence continues the positive report rather than opposing it.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For instance' would make the sales figures an example of the budget result, which they are not.
per_choice_rationale.D: The second sentence stacks a second, separate benefit onto the first — exactly what this additive transition signals.

why_correct_md: The sentences stack **two separate benefits**, so an additive transition fits.
why_tempted_md: Both sentences are positive, so 'Similarly' feels harmonious even though the facts aren't actually alike.
rule_md: 1) Summarize sentence 1 in five words. 2) Summarize sentence 2. 3) Name the relationship: same point restated, new point stacked on, contrast, example, or result. 4) Match the transition to that relationship. 5) Re-read with your pick in place.

subject: act-english
context_html: Planners braced for the road diet to slow fire-truck response times along Cedar Avenue. <u>Therefore,</u> engines reached calls faster once double-parking disappeared from the corridor.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Therefore' treats faster responses as the expected result of the planners' worry, but the outcome defied the expectation.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Consequently' repeats the same false cause-effect link as 'Therefore.'
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In fact' signals that reality contradicted or outstripped the expectation, which is exactly the relationship here.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Likewise' claims similarity, but the sentences set up an expectation and then overturn it.

why_correct_md: The second sentence **overturns the expectation** set up in the first — the precise job of this corrective transition.
why_tempted_md: Students see a setup sentence followed by an outcome and reflexively reach for a cause-effect word like 'Therefore.'
rule_md: 1) Ask what the first sentence predicts or expects. 2) Ask whether the second sentence fulfills that expectation or defies it. 3) Fulfilled: use a result word. Defied: use a correction or contrast word. Parallel: use a likeness word. 4) Re-read with your choice.

subject: act-english
context_html: Over the past decade, the city has converted more than thirty vacant lots into pocket parks. Most are no larger than a house lot, yet each has become a gathering spot, with benches, shade trees, and room for a food cart or two. Crime reports near the converted lots have declined, and adjacent storefronts report steadier foot traffic.
stem_md: The writer wants to conclude the paragraph with a sentence that reinforces its main point. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Public parks have been part of American city planning since the nineteenth century.
Fencing and irrigation account for most of a pocket park's start-up costs.
In these modest plots, the city has discovered that a park's impact does not depend on its acreage.
The city's next campaign will ask voters to approve a downtown convention center.

per_choice_rationale.A: This reaches for broad history the paragraph never discusses — the misconception that a sweeping statement makes a strong ending.
per_choice_rationale.B: This adds a stray cost detail instead of pulling the paragraph's evidence together.
per_choice_rationale.C: This distills the paragraph's evidence — small sites, big neighborhood gains — into a closing generalization.
per_choice_rationale.D: This swerves to an unrelated future project, abandoning the paragraph's subject entirely.

why_correct_md: A strong conclusion **generalizes from the paragraph's own evidence** — here, that tiny sites produced big gains.
why_tempted_md: The historical statement sounds authoritative and park-related, so its disconnection from this paragraph's evidence is easy to miss.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's main point in one clause. 2) Cross out any option introducing information the paragraph never developed. 3) Cross out any option narrower than the main point. 4) Keep the option that restates the point using the paragraph's own thrust. 5) Re-read the paragraph plus your ending.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Last year, the downtown alliance launched a pilot program to replace its confusing wayfinding signs. [2] Designers began by interviewing visitors who had gotten lost near the transit mall. [3] The interviews revealed that most people navigate by landmarks rather than by street names. [4] The new signs therefore feature bold icons of the clock tower, the river, and other familiar reference points. [5] That discovery surprised the design team, which had expected to build a map-heavy layout.
stem_md: For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, the writer wants to place Sentence 5 where it functions best. Sentence 5 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Left at the end, 'That discovery' sits far from the finding it names, and the surprise lands after the design it motivated has already been described.
per_choice_rationale.B: After Sentence 1 there is no discovery yet for the pronoun phrase to point to.
per_choice_rationale.C: After Sentence 2 the interviews have happened, but no finding has been stated for 'That discovery' to name.
per_choice_rationale.D: Sentence 3 states the finding; Sentence 5's 'That discovery' points straight at it, and the team's surprise then motivates the design in Sentence 4.

why_correct_md: 'That discovery' must sit **immediately after the sentence that states the discovery**, and the team's surprise then explains the design change.
why_tempted_md: The paragraph reads smoothly enough to the ear at first pass, so leaving the sentence where it is feels safe.
rule_md: 1) Find pointing words in the movable sentence ('that,' 'this,' 'such'). 2) Identify what they must refer to. 3) Place the sentence right after its referent. 4) Re-read to confirm each sentence now leads logically to the next.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] The Parkway Viaduct opened in 1954 as the city's first limited-access highway. [2] At the time, engineers celebrated it for whisking suburban drivers over the crowded riverfront wards. [3] Within two decades, however, maintenance costs were climbing and the neighborhoods beneath it had emptied. [4] Today, a coalition of residents and business owners is campaigning to tear the viaduct down. [5] Their proposal would replace it with a surface boulevard, twelve acres of housing, and a riverfront trail. [6] City engineers are studying whether the boulevard could absorb the viaduct's traffic.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide this paragraph into two paragraphs, separating the viaduct's history from the current campaign to remove it. The most logical place to begin the new paragraph is at:

per_choice_rationale.A: Sentence 2 continues the 1954 opening story; splitting there strands the history's first detail.
per_choice_rationale.B: Sentence 3's 'however' marks a turn, but it still narrates the viaduct's past decades — the misconception that any contrast word starts a new paragraph.
per_choice_rationale.C: Sentence 4's 'Today' shifts from the structure's past to the present-day removal campaign, exactly the seam the writer wants.
per_choice_rationale.D: Sentence 5 elaborates the proposal introduced in Sentence 4; starting there separates a detail from its topic sentence.

why_correct_md: **'Today'** pivots the paragraph from decades of history to the current campaign — the seam the writer asked for.
why_tempted_md: 'However' in Sentence 3 feels like a hinge, but the contrast it marks happens within the historical narrative.
rule_md: 1) Restate the two intended topics. 2) Label each sentence with the topic it serves. 3) Find where the labels switch. 4) Begin the new paragraph at the first sentence of the second topic. 5) Check that both halves stand alone.

subject: act-english
context_html: The Marsh Street depot, <u>a brick landmark completed in 1911,</u> will anchor the new transit plaza.
stem_md: Which choice provides the best punctuation for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: The appositive is nonessential, so the paired commas around it are correct as written.
per_choice_rationale.B: Dropping the closing comma leaves the appositive half-fenced, welding it onto the verb — the misconception that one comma is enough.
per_choice_rationale.C: The extra comma after 'landmark' chops the appositive itself in two for no grammatical reason.
per_choice_rationale.D: A semicolon cannot close an appositive; it needs an independent clause on each side.

why_correct_md: A **nonessential appositive** takes a comma on both sides, and the original supplies both.
why_tempted_md: The comma-heavy look of the original makes students want to delete one, especially the closing comma.
rule_md: 1) Find the interrupter. 2) Test: can the sentence stand without it? 3) If yes, fence it with a comma at the start AND the end. 4) Never use stronger marks like semicolons unless both sides are full clauses. 5) Re-read the sentence, skipping the interrupter.

subject: act-english
context_html: The ferry terminal opened in <u>May, ridership</u> doubled by the end of August.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses — this is a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: The semicolon-plus-conjunction doubles up: use one joiner or the other, not both.
per_choice_rationale.C: A semicolon correctly joins the two related independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.D: Removing all punctuation fuses the clauses into a run-on.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses may be joined by a **semicolon alone**.
why_tempted_md: The clauses are short and closely related, so the bare comma feels sufficient.
rule_md: 1) Find the subject-verb pairs. 2) If both sides could stand as sentences, a bare comma is illegal. 3) Legal joins: period, semicolon, or comma plus coordinating conjunction. 4) Pick the join that fits the relationship. 5) Re-read both clauses.

subject: act-english
context_html: The preservation board must review alterations to <u>buildings, which stand</u> within the historic district; owners elsewhere may renovate freely.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: The comma plus 'which' marks the clause as nonessential, implying the board reviews all buildings — but the second half of the sentence shows only district buildings are covered.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'That' with no comma makes the clause restrictive, correctly limiting review to buildings inside the district.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'That' introduces restrictive clauses, which never take a comma before them — the misconception that a pause always earns a comma.
per_choice_rationale.D: Dropping the comma helps, but the singular verb 'stands' clashes with the plural 'buildings.'

why_correct_md: The clause **limits** which buildings need review, so it must be restrictive: 'that' with no comma.
why_tempted_md: The comma-plus-'which' construction looks polished and formal, so students miss that it quietly changes the sentence's meaning.
rule_md: 1) Ask: does the clause limit which nouns you mean, or just add bonus detail? 2) If it limits, use the restrictive pronoun with no comma. 3) If it's bonus detail, use a comma plus 'which.' 4) Check the rest of the sentence for evidence of which meaning is intended. 5) Confirm the clause's verb agrees with the noun it describes.

subject: act-english
context_html: During rush hour, Route 9 buses <u>move</u> along the new bus-only lane while car traffic idles beside them.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize how fast the buses travel in the new lane compared with the cars beside them. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Move' states motion without any sense of pace, so it does nothing for the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Proceed' sounds more formal but is just as neutral about speed — the misconception that elevated diction equals effectiveness.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Streak' builds rapid motion into the verb itself, sharpening the contrast with the idling cars.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Crawl' emphasizes slowness — the opposite of the writer's stated goal.

why_correct_md: Only this verb carries **speed** in its own meaning, achieving the writer's stated emphasis.
why_tempted_md: 'Proceed' sounds official and polished, so students mistake formality for accomplishing the goal.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's goal in your own words. 2) Test each verb alone: does it carry the target quality without help from other words? 3) Eliminate neutral verbs, then verbs suggesting the opposite quality. 4) Keep the verb whose built-in picture matches the goal. 5) Re-read the sentence to confirm the contrast lands.

subject: act-english
context_html: A canopy survey found that shade trees cover 38 percent of the streets in Oak Hill but only 9 percent of those near the freight yards, a difference the report's authors describe as <u>notable</u>.
stem_md: The writer wants to convey the severity of the gap in tree cover between the two neighborhoods. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Notable' concedes the gap deserves attention but says nothing about how severe it is.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Stark' presents the difference as harsh and extreme, delivering exactly the severity the writer wants.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Detectable' nearly erases the gap, implying it can barely be measured — the opposite of severe.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Surprising' asserts unexpectedness, a different quality from severity.

why_correct_md: The goal demands an adjective that asserts **harsh magnitude**, and only one option does.
why_tempted_md: 'Notable' sounds appropriately serious, so its actual mildness is easy to miss.
rule_md: 1) Name the exact quality the stem asks for. 2) For each adjective, state the single quality it asserts. 3) Strike options asserting a different quality. 4) Strike options asserting the right quality at a weaker degree. 5) Keep the survivor and re-read the sentence with the numbers in view.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each spring, the Riverside Night Market fills two blocks of Dock Street with food stalls, craft tables, and live music. Vendors pay a modest fee that funds trash pickup and off-duty police patrols. The market has become the district's most reliable draw for weekend visitors.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following true statement after the second sentence: "Last year those fees covered every cleanup and security bill, so the market needed no money from the city." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it demonstrates that the fee arrangement described in the previous sentence works.
Yes, because it reveals how much each vendor pays under the fee arrangement.
No, because the previous sentence already describes what the fees pay for.
No, because budget details distract from the paragraph's point about weekend visitors.

per_choice_rationale.A: The new sentence proves the fee system actually covered its costs, directly extending the point of the sentence it follows.
per_choice_rationale.B: The proposed sentence never states any individual vendor's payment — this reason misdescribes its content.
per_choice_rationale.C: Purpose and outcome are different facts: the paragraph says what the fees are for, not whether they sufficed — the misconception that shared topic equals repetition.
per_choice_rationale.D: The paragraph portrays a well-run market, so a sentence showing the market pays its own way supports rather than distracts.

why_correct_md: The addition supplies the **outcome** of the fee system the previous sentence set up, strengthening the paragraph's portrait.
why_tempted_md: The proposed sentence and the one before it both mention fees, so the addition can look like mere repetition.
rule_md: 1) State what the proposed sentence adds that the paragraph lacks. 2) Ask whether that addition supports the paragraph's focus. 3) If yes, the winning 'Yes' reason must accurately restate the sentence's content; if no, the winning 'No' reason must, too. 4) Reject any reason that misdescribes the sentence or the paragraph. 5) Choose the verdict-plus-reason pair that survives.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] When the city legalized backyard cottages in 2021, planners predicted a construction boom. [2] Instead, only forty permits were issued in the first year. [3] Interviews with homeowners traced the shortfall to a single rule: each cottage required an off-street parking space, which many small lots cannot fit. [4] This spring, the council voted to drop that requirement.
stem_md: The writer is considering deleting Sentence 3. If the writer were to delete this sentence, the paragraph would primarily lose:

choices.label: the explanation that connects the weak permit numbers to the council's vote.
evidence that homeowners opposed the cottage program from the start.
the statistic that shows how slowly the program began.
a transition between the planners' prediction and the permit totals.

per_choice_rationale.A: Sentence 3 supplies the cause — the parking rule — that makes Sentence 4's remedy comprehensible; without it, the vote comes from nowhere.
per_choice_rationale.B: The interviews show homeowners were blocked by a rule, not that they opposed cottages — a misreading of the sentence.
per_choice_rationale.C: The forty-permit figure sits in Sentence 2, which would remain after the deletion.
per_choice_rationale.D: Sentence 3 comes after both the prediction and the totals, so it cannot bridge them.

why_correct_md: Sentence 3 is the paragraph's **causal link**: it explains the slow start and sets up the council's fix.
why_tempted_md: Because Sentence 2 already establishes the slow start, Sentence 3 can feel like extra detail rather than the paragraph's hinge.
rule_md: 1) State each sentence's job in the paragraph. 2) Delete the target sentence mentally and re-read. 3) Name precisely what no longer makes sense. 4) Match that loss to an option, rejecting options that describe content living in other sentences. 5) Verify the surviving option describes the target sentence accurately.

subject: act-english
context_html: For twenty years after the tannery closed, Grafton Pier sat behind a chain-link fence while the city argued over its future. Preservationists wanted the timber warehouse restored; the parks department wanted open lawn to the waterline; a hotel group promised tax revenue. The compromise that finally passed a citywide vote — a public promenade wrapping a smaller, restored warehouse — satisfied no faction completely, which several council members now cite as proof it was the right call.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to describe the engineering challenges of building on an aging pier. Would this paragraph accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it explains how the restored warehouse was anchored to the pier.
Yes, because the promenade it describes was built out over the water.
No, because it focuses on the community's fight over the site rather than on how anything was built.
No, because the paragraph discusses a warehouse rather than a pier.

per_choice_rationale.A: The paragraph never explains any anchoring or construction method — this reason invents content.
per_choice_rationale.B: A structure's location over water does not mean the paragraph covers the difficulties of building there — the misconception that a surface link satisfies the goal.
per_choice_rationale.C: Every sentence concerns the political contest over the pier's future, not technical challenges, so the paragraph fails the supposed goal.
per_choice_rationale.D: The verdict is right but the reason misreads the passage: the pier and its redevelopment are the paragraph's clear subject.

why_correct_md: The paragraph's content is **political, not technical**, so it cannot serve an engineering-focused purpose.
why_tempted_md: Because the setting involves water and construction, the reason about building over the water feels plausible without checking what the sentences actually develop.
rule_md: 1) Restate the supposed goal precisely. 2) List what each sentence of the paragraph actually develops. 3) Judge the verdict: does the content match the goal? 4) Among options with the correct verdict, keep only the reason that accurately describes the paragraph. 5) Reject reasons that invent, misread, or rely on surface connections.

subject: act-english
context_html: The transit agency installed forty new bus shelters along the crosstown line. <u>Each one equipped</u> with solar lighting and a screen showing arrival times.
stem_md: Which choice makes the second statement a complete sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Equipped' is a bare participle, leaving the subject with no main verb — a fragment.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Being equipped' is still a participle; adding '-ing' does not create a finite verb.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Is equipped' supplies the finite verb the subject needs, completing the sentence.
per_choice_rationale.D: A comma cannot substitute for a verb; the statement remains a fragment.

why_correct_md: A complete sentence needs a **finite verb**, and only this option provides one.
why_tempted_md: The fragment reads smoothly after the first sentence, so the missing verb is easy to overlook.
rule_md: 1) Isolate the statement and find its subject. 2) Hunt for a finite verb — one that changes form for past or future. 3) If every verb-like word is a participle, the statement is a fragment. 4) Fix it by adding a helping verb or attaching the fragment to the previous sentence. 5) Re-read the repaired statement alone.

subject: act-english
context_html: Crews converted every streetlight in the Fairmont district to LEDs over a single <u>summer, residents</u> noticed the whiter light before the utility announced the project was finished.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: A bare comma cannot join two independent clauses — this is a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Removing the comma fuses the clauses and even invites the misreading 'summer residents.'
per_choice_rationale.C: 'However' set off by commas is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction, so the splice survives — the misconception that any connector legalizes the join.
per_choice_rationale.D: A comma plus a coordinating conjunction legally joins the two independent clauses.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses may be joined by a **comma plus a coordinating conjunction**.
why_tempted_md: 'However' feels like a strong connector, so students assume it can join clauses the way a conjunction does.
rule_md: 1) Find the subject-verb pair on each side of the underlined area. 2) If both sides could stand as sentences, a bare comma is illegal. 3) Legal joins: period, semicolon, or comma plus coordinating conjunction. 4) Remember that words like 'however' are adverbs, not conjunctions. 5) Re-read with your repair in place.

subject: act-english
context_html: The council eliminated parking minimums for downtown apartment buildings <u>last fall, since then</u> three stalled projects have broken ground.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Since then three stalled projects have broken ground' is a full independent clause, so the bare comma creates a splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Removing the only mark fuses the two clauses into a run-on.
per_choice_rationale.C: Fencing the time phrase with commas does not repair the illegal clause join — the misconception that more commas mean more correctness.
per_choice_rationale.D: A period properly ends the first clause, and the time phrase then opens a new sentence with its own comma.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses need a **full boundary** — here, a period before the new sentence begins.
why_tempted_md: 'Since then' feels like a subordinating link, so the second clause doesn't register as independent.
rule_md: 1) Locate every subject-verb pair. 2) Ask whether each side of the seam could stand alone as a sentence. 3) If both can, choose a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. 4) Beware of time phrases that look like subordinators but aren't. 5) Re-read each half separately to confirm completeness.

subject: act-english
context_html: Having spent weeks mailing a survey to every household in the annexation area, <u>the low response rate frustrated the planners</u>.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: the response rate frustrated the planners with its lowness
frustration over the low response rate grew among the planners
the planners were frustrated by the low response rate

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening participial phrase attaches to 'the low response rate,' which did not mail any surveys — a dangling modifier.
per_choice_rationale.B: Rewording the tail still leaves 'the response rate' as the noun the opener grabs, so the dangle remains.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Frustration' becomes the subject, but an emotion cannot have spent weeks mailing surveys either — the misconception that any rewrite fixes the problem.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'The planners,' the actual doers of the mailing, now follow the modifier directly, repairing the dangle.

why_correct_md: An introductory participial phrase must be followed immediately by its **doer** — the planners.
why_tempted_md: The original's meaning is perfectly clear to the ear, so the structural mismatch goes unnoticed.
rule_md: 1) Find the opening '-ing' or 'having' phrase. 2) Ask who performed that action. 3) Check the first noun after the comma. 4) If the noun and the doer don't match, the modifier dangles. 5) Re-choose or rewrite so the doer sits right after the comma, then re-read.

subject: act-english
context_html: Next spring, the transit authority will <u>combine</u> the two overlapping bus routes into a single crosstown line.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most concise while preserving its meaning?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Combine' alone carries the full meaning, and 'into a single crosstown line' already states the result.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Together' is built into the meaning of 'combine' — a redundant particle adding no information.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Merge' repeats 'combine'; pairing synonyms adds words, not meaning — the redundant-synonym trap.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Uniting them as one' restates both the verb and 'into a single line,' doubling the redundancy.

why_correct_md: The verb already contains the idea of joining, and **'into a single crosstown line'** states the result — nothing needs repeating.
why_tempted_md: 'Combine and merge' feels thorough, as though two verbs make the action more complete.
rule_md: 1) Ask what the underlined verb already means. 2) Scan the rest of the sentence for words that repeat that meaning. 3) Strike any word or phrase whose idea is already present elsewhere. 4) Prefer the version that expresses each idea exactly once. 5) Re-read to confirm no meaning was lost.

subject: act-english
context_html: Residents who wish to comment on the draft comprehensive plan <u>are able to make use of the online portal for the purpose of submitting</u> their remarks before the June hearing.
stem_md: Which choice expresses the idea most clearly and concisely?

choices.label: may use the online portal to submit
are able to utilize the online portal so as to submit
may, through the use of the online portal, submit

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Are able to,' 'make use of,' and 'for the purpose of' are three stacked padding phrases, each replaceable by a single plain word.
per_choice_rationale.B: Every padded phrase is replaced by its plain one-word equivalent, cutting the span to its working words.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Utilize' and 'so as to' merely swap one set of inflated phrases for another — the misconception that formal-sounding words are more correct.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Through the use of' buries the action in a prepositional detour that a direct construction handles in fewer words.

why_correct_md: The concise version replaces each **inflated phrase** with its plain one-word equivalent and loses no information.
why_tempted_md: 'Utilize' and 'so as to' sound elevated, so that rewrite feels like an upgrade rather than a repackaging of the same padding.
rule_md: 1) Underline each multi-word phrase in the span. 2) For each, ask whether a one-word equivalent exists. 3) Substitute the plain equivalents. 4) Compare the candidates and reject any that trade one inflated phrase for another. 5) Re-read to confirm the trimmed sentence keeps the full meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: The sidewalk repair fund, approved by voters last November, <u>covers</u> the full cost of replacing broken panels on residential blocks.
stem_md: Which choice is most effective for the underlined portion?

choices.label: covers, for all intents and purposes,

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Covers' states the fact directly; the sentence needs no qualifier or padding.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Basically' is an empty hedge that adds vagueness, not information.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For all intents and purposes' is a filler idiom that muddies a straightforward factual claim.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Is the thing that' inflates the verb into a wordy frame without adding meaning.

why_correct_md: The plain verb already makes the claim; every alternative adds a **filler** word or phrase that contributes nothing.
why_tempted_md: 'Basically' feels like it appropriately softens the claim, so the empty hedge passes as careful writing.
rule_md: 1) Read the sentence with the candidate in place. 2) Delete each added word or phrase and re-read. 3) If the meaning is unchanged, the addition is filler. 4) Keep only words that add information the sentence needs. 5) Confirm the final version states the fact directly.

subject: act-english
context_html: The new noise ordinance <u>limits</u> amplified music near the hospital district to sixty decibels after 10 p.m.
stem_md: Which choice conveys the sentence's meaning most precisely?

per_choice_rationale.A: The original verb precisely expresses a cap set at a stated level, fitting the 'to sixty decibels' phrase.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Restrains' suggests physically holding something back and does not idiomatically pair with 'to sixty decibels.'
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Shortens' concerns duration, not volume — the wrong dimension for a decibel figure.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Lessens' means reduces but cannot express a maximum; 'lessens ... to sixty decibels' garbles the intended cap.

why_correct_md: Only the original verb expresses a **cap at a stated level**, which the decibel figure requires.
why_tempted_md: 'Lessens' shares the idea of reduction, so it feels interchangeable until it is tested against the 'to sixty decibels' phrase.
rule_md: 1) Identify what the verb must do in this exact sentence. 2) Note the phrases the verb must connect to — here, a measured level. 3) Test each candidate in the frame: does it fit the dimension (volume, not time) and the structure ('to' plus a level)? 4) Reject near-synonyms that fail either test. 5) Re-read with the survivor in place.

subject: act-english
context_html: In its annual report to the council, the planning commission <u>conceded</u> that the permit backlog had grown despite the addition of two reviewers.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the formal tone of the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: The original verb matches the formal register of an official report while conveying a reluctant admission.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Let on' is conversational and also implies revealing a secret rather than formally admitting a shortfall.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Fessed up' is slang, far below the register of a report addressed to a council.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Was straight with everybody' is a breezy colloquialism that trades precision for chattiness.

why_correct_md: The original verb keeps the sentence's **formal, official register** while preserving the sense of an admission.
why_tempted_md: 'Fessed up' vividly captures admitting fault, so its casual register slips past students focused only on meaning.
rule_md: 1) Identify the passage's register from its setting and diction — here, an official report. 2) Rate each option on a scale: slang, conversational, neutral, formal. 3) Eliminate options below (or absurdly above) the passage's register. 4) Among survivors, check that the meaning fits the context. 5) Re-read the sentence in the passage's voice.

subject: act-english
context_html: Every spring, the beekeeping club invites new members <u>to assemble</u> their first hive frames under a mentor's supervision.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: 'invite' plus a person takes an infinitive, and 'to' plus the base verb 'assemble' is exactly that form.
per_choice_rationale.B: Treats 'to' as a preposition and attaches an -ing form to it, but the infinitive marker must be followed by the base verb.
per_choice_rationale.C: Pairs the preposition 'for' with a bare verb, a combination that matches neither the infinitive pattern nor any preposition-plus-gerund idiom.
per_choice_rationale.D: Drops the infinitive marker entirely, leaving a bare gerund that 'invites new members' cannot govern.

why_correct_md: After **invite** plus a person, English requires the infinitive — 'to' plus the base verb — so the original form is already right.
why_tempted_md: Students who have learned that prepositions take -ing forms misread this 'to' as a preposition and reach for 'to assembling.'
rule_md: 1) Find the main verb and check whether it names a person before the action (invite someone, ask someone, encourage someone). 2) If it does, the action that follows takes 'to' plus the base verb. 3) Test each option in a simple frame: 'She invited us to ___ a cake.' 4) Reject any option that puts an -ing form after 'to' or swaps in a different preposition.

subject: act-english
context_html: By late summer, each colony fiercely defends <u>its</u> honey stores against raiding wasps.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: 'each colony' is a singular antecedent, and the singular possessive 'its' agrees with it.
per_choice_rationale.B: Uses a plural pronoun for the singular antecedent 'each colony,' a number-agreement error triggered by picturing many colonies.
per_choice_rationale.C: Substitutes the contraction of 'it is' where the sentence needs a possessive pronoun.
per_choice_rationale.D: Puts an apostrophe on a possessive pronoun, producing a form that does not exist in English.

why_correct_md: Because **each** makes its noun singular, the singular possessive pronoun agrees with 'each colony.'
why_tempted_md: Students picture many colonies across the apiary and reach for the plural 'their,' ignoring that 'each' forces a one-at-a-time reading.
rule_md: 1) Circle the pronoun and draw an arrow back to its antecedent. 2) If the antecedent starts with 'each,' 'every,' or 'either,' treat it as singular. 3) Match the pronoun's number to the antecedent's. 4) If an apostrophe appears, expand it ('it is') to test whether a contraction fits; possessive pronouns never take apostrophes.

subject: act-english
context_html: Volunteers at the teaching apiary spend their mornings <u>checking frames, refilling feeders, and recording queen activity</u>.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the pattern established in the sentence?

choices.label: checking frames, refilling feeders, and to record queen activity
checking frames, to refill feeders, and recording queen activity
to check frames, refilling feeders, and record queen activity

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: all three items in the series are -ing forms, keeping the list perfectly parallel after 'spend their mornings.'
per_choice_rationale.B: Switches the final item to an infinitive, breaking the -ing pattern set by the first two items.
per_choice_rationale.C: Drops an infinitive into the middle of an otherwise -ing series, breaking parallelism and the 'spend time doing' idiom.
per_choice_rationale.D: Mixes three different verb shapes — infinitive, gerund, and bare form — in a single series.

why_correct_md: A series must keep one grammatical form throughout, and the original gives three matched **-ing** forms.
why_tempted_md: The final list slot is where students most often drift to an infinitive, so the version ending 'and to record' feels natural to the ear.
rule_md: 1) Bracket every item in the series. 2) Label each item's grammatical form (to-form, -ing form, bare verb). 3) Confirm every label matches the first item's. 4) Also test each item alone after the lead-in ('spend their mornings ___') to catch idiom breaks.

subject: act-english
context_html: Honeybees can forage in a light drizzle. <u>Therefore,</u> a sudden downpour can strand hundreds of workers far from the hive.
stem_md: Which transition word or phrase is most logical in context?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Therefore' claims the stranding follows logically from bees' tolerance of drizzle, but the second sentence pushes against the first rather than concluding from it.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'As a result' makes the same cause-and-effect error in different words: tolerating drizzle does not cause stranding.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For example' would require the downpour to illustrate the drizzle claim, but it presents an opposing situation instead.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the second sentence limits the first with an opposite-direction fact, so a contrast transition is required.

why_correct_md: The two sentences pull in opposite directions — mild rain is manageable, heavy rain is dangerous — so a **contrast** transition is the only logical link.
why_tempted_md: Because both sentences are about rain and bees, students assume a cause-and-effect chain and keep 'Therefore.'
rule_md: 1) State each sentence's idea in five words or fewer. 2) Name the relationship between the ideas: continuation, cause-effect, example, or contrast. 3) Match the transition to that named relationship. 4) Re-read both sentences with your choice inserted to confirm the logic holds.

subject: act-english
context_html: Requeening usually calms an aggressive colony. <u>Even so,</u> the hive's temperament may take six weeks to soften, because the old queen's defensive daughters must live out their lifespans first.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the second sentence concedes a lingering complication that qualifies the calming claim, exactly the yes-but relationship 'Even so' signals.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Consequently' would present the six-week delay as flowing naturally from the calming claim, but the delay tempers that claim rather than resulting from it.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In other words' signals a paraphrase, yet the second sentence adds new, qualifying information instead of restating the first.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'For instance' would require the delay to be an example of requeening's calming effect, but it is a caveat working against that effect.

why_correct_md: The second sentence attaches a **concession** — the fix works, but slowly — so a yes-but transition fits the logic.
why_tempted_md: Because requeening does eventually calm the hive, students read the delay as a consequence of the fix and pick 'Consequently.'
rule_md: 1) Summarize sentence one's claim. 2) Ask what sentence two does to that claim: extends it, restates it, illustrates it, or qualifies it. 3) If sentence two admits a complication while leaving the claim standing, choose a concessive transition. 4) Confirm by reading the pair with a plain 'but still' in the slot — if that works, the concession reading is right.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] ___ [2] A worker's dance points nestmates toward a food source, encoding both the direction and the distance of the flowers. [3] The angle of the waggle run relative to vertical signals the direction; the length of the run signals how far to fly.
stem_md: The writer wants an opening sentence that introduces the paragraph's focus on how bees communicate the location of food. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: The waggle dance is one of nature's most precise systems for sharing directions.
Honeybees have fascinated naturalists for many centuries.
A single hive may contain tens of thousands of individual workers.
Bees also communicate danger by releasing alarm pheromones.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: it names the dance and frames it as a system for sharing directions, previewing the exact topic the following sentences develop.
per_choice_rationale.B: Offers a broad historical remark that never mentions communicating food location, so it fails to set up the paragraph.
per_choice_rationale.C: States a colony-size fact unrelated to how bees signal a food source.
per_choice_rationale.D: Introduces a different communication channel — alarm — that the paragraph does not go on to discuss.

why_correct_md: A good opener names the paragraph's **specific topic**, and only this sentence forecasts a system for sharing directions to food.
why_tempted_md: The broad 'fascinated naturalists' opener sounds like a classic essay introduction, so students pick it for tone even though it misses the topic.
rule_md: 1) Read the sentences that follow the blank and note their shared subject. 2) State that subject in a phrase ('how bees signal food location'). 3) Choose the opener that names that exact subject. 4) Reject openers that are broader, narrower, or about a different subject even if they sound essay-like.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Before installing a package of bees, the keeper sprays the screen lightly with sugar water. [2] The keeper then removes the queen cage and checks that she is alive. [3] Finally, the open package is set inside the hive body so the workers can crawl onto the frames. [4] Calm, well-fed bees are far less likely to fly off during this transfer.
stem_md: The writer wants to add the following sentence to the paragraph: "This feeding keeps the bees occupied and gentle." To make the paragraph's logic clearest, where should the sentence be placed?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: 'This feeding' refers directly to the sugar-water spraying in Sentence 1, so the new sentence belongs immediately after it.
per_choice_rationale.B: Placing it after the queen-cage step separates 'This feeding' from the feeding action it names, breaking the reference.
per_choice_rationale.C: After the frame-transfer step, the phrase 'This feeding' has no nearby antecedent and interrupts the sequence.
per_choice_rationale.D: At the very end, the sentence would follow an unrelated summary and leave 'This feeding' pointing back across three intervening steps.

why_correct_md: The added sentence opens with **'This feeding,'** a backward reference that must sit right after the sentence describing the feeding.
why_tempted_md: Because the last sentence is also about keeping bees calm, students group the new calm-related sentence there instead of tracking the 'This feeding' reference.
rule_md: 1) Find the pointing word or phrase in the sentence to be added ('This feeding'). 2) Locate the sentence that supplies its antecedent (the spraying with sugar water). 3) Place the new sentence immediately after that antecedent. 4) Confirm the surrounding steps still read in order.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] In midwinter, a colony forms a tight cluster and shivers its flight muscles to generate heat. [2] The bees rotate from the cold outer shell of the cluster to the warm core, sharing the burden of staying warm. [3] A well-provisioned hive can hold its center near ninety degrees even when snow buries the entrance. [4] Spring brings an entirely different rhythm to the hive. [5] As days lengthen, the queen resumes laying, and foragers stream out after the first pollen. [6] Within weeks the colony's population begins to climb toward its summer peak.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide this passage into two paragraphs so that each paragraph covers a single season. The second paragraph should begin at which sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: Sentence 2 continues the midwinter clustering description, so a break here splits the winter material in two.
per_choice_rationale.B: Sentence 3 still describes the winter cluster's temperature, keeping it inside the first season's paragraph.
per_choice_rationale.C: Sentence 5 is already inside the spring discussion; starting the paragraph here strands the spring topic sentence in the winter paragraph.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: Sentence 4 announces the shift to spring, so it opens the second paragraph and keeps each season whole.

why_correct_md: A paragraph break belongs where the **topic shifts**, and the move from winter to spring is announced precisely at that sentence.
why_tempted_md: The vivid spring details in the next sentence read like a fresh start, so students break there and accidentally leave the spring topic sentence behind.
rule_md: 1) Label each sentence with its subtopic (winter cluster / spring buildup). 2) Find the first sentence that switches to the new subtopic. 3) Begin the new paragraph at that switch sentence, not before or after it. 4) Check that neither resulting paragraph contains stray sentences from the other subtopic.

subject: act-english
context_html: The beekeeper's smoker, <u>a dented tin canister with a leather bellows produces</u> cool smoke that masks the colony's alarm signals.
stem_md: Which choice correctly punctuates the underlined portion?

choices.label: a dented tin canister with a leather bellows, produces
a dented tin canister with a leather bellows produces,
a dented tin canister with a leather bellows; produces

per_choice_rationale.A: Opens the nonrestrictive appositive with a comma but never closes it, so the description runs into the verb without a break.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: commas both open and close the nonrestrictive appositive, letting the subject 'smoker' meet its verb 'produces' cleanly.
per_choice_rationale.C: Puts the comma after the verb, separating 'produces' from its object and leaving the appositive unclosed.
per_choice_rationale.D: Uses a semicolon where the appositive should close, but a semicolon must join independent clauses, and the second part is not one.

why_correct_md: A nonrestrictive appositive needs a comma on **both** sides, so the description must be closed before the verb.
why_tempted_md: The opening comma already sits in the original, so students accept it and never notice the missing closing comma before 'produces.'
rule_md: 1) Find the subject and its main verb ('smoker … produces'). 2) Notice any description inserted between them. 3) If the description is extra information, fence it with a comma on each side. 4) Make sure nothing separates the verb from its subject or object once the fence is closed.

subject: act-english
context_html: The nectar flow had ended <u>early that year, the</u> bees turned to goldenrod for their last stores.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Joins two independent clauses with only a comma, the classic comma-splice error.
per_choice_rationale.B: Removes the comma but leaves two full clauses fused with no punctuation at all — a run-on.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a semicolon links the two closely related independent clauses without any splice.
per_choice_rationale.D: Moves the comma to a spot that breaks up 'early that year' while still leaving the two clauses joined by a comma.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses need a semicolon (or period) between them, so the **semicolon** repairs the splice.
why_tempted_md: The comma-plus-clause version reads smoothly aloud, so students hear it as a single flowing sentence rather than two spliced clauses.
rule_md: 1) Split the sentence at the punctuation and test each half for a subject and a verb. 2) If both halves are complete sentences, a comma alone cannot join them. 3) Use a semicolon or period between two independent clauses. 4) Reject any option that still leaves a comma or nothing between two complete clauses.

subject: act-english
context_html: Beekeepers in cold climates favor the Carniolan honeybee, <u>bee, that overwinters</u> on remarkably small stores.
stem_md: Which choice correctly punctuates and introduces the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Introduces extra, non-essential information with 'that,' but a clause adding a detail to an already-identified subspecies calls for the nonrestrictive relative word, not the restrictive one.
per_choice_rationale.B: Drops the comma and keeps 'that,' treating the overwintering detail as essential to identifying which bee, though the subspecies is already named.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the subspecies is already identified, so the extra detail is nonrestrictive and takes a comma plus the nonrestrictive relative word.
per_choice_rationale.D: Uses the nonrestrictive relative word but omits the comma that a nonrestrictive clause requires to be set off.

why_correct_md: Because the subspecies is already named, the following clause is **nonrestrictive** — extra information — so it needs a comma and the nonrestrictive relative word.
why_tempted_md: Students hear the overwintering fact as important and treat it as essential, keeping the restrictive 'that' with no comma.
rule_md: 1) Decide whether the relative clause identifies which thing (essential) or just adds a detail about an already-named thing (extra). 2) If the noun is already fully identified, the clause is nonrestrictive. 3) Set a nonrestrictive clause off with a comma and use the nonrestrictive relative word. 4) Reject any option that either omits that comma or uses the restrictive word for extra information.

subject: act-english
context_html: Buckwheat honey has a dark, <u>strong</u> flavor that many bakers prize for their winter gingerbread.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely conveys a rich, full-bodied flavor?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Strong' is serviceable but generic; it names intensity without capturing the full-bodied richness the sentence sets up.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Big' is a colloquial, imprecise word for describing flavor and lowers the register of the sentence.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: 'robust' names a rich, full-bodied intensity in a register that fits the descriptive sentence.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Loud' is figurative slang for flavor and clashes with the descriptive, measured tone of the passage.

why_correct_md: The most **precise** word names full-bodied richness exactly, which is what distinguishes the best option from merely intense-sounding ones.
why_tempted_md: 'Strong' already reads as intense, so students accept it without asking whether a more exact word captures the fullness of the flavor.
rule_md: 1) Name the exact quality the sentence is reaching for (here, rich fullness, not just power). 2) Test each option against that quality and against the sentence's register. 3) Eliminate words that are merely vague, too casual, or figurative slang. 4) Keep the one word that matches both meaning and tone.

subject: act-english
context_html: As the afternoon warmed, the clustered swarm grew restless and finally <u>lifted</u> into the air, streaming toward a hollow oak the scouts had already chosen.
stem_md: Which choice is the most precise word for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: 'lifted' naturally describes the swarm rising into the air under its own power, matching the living, self-propelled motion.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Hoisted' implies an external force raising a load, but no outside agent lifts the swarm here.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Elevated' is clinical and abstract, ill-suited to the vivid physical motion of a swarm taking flight.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Boosted' is colloquial and suggests a push or an increase in amount, not self-propelled flight.

why_correct_md: The best word describes motion the swarm produces itself, so a verb of **self-propelled rising** fits where verbs implying an outside force or the wrong register do not.
why_tempted_md: Each alternative loosely means 'raised,' so students who scan only for a synonym of 'went up' accept one without testing its connotation.
rule_md: 1) Identify who or what performs the action and whether an outside force is involved. 2) List the connotation each candidate carries (external lifting, clinical rise, casual push). 3) Keep only the word whose connotation matches self-powered motion in a vivid register. 4) Reject near-synonyms whose implied agent or tone does not fit.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Bees gather sticky resin from tree buds and carry it home as propolis. [2] Inside the hive, they pack propolis into cracks, sealing out drafts and dampening vibrations. [3] The resin also has antimicrobial properties that help keep the colony free of disease.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence to the paragraph: "Pine and poplar are among the trees whose buds supply this resin." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it supplies useful background about where the paragraph's resin comes from.
Yes, because it offers a concrete example that supports the paragraph's point.
Yes, because it corrects a vague statement in the paragraph's opening sentence.
No, because the new sentence drifts from the paragraph's focus on what propolis does.

per_choice_rationale.A: The paragraph never sets out to trace the resin's botanical origin, so naming source trees supplies a detail the passage does not need.
per_choice_rationale.B: The proposed sentence names sources rather than illustrating how propolis works, so it does not exemplify the paragraph's point.
per_choice_rationale.C: The opening's phrase 'resin from tree buds' is not vague enough to require correction; the sentence would change focus, not fix accuracy.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: after the first sentence the paragraph is about what propolis does inside the hive, so a note on source trees pulls attention off-topic.

why_correct_md: A sentence should be added only if it advances the paragraph's **focus**, and this one veers into where resin originates rather than what propolis does.
why_tempted_md: The source detail is factually true and relates to bees, so students accept it without checking whether it serves the paragraph's actual topic.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's controlling focus after its opening sentence (here, how propolis functions in the hive). 2) Ask whether the proposed sentence advances that focus. 3) If it introduces a side topic, it should not be added, no matter how true it is. 4) Match the reason to the real relationship between the sentence and the paragraph's focus.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Each February, commercial beekeepers truck millions of hives to California's almond orchards. [2] The trees bloom for only a few weeks, and every blossom must be visited by a bee to set a nut. [3] Growers pay rental fees that now form a major share of many beekeepers' yearly income.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after Sentence 2: "Wild pollinators alone are far too few to service orchards that stretch for miles." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it explains why growers depend on rented hives rather than on native bees.
Yes, because it adds data about the growers' rental income.
No, because it merely restates the need to rent colonies mentioned elsewhere.
No, because the length of the bloom is not relevant to the paragraph.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: it supplies the missing reason the orchards depend on trucked-in hives, connecting the bloom's demand to the rental market described in Sentence 3.
per_choice_rationale.B: The proposed sentence offers no numbers or figures, so it adds no data at all.
per_choice_rationale.C: The paragraph never states why wild bees fall short, so the sentence adds a reason rather than repeating one.
per_choice_rationale.D: The short bloom is exactly what makes rented hives necessary, so it is central to the paragraph, not irrelevant.

why_correct_md: A sentence earns a place when it fills a **logical gap**, and this one explains why paid pollination is needed at all.
why_tempted_md: Because the paragraph flows without it, students assume the sentence is optional and overlook the causal link it supplies between the bloom and the rental market.
rule_md: 1) Trace the paragraph's logic and look for a step that is assumed but never stated. 2) Ask whether the proposed sentence supplies that missing step. 3) If it fills a real gap in reasoning, adding it strengthens the paragraph. 4) Match the reason to what the sentence actually contributes, not to a fact it lacks.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] This essay traces the year of an urban rooftop hive from the first cleansing flights of March to the wrapping of the boxes in November. [2] It follows one keeper's decisions week by week, weighing when to add space, when to harvest, and when to leave the bees alone. [3] Along the way it shows how a single colony reflects the rhythm of the city's blooming trees and vacant-lot wildflowers.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to argue that cities should pass ordinances protecting rooftop apiaries. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it describes a rooftop hive located within a city.
Yes, because it mentions the keeper's week-by-week decisions about the colony.
No, because it focuses only on the springtime portion of the beekeeping year.
No, because it narrates one hive's yearly cycle rather than advocating for any policy.

per_choice_rationale.A: The mere presence of an urban setting does not make the essay an argument for legislation; a shared subject is not the same as a shared purpose.
per_choice_rationale.B: Describing a keeper's choices is narration, not advocacy, so this reason confuses recounting events with arguing for a law.
per_choice_rationale.C: The essay covers the full year from March to November, so the claim that it stops at spring misreads its scope.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the essay is a chronological account of one colony's year and never argues for protective ordinances, so it does not serve an advocacy goal.

why_correct_md: An essay accomplishes an argumentative goal only if it actually **argues**, and this one narrates a yearly cycle without urging any policy.
why_tempted_md: Because the essay is genuinely about urban beekeeping, students match the topic and answer 'yes,' overlooking that topic overlap is not the same as making a case.
rule_md: 1) State the stated goal as a verb (here, 'argue for a law'). 2) State what the essay actually does as a verb (narrate a year). 3) Compare the two verbs, not the shared subject matter. 4) If the essay's action does not match the goal's action, it fails the goal no matter how related the topic is.

subject: act-english
context_html: The apprentice lifted the heavy super off the stack. <u>Straining under the weight of forty pounds of capped comb.</u>
stem_md: Which choice makes the underlined portion a complete sentence?

choices.label: She strained under the weight of forty pounds of capped comb.
Straining under the weight of forty pounds of capped comb,
Under the weight of forty pounds of capped comb straining.

per_choice_rationale.A: The '-ing' phrase has no subject and no finite verb, so it is a fragment standing where a sentence should be.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: adding the subject 'she' and the finite verb 'strained' turns the fragment into a complete sentence.
per_choice_rationale.C: Merely swapping the period for a comma still leaves a subjectless participial phrase with no main clause attached.
per_choice_rationale.D: Rearranges the same words but still supplies no subject and no finite verb, so the fragment remains.

why_correct_md: A complete sentence needs a **subject and a finite verb**, and only this version supplies both.
why_tempted_md: The original sounds descriptive and full, so students accept the vivid participial phrase as if it were a sentence.
rule_md: 1) Look for the subject: who or what performs the action? 2) Look for a finite verb that can carry tense (not just an '-ing' or '-ed' word). 3) If either is missing, the string is a fragment. 4) Fix it by supplying the missing subject, the missing finite verb, or both.

subject: act-english
context_html: The observation hive sits against a south window, <u>visitors watch</u> the workers build comb in real time.
stem_md: Which choice most effectively repairs the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Joins two independent clauses with only a comma, producing a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Adds a stray comma after 'visitors' but leaves the two independent clauses spliced together.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: 'where' turns the second clause into a subordinate clause, so a single comma now correctly joins a main clause to a modifier.
per_choice_rationale.D: Uses a semicolon before an '-ing' form, but a semicolon requires a complete independent clause on its right, and 'watching…' is not one.

why_correct_md: Turning the second clause into a **subordinate** clause with 'where' cures the splice, so one clause depends on the other.
why_tempted_md: The original reads smoothly as two related facts, so students hear one flowing sentence and miss that two complete clauses are spliced by a comma.
rule_md: 1) Split the sentence at the comma and test each side for a subject and verb. 2) If both sides are independent clauses joined only by a comma, it is a splice. 3) Fix it by subordinating one clause, adding a coordinating conjunction, or using a semicolon or period. 4) Reject any fix that still leaves two independent clauses joined by a comma alone or misuses a semicolon.

subject: act-english
context_html: The queen excluder keeps her below the honey supers <u>the metal grid lets</u> smaller workers pass while blocking her wider body.
stem_md: Which choice best establishes the boundary between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: Runs two complete independent clauses together with no punctuation at all — a fused sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: Inserts a comma between the two independent clauses, downgrading the fused sentence to a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.C: Drops a comma inside the second clause, splitting its subject from its verb while still fusing the two clauses.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: a period ends the first complete statement and a capital opens the second, giving each independent clause its own sentence.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses need a real boundary, and a **period** cleanly closes one sentence and starts the next.
why_tempted_md: The two clauses share a topic and flow together, so students read them as one sentence and leave them fused.
rule_md: 1) Locate where the first complete thought ends. 2) Test whether what follows is also a complete thought with its own subject and verb. 3) If both are complete, put a period (or semicolon) at the boundary, not a comma or nothing. 4) Reject fixes that leave the clauses fused or joined by a comma alone.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Peering through the mesh veil, the keeper spotted</u> the supersedure cell hanging from the bottom bar of the frame.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: Peering through the mesh veil, the supersedure cell was spotted by the keeper
Peering through the mesh veil, the frame held
The supersedure cell, peering through the mesh veil, was spotted

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the opening modifier 'Peering through the mesh veil' attaches to 'the keeper,' the only one in the sentence who can peer.
per_choice_rationale.B: The passive construction makes 'the supersedure cell' the subject the modifier lands on, but a cell cannot peer through a veil.
per_choice_rationale.C: Puts 'the frame' right after the modifier, illogically implying the frame did the peering.
per_choice_rationale.D: Wedges the modifier next to 'the supersedure cell,' the one thing in the sentence that cannot look through a veil.

why_correct_md: An introductory participial phrase must modify the **subject that follows it**, and only the keeper can peer through a veil.
why_tempted_md: The passive rewrite sounds formal and objective, so students pick it without checking that its new subject cannot perform the opening action.
rule_md: 1) Read the introductory '-ing' phrase and ask who or what performs its action. 2) Find the subject that comes right after the comma. 3) Confirm that subject is the doer of the phrase's action. 4) Reject any version whose post-comma subject cannot logically perform the opening action.

subject: act-english
context_html: The forager returns to the hive and <u>shares and distributes the nectar</u> to several house bees waiting near the entrance.
stem_md: Which choice best eliminates the redundancy in the underlined portion?

choices.label: shares and gives out the nectar
shares, distributes, and passes the nectar

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Shares and distributes' pairs two verbs that mean essentially the same thing, so one is redundant.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Shares and gives out' still doubles up two near-synonymous verbs, keeping the redundancy in new words.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a single precise verb conveys the whole action with no repetition.
per_choice_rationale.D: Piles up three overlapping verbs, making the redundancy worse rather than removing it.

why_correct_md: When two words carry the same meaning, keep only one, so a **single** verb says everything the pair did.
why_tempted_md: The paired verbs sound thorough and emphatic, so students read the doubling as richness rather than repetition.
rule_md: 1) Underline each verb in the span and paraphrase its meaning. 2) If two verbs mean the same thing, one is redundant. 3) Keep the single verb that best carries the action and delete the twin. 4) Reject any option that keeps or adds a second same-meaning verb.

subject: act-english
context_html: The mentor explained that a small entrance matters <u>because</u> a weak colony can guard it against robbing bees more easily.
stem_md: Which choice is most concise while keeping the sentence's meaning?

choices.label: on account of the fact that

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: a single plain connector states the cause directly with no padding.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Due to the fact that' is a bulky, four-word stand-in for a one-word cause connector.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For the reason that' pads the cause link into a multi-word phrase that adds no meaning.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'On account of the fact that' is the wordiest cause frame of the set, stacking filler onto a simple link.

why_correct_md: Wordiness is cured by keeping the tightest form, and a single plain **connector** already states the cause with no padding.
why_tempted_md: The longer cause frames sound more formal, so students swap in bulk, mistaking extra words for greater rigor.
rule_md: 1) Find the words that link cause to effect. 2) Ask whether a single connector can do that job. 3) Prefer the one-word link over any multi-word 'due to the fact that' style frame. 4) Reject any option that expands a simple cause link into a padded phrase.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>It is important to note that when</u> the temperature drops below fifty degrees, foragers stop leaving the hive.
stem_md: Which choice best removes the empty phrasing from the sentence?

choices.label: For all intents and purposes, when
It should be understood that when

per_choice_rationale.A: 'It is important to note that' is a filler opener that adds no information before the real clause.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'For all intents and purposes' is an empty stock phrase that pads the sentence with no added meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: cutting straight to 'When' removes the filler and lets the real idea begin at once.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'It should be understood that' is the same kind of empty announcer, swapping one filler for another.

why_correct_md: Empty announcer phrases can simply be **deleted**, so the sentence should open directly with the real clause.
why_tempted_md: The 'it is important to note that' opener sounds thoughtful and academic, so students keep it as if it signaled significance.
rule_md: 1) Check whether the opening words announce that something matters rather than saying anything. 2) Test whether deleting them changes the meaning; if not, they are filler. 3) Cut the filler and start with the substantive clause. 4) Reject any option that trades one empty announcer for another.

subject: act-english
context_html: Before the inspection, the keeper <u>looked at</u> each frame against the sunlight to judge how much brood the queen had laid.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely conveys careful, deliberate observation?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Looked at' is neutral and vague, giving no sense of the close, purposeful scrutiny the sentence describes.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: 'examined' names a careful, methodical inspection that fits judging brood on each frame.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Glimpsed' means a brief, partial look — the opposite of the deliberate study the sentence requires.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Eyed' suggests a casual or suspicious glance, not the careful assessment being described.

why_correct_md: The most **precise** verb names deliberate, close inspection, which is exactly what judging brood frame by frame demands.
why_tempted_md: 'Looked at' is true and safe, so students accept it without asking whether a sharper verb captures the care involved.
rule_md: 1) Name the exact manner of the action the sentence describes (here, careful, methodical study). 2) Test each candidate verb's connotation against that manner. 3) Eliminate verbs that are vague, too brief, or too casual. 4) Keep the verb whose precise sense matches the described care.

subject: act-english
context_html: The county's guide to backyard beekeeping advises that novices <u>consult</u> an experienced mentor before installing their first colony.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the formal register of the passage?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: 'consult' is a formal, precise verb that matches the register of an official county guide.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Hit up' is slang that clashes with the formal tone of an advisory document.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Touch base with' is casual business jargon, too colloquial for this formal guide.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Get the lowdown from' is informal, idiomatic speech unsuited to an official publication.

why_correct_md: An official guide calls for **formal** diction, and only the original verb keeps that professional register.
why_tempted_md: The casual alternatives sound friendly and approachable, so students pick them to make the advice feel welcoming.
rule_md: 1) Identify the passage's register from its context (here, an official county guide = formal). 2) Rate each option as formal, neutral, or colloquial. 3) Keep the option whose register matches the passage. 4) Reject slang or casual idioms even when they feel warmer or friendlier.

subject: act-english
context_html: Before threading her first roll onto the steel reel, Marisol practiced <u>to wind</u> a strip of scrap film in total darkness.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Reflects the misconception that 'practiced' can take an infinitive (infinitive_after_practice); idiomatic English requires a gerund object after 'practiced.'
per_choice_rationale.B: Stacks the infinitive marker 'to' onto a gerund (double_verb_marker), a form English never allows.
per_choice_rationale.C: Inserts a full new clause where the verb needs an object (clause_for_object), leaving 'practiced she wound' ungrammatical.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: 'practiced' takes a gerund object, so 'winding' properly names the rehearsed activity.

why_correct_md: The verb *practiced* takes a **gerund** object, so the -ing form correctly names the activity Marisol rehearsed.
why_tempted_md: The infinitive 'to wind' sounds purposeful, as if it meant 'in order to wind,' so many students accept it by ear.
rule_md: 1) Find the main verb ('practiced'). 2) Ask what form that verb takes for an activity that follows it — test with a familiar activity: 'practiced swimming,' never 'practiced to swim.' 3) Reject any option that stacks 'to' on an -ing form or adds a second subject-verb pair. 4) Choose the single form that names the activity.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each new member of the photo club must label <u>their</u> box of printing paper before storing it in the paper safe.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Uses a plural pronoun for the grammatically singular 'each new member' (plural_for_each), which the ACT counts as an agreement error.
per_choice_rationale.B: Puts an object pronoun where a possessive is required before the noun 'box' (object_for_possessive).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: 'each new member' is singular and human, so the singular personal possessive agrees in number and kind.
per_choice_rationale.D: Chooses a singular pronoun but one reserved for things, not people (nonhuman_pronoun), so it cannot refer to a club member.

why_correct_md: 'Each new member' is grammatically **singular**, so the pronoun must be a singular possessive that can refer to a person.
why_tempted_md: 'Their' matches how most people speak, so students accept the plural pronoun without noticing that 'each' forces a singular antecedent on the ACT.
rule_md: 1) Find the pronoun's antecedent. 2) Check its number — words like 'each,' 'every,' and 'neither' are singular. 3) Check its kind — person or thing. 4) Confirm the pronoun's job (possessive before a noun, subject, or object). 5) Pick the pronoun matching all three: number, kind, and job.

subject: act-english
context_html: The instructor's checklist covered mixing the chemistry, setting the timer, and <u>labeling each tray with tape</u>.
stem_md: Which choice is most consistent with the structure of the sentence?

choices.label: to label each tray with tape
each tray should be labeled with tape
how each tray gets labeled with tape

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: 'labeling' matches the gerund pattern set by 'mixing' and 'setting,' keeping the series parallel.
per_choice_rationale.B: Switches the final item to an infinitive (parallel_mixed_form), breaking the -ing pattern of the first two items.
