per_choice_rationale.C: Drops a complete clause into the series (clause_in_series), which cannot hang from 'covered' the way the other items do.
per_choice_rationale.D: Wraps the item in a 'how' clause (noun_clause_padding), abandoning the parallel gerund shape and adding needless words.

why_correct_md: The series items 'mixing' and 'setting' establish a **gerund** pattern, and the original third item matches it exactly.
why_tempted_md: The infinitive version sounds complete and purposeful on its own, so students miss that it breaks the -ing rhythm of the list.
rule_md: 1) Locate the series and list its items in a column. 2) Identify the grammatical shape of the first item. 3) Check each later item against that shape. 4) Test every item by hanging it directly off the shared verb ('covered ___'). 5) Choose the option matching the established shape.

subject: act-english
context_html: Many beginners assume the amber safelight is completely harmless to photographic paper. <u>Similarly,</u> a sheet left under the lamp for several minutes will slowly fog.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: Treats the two sentences as alike (transition_false_similarity), but the second sentence contradicts the beginners' assumption rather than resembling it.
per_choice_rationale.B: Claims the fogging results from the assumption (transition_false_cause), though a belief cannot cause paper to fog.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the second sentence reverses the expectation set up by the first, so a contrast word fits the logic.
per_choice_rationale.D: Presents the fogging as an illustration of the assumption (transition_false_example), when it actually disproves that assumption.

why_correct_md: The second sentence **contradicts** the beginners' assumption, so the transition must signal contrast.
why_tempted_md: Both sentences mention the safelight and paper, so 'Similarly' feels superficially right to students who match topics instead of logic.
rule_md: 1) Restate each sentence in five plain words. 2) Name the relationship between them: same direction, contrast, cause-effect, or example. 3) Match the transition word to that named relationship. 4) Re-read the pair with your choice inserted to confirm the logic clicks.

subject: act-english
context_html: A bottle of stop bath costs less than a movie ticket and lasts for months on a darkroom shelf. <u>In other words,</u> some home printers skip it entirely, trusting a plain water rinse to halt development.
stem_md: Which choice best expresses the relationship between these two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: Treats the second sentence as a restatement of the first (transition_false_restatement), but skipping a product is not another way of saying it is cheap.
per_choice_rationale.B: Claims cheapness causes printers to skip the product (transition_false_cause), the reverse of what low cost would predict.
per_choice_rationale.C: Offers the skipping as a specific case of the cheapness (transition_false_example), though it is a surprising departure, not an instance.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the second sentence describes behavior that persists despite the first sentence's facts, so a concessive transition fits.

why_correct_md: Printers skip the stop bath **despite** its low cost and long life, so the transition must concede the first sentence before pivoting.
why_tempted_md: 'As a result' attracts students who see any two adjacent facts as cause and effect without testing whether the second actually follows from the first.
rule_md: 1) Summarize sentence one and sentence two separately. 2) Ask: given sentence one, is sentence two expected or surprising? 3) If expected, consider cause-effect or continuation words; if surprising, use a concession word. 4) Plug in your choice and confirm the surprise or expectation reads correctly.

subject: act-english
context_html: A test strip is a sliver of photographic paper exposed in timed bands. The printer covers the strip with a card, sliding it back every few seconds so each band receives more light than the one before. After development, the bands range from ghostly gray to nearly black.
stem_md: The writer wants to conclude the paragraph with a sentence that emphasizes the test strip's practical value to the printer. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Photographic paper is sold in boxes of twenty-five, fifty, or one hundred sheets.
Reading those bands tells printers which exposure time to give the final print.
Some printers save old strips for years, though few ever look at them again.
A test strip needs the same developer, stop bath, and fixer as a full print.

per_choice_rationale.A: Introduces packaging trivia unrelated to the strip's usefulness (add_offtopic), abandoning the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it converts the bands just described into the printer's key decision, directly emphasizing practical value.
per_choice_rationale.C: Describes strips being kept but never used (goal_wrong_emphasis), which undercuts rather than emphasizes their value.
per_choice_rationale.D: States an accurate processing fact that shows no benefit to the printer (true_but_irrelevant), so it fails the goal.

why_correct_md: It ties the bands described in the paragraph to the **decision** they enable, which is exactly the practical value the goal demands.
why_tempted_md: The processing-steps sentence is factually true and on-topic, so students confuse accuracy with accomplishing the stated goal.
rule_md: 1) Underline the goal words in the stem. 2) For each option, ask: does this sentence do that job, or is it merely true and related? 3) Eliminate options that add new topics, undercut the goal, or state inert facts. 4) Confirm the survivor links back to the paragraph's content.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Every printing session begins with the same quiet ritual. [2] The printer mixes fresh developer and brings each tray to the proper temperature. [3] Next, the paper safe is checked to make sure its lid is latched tight. [4] Finally, the overhead white light goes off and the amber safelight comes on. [5] A lid left open for a single minute can ruin fifty sheets of paper.
stem_md: The writer wants the paragraph's warning to reinforce the step it describes. For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, Sentence 5 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Leaves the lid warning after the lighting step (placement_stranded), two steps away from the paper safe it comments on.
per_choice_rationale.B: Opens the paragraph with a warning about a lid the reader has not yet met (placement_before_referent).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the warning lands directly beside the latching step it reinforces, keeping the ritual's order intact.
per_choice_rationale.D: Drops the warning after the opener, before the paper safe has been introduced (placement_premature).

why_correct_md: The warning is about the **paper safe's lid**, so it belongs immediately beside the latching step it reinforces.
why_tempted_md: Leaving the warning at the end feels safe because final sentences often summarize, but this one comments on a specific mid-paragraph step.
rule_md: 1) Find the noun or idea the movable sentence points back to. 2) Locate where that referent is introduced. 3) Place the sentence immediately beside its referent. 4) Re-read the paragraph in the new order to confirm each step still flows.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] The first darkrooms were portable tents that traveled by wagon alongside photographers of the 1850s. [2] Wet-plate negatives had to be developed within minutes, so the tent went wherever the camera did. [3] A modern darkroom, by contrast, is a fixed room built around running water and total control of light. [4] Its walls are painted a deep matte black, and its door is sealed with a folding light trap. [5] A ventilation fan pulls chemical fumes up and away from the printing bench.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide this paragraph into two paragraphs so that each one has a single focus. The most logical place to begin the new paragraph is at:

per_choice_rationale.A: Splits the tent history from its own explanation (divide_midtopic), since Sentence 2 still explains why the tents existed.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the paragraph pivots from 1850s tents to the modern room exactly at the 'by contrast' sentence.
per_choice_rationale.C: Breaks after the modern room has already been introduced (divide_late), stranding the topic sentence with the history.
per_choice_rationale.D: Leaves nearly all of the modern-room description in the first paragraph (divide_last_sentence), creating a one-sentence orphan.

why_correct_md: The topic **pivots** from historical tents to the modern room at the 'by contrast' sentence, so the new paragraph begins there.
why_tempted_md: Sentence 4's shift to physical details feels like a fresh start, but the modern-darkroom topic has already begun one sentence earlier.
rule_md: 1) Label each sentence's topic in two or three words. 2) Find where the labels change from one subject to another. 3) Start the new paragraph at the first sentence of the new subject. 4) Verify both resulting paragraphs read as single-focus units.

subject: act-english
context_html: Every printing session depends on three trays lined up in order: <u>developer, stop bath and, fixer</u>, each one mixed fresh that morning.
stem_md: Which choice best punctuates the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Places a comma after the conjunction instead of before it (comma_after_conjunction), splitting 'and' from the item it introduces.
per_choice_rationale.B: Omits the divider after the first series item (missing_series_comma), letting 'developer' and 'stop bath' run together.
per_choice_rationale.C: Cuts the two-word chemical name in half (comma_inside_item), inventing a fourth item that does not exist.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: commas separate the three whole items, with the final comma before 'and.'

why_correct_md: A three-item series needs a comma **between items** — after the first and second — with none trailing the conjunction.
why_tempted_md: The original keeps the right number of commas, so students who count commas instead of checking their positions accept it.
rule_md: 1) Count the items in the series by naming each one aloud. 2) Keep multi-word items whole — no comma inside a single name. 3) Place a comma after each item except the last. 4) Check that no comma directly follows the conjunction.

subject: act-english
context_html: Loading film onto a steel reel takes real <u>practice; most</u> students fumble their first roll inside the changing bag.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: a semicolon legally joins the two independent clauses on either side of it.
per_choice_rationale.B: Joins two independent clauses with only a comma (comma_splice).
per_choice_rationale.C: Puts a dependent clause after the semicolon (semicolon_fragment), since 'although' demotes the second clause.
per_choice_rationale.D: Uses a conjunctive adverb after a bare comma (comma_conjunctive_adverb_splice), which still leaves the clauses unjoined.

why_correct_md: Both halves are **independent clauses**, and a semicolon is a legal junction between two independent clauses.
why_tempted_md: The comma version matches the light pause students hear when reading, so the splice slips past anyone who trusts the ear over the clause test.
rule_md: 1) Read each side of the mark alone and label it independent or dependent. 2) If both sides are independent, require a junction rated for that: strong stop or comma plus coordinating conjunction. 3) If a subordinating word appears, re-test the demoted side. 4) Reject any junction that leaves two independent clauses held by a comma alone.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Negatives which have dried overnight</u> can be handled freely; a sheet pulled early from the drying cabinet will smear at the slightest touch.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence both clear and grammatically correct?

per_choice_rationale.A: Uses 'which' with no commas for an essential clause (which_for_restrictive); ACT convention reserves the comma-free essential clause for 'that.'
per_choice_rationale.B: Sets the clause off with commas (nonrestrictive_meaning_change), turning essential information into an aside and implying that every negative has dried overnight.
per_choice_rationale.C: Picks the right relative pronoun but strands a lone comma between the subject and its verb (comma_splits_subject_verb).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the clause identifies which negatives are safe to handle, so it takes 'that' with no commas.

why_correct_md: The clause **restricts** the noun — only negatives that finished drying are safe — so it takes 'that' with no commas.
why_tempted_md: 'Which' sounds slightly more formal than 'that,' so students upgrade to it without testing whether the clause is essential.
rule_md: 1) Cover the relative clause and re-read the sentence. 2) If the meaning over-generalizes or changes, the clause is essential. 3) Essential clauses take 'that' with no commas; incidental ones take 'which' set off by commas. 4) Finally, confirm no lone comma separates the subject from its verb.

subject: act-english
context_html: Using bamboo tongs, the printer <u>moves</u> the dripping print from the developer tray into the stop bath.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize the delicate care the printer takes with the wet print. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Moves' is accurate but neutral (goal_neutral_verb), conveying no special care.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Shoves' signals rough force (goal_opposite_connotation), the reverse of the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: 'eases' pictures a slow, careful motion, directly conveying delicate handling.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Transfers' is clinical and procedural (goal_flat_technical), emphasizing logistics rather than care.

why_correct_md: The goal asks for **care**, and only a verb that pictures slow, gentle motion delivers it.
why_tempted_md: 'Transfers' sounds precise and writerly, so students pick polish over the connotation the goal demands.
rule_md: 1) Underline the goal words in the stem. 2) For each verb, name its connotation in one word (rough, neutral, careful, clinical). 3) Eliminate any verb whose connotation misses the goal, even if it is accurate. 4) Pick the verb whose picture matches the goal exactly.

subject: act-english
context_html: Because a two-degree drift can shift a print's contrast, Priya <u>checks</u> the developer's temperature throughout the entire two-hour session.
stem_md: The writer wants to stress that Priya keeps constant watch over the developer's temperature for the whole session. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Checks' names discrete, occasional acts (verb_discrete_acts), not the unbroken vigilance the goal demands.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Verifies' means confirming a fact once (verb_one_time_confirmation), so it cannot stretch across two hours.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: 'monitors' denotes sustained, continuous observation, matching 'constant watch' exactly.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Inspects' pictures a single close examination (verb_momentary_scrutiny), not ongoing attention.

why_correct_md: Only a verb of **sustained** observation matches 'constant watch' over 'the whole session.'
why_tempted_md: 'Checks' pairs naturally with 'throughout,' so students assume repeated checking adds up to the continuous vigilance the goal requires.
rule_md: 1) Circle the duration cues in the stem and sentence ('constant,' 'whole session,' 'throughout'). 2) Ask of each verb: does it happen once, repeatedly, or continuously? 3) Eliminate one-time and intermittent verbs. 4) Choose the verb whose built-in duration matches the cues.

subject: act-english
context_html: After developing a roll of film, many photographers make a contact sheet before printing anything at full size. The negatives are laid directly on a sheet of photographic paper and exposed, producing a page of frame-sized images. Studying these tiny previews, the photographer circles the frames worth enlarging with a grease pencil.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence at the end of the paragraph: "The grease pencil's waxy marks wipe off with a soft cloth, so no selection is ever permanent." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it demonstrates that grease pencils outperform every other marking tool.
Yes, because it adds a relevant detail about the marking tool described in the final sentence.
No, because it introduces information about a tool unrelated to reviewing the contact sheet.
No, because it repeats a detail already stated earlier in the paragraph.

per_choice_rationale.A: Reaches the right verdict for a wrong reason (yes_overclaim): the new sentence compares the pencil to nothing, so it cannot show superiority.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the sentence extends the grease-pencil detail just introduced, explaining why circling frames is a low-stakes step.
per_choice_rationale.C: Misreads the sentence's subject (no_false_irrelevance): the pencil is exactly the tool the paragraph's last sentence puts in the photographer's hand.
per_choice_rationale.D: Claims repetition that never occurred (no_false_repetition): erasability appears nowhere earlier in the paragraph.

why_correct_md: The new sentence **builds on** the grease-pencil detail that immediately precedes it, so it belongs.
why_tempted_md: Students who skim past the last sentence assume the pencil is new, off-topic equipment and reject the addition as irrelevant.
rule_md: 1) Find what the proposed sentence is about. 2) Locate that subject in the paragraph — is it present, and where? 3) If present and adjacent, the sentence likely belongs; if absent, it likely does not. 4) Then audit the stated reason: accept an option only when both its verdict and its reason are true.

subject: act-english
context_html: Fixer makes a photographic image permanent, but any fixer left behind in the paper will slowly bleach it. Prints are therefore washed for up to an hour in gently running water. Some museums store their finest prints in climate-controlled vaults. A residue test at the end of the wash confirms that the last traces of the chemical are gone.
stem_md: The writer is considering deleting the sentence "Some museums store their finest prints in climate-controlled vaults." Should the sentence be kept or deleted?

choices.label: Kept, because it emphasizes how valuable a fully washed print can become.
Deleted, because it shifts the focus away from removing fixer from the print.
Kept, because it supplies a step that belongs between the fixer wash and the residue test.
Deleted, because the essay never explains what fixer is made of.

per_choice_rationale.A: Keeps the sentence for an unearned payoff (kept_false_implication): the paragraph never links washing to museum value, so the sentence cannot emphasize it.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the paragraph traces fixer from threat to wash to residue test, and the museum aside breaks that chain.
per_choice_rationale.C: Invents a procedural role (kept_false_step): storing prints in vaults is not a stage between washing and testing.
per_choice_rationale.D: Reaches the right verdict with an irrelevant reason (deleted_wrong_reason): the paragraph's job is removal, not chemistry, so the missing formula is beside the point.

why_correct_md: The paragraph follows one thread — getting fixer **out** of the print and proving it is gone — and the museum sentence stands outside that thread.
why_tempted_md: The museum sentence flatters the paragraph's subject, so students keep it for its pleasant association with permanence and value.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's job in one sentence. 2) Test the candidate sentence: does it advance that job or merely sit near it? 3) If it does not advance the job, lean toward deletion. 4) Then vet the reason attached to your verdict — both the decision and its justification must be true of the text.

subject: act-english
context_html: An enlarger is little more than a lamp, a negative carrier, and a lens mounted on a vertical column. Light passes through the negative, and the lens focuses that image onto the easel below; raising the head makes the projected picture larger, while lowering it makes the picture smaller. A set of bellows lets the printer fine-tune focus at any height.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to explain how one basic piece of darkroom equipment forms an image. Would this passage accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it recounts one printer's early struggles to focus a negative sharply.
Yes, because it identifies the machine's main parts and explains how light projects the negative onto the paper.
No, because it explains darkroom safety procedures rather than any one piece of equipment.
No, because it never explains how the projected image is developed into a finished print on paper.

per_choice_rationale.A: Reaches the right verdict with a false description (yes_wrong_description): the passage is a general explanation, not a narrative about any one printer's struggles.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the passage names the enlarger's components and traces how light carries the image from negative to easel, which is exactly the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.C: Misdescribes the passage entirely (no_false_focus): not one sentence discusses safety procedures.
per_choice_rationale.D: Applies a criterion the goal never set (no_irrelevant_criterion): the goal asked how the image is formed, not how the print is later developed.

why_correct_md: Both the **verdict** and the **reason** must match the passage, and only this option's reason truthfully describes what the passage does.
why_tempted_md: It is true the passage omits development, so students accept that criticism without checking whether the stated goal ever demanded that topic.
rule_md: 1) Restate the stated goal in your own words. 2) Summarize what the passage actually does in one sentence. 3) Compare the two: does the passage do the goal's job? That fixes the yes/no verdict. 4) Then test each option's reason against the text, discarding any reason that misdescribes the passage or invokes a requirement the goal never set. 5) Choose the option whose verdict and reason are both true.

subject: act-english
context_html: Dodging happens while the enlarger lamp is on. <u>The printer waving a small paddle over areas that would otherwise print too dark</u>.
stem_md: Which choice is most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: The printer, waving a small paddle over areas that would otherwise print too dark
Because the printer waves a small paddle over areas that would otherwise print too dark
The printer waves a small paddle over areas that would otherwise print too dark

per_choice_rationale.A: Leaves a bare -ing form as the only verb candidate (fragment_participle), so the word group never makes an assertion.
per_choice_rationale.B: Adds a comma but no tensed verb (comma_patch); punctuation cannot complete a fragment.
per_choice_rationale.C: Attaches a subordinator to the clause (fragment_subordinator), demoting it to a dependent piece with no main clause to lean on.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the tensed verb 'waves' pairs with the subject to form a complete sentence.

why_correct_md: Pairing the subject with the **tensed** verb 'waves' turns the word group into a complete sentence.
why_tempted_md: The original sounds complete when read quickly because 'waving' feels verb-like, so students miss that it carries no tense.
rule_md: 1) Find the subject of the word group. 2) Hunt for a verb with tense — a bare -ing form does not count. 3) If no tensed verb exists, the group is a fragment. 4) Prefer the revision that supplies a tensed verb; reject patches that only add punctuation or a subordinating word.

subject: act-english
context_html: Selenium toner deepens a print's <u>shadows, it also protects</u> the silver image from fading over decades of display.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Joins two independent clauses with only a comma (comma_splice).
per_choice_rationale.B: Places a conjunctive adverb after a bare comma (conjunctive_adverb_splice), which still leaves the clauses unjoined and falsely signals cause-effect.
per_choice_rationale.C: Deletes the comma without adding a connector (comma_delete_fuse), turning the splice into a fused sentence.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: a comma plus the coordinating conjunction 'and' legally joins the two independent clauses.

why_correct_md: A comma plus the **coordinating conjunction** 'and' is a legal junction between two independent clauses.
why_tempted_md: 'Therefore' feels like a strong connector, so students accept it after a comma without realizing conjunctive adverbs cannot join clauses.
rule_md: 1) Test each side of the junction for independence by reading it alone. 2) If both sides are independent, require one of: a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS). 3) Treat conjunctive adverbs like 'therefore' and 'however' as impostors — after a comma they still leave a splice. 4) Re-read the sentence with your junction installed to confirm it holds.

subject: act-english
context_html: Resin-coated paper dries flat in <u>minutes fiber paper</u> can curl for a whole day unless it is pressed.
stem_md: Which choice best punctuates the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Lets two independent clauses touch with no boundary at all (fused_sentence).
per_choice_rationale.B: Swaps the missing boundary for a bare comma (comma_splice), which is still too weak to join two independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a semicolon legally joins the two related independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.D: Adds 'although' after the semicolon (semicolon_fragment), demoting the second clause when the semicolon demands independence on both sides.

why_correct_md: A **semicolon** legally joins the two related independent clauses about the two kinds of paper.
why_tempted_md: The comma version matches the small pause readers hear between the two claims, so the splice sneaks past anyone trusting the ear.
rule_md: 1) Read each side of the boundary alone and label it independent or dependent. 2) Two independent clauses need a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. 3) If a subordinating word appears, re-test the demoted side — a semicolon cannot precede a dependent clause. 4) Pick the boundary that matches your labels and re-read.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Inverting the tank every thirty seconds, fresh developer washes over</u> each frame of the film.
stem_md: Which choice results in the clearest, most logical sentence?

choices.label: Inverting the tank every thirty seconds, it is ensured that fresh developer washes over
By inverting the tank every thirty seconds, the photographer washes fresh developer over
Inverted every thirty seconds, fresh developer washes over

per_choice_rationale.A: Leaves the opening phrase dangling (dangling_modifier): the noun after the comma is the developer, which cannot invert a tank.
per_choice_rationale.B: Hides the doer behind an empty 'it is ensured' construction (dangling_passive_patch), so the modifier still has nothing to attach to.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the person who performs the inverting now stands immediately after the modifier.
per_choice_rationale.D: Re-aims the participle at the liquid (misattached_participle), absurdly claiming the developer itself is inverted.

why_correct_md: Naming **the photographer** right after the modifier gives the opening phrase a doer that can actually invert the tank.
why_tempted_md: The original keeps the sentence's spotlight on the developer, which feels natural because the developer is what the sentence is really about.
rule_md: 1) Find the opening modifier and ask who performs its action. 2) Check the first noun after the comma. 3) If that noun cannot perform the action, the modifier dangles. 4) Choose the version that places the true doer immediately after the comma, and reject rewrites that merely bury the problem in passive padding.

subject: act-english
context_html: A grain magnifier lets the printer focus the enlarger with real <u>precision, sharpening the projected image until the film's grain itself is visible</u>.
stem_md: Which choice most effectively expresses the idea without redundancy?

choices.label: precision, sharpening the projected image until the film's grain itself is visible to the eye
precision and exactness, sharpening the projected image until the film's grain itself is visible
precision, sharpening and refining the projected image until the film's grain itself is visible

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: every word does distinct work, and no idea is repeated.
per_choice_rationale.B: Appends 'to the eye' (redundant_tail), restating an idea already built into 'visible.'
per_choice_rationale.C: Pairs 'precision' with its synonym 'exactness' (redundant_synonym_pair), saying one thing twice.
per_choice_rationale.D: Doubles the verb with 'refining' (redundant_verb_pair), which re-performs the job 'sharpening' already does.

why_correct_md: Every word in the original does **distinct** work; each revision smuggles in a synonym or an already-built-in idea.
why_tempted_md: 'Visible to the eye' sounds like a natural, complete-feeling phrase, so students add it without noticing that 'visible' already contains the idea.
rule_md: 1) Read each option word by word. 2) For every added word, ask: does it introduce a new idea, or restate one already present? 3) Check pairs joined by 'and' for synonym doubling, and check modifiers for meanings already built into their headwords. 4) Keep the version in which nothing repeats.

subject: act-english
context_html: Test prints pile up quickly, so most printers <u>reuse</u> the backs of failed sheets for notes.
stem_md: Which choice expresses the idea most concisely while preserving the meaning?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the single verb already carries the complete idea.
per_choice_rationale.B: Buries the action in a noun propped up by 'make' (nominalization_padding), adding words but no meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: Adds 'once again' (redundant_re_prefix) even though the re- prefix already means the action is repeated.
per_choice_rationale.D: Bolts on 'utilize' (doubled_verb), a dressed-up synonym that contributes nothing new.

why_correct_md: The single verb already carries the **complete** idea; every alternative adds words without adding meaning.
why_tempted_md: 'Make reuse of' sounds formal and deliberate, so students mistake extra bulk for extra sophistication.
rule_md: 1) Identify the core action of the underlined portion. 2) Strip each option down to the words that add information. 3) Cross out helper constructions like 'make ... of,' repetitions of a prefix's meaning, and synonym pairs. 4) Select the option with zero crossed-out words.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Due to the fact that</u> fixer exhausts itself with use, busy labs test its strength every morning.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the sentence's concise, formal style?

choices.label: In light of the fact that

per_choice_rationale.A: Opens with a five-word filler formula (filler_phrase) that does the work of a single word.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: one subordinating conjunction states the causal link directly and formally.
per_choice_rationale.C: Swaps one inflated 'the fact that' formula for another (filler_swap), keeping all the padding.
per_choice_rationale.D: Compresses the opener but into a nonstandard, conversational connector (colloquial_nonstandard).

why_correct_md: **Because** states the causal link in one direct, formal word.
why_tempted_md: 'In light of the fact that' sounds elevated and scholarly, so students read its extra bulk as extra formality.
rule_md: 1) Name the relationship the opener must signal (here, cause). 2) Weigh each option's word count against that single job. 3) Reject stock formulas built on 'the fact that' and any connector that belongs to casual speech. 4) Choose the connector that is both compact and standard written English.

subject: act-english
context_html: Thirty seconds into the developer, gray tones begin to <u>occur</u> across the white sheet.
stem_md: Which word most precisely describes how the gray tones appear on the sheet?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Occur' merely reports that something happened (vague_verb), painting no picture of gradual appearance.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it precisely pictures tones gradually coming into view, matching the slow development.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Erupt' injects sudden violence (overstated_verb) that contradicts a thirty-second, gentle process.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Accumulate' describes quantity piling up (wrong_mechanism), not an image becoming visible in place.

why_correct_md: **Emerge** captures tones gradually coming into view, matching both the timescale and the mechanism of development.
why_tempted_md: 'Accumulate' appeals because the tones do intensify over time, but it pictures quantity piling up rather than an image appearing.
rule_md: 1) Picture the literal scene the sentence describes. 2) Define each option verb in your own words. 3) Match each definition against the scene's speed, force, and mechanism. 4) Eliminate verbs that are vague, overstated, or mechanically wrong, and pick the one whose picture matches exactly.

subject: act-english
context_html: A darkroom depends on steady airflow to carry chemical vapor away from the trays. When the ventilation fan fails, chemical fumes <u>get pretty gnarly</u> within minutes.
stem_md: Which choice best matches the tone of the passage?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Pretty gnarly' is casual slang (colloquial_slang) that clashes with the passage's plain, informative voice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it states the danger plainly, at the same level of formality as the surrounding sentences.
per_choice_rationale.C: Trades one slang phrase for another (colloquial_swap), leaving the register just as casual.
per_choice_rationale.D: Overshoots into inflated, showy diction (register_overshoot), which breaks the plain voice as surely as slang does.

why_correct_md: The phrase conveys the danger in the same **plain, informative register** as the rest of the passage.
why_tempted_md: 'Escalate into an olfactory catastrophe' impresses students who equate fancier vocabulary with better writing.
rule_md: 1) Read the surrounding sentences and name the passage's register in one word (here: plain, informative). 2) Rate each option: slang, plain standard, or inflated. 3) Reject both undershoots (slang) and overshoots (showy diction). 4) Choose the option that sits level with the passage's voice.

subject: act-english
context_html: Determined <u>to making</u> a fresh start, my great-uncle Emil sold his cobbler's bench and booked third-class passage on a steamer bound for Halifax.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Pairs the infinitive marker 'to' with an -ing form, a mixed verb form that standard English rejects after 'determined.'
per_choice_rationale.B: Uses a perfect infinitive, which wrongly places the fresh start before the determination in time.
per_choice_rationale.C: Swaps the infinitive that 'determined' idiomatically requires for a preposition-plus-gerund pattern.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: 'determined' takes a plain infinitive complement, so the base verb follows 'to.'

why_correct_md: After **determined**, English requires a plain infinitive, so the base form of the verb must follow *to*.
why_tempted_md: 'For making' mirrors familiar patterns like 'responsible for making,' so the preposition-plus-gerund construction sounds idiomatic.
rule_md: 1) Find the governing word before the underlined verb (here, *determined*). 2) Recall which complement that word takes: infinitive, gerund, or preposition + gerund. 3) If infinitive *to* is present, put the bare base form after it — never an -ing form. 4) Check that the option does not shift the action's time with *have* + participle. 5) Pick the option that passes every check.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each of my cousins has traced <u>their</u> branch of the family back to the village outside Guadalajara where our great-grandparents were married.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Their' is plural, but the true subject 'each' is grammatically singular, so the pronoun clashes with its antecedent in number.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the singular subject 'each' requires a singular, person-appropriate possessive.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Its' is singular but refers to things, not people; the cousins are human beings.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'They're' is the contraction of 'they are,' not a possessive form at all.

why_correct_md: **Each** is grammatically singular, so the possessive that refers back to it must be singular and suited to people.
why_tempted_md: 'Their' matches everyday speech and avoids awkwardness, but the ACT requires number agreement with the singular 'each.'
rule_md: 1) Find the pronoun and ask what noun it points back to. 2) Cross out the prepositional phrase after the subject — *of my cousins* — leaving *each*. 3) Classify the antecedent: *each* is always singular. 4) Ask whether the antecedent is a person or a thing. 5) Choose a singular, person-appropriate possessive; reject contractions posing as possessives.

subject: act-english
context_html: In her taped interview, my grandmother described <u>packing one trunk, hiding coins in its lining, and kissing the doorframe of the house</u> before the family walked to the station.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: packing one trunk, hiding coins in its lining, and to kiss the doorframe of the house
packing one trunk, to hide coins in its lining, and kissing the doorframe of the house
to pack one trunk, hiding coins in its lining, and kissed the doorframe of the house

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: all three listed actions use the same gerund form, keeping the series parallel.
per_choice_rationale.B: Breaks parallelism by switching only the third item to an infinitive after two gerunds.
per_choice_rationale.C: Switches the middle item to an infinitive, breaking the gerund series where readers check least.
per_choice_rationale.D: Mixes an infinitive, a gerund, and a past-tense verb — three different forms in one list.

why_correct_md: All three items in the series keep the same **gerund** form, so the list is already parallel.
why_tempted_md: Choices that alter only one item are tempting because the ear relaxes after matching items and tolerates a quiet form shift.
rule_md: 1) Bracket every item in the list. 2) Label each item's opening verb form: gerund, infinitive, or finite verb. 3) Require identical labels across all items. 4) Confirm each item still attaches sensibly to the main verb (*described*). 5) If the original already passes, resist the urge to fix it.

subject: act-english
context_html: The manifest of the S.S. Providence lists my great-grandfather's occupation as 'farmer.' <u>However,</u> the letters he mailed home during his first year describe twelve-hour shifts in a Rhode Island textile mill.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the letters contradict the manifest's record, so a contrast transition is the logical connector.
per_choice_rationale.B: Falsely marks the mill work as a result of the manifest's farming label; no cause-effect link exists.
per_choice_rationale.C: Presents the mill shifts as an example of farming, though they conflict with that record.
per_choice_rationale.D: Claims the two records point the same way when they actually disagree.

why_correct_md: The letters **contradict** the manifest's record, so a contrast transition is the logical connector.
why_tempted_md: 'Therefore' attracts readers who assume the second sentence simply continues the first instead of testing the actual logical relationship.
rule_md: 1) State sentence one's claim in your own words. 2) State sentence two's claim. 3) Name the relationship: contrast, cause-effect, example, or addition. 4) Match the transition word to that named relationship. 5) Re-read the pair with your choice to confirm the logic clicks.

subject: act-english
context_html: For decades, my aunt repeated the story that an impatient clerk at Ellis Island shortened our surname. <u>Likewise,</u> the manifest we finally located shows the abbreviated spelling in my great-grandfather's own handwriting, recorded before the ship ever left Genoa.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Likewise' signals similarity, but the manifest disproves the aunt's story rather than paralleling it.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Consequently' invents a causal chain; the retold story did not produce the handwriting on the manifest.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For instance' would make the manifest an example of the clerk legend, when it is evidence against it.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the manifest corrects the long-held assumption, and this transition signals that corrective turn.

why_correct_md: The manifest **corrects** the family's assumption, so the transition must signal reality overturning the story.
why_tempted_md: 'Consequently' tempts readers who see 'finally located' as the outcome of decades of retelling rather than checking what the manifest does to the story's truth.
rule_md: 1) Summarize the first sentence: a belief held for decades. 2) Summarize the second: evidence that disproves it. 3) Name that move — a correction of an assumption. 4) Test each transition against the pattern 'belief, then corrective reality.' 5) Choose the one that signals the correction.

subject: act-english
context_html: For years, the letters my great-grandfather mailed from Buenos Aires sat in a shoebox labeled 'miscellaneous.' Last spring, my mother and I scanned all ninety-four of them and tagged each with its date and postmark. As we worked, we watched his Spanish creep into his Yiddish sentences, one borrowed word at a time.
stem_md: The writer wants to conclude the paragraph with a sentence that reinforces its main point about what the letters reveal. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Scanning fragile letters requires patience and a steady flatbed scanner.
Read in order, the letters trace a man slowly turning into someone new.
Buenos Aires drew thousands of Eastern European immigrants into its port neighborhoods in the early twentieth century.
My mother hopes to read and digitize our photo albums next winter.

per_choice_rationale.A: Ends on equipment and procedure, abandoning the paragraph's point about what the letters reveal.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it restates the paragraph's discovery — a gradual transformation visible across the letters — in a closing image.
per_choice_rationale.C: Zooms out to a broad historical statistic, widening the lens far beyond this one family's papers.
per_choice_rationale.D: Pivots to a future project, introducing material the paragraph never developed.

why_correct_md: It **restates the paragraph's discovery** — the gradual transformation visible across the letters — in a single closing image.
why_tempted_md: The historical statistic feels weighty and on-theme for immigration, but it widens the lens far beyond what these letters reveal.
rule_md: 1) Restate the paragraph's main point in your own words. 2) Ask what the stem requires the final sentence to do. 3) Test each option: does it return to that point, or drift to process, background, or future plans? 4) Eliminate any sentence introducing material the paragraph never developed. 5) Choose the one that echoes the main point.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] My aunt Priya keeps our family's immigration papers in a fireproof box under her bed. [2] The oldest item is a 1968 airline ticket from Bombay to London, its carbon copy still crisp. [3] Beside it lies my grandfather's first British payslip, folded into eighths. [4] The box even holds the rejected visa application that delayed my grandmother's arrival by two years.
stem_md: The writer wants to add the following sentence to the paragraph: 'Each document, my aunt says, is a chapter no one thought to write down.' To make the paragraph most logical, the sentence should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Places a summary of 'each document' before the reader has met a single item in the box.
per_choice_rationale.B: Generalizes about every document when only the airline ticket has been introduced.
per_choice_rationale.C: Leaves the visa application stranded outside the summary that is supposed to gather everything.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: after the full inventory, the generalization about 'each document' has all its referents in place.

why_correct_md: The added sentence **generalizes about every document**, so it must follow the complete inventory it sums up.
why_tempted_md: Placing it right after the opening keeps 'my aunt says' beside its antecedent, but the summary would then precede everything it summarizes.
rule_md: 1) Classify the sentence to add: introducer, detail, or summarizer. 2) If it generalizes ('each document'), locate the point where all its referents have appeared. 3) Check that pronouns and pointers still have clear antecedents at that spot. 4) Insert it and re-read the paragraph for flow. 5) Confirm no listed item is stranded after the summary.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] According to family legend, my great-grandfather chose Minnesota because a steamship poster showed wheat fields that reminded him of home. [2] My grandmother swore the poster hung for years in a shop window in Bergen. [3] The documents, however, tell a less romantic story. [4] A labor contract preserved in the county archive shows that a railroad agent recruited him and paid his passage. [5] The contract bound him to two years of track work at a fixed wage. [6] Whatever drew him across the ocean, he stayed, and four generations of us have followed.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide the paragraph into two paragraphs in order to separate the family legend from the documentary record. The most logical place to begin the second paragraph is at:

per_choice_rationale.A: Splits the legend material in half, since the grandmother's memory of the poster is still part of the legend.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: this sentence announces the pivot from legend to documents, so it should open the second paragraph.
per_choice_rationale.C: Starts with the first archival detail but strands the pivot sentence back with the legend.
per_choice_rationale.D: Breaks in the middle of the contract discussion, splitting the documentary record itself.

why_correct_md: Sentence 3 **announces the pivot** from legend to documents, so the second paragraph should open with it.
why_tempted_md: Sentence 4 attracts readers because it contains the first archival detail, but choosing it strands the pivot sentence with the legend.
rule_md: 1) Label each sentence by topic: legend or record. 2) Find the boundary where the labels flip. 3) Look for a signpost sentence that announces the new topic — it belongs at the top of the new paragraph. 4) Verify each resulting paragraph is unified. 5) Choose that boundary sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: My great-grandmother's steamer <u>trunk a battered cedar box with a broken hasp</u> still anchors one corner of our attic.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: trunk, a battered cedar box with a broken hasp
trunk, a battered cedar box with a broken hasp,
trunk a battered cedar box with a broken hasp,

per_choice_rationale.A: Leaves the appositive completely unmarked, fusing the renaming phrase into the main clause.
per_choice_rationale.B: Opens the appositive with a comma but never closes it before the verb.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: paired commas fence off the nonessential appositive on both sides.
per_choice_rationale.D: Closes the aside without ever opening it, so 'trunk a battered cedar box' reads as one noun pile.

why_correct_md: A nonessential appositive must be set off by **paired commas**, one before and one after.
why_tempted_md: A single opening comma satisfies the ear at the pause, so readers often forget the aside must also be closed.
rule_md: 1) Find the phrase that renames a nearby noun. 2) Test removal: if the sentence survives, the phrase is nonessential. 3) Fence it with a comma on each side. 4) Re-read to confirm the subject and verb reconnect cleanly around the aside. 5) Reject any option that marks only one boundary.

subject: act-english
context_html: My grandfather stepped off the train in Chicago with twelve <u>dollars, he</u> spent half of it on a warm coat before nightfall.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Joins two independent clauses with only a comma — a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Adds the adverb 'then,' which supplies timing but no grammatical connection, so the splice remains.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a semicolon legally joins the two independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.D: Puts a dependent 'because' clause after a semicolon, which requires an independent clause on each side.

why_correct_md: A **semicolon** legally joins the two independent clauses that the comma alone spliced together.
why_tempted_md: Adding 'then' feels like it links the actions in time, but an adverb has no power to join two complete sentences.
rule_md: 1) Test each side of the mark: subject + verb + complete thought? 2) If both sides are independent, a bare comma is illegal. 3) Legal joins: period, semicolon, or comma + coordinating conjunction. 4) If a subordinator is added, confirm the logic is real and the punctuation still matches. 5) Pick the option using a legal join with sensible meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: Of all the papers in the strongbox, the <u>notebook that my great-grandmother carried from Naples</u> is the only one written in her own hand.
stem_md: Which choice provides the correct punctuation for the underlined portion?

choices.label: notebook, which my great-grandmother carried from Naples,
notebook that my great-grandmother carried from Naples,
notebook, that my great-grandmother carried from Naples,

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the clause identifies which paper is meant, so restrictive 'that' with no commas is right.
per_choice_rationale.B: Paired commas mark the clause as removable, but removing it leaves the notebook unidentified among the papers in the strongbox.
per_choice_rationale.C: Adds a stray comma after a restrictive clause, cutting the subject off from its verb.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'That' heads only restrictive clauses, so it can never be framed by nonrestrictive commas.

why_correct_md: The clause is **restrictive** — it singles out which paper is meant — so 'that' with no commas is correct.
why_tempted_md: The comma-wrapped 'which' version sounds polished, so students default to it without testing whether the clause is essential.
rule_md: 1) Drop the clause and re-read the sentence. 2) If the reader can no longer tell which thing is meant, the clause is essential. 3) Essential clauses take 'that' and no commas; nonessential ones take 'which' with paired commas. 4) Reject any mix of the two systems. 5) Confirm no stray comma separates subject from verb.

subject: act-english
context_html: When the ferry docked at last, my grandmother <u>walked</u> down the gangway toward the crowd of strangers on the pier, her documents pinned inside her coat.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize the grandmother's hesitation as she left the ship. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Walked' reports motion neutrally and conveys none of the hesitation the writer wants to emphasize.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Strolled' suggests leisure and ease, the opposite of a nervous arrival.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: 'edged' conveys slow, cautious, reluctant movement, matching the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Hurried' signals eagerness or urgency rather than hesitation.

why_correct_md: Only this verb's **connotation** of slow, wary movement delivers the hesitation the stem requires.
why_tempted_md: 'Walked' tempts students because it is unobjectionable, but a goal question rewards the verb that accomplishes the stated emphasis, not merely a grammatical one.
rule_md: 1) Underline the goal stated in the stem. 2) For each verb, name its connotation in one word (neutral, relaxed, cautious, rushed). 3) Match the connotations against the goal. 4) Reject grammatical options that miss the emphasis. 5) Choose the verb whose picture fits the goal exactly.

subject: act-english
context_html: From ship manifests, census sheets, and a water-stained synagogue ledger, my cousin <u>reconstructs</u> the route our family took across three borders.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize the painstaking, piece-by-piece nature of the cousin's research. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: 'reconstructs' pictures rebuilding something lost from fragments, exactly the painstaking effort the writer wants.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Retraces' implies following a route already known, erasing the piece-by-piece assembly.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Imagines' cuts the work loose from the documents, suggesting invention rather than research.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Records' implies merely writing down finished information, minimizing the labor.

why_correct_md: The original verb alone conveys **rebuilding from fragments**, which matches the stated emphasis on painstaking effort.
why_tempted_md: 'Retraces' tempts because it involves routes and journeys, but it presumes the path is already mapped rather than pieced together.
rule_md: 1) Restate the stem's goal in your own words. 2) Ask what each verb presupposes about the starting materials. 3) Keep only verbs implying effortful assembly from evidence. 4) Test the survivor against the sources listed in the sentence. 5) If the original passes best, keep it.

subject: act-english
context_html: After twelve-hour shifts at the cannery, my grandfather walked to English classes held in a church basement. His notebook, which my mother still keeps, shows column after column of vocabulary words copied in careful script. Within two years, he was translating letters for neighbors up and down the block.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the second sentence: 'Classmates later remembered that he stayed after each lesson to practice conversation with the volunteer teacher.' Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it explains why the cannery demanded such long shifts.
Yes, because it offers further evidence of the grandfather's commitment to learning English.
No, because it repeats information the paragraph has already provided about the notebook.
No, because it shifts attention from the grandfather's studying to the volunteer teacher.

per_choice_rationale.A: The addition is justified, but not for this reason — the sentence says nothing about the cannery's schedule.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the detail extends the paragraph's picture of the grandfather working doggedly at English.
per_choice_rationale.C: The proposed sentence adds spoken practice, a new fact, not a repetition of the written notebook detail.
per_choice_rationale.D: The grandfather remains the subject and focus; the teacher is incidental background.

why_correct_md: The sentence adds a **supporting** detail that deepens the paragraph's single focus on the grandfather's determination.
why_tempted_md: The repetition objection tempts students because the notebook and the after-class practice both involve studying, though they are different facts.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's focus in one phrase. 2) Ask whether the proposed sentence develops that focus, repeats it, or derails it. 3) Decide add or omit. 4) Then vet the stated reason: it must match what the sentence actually does. 5) Reject right verdicts wearing wrong reasons.

subject: act-english
context_html: The 1920 census lists my great-grandparents in a boardinghouse on Mulberry Street, along with eleven other lodgers. The enumerator recorded my great-grandfather's occupation as 'presser' and my great-grandmother's as 'none.' Her account book from that same year, however, records payments for taking in sewing from half the block. The census, I have come to understand, counted only what its forms had room to ask.
stem_md: The writer is considering deleting the sentence about the great-grandmother's account book. Should the writer make this deletion?

choices.label: Yes, because it introduces a source other than the census and blurs the paragraph's focus.
Yes, because the great-grandmother's earnings are not relevant to a paragraph about the census.
No, because it proves the enumerator deliberately falsified the family's entry.
No, because it supplies the contradiction on which the paragraph's final point depends.

per_choice_rationale.A: The account book is not a distraction; it is the counter-record that makes the closing sentence possible.
per_choice_rationale.B: Her earnings matter precisely because the census recorded her occupation as 'none.'
per_choice_rationale.C: Keeping the sentence is right, but the passage blames the form's limits, not deliberate dishonesty.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the account book contradicts the census entry and sets up the paragraph's closing insight.

why_correct_md: The sentence supplies the **contradiction** between record and reality on which the paragraph's conclusion rests.
why_tempted_md: The falsification option tempts because the enumerator did record something untrue, but the passage attributes the gap to the form, not to fraud.
rule_md: 1) Find the paragraph's concluding claim. 2) List which sentences that claim rests on. 3) If the candidate sentence is load-bearing, keep it. 4) Check the offered reason against the passage's actual argument. 5) Accept only the verdict-plus-reason pair in which both parts hold.

subject: act-english
context_html: On the morning of her naturalization ceremony, my grandmother pressed the navy dress she had sewn from a pattern her sister mailed from Krakow. At the courthouse, she repeated the oath in careful English, her accent softening the vowels. Afterward, my grandfather photographed her on the steps, certificate held against the wind. She kept the dress, the photograph, and the flag pin in one box for the rest of her life.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to provide a step-by-step account of how immigrants obtained citizenship in the 1930s. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it describes the day the grandmother completed her naturalization.
Yes, because the oath mentioned in the essay was a legal requirement for citizenship.
No, because the essay is a personal portrait of a single celebration, not an explanation of legal procedures.
No, because the essay focuses mainly on the courthouse rather than on the grandmother.

per_choice_rationale.A: Describing the ceremony day narrates an outcome; it does not lay out the legal steps the supposed goal requires.
per_choice_rationale.B: One glancing reference to the oath cannot stand in for a step-by-step account of the whole process.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the essay is an intimate family scene, not an explanation of how citizenship was legally obtained.
per_choice_rationale.D: The essay centers on the grandmother throughout; the courthouse is only a setting.

why_correct_md: The essay's scope is a **family memory**, so it cannot serve a goal that demands a procedural account.
why_tempted_md: The oath detail tempts students to answer yes because it is genuinely legal, but one step is not a whole process.
rule_md: 1) Restate the hypothetical goal precisely. 2) Summarize what the essay actually does in one sentence. 3) Compare scope: process account versus intimate scene. 4) Give the yes/no verdict. 5) Then screen the reasons: keep only the one that describes the essay accurately.

subject: act-english
context_html: My great-aunt saved every boarding pass and luggage <u>tag. Because she believed</u> the family would someday want proof of the journey.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Punctuating the 'Because' clause as its own sentence strands a dependent fragment.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: attaching the subordinate clause directly to the main clause completes the thought.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Believing' is a participle, not a finite verb, so the second word group remains a fragment.
per_choice_rationale.D: A semicolon demands an independent clause on each side, and the 'because' clause is dependent.

why_correct_md: A **subordinate** clause must attach to the independent clause it explains rather than stand alone.
why_tempted_md: The period version tempts because speech often pauses before 'because,' making the fragment sound complete.
rule_md: 1) Read each word group after a period by itself. 2) Check for a subject, a finite verb, and a complete thought. 3) If it opens with a subordinator, it must join a main clause. 4) Match the punctuation to the join: no semicolon before a lone dependent clause. 5) Re-read the repaired sentence whole.

subject: act-english
context_html: The consulate stamped her passport on a <u>Tuesday, she</u> had sold the family piano by Friday.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Then' is an adverb with no joining power, so the splice remains.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a comma plus the coordinating conjunction 'and' legally joins the clauses.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Because' plus a period strands a fragment and invents a cause-effect link the sentence never asserts.

why_correct_md: A comma needs a **coordinating conjunction** beside it to join two independent clauses.
why_tempted_md: 'Then' feels like a connector because it orders the events in time, but adverbs cannot glue clauses together.
rule_md: 1) Test each side of the mark for subject + verb + complete thought. 2) If both sides pass, a bare comma is illegal. 3) Legal repairs: period, semicolon, or comma + FANBOYS word. 4) If a subordinator is used instead, confirm the clause attaches and the logic is real. 5) Pick the repair that is both legal and sensible.

subject: act-english
context_html: The archive reading room closed at <u>five we</u> photographed the last ledger pages in the parking lot.
stem_md: Which choice makes the underlined portion grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Nothing separates the two independent clauses — a fused sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: Substituting a comma converts the fused sentence into a comma splice, still illegal.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'However' is a conjunctive adverb, powerless to join clauses across a mere comma, and its contrast logic is wrong here besides.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: a period gives each independent clause its own sentence.

why_correct_md: A **period** legally separates the two complete statements that were fused together.
why_tempted_md: The comma version tempts because a pause clearly belongs at the seam, but a pause mark is not a boundary mark.
rule_md: 1) Locate each subject-verb core. 2) Mark where the first complete thought ends. 3) At that seam, require a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. 4) Treat words like 'however' as adverbs, not glue. 5) Choose the option that meets the requirement.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Yellowed and brittle, my mother unfolded the telegram</u> that had announced her grandfather's safe arrival in 1923.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: Yellowed and brittle, my mother carefully unfolded the telegram
My mother unfolded the yellowed, brittle telegram
Yellowed and brittle, my mother's hands unfolded the telegram

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening modifier attaches to 'my mother,' absurdly describing her as yellowed and brittle.
per_choice_rationale.B: Adding 'carefully' decorates the verb but leaves the modifier still pointing at the mother.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: moving the description next to 'telegram' lets the adjectives modify the paper they describe.
per_choice_rationale.D: Shifting the description onto her hands still misassigns it; the document, not the hands, is aged.

why_correct_md: Adjectives must sit **next to the noun they describe**, so the description belongs beside the telegram.
why_tempted_md: The 'hands' version tempts because hands touch the paper, so the image feels almost sensible while remaining misattached.
rule_md: 1) Find the opening descriptive phrase. 2) Identify the first noun after the comma — that is what it modifies. 3) Ask whether that pairing makes sense. 4) If not, rearrange so describer and described are adjacent. 5) Re-read to confirm no new misattachment appears.

subject: act-english
context_html: The passage cost forty dollars, a sum my great-grandfather <u>saved</u> over three winters of cutting lake ice.
stem_md: Which choice is the most effective wording for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: 'saved' says everything once; the three-winter timeframe already conveys the slow accumulation.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Saved up and accumulated' states the same action twice.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Gradually' duplicates the pace already established by 'over three winters.'
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Was able to save' pads the verb with an ability phrase made pointless by the completed action.

why_correct_md: The lone verb is already complete because **'over three winters'** carries the idea of slow accumulation.
why_tempted_md: 'Gradually saved' tempts because the adverb sounds informative until you notice the timeframe already guarantees it.
rule_md: 1) Identify the core action. 2) For every added word, name the new information it contributes. 3) Cross out words whose meaning is already elsewhere in the sentence. 4) Check that the surviving version reads cleanly. 5) Prefer it, even if it is the original.

subject: act-english
context_html: Customs officials <u>made an inspection of</u> every trunk stacked on the pier.
stem_md: Which choice expresses the idea most concisely?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Made an inspection of' stretches one action into a padded verb-plus-noun phrase.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the single verb delivers the entire action without padding.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Conducted an inspection of' dresses the padding in a fancier verb but keeps every extra word.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Gave an inspection to' is unidiomatic as well as wordy.

why_correct_md: One **strong verb** carries the whole action that the noun phrase buries.
why_tempted_md: 'Conducted an inspection of' tempts because it sounds official and formal, which masks the wordiness.
rule_md: 1) Find the action hiding inside a noun. 2) Rewrite the sentence with that action as the verb. 3) Compare: if the meaning is identical, prefer the tighter version. 4) Reject swaps still built around the buried noun. 5) Check the survivor for idiom and tense.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>It is interesting to note that the</u> family's first apartment stood two blocks from the harbor, close enough to hear the ferry horns.
stem_md: Which choice expresses the idea most directly?

choices.label: As a matter of fact, the
It should be noted that the

per_choice_rationale.A: 'It is interesting to note that' announces interest without adding any information.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'As a matter of fact' swaps one empty opener for another; nothing is being corrected or emphasized.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: deleting the filler lets the sentence begin with its actual subject.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'It should be noted that' is throat-clearing in an academic costume.

why_correct_md: Cutting the **filler** phrase lets the sentence lead with its real content at no cost in meaning.
why_tempted_md: 'It should be noted that' tempts because it sounds scholarly, but formality is not the same as content.
rule_md: 1) Bracket the opening phrase. 2) Delete it mentally and re-read. 3) If no meaning is lost, the phrase is filler — cut it. 4) Watch for replacement fillers sneaking in. 5) Keep the version that starts with the subject.

subject: act-english
context_html: A single line in the parish register — 'both sons to America, spring' — <u>proves</u> that the brothers left the village together.
stem_md: Which word most precisely characterizes what the register entry shows?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Proves' claims a certainty that a five-word register entry cannot supply.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it matches the tentative inference that a terse line can support.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Confirms' presupposes a prior claim awaiting verification, which the passage never presents.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Mentions' overstates explicitness: the entry never states that the brothers traveled together.

why_correct_md: The key verb matches the **strength of the evidence**: the line implies, but cannot establish, a joint departure.
why_tempted_md: 'Proves' tempts because the entry names both sons and one season, which feels decisive at a glance.
rule_md: 1) Quote the evidence to yourself. 2) List what it states outright versus what a reader infers. 3) Grade each verb's strength, from establishing certainty down to implying. 4) Match verb strength to evidence strength. 5) Choose the verb that neither overstates nor understates.

subject: act-english
context_html: The historical society's newsletter praised the exhibit, noting that the curators had <u>pulled together a bunch of</u> documents from a dozen family collections.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the tone established in the passage?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Pulled together a bunch of' is conversational slang inside a formal newsletter sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Scraped up a pile of' is slangier still and belittles the curators' work.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Effectuated the amalgamation of numerous' overcorrects into pompous, inflated diction.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it is formal, natural, and precise — matching the newsletter's register.

why_correct_md: **Register** must match the passage: standard formal diction, neither slang nor pomposity.
why_tempted_md: The Latinate option tempts because bigger words feel more formal, but inflation is its own register error.
rule_md: 1) Sample the passage's diction ('praised,' 'curators,' 'collections'). 2) Label each option: slang, standard formal, or inflated. 3) Discard both extremes. 4) Confirm the survivor keeps the original meaning. 5) Re-read the sentence for smooth fit.

subject: act-english
context_html: Rangers measuring Grinnell Glacier in Glacier National Park found that the ice <u>had shrank</u> to half of its 1966 footprint.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Uses the simple past 'shrank' where the past-perfect helper 'had' requires the past participle.
per_choice_rationale.B: Invents a regular '-ed' participle for a verb that is irregular in every form.
per_choice_rationale.C: Swaps the helper without fixing the form: 'shrank' is still not a participle, and the present-perfect helper misstates an already-completed event.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correctly pairs the helper 'had' with the past participle of the irregular verb.

why_correct_md: After the helping verb **had**, an irregular verb must appear in its past-participle form.
why_tempted_md: 'Had shrank' sounds acceptable because the simple past form appears constantly in speech while the participle rarely does.
rule_md: 1) Spot a helping verb (has/have/had) before the main verb. 2) Recite the verb's three forms: base, simple past, past participle. 3) After has/have/had, use only the third form. 4) If the correct pairing sounds odd, trust the verb chart, not your ear.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each of Bryce Canyon's horseback guides must renew <u>their</u> outfitter permit before the summer season begins.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Matches the plural noun 'guides' inside the prepositional phrase instead of the true singular subject 'Each.'
per_choice_rationale.B: Agrees in number with the singular pronoun 'Each' and correctly refers to people.
per_choice_rationale.C: Is singular but refers to things, not to human guides.
per_choice_rationale.D: Shifts to the impersonal 'one' even though the sentence names specific guides.

why_correct_md: The subject is **Each**, a singular pronoun, so the possessive that follows must be singular and refer to people.
why_tempted_md: The plural noun 'guides' sits closest to the pronoun, luring students into matching the nearest noun instead of the true antecedent.
rule_md: 1) Find the pronoun and ask what noun it stands for. 2) Cross out any 'of the ...' phrase after words like each, either, neither, every. 3) Match the pronoun's number to what remains. 4) Confirm the pronoun's type fits the antecedent (person vs. thing).

subject: act-english
context_html: The trail crew at Acadia spends early summer clearing drainage bars, rebuilding granite steps, and <u>they repaint</u> the faded blazes that mark the summit routes.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the pattern established earlier in the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: Breaks the list of '-ing' phrases by restarting with the subject 'they,' turning the third item into a mismatched clause.
per_choice_rationale.B: Matches 'clearing' and 'rebuilding,' completing the series in the same grammatical form.
per_choice_rationale.C: Switches the third item to an infinitive, mismatching the two '-ing' items before it.
per_choice_rationale.D: Uses a perfect participle that wrongly signals completed prior action and still breaks the series' form.

why_correct_md: Items in a series must share one grammatical form, and the first two items here are **-ing** phrases.
why_tempted_md: Adding 'they' feels natural in speech, so students overlook that it snaps the list into a mismatched independent clause.
rule_md: 1) Find the series and its conjunction. 2) Label the form of each item (noun, -ing phrase, infinitive, clause). 3) Make every item wear the same label as the first. 4) Re-read the list skipping the middle item to test the last against the first.

subject: act-english
context_html: Most first-time visitors picture Congaree National Park as a gloomy swamp. <u>Similarly,</u> the park is a floodplain forest that drains and refills as its river rises and falls.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: Signals similarity, but the second sentence corrects the first impression rather than resembling it.
per_choice_rationale.B: Claims the second sentence results from the first, yet no cause-effect link exists between an impression and the park's hydrology.
per_choice_rationale.C: Signals that the second sentence sets the record straight, which matches the correction of a mistaken picture.
per_choice_rationale.D: Promises an illustration, but the second sentence reclassifies the park instead of giving an instance of the swamp idea.

why_correct_md: The second sentence **corrects** a common misconception, so the transition must signal contradiction-plus-clarification.
why_tempted_md: 'Therefore' tempts readers who treat any logical connector as interchangeable glue between related sentences.
rule_md: 1) State each sentence's idea in five words. 2) Name the relationship: cause, contrast, example, addition, or correction. 3) Test the transition by substituting its plain meaning ('as a result,' 'likewise,' 'for instance'). 4) Keep only the transition whose meaning survives the substitution.

subject: act-english
context_html: Only a few hundred private cars win Denali's September road lottery each year. <u>Consequently,</u> the animals along the park road have never learned to fear traffic, and roadside sightings remain remarkably common.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correctly signals that scarce traffic causes the animals' indifference and the frequent sightings.
per_choice_rationale.B: Signals contrast, but the second sentence follows from the first rather than opposing it.
per_choice_rationale.C: Claims a restatement, yet the second sentence reports a new effect instead of rephrasing the lottery.
per_choice_rationale.D: Implies two simultaneous, unrelated happenings, ignoring the causal chain.

why_correct_md: Scarce traffic **causes** unwary wildlife, so a result-signaling transition is exactly right.
why_tempted_md: 'However' attracts students who sense surprise in animals ignoring cars and mistake surprise for contrast.
rule_md: 1) Paraphrase sentence one and sentence two. 2) Ask: does the second happen *because of* the first, *despite* it, or merely *alongside* it? 3) Match the transition to that exact relationship. 4) Re-read with your pick to confirm the logic clicks.

subject: act-english
context_html: Great Smoky Mountains National Park receives more visitors than any other national park, yet its maintenance budget is among the leanest per guest. Volunteer crews clear storm-downed trees, staff the visitor desks, and monitor backcountry campsites. Last year, these crews donated more than 400,000 hours of work.
stem_md: The writer wants to conclude the paragraph with a sentence that reinforces its main idea. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: The park's synchronous fireflies draw thousands of spectators every June.
Many national parks were established in the early twentieth century.
Such unpaid labor keeps the nation's busiest park running.
Visitors to the park should always pack rain gear before hiking.

per_choice_rationale.A: Introduces a new attraction instead of returning to the volunteers-versus-budget point.
per_choice_rationale.B: Zooms out to unrelated park-system history, abandoning the paragraph's focus entirely.
per_choice_rationale.C: Ties the volunteer hours back to the gap between heavy visitation and a thin budget—the paragraph's central idea.
per_choice_rationale.D: Offers practical advice that no sentence in the paragraph prepared.

why_correct_md: A strong conclusion **restates the paragraph's central tension**—huge crowds, small budget, volunteers filling the gap.
why_tempted_md: The firefly sentence stays inside the same park and sounds vivid, so students mistake topical proximity for relevance.
