rule_md: 1) Write the paragraph's main idea in one clause. 2) Test each closer: does it circle back to that clause? 3) Reject closers that add new topics, zoom too far out, or give unprepared advice. 4) Pick the one that echoes the opening tension.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Zion's shuttle system did not exist before 2000. [2] Back then, cars idled bumper to bumper along the canyon's only road, and overflow parking crushed fragile streamside ground. [3] Park managers responded by banning most private vehicles and running quiet propane buses instead. [4] Today, birdsong rather than engine noise fills the canyon. [5] The ban met fierce resistance from local businesses at first.
stem_md: The writer wants Sentence 5 placed where it will best preserve the paragraph's logical sequence of events. Where should Sentence 5 appear?

per_choice_rationale.A: Leaves the initial resistance dangling after the present-day payoff, scrambling the timeline.
per_choice_rationale.B: Inserts the reaction before either the problem or the ban has been described.
per_choice_rationale.C: Places resistance to a ban that has not yet been announced.
per_choice_rationale.D: Puts the reaction immediately after the ban it responds to and before the present-day result.

why_correct_md: 'At first' marks the sentence as the **immediate reaction to the ban**, so it belongs right after the ban is introduced.
why_tempted_md: Leaving the sentence where it is feels safe because it reads grammatically, even though the chronology breaks.
rule_md: 1) Find the moving sentence's time cues and pointing words ('the ban,' 'at first'). 2) Locate the sentence that introduces what those cues point to. 3) Place the mover directly after that anchor. 4) Re-read the paragraph in order to confirm the timeline runs one direction.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Carlsbad Caverns began as a limestone reef beneath an ancient inland sea. [2] Over millions of years, acidic groundwater hollowed the reef into chambers of astonishing size. [3] Today, though, the park is famous less for its geology than for its bats. [4] On summer evenings, hundreds of thousands of Brazilian free-tailed bats spiral out of the natural entrance. [5] Rangers run an amphitheater program so visitors can watch the nightly exodus.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide this paragraph into two paragraphs, each focused on a single subject. Beginning the second paragraph with which sentence best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: Splits the two geology sentences apart, stranding the opener as a one-sentence paragraph.
per_choice_rationale.B: Opens the new paragraph exactly where the topic pivots from geology to bats, with 'Today, though' signaling the shift.
per_choice_rationale.C: Strands the pivot sentence with the geology material it explicitly turns away from.
per_choice_rationale.D: Separates the amphitheater detail from the bat flight it depends on.

why_correct_md: Sentence 3 carries the **topic-shift signal** ('Today, though...') that turns from cave formation to bats.
why_tempted_md: Sentence 4 attracts students because it is the first sentence packed with bat imagery, but the pivot actually happens one sentence earlier.
rule_md: 1) Label each sentence's topic in one word. 2) Find where the label changes. 3) Check for a pivot cue (today, however, but) at that seam. 4) Start the new paragraph at the first sentence bearing the new label.

subject: act-english
context_html: Theodore Roosevelt<u>, an avid outdoorsman,</u> used the Antiquities Act of 1906 to protect Devils Tower as the first national monument.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correctly frames the nonessential appositive with a matched pair of commas.
per_choice_rationale.B: Opens the appositive with a comma but never closes it, leaving the interrupter half-fenced.
per_choice_rationale.C: Closes the appositive without opening it, running the name straight into the description.
per_choice_rationale.D: Mixes a dash with a comma—an unmatched pair that cannot fence a single interrupter.

why_correct_md: A nonessential appositive must be enclosed by a **matched pair** of commas, which the sentence already has.
why_tempted_md: The missing-second-comma version sounds identical when read aloud, so the ear cannot catch the unclosed fence.
rule_md: 1) Find the interrupter and read the sentence without it. 2) If the sentence survives, the interrupter is nonessential. 3) Fence it with a matched pair: two commas, two dashes, or two parentheses. 4) Never mix fence types around one interrupter.

subject: act-english
context_html: The air in Mammoth Cave stays near 54 <u>degrees, rangers</u> recommend a light jacket even in July.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Joins two complete sentences with only a comma, creating a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Fuses the two complete sentences with no punctuation at all.
per_choice_rationale.C: Piles a semicolon on top of a coordinating conjunction, doubling the connectors.
per_choice_rationale.D: Uses a semicolon alone—the correct weld between two closely related independent clauses.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses may be joined by a **semicolon standing alone**.
why_tempted_md: The comma splice sounds natural because speakers pause only briefly between the two statements.
rule_md: 1) Cover the punctuation and test each side: subject + verb + complete thought? 2) If both sides pass, a comma alone is illegal. 3) Join with a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. 4) Never stack a semicolon and a conjunction together.

subject: act-english
context_html: The quota system <u>which</u> limits raft launches on the Colorado River each day protects the canyon's famous quiet.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Uses 'which' without commas for a clause the sentence needs to identify its subject—restrictive clauses take 'that.'
per_choice_rationale.B: Adds one comma as if the clause were a removable aside, but the sentence needs the clause to say which system is meant, and the aside is never closed.
per_choice_rationale.C: Applies a pronoun reserved for people to a system.
per_choice_rationale.D: Introduces the identifying (restrictive) clause with 'that' and no comma, exactly as required.

why_correct_md: The clause **defines which system** is meant, so it is restrictive and takes 'that' with no comma.
why_tempted_md: 'Which' sounds more formal than 'that,' so students upgrade to it even where the clause is essential.
rule_md: 1) Delete the clause and re-read. 2) If the sentence loses its meaning or the noun turns vague, the clause is essential. 3) Essential clause: use 'that' with no commas. 4) Nonessential clause: use comma + 'which' + comma.

subject: act-english
context_html: By noon in July, the salt flats of Death Valley <u>get warm</u> beneath a cloudless sky.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize the extreme intensity of the desert heat. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Get warm' describes mild, pleasant heat, undercutting the intended extremity.
per_choice_rationale.B: Evokes oven-level heat in a single vivid verb, matching the writer's goal.
per_choice_rationale.C: Adds a pace but keeps the temperature mild.
per_choice_rationale.D: Abandons temperature altogether for a neutral image.

why_correct_md: The goal is **intensity**, and only one verb conveys punishing, oven-like heat.
why_tempted_md: 'Warm up steadily' feels more descriptive than the original, so students credit added words instead of added heat.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's stated goal in one word. 2) Rate each option against that word only. 3) Ignore which option sounds fanciest or longest. 4) Pick the option scoring highest on the goal, provided it stays grammatical.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each dawn at Katmai, the bear biologist <u>looks over</u> the overnight signals from the sows' tracking collars.
stem_md: The writer wants to portray the biologist as examining the data with painstaking care. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Looks over' implies a quick, casual skim—the opposite of painstaking care.
per_choice_rationale.B: Denotes close, critical, detail-by-detail examination, exactly the care the writer wants.
per_choice_rationale.C: Names a whole scholarly activity, far too broad for the daily act of reading collar signals.
per_choice_rationale.D: Reduces the examination to passive, incidental awareness.

why_correct_md: Only one verb specifically means **examining minutely and critically**.
why_tempted_md: 'Researches' sounds scientific and serious, so students equate professional flavor with careful attention.
rule_md: 1) Underline the goal's key qualities (here: care and thoroughness). 2) Define each verb candidate precisely. 3) Eliminate verbs that are too casual, too broad, or too passive for those qualities. 4) Keep the verb whose core meaning *is* the goal.

subject: act-english
context_html: Saguaro cactuses grow with almost comic slowness. A ten-year-old saguaro may stand barely two inches tall. At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence: Even at fifty, most have yet to sprout their first arm.
stem_md: Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it extends the paragraph's point about slow growth with a second vivid benchmark.
Yes, because it explains why saguaros grow so slowly.
No, because it contradicts the claim made in the preceding sentence.
No, because the paragraph focuses on desert animals rather than plants.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correctly identifies both the right decision and the right reason—the sentence adds a second age-based illustration of slowness.
per_choice_rationale.B: Reaches the right decision for a wrong reason: the sentence gives another example, not a cause.
per_choice_rationale.C: Misreads the sentence, which reinforces rather than contradicts the two-inch example.
per_choice_rationale.D: Misstates the paragraph's topic, which is plainly the cactus itself.

why_correct_md: The proposed sentence supplies a **second concrete benchmark** of slow growth, directly supporting the paragraph's point.
why_tempted_md: The 'explains why' justification tempts students who treat any added information as an explanation.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's point. 2) Ask whether the new sentence supports, contradicts, or ignores it. 3) Decide add or don't add. 4) Then vet the *reason*: it must describe what the sentence actually does, not merely reach the right verdict.

subject: act-english
context_html: Since 2017, the Everglades python elimination program has paid contractors to hunt invasive Burmese pythons. The snakes have devastated native mammals; marsh rabbits have all but vanished from parts of the park. One veteran contractor also competes in bass-fishing tournaments on weekends. Together, the hunters have removed more than 11,000 pythons. The writer is considering deleting the sentence in italics.
stem_md: Should the sentence in italics be kept or deleted?

choices.label: Deleted, because it repeats information stated earlier in the paragraph.
Deleted, because it shifts attention away from the program's results.
Kept, because it provides essential background on python biology.
Kept, because it creates a smooth transition to the removal total that follows.

per_choice_rationale.A: Reaches the right verdict with a false reason—no earlier sentence mentions the contractor's hobby.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correctly deletes and correctly explains: the hobby detail interrupts the line from problem to outcome.
per_choice_rationale.C: Misdescribes the sentence, which says nothing about python biology.
per_choice_rationale.D: Claims a transition, but weekend fishing has no logical link to the 11,000-python total.

why_correct_md: The italicized sentence is a **tangent**—it breaks the paragraph's thread from invasion problem to removal outcome.
why_tempted_md: The 'transition' justification tempts students because the sentence sits physically between two others, and position gets mistaken for function.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's through-line. 2) Ask what the target sentence contributes to it. 3) If nothing, delete. 4) Vet the stated reason: it must match what the sentence actually does or fails to do.

subject: act-english
context_html: What began in the 1930s as scattered nature clubs for campers' children slowly hardened into a curriculum: by the 1960s, individual parks were printing their own activity booklets. In the 1990s, the National Park Service standardized the Junior Ranger badge across the system, and today more than two hundred parks—plus an online version for children who have never set foot in a park—award it.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to trace how a single national park program developed over time. Would this passage accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it follows one program from informal beginnings to its standardized, nationwide present.
Yes, because it lists the specific activities children complete to earn the badge.
No, because it evaluates the program's educational effectiveness rather than its history.
No, because it describes several unrelated park programs rather than a single one.

per_choice_rationale.A: Accurately matches the passage's decade-by-decade arc of one program to the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.B: Reaches the right verdict on a false basis—the passage never lists any activities.
per_choice_rationale.C: Inverts the passage, which narrates history and offers no judgment of effectiveness.
per_choice_rationale.D: Miscounts the subject: clubs, booklets, and badge are stages of one program, not separate programs.

why_correct_md: The passage moves **chronologically through one program's stages**—exactly what the supposed goal demands.
why_tempted_md: The stages look different enough (clubs, booklets, badges) that students mistake one evolving program for several distinct ones.
rule_md: 1) Restate the supposed goal precisely (how many subjects? what kind of coverage?). 2) Outline what the passage actually does, decade by decade or point by point. 3) Compare outline to goal for both scope and type. 4) Pick the verdict whose reason matches your outline, not just the right yes or no.

subject: act-english
context_html: Hundreds of bison <u>graze</u> in Yellowstone's Lamar Valley on long summer evenings.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Keeps a finite main verb, so the sentence remains complete.
per_choice_rationale.B: Swaps the verb for a participle, leaving the subject with no main verb.
per_choice_rationale.C: Buries the only verb inside a relative clause, so nothing is left to complete the sentence.
per_choice_rationale.D: Replaces the verb with an infinitive, which cannot serve as a sentence's main verb.

why_correct_md: A sentence needs a **finite main verb**, and the original is the only version that provides one.
why_tempted_md: 'Grazing' paints an appealing picture and sounds fluid aloud, masking that it strands the subject.
rule_md: 1) Find the subject. 2) Ask: what does the subject *do*—is there a verb with tense? 3) Words ending in -ing or starting with 'to' don't count as main verbs by themselves. 4) If no tensed verb survives, it's a fragment—restore one.

subject: act-english
context_html: The fire lookout on Mount Harkness was built in <u>1933, and it</u> still shelters a volunteer spotter every summer.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Joins the two independent clauses correctly with a comma plus the coordinating conjunction 'and.'
per_choice_rationale.B: Drops the conjunction, leaving a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.C: Stacks a semicolon on the conjunction, doubling the join.
per_choice_rationale.D: Treats 'however' like a conjunction, but a conjunctive adverb set off by commas still leaves a splice.

why_correct_md: Comma **plus coordinating conjunction** is a legal weld between independent clauses—and it is already in place.
why_tempted_md: 'However' feels like a strong connector, so students assume it can legally join clauses with commas alone.
rule_md: 1) Confirm both sides are independent clauses. 2) Legal joins: period; semicolon; comma + FANBOYS. 3) Conjunctive adverbs (however, therefore) need a semicolon before them, not a comma. 4) Never combine a semicolon with a FANBOYS word.

subject: act-english
context_html: Haleakala's summit rises above the island's cloud <u>layer. Which</u> means sunrise visitors look down on a rolling sea of white.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Cuts the relative clause off as its own 'sentence,' creating a fragment.
per_choice_rationale.B: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and the 'which' clause is not one.
per_choice_rationale.C: Attaches the nonrestrictive 'which' clause to the main clause with a comma, as required.
per_choice_rationale.D: A colon cannot introduce a relative clause that leans back on the sentence.

why_correct_md: A 'which' clause is **dependent**—it must be attached to its sentence with a comma, not severed by end-stop punctuation.
why_tempted_md: The period version mimics a casual written style ('Which means...') common in blogs and texts, so it looks familiar.
rule_md: 1) Ask whether the words after the punctuation could stand alone as a sentence. 2) A clause beginning with a relative pronoun cannot. 3) Periods, semicolons, and colons all demand more independence than such a clause has. 4) Attach dependent add-ons with a comma.

subject: act-english
context_html: Paddling through Voyageurs' island channels at dusk, <u>loons startled the kayakers</u> at nearly every bend.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: the kayakers were startled by loons
loons were startling to the kayakers
the loons' cries startled the kayakers

per_choice_rationale.A: Makes the loons the paddlers—the opening modifier grabs the first noun after the comma.
per_choice_rationale.B: Places 'the kayakers,' the actual paddlers, right after the modifier, repairing the dangler.
per_choice_rationale.C: Keeps 'loons' in the modifier's grip, so the birds are still doing the paddling.
per_choice_rationale.D: Hands the paddling to the loons' cries, which is even less plausible.

why_correct_md: An introductory participial phrase must be followed **immediately by its true doer**—the kayakers.
why_tempted_md: The 'cries' version adds vivid detail while leaving the dangling structure untouched, so it feels like an upgrade.
rule_md: 1) Find the opening modifier and ask: who performs this action? 2) Check the first noun after the comma. 3) If doer and noun don't match, the modifier dangles. 4) Rewrite so the doer lands directly after the comma—even if that means the passive voice.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each January, Isle Royale's wolf-count team <u>collaborates together with</u> volunteer pilots to spot the island's packs from the air.
stem_md: Which choice best improves the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Together' repeats the togetherness already built into 'collaborates.'
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Jointly' duplicates the same built-in meaning in a dressier word.
per_choice_rationale.C: Trims to the verb alone, which already contains the idea of working together.
per_choice_rationale.D: Piles three redundant layers onto a single idea.

why_correct_md: The prefix in 'collaborates' already means together, so the verb alone is complete—**redundancy adds no meaning**.
why_tempted_md: 'Jointly' sounds technical and precise, so students read the duplication as added rigor.
rule_md: 1) Define the underlined verb: does its meaning already include the modifier's idea? 2) Delete any word restating that built-in meaning. 3) Re-read: if the sentence loses nothing, the deletion stands. 4) Prefer the tightest version that keeps the full meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: Rangers at Grand Teton close the cliff trail <u>due to the fact that</u> ice glazes the ledges each January.
stem_md: Which choice best improves the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Stretches one connecting idea across five words.
per_choice_rationale.B: Expresses the causal link in a single exact word.
per_choice_rationale.C: Swaps in an equally bloated five-word formula.
per_choice_rationale.D: Trades one wordy formula for another four-word one.

why_correct_md: One word can carry the causal link, and ACT style always prefers the **shortest grammatical option that preserves meaning**.
why_tempted_md: 'Due to the fact that' appears constantly in official-sounding writing, so it reads as extra formality rather than padding.
rule_md: 1) Identify the job the underlined phrase does (here: linking cause to effect). 2) Ask if a single word does the same job. 3) Substitute and re-read for meaning. 4) If nothing is lost, take the shorter version.

subject: act-english
context_html: At Rocky Mountain National Park, visitors should <u>basically just plan on trying to</u> reach the Bear Lake lot before eight in the morning.
stem_md: Which choice best improves the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Strings three fillers—'basically,' 'just,' and 'trying to'—around the real advice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Deletes some padding but keeps the empty qualifier 'basically.'
per_choice_rationale.C: Strips every filler, leaving the complete instruction.
per_choice_rationale.D: Trades one filler for another and keeps the casual idiom 'plan on.'

why_correct_md: 'Basically,' 'just,' and 'trying to' add **no information**—the bare instruction says everything.
why_tempted_md: Keeping 'basically' feels like preserving the sentence's easygoing tone rather than deleting dead weight.
rule_md: 1) Delete each qualifier one at a time. 2) After each deletion, ask: did any meaning vanish? 3) If not, the word was filler—leave it out. 4) Keep only words that change what the reader knows or must do.

subject: act-english
context_html: Dye tests at Wind Cave revealed how quickly rainwater <u>percolates</u> through fractured limestone into pools far below.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most precise word for this context?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Percolates' names precisely the slow filtering of water down through porous rock.
per_choice_rationale.B: Personifies the water as aimless, losing the downward-filtering precision.
per_choice_rationale.C: Names the wrong process entirely—turning to vapor, not sinking through stone.
per_choice_rationale.D: Is so generic it could describe traffic, saying nothing about filtering.

why_correct_md: The sentence needs the verb that specifically means **filtering downward through a porous medium**.
why_tempted_md: 'Evaporates' is a familiar science word about water, so it borrows unearned credibility.
rule_md: 1) Identify exactly what is happening physically. 2) Define each verb candidate. 3) Eliminate verbs that name a different process or are too vague to name any. 4) Keep the verb whose definition matches the physics.

subject: act-english
context_html: The restoration crew at Indiana Dunes <u>was totally psyched to</u> begin replanting marram grass along the storm-scoured foredunes.
stem_md: Which choice best matches the tone of the passage?

choices.label: was desirous of the opportunity to

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Totally psyched' is slang, clashing with the passage's reportorial register.
per_choice_rationale.B: Conveys the same enthusiasm in standard, register-neutral English.
per_choice_rationale.C: Replaces one slang phrase with another.
per_choice_rationale.D: Overcorrects into stilted, antique formality that sticks out as much as slang does.

why_correct_md: Formal prose needs a **standard-register** word for enthusiasm—neither slang nor starch.
why_tempted_md: The stiff, elaborate option sounds extra formal, and students often equate maximal formality with correctness.
rule_md: 1) Read the surrounding sentences and name the register (conversational, standard, academic). 2) Flag any option that is slang for that register—or costume-formal beyond it. 3) The right word should be invisible: same meaning, no register spike. 4) Re-read the sentence with your pick to confirm it blends in.

subject: act-english
context_html: Before cutting a single punch, a foundry apprentice spent years learning <u>to carving</u> letterforms in soft steel.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Learning to carving' mixes the infinitive marker 'to' with an -ing form; after 'to,' the base verb is required.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Learning carve' drops the infinitive marker that 'learning' needs before a following verb.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Learning to carve' correctly pairs the verb 'learning' with a to + base-verb infinitive.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'To have carved' adds a perfect form that wrongly places the carving before the years of learning.

why_correct_md: After **learning**, the following action takes a to + base-verb infinitive: 'learning to carve.'
why_tempted_md: 'To carving' sounds plausible because -ing verbs legitimately follow many other verbs, such as 'enjoy carving.'
rule_md: 1) Find the main verb and the second verb that follows it. 2) If the marker 'to' is present, the next verb must be the base form. 3) Test the pair alone: 'to' plus the base form should sound complete. 4) Reserve 'to have' plus a past participle for actions finished before the main verb. 5) Re-read the sentence with the corrected form.

subject: act-english
context_html: A foundry that lost <u>their</u> master matrices could not cast replacement type for its customers.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Their' is plural, but the antecedent 'a foundry' is singular.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'They're' is the contraction of 'they are,' which makes no sense before a noun here and is also plural.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'It's' means 'it is'; the sentence needs a possessive, not a contraction.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Its' is the singular possessive that matches the singular antecedent 'a foundry.'

why_correct_md: The singular antecedent **a foundry** requires the singular possessive form of the pronoun.
why_tempted_md: Students default to 'their' because everyday speech uses it for any owner, singular or plural.
rule_md: 1) Find the pronoun and ask what noun it stands for. 2) Decide whether that noun is singular or plural. 3) Match the pronoun's number to the noun's number. 4) If the pronoun shows ownership, expand any apostrophe form into two words and re-read to catch contraction traps. 5) Re-check the sentence with the matched pronoun.

subject: act-english
context_html: Composing a page by hand meant plucking each letter from its case, aligning it in the stick, and <u>to lock the finished lines</u> into a heavy iron chase.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

choices.label: to have locked the finished lines

per_choice_rationale.A: 'To lock' breaks the -ing pattern established by 'plucking' and 'aligning.'
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Locking' matches the -ing form of the other two items in the series.
per_choice_rationale.C: This passive clause abandons the list structure altogether, leaving the series unbalanced.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'To have locked' is both a non-matching infinitive and a perfect form that misorders the actions.

why_correct_md: Items in a series must share one grammatical shape; the third action must **match** 'plucking' and 'aligning.'
why_tempted_md: 'To lock' tempts because infinitives often express purpose, and securing the chase feels like the goal of the whole process.
rule_md: 1) Locate the series and list each item. 2) Label each item's form: -ing, infinitive, or clause. 3) Identify the form the first items establish. 4) Rewrite the odd item to copy that form exactly. 5) Re-read the full series to confirm the rhythm matches.

subject: act-english
context_html: At poster sizes, metal type was ruinously heavy and expensive to cast. <u>For example,</u> printers of the 1830s turned to letters sawn from close-grained wood.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'For example' promises an illustration of metal's heaviness or expense, but the second sentence gives an outcome instead.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'As a result' correctly signals that the switch to wood followed from metal's cost and weight.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Similarly' claims the two sentences make parallel points, but the second reacts to the first.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Meanwhile' implies two simultaneous, unrelated events, not a problem followed by its solution.

why_correct_md: The second sentence is the **consequence** of the first, so a cause-and-effect transition is required.
why_tempted_md: 'For example' attracts readers who see the specific 1830s detail as an illustration rather than an effect.
rule_md: 1) State the first sentence's idea in five words. 2) State the second sentence's idea in five words. 3) Name the logical relationship between them: cause, contrast, example, addition, or time. 4) Match the transition to that relationship. 5) Re-read with the chosen transition to confirm the logic clicks.

subject: act-english
context_html: A hand compositor who spotted a wrong letter could pluck it from the set line and drop in the correct sort within seconds. <u>Likewise,</u> a Linotype operator who caught an error had to melt down and recast the entire slug.
stem_md: Which transition word or phrase best fits at this point in the passage?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Likewise' asserts the two workflows match, but one fix takes seconds while the other requires recasting an entire line.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'By contrast' correctly frames the Linotype's laborious correction against the compositor's quick swap.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In fact' intensifies or confirms a prior claim, but the second sentence does not restate or sharpen the first.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'As a result' invents causation; the operator's burden was not caused by the compositor's ease.

why_correct_md: The sentences describe **opposite** correction workflows, so an opposition transition is required.
why_tempted_md: 'Likewise' lures readers who notice the parallel structure — two workers spotting errors — and miss that the outcomes diverge.
rule_md: 1) Identify the topic both sentences share. 2) Note what each sentence says about that topic. 3) Ask: same direction, opposite direction, cause, or emphasis? 4) Discard any transition whose direction disagrees with your answer. 5) Re-read the pair with the survivor to confirm the turn feels natural.

subject: act-english
context_html: Writing ink of the fifteenth century was water-based and flowed easily from a quill, but it beaded and smeared on metal type. Gutenberg's workshop instead blended lampblack with linseed varnish, producing a paste sticky enough to cling to each letter. The mixture transferred cleanly under pressure and dried to a durable sheen.
stem_md: The writer wants to add a sentence at the beginning of the paragraph that introduces its main idea. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Ink has been made from countless materials over the centuries.
Lampblack is a fine soot gathered from burning oil or resin.
Printing from metal type demanded an ink unlike any a scribe had ever used.
Gutenberg borrowed the screw mechanism of his press from local wine makers.

per_choice_rationale.A: This sentence is far broader than the paragraph, which concerns one specific formulation problem.
per_choice_rationale.B: This zooms in on a single ingredient before the paragraph has established why a new recipe was needed.
per_choice_rationale.C: This states the paragraph's controlling idea — a new craft required an entirely new ink — which every following sentence supports.
per_choice_rationale.D: The press's mechanics are a different subject; the paragraph never discusses machinery.

why_correct_md: The best introduction previews the paragraph's **controlling idea**, which each later sentence then develops.
why_tempted_md: The broad ink-history opener attracts students who equate 'introduction' with 'general background.'
rule_md: 1) Read the body sentences first and summarize their shared subject in one phrase. 2) Ask of each candidate: does it promise exactly that subject? 3) Reject candidates that are wider, narrower, or about something else. 4) Confirm the survivor lets the next sentence follow naturally. 5) Re-read the assembled paragraph from the top.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] In 1886, the New-York Tribune installed the first commercial Linotype machine. [2] Each keystroke released a small brass mold, called a matrix, from a magazine overhead. [3] When a line of molds was complete, the machine cast it in molten metal as a single fresh slug. [4] Finished slugs were then locked into page frames and hurried to the press.
stem_md: The writer wants to add the following true sentence to the paragraph: Its keyboard resembled a typewriter's, but each key summoned a mold rather than striking a letter onto paper. For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, the sentence should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Placed first, 'Its keyboard' has no machine to refer back to, leaving the pronoun stranded.
per_choice_rationale.B: After Sentence 1, 'Its' clearly refers to the newly introduced machine, and the keyboard description sets up the keystroke in Sentence 2.
per_choice_rationale.C: By Sentence 3 the paragraph has moved on to casting; doubling back to the keyboard breaks the process order.
per_choice_rationale.D: At the end, the keyboard detail trails the finished slugs, far from the keystroke it explains.

why_correct_md: The sentence must sit where its pronoun finds its noun and where it **sets up** the keystroke that follows.
why_tempted_md: The end position tempts students who treat added sentences as afterthoughts rather than links in a step-by-step process.
rule_md: 1) Find every pointer in the new sentence — pronouns, time words, repeated terms. 2) Locate the sentence each pointer needs to follow. 3) Locate the sentence the new material must come before, based on what it sets up. 4) The slot between those anchors is the placement. 5) Re-read the paragraph with the sentence inserted to confirm the chain of steps.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] For centuries, European paper was made one sheet at a time, as a vatman dipped a wire mold into a tub of beaten pulp. [2] Each sheet was then pressed, hung to dry, and inspected against the light. [3] The Fourdrinier machine, patented in 1806, replaced this rhythm with a continuous roll. [4] Pulp streamed onto a moving wire belt, shedding water as the belt traveled. [5] Within decades, a single machine could outproduce a hundred vatmen.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide this paragraph into two paragraphs, the first on handmade paper and the second on machine-made paper. The best place to begin the second paragraph is at:

per_choice_rationale.A: Sentence 3 introduces the machine, so the shift in topic — and the new paragraph — begins there.
per_choice_rationale.B: Sentence 2 continues describing handwork; splitting there strands half of the handmade process.
per_choice_rationale.C: Sentence 4 explains the machine introduced in Sentence 3; dividing there separates the machine from its own description.
per_choice_rationale.D: Sentence 5 gives the machine era's payoff; starting there leaves the machine's debut buried in the handmade paragraph.

why_correct_md: A new paragraph begins exactly where the **topic shifts** — here, at the first sentence about the machine.
why_tempted_md: Sentence 4 tempts readers who take the patent date in Sentence 3 as historical backdrop rather than the machine topic's true start.
rule_md: 1) Label each sentence with its topic in one or two words. 2) Find the first sentence whose label switches to the second topic. 3) Begin the new paragraph at that exact sentence. 4) Check that everything before the break belongs to topic one and everything after to topic two. 5) Re-read both halves for completeness.

subject: act-english
context_html: Claude Garamond<u>, a Parisian punch cutter,</u> designed romans so graceful that rival foundries copied them for two centuries.
stem_md: Which choice punctuates the sentence correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: The appositive 'a Parisian punch cutter' is nonessential, so it is correctly enclosed by a pair of commas.
per_choice_rationale.B: Dropping the second comma leaves the appositive open, fusing it into the main clause.
per_choice_rationale.C: Dropping the first comma runs the name straight into the description, with no signal that an aside has begun.
per_choice_rationale.D: Opening with a dash but closing with a comma mismatches the pair; interrupters need matching marks on both sides.

why_correct_md: A nonessential appositive must be **enclosed** by a matched pair of commas.
why_tempted_md: The single-comma versions tempt because each half sounds fine read quickly; only tracing both boundaries reveals the missing mark.
rule_md: 1) Find the interrupting phrase and cover it with a finger. 2) Confirm the sentence still works without it — that makes it nonessential. 3) Mark both boundaries of the interrupter. 4) Place matching punctuation at each boundary: two commas or two dashes, never one of each. 5) Re-read with and without the phrase.

subject: act-english
context_html: Movable metal type was not a European invention<u>; Korean printers cast bronze characters decades before Gutenberg</u> set his first line.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

choices.label: , Korean printers cast bronze characters decades before Gutenberg
Korean printers cast bronze characters decades before Gutenberg
; although Korean printers cast bronze characters decades before Gutenberg

per_choice_rationale.A: The semicolon correctly joins two complete, closely related statements.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma alone between two complete statements creates a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.C: No punctuation at all fuses the two statements into a run-on.
per_choice_rationale.D: Adding 'although' turns the second half into a subordinate clause, which cannot follow a semicolon.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses may be joined by a **semicolon** when their ideas are closely linked.
why_tempted_md: The comma version tempts because the pause feels natural in speech, masking that both halves are full sentences.
rule_md: 1) Cover the punctuation and read each half alone. 2) Ask whether each half has its own subject and verb and can stand alone. 3) If both stand alone, join them with a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. 4) If one half cannot stand alone, a semicolon is the wrong bridge. 5) Re-read the joined sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: A compositor's case held everything a line of verse required<u>: letters, spacers, and tied ligatures</u> sorted into little compartments.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

choices.label: , such as: letters, spacers, and tied ligatures

per_choice_rationale.A: A complete statement precedes the list, so the colon properly introduces it.
per_choice_rationale.B: A semicolon cannot introduce a list; it joins two complete statements.
per_choice_rationale.C: The comma after 'and' interrupts the final list item; no comma follows the conjunction in a series.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Such as' already introduces examples, so a colon after it is redundant and interrupts the phrase's flow.

why_correct_md: A colon may introduce a list only after a **complete** statement, which 'the case held everything a line of verse required' is.
why_tempted_md: The semicolon version tempts students who treat semicolons and colons as interchangeable 'strong' marks.
rule_md: 1) Read the words before the mark and ask whether they form a complete statement. 2) If yes, a colon may introduce the list that follows. 3) If the lead-in ends with a phrase like 'such as' or 'including,' use no mark at all. 4) Scan the list itself: commas between items, none after the final conjunction. 5) Re-read the whole sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: The dampened sheets were <u>whisper-thin</u>, so pressmen lifted each one with wooden tongs to keep it whole.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize how fragile the dampened paper was. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Whisper-thin' evokes near-weightless delicacy, directly serving the goal of emphasizing fragility.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Fairly thin' is a mild hedge that reports thickness without conveying fragility.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Not very thick' states a negative measurement and carries no sense of delicacy.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Inexpensive to produce' abandons the goal entirely, describing cost rather than fragility.

why_correct_md: The vivid compound most strongly conveys **fragility**, which is the writer's stated goal.
why_tempted_md: 'Fairly thin' tempts because it is factually consistent with the sentence, though it fails the emphasis goal.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's goal in your own words. 2) Test each candidate only against that goal, not against grammar. 3) Discard candidates that are merely accurate but flat. 4) Discard candidates that change the subject. 5) Keep the one that delivers the goal most forcefully, then re-read the sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: By 1890, the pressroom of a metropolitan daily <u>hummed</u> from dusk to dawn, and pressmen stuffed cotton in their ears against the din.
stem_md: The writer wants to convey that the presses were overwhelmingly, almost violently loud. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Hummed' suggests a soft, steady murmur — the opposite of overwhelming noise.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Thundered' delivers the crushing, room-shaking volume the writer wants, and it fits the detail about earplugs.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Clattered' conveys a busy rattling, but its light, tinny register falls short of violent loudness.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Operated' says nothing about sound at all, ignoring the goal.

why_correct_md: Only the most forceful verb matches the goal of **overwhelming** loudness and the earplug detail.
why_tempted_md: 'Clattered' tempts because it is genuinely noisy; the question is whether it reaches the violent intensity the goal specifies.
rule_md: 1) Underline the intensity words in the stated goal. 2) Rank the candidate verbs from softest to loudest. 3) Eliminate verbs below the goal's intensity, even if they are 'noisy.' 4) Check the survivor against nearby context clues. 5) Re-read the sentence for fit of tone.

subject: act-english
context_html: After each day's run, printers scrubbed their type with lye to strip away the sticky ink, then rinsed the letters in a trough. Type left dirty printed smudges instead of crisp strokes. Careful washing kept a font sharp through thousands of impressions.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the first sentence: Lye was also prized by launderers for whitening linen shirts. Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it explains why printers preferred lye to gentler cleansers.
Yes, because it offers a vivid glimpse of daily life inside a print shop.
No, because it repeats information provided elsewhere in the paragraph.
No, because it strays from the paragraph's focus on keeping type clean.

per_choice_rationale.A: The proposed sentence says nothing about why lye suited printers; it describes a different trade's use.
per_choice_rationale.B: The glimpse it offers is of laundry work, not of life inside a print shop.
per_choice_rationale.C: Nothing in the paragraph mentions launderers or shirts, so no repetition occurs.
per_choice_rationale.D: The sentence veers to laundry, an unrelated use of lye, so it does not belong in a paragraph about type upkeep.

why_correct_md: The addition fails the **relevance** test: it develops laundry, not the paragraph's subject.
why_tempted_md: The 'vivid detail' justification tempts because the image is concrete — but it is concrete about the wrong topic.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's subject in one phrase. 2) Ask whether the proposed sentence develops that subject. 3) If yes, pick the 'yes' reason that names its actual contribution. 4) If no, pick the 'no' reason that names its actual flaw. 5) Verify the chosen justification matches what the sentence really does.

subject: act-english
context_html: Aldus Manutius introduced italic type in 1501 so that more words could fit on a small page. His pocket-sized editions of the classics sold briskly across Europe. Within two years, a rival Lyonnaise workshop was counterfeiting the slanted letters so faithfully that Aldus petitioned the Venetian senate for protection.
stem_md: The writer is considering deleting the final sentence. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?

choices.label: Kept, because it shows that italic type quickly spread to readers in other countries.
Kept, because the rival's counterfeiting demonstrates how commercially valuable the new type had become.
Deleted, because it repeats the earlier point that the pocket editions sold briskly.
Deleted, because it interrupts the paragraph's account of how italic letters were designed.

per_choice_rationale.A: The rival was indeed abroad, but the sentence's point is imitation, not geographic spread — the previous sentence already covers sales across Europe.
per_choice_rationale.B: Counterfeiting is costly to attempt, so the rival's effort — and Aldus's plea for protection — proves the invention's commercial worth.
per_choice_rationale.C: Brisk sales and criminal imitation are different evidence; the sentence adds escalation, not repetition.
per_choice_rationale.D: The paragraph traces the invention's fortunes, not its design process, so no such account is interrupted.

why_correct_md: The final sentence supplies **evidence of worth** — imitation and a plea for protection — that no earlier sentence provides.
why_tempted_md: The 'spread to other countries' reading tempts because Lyon is indeed abroad, but that mistakes a detail of the sentence for its purpose.
rule_md: 1) State what the sentence in question uniquely contributes. 2) Ask whether any other sentence already does that job. 3) If the contribution is unique and on-topic, keep it. 4) Match your verdict to the justification that names the sentence's actual role. 5) Re-read the paragraph both with and without the sentence to confirm.

subject: act-english
context_html: Printers stored capital letters in an upper case mounted above the small letters' lower case, giving English 'uppercase' and 'lowercase.' The strips of lead once wedged between lines survive in 'leading,' the term designers still use for line spacing. Even 'out of sorts' may recall a compositor who had exhausted the pieces of type called sorts. Each phrase preserves a gesture from the composing room long after the room itself fell silent.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to show how the printing trade left lasting marks on ordinary English. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it identifies the individual printers who coined each term.
Yes, because it connects common expressions to the trade's physical objects and routines.
No, because it concerns page layout rather than the history of language.
No, because it discusses only vocabulary that professional typographers still use.

per_choice_rationale.A: The essay names no coiners; this 'yes' rests on evidence the essay never gives.
per_choice_rationale.B: The essay repeatedly ties everyday terms to concrete shop practice, exactly the mark-leaving the goal describes.
per_choice_rationale.C: Language history is the essay's whole subject; page layout is only the source domain of the terms.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Out of sorts' is everyday idiom, not professional jargon, so the essay reaches beyond specialists.

why_correct_md: The essay traces everyday terms to shop practice, which **fulfills** the stated goal directly.
why_tempted_md: The 'only professional vocabulary' objection tempts because 'leading' is indeed jargon; it takes the idiom example to defeat that reading.
rule_md: 1) Restate the hypothetical goal precisely. 2) List what the essay actually does, sentence by sentence. 3) Judge yes or no by matching the list to the goal. 4) Then vet the reason: a right verdict with a wrong reason is still wrong. 5) Confirm the chosen reason cites evidence actually present in the essay.

subject: act-english
context_html: Because oil-based ink dried slowly, <u>pressmen hung the printed sheets on ropes strung overhead</u>.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence grammatically complete?

choices.label: pressmen hanging the printed sheets on ropes strung overhead
the printed sheets hanging on ropes strung overhead
with the printed sheets hung on ropes strung overhead

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Pressmen hung' supplies a subject and a finite verb, completing the sentence that the 'Because' clause depends on.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Pressmen hanging' has no finite verb, leaving the opening clause attached to a fragment.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Sheets hanging' likewise lacks a finite verb; nothing in the sentence can stand alone.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'With...' is a prepositional phrase, so the sentence never gets a main clause at all.

why_correct_md: A sentence opening with a 'Because' clause must be completed by an **independent clause** with a finite verb.
why_tempted_md: The -ing versions tempt because they sound fluid aloud, disguising the missing finite verb.
rule_md: 1) Bracket the opening dependent clause. 2) Look at what remains and hunt for a subject plus a finite verb. 3) Remember that an -ing form or a 'with' phrase alone does not count as finite. 4) If no finite verb remains, the sentence is a fragment — repair it. 5) Re-read the whole sentence from the start.

subject: act-english
context_html: Type metal had to melt at an unusually low temperature<u>, otherwise the</u> brass matrices would wear out after a few castings.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: A comma before 'otherwise' leaves two complete statements joined by only a comma — a splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Adding a second comma decorates the splice without fixing it; the joint is still just a comma.
per_choice_rationale.C: Removing all punctuation fuses the two statements into a run-on.
per_choice_rationale.D: A semicolon before 'otherwise' properly separates the independent clauses, with a comma after the connecting adverb.

why_correct_md: Conjunctive adverbs like 'otherwise' need a **semicolon** (or period) before them when they join two complete statements.
why_tempted_md: The comma version tempts because 'otherwise' feels like a conjunction, but adverbs cannot glue clauses the way 'and' or 'but' can.
rule_md: 1) Test each side of the joint for a subject and finite verb. 2) If both sides stand alone, identify the joining word's part of speech. 3) A true coordinating conjunction may take a comma; a connecting adverb may not. 4) Before a connecting adverb, use a stronger stop, with a comma after the adverb. 5) Re-read the repaired sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: William Caslon knew buyers could not judge a typeface from loose letters<u> he therefore printed</u> broadside specimen sheets displaying every size he cast.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: With no punctuation, two complete statements are fused into a run-on.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma cannot join two independent clauses; 'therefore' is an adverb, not a conjunction, so this is a splice.
per_choice_rationale.C: A period ends the first complete statement and lets the second begin cleanly.
per_choice_rationale.D: After the semicolon, 'therefore printing' has no subject or finite verb — a fragment.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses need a full **boundary** — here a period cleanly separates them.
why_tempted_md: The comma version tempts because 'therefore' feels strong enough to carry the joint, but adverbs cannot join clauses.
rule_md: 1) Locate where one complete thought ends and another begins. 2) Check each side for its own subject and finite verb. 3) Join two independents only with a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. 4) Confirm any words after the mark still form a complete clause. 5) Re-read both statements.

subject: act-english
context_html: After inking the rollers by hand, <u>the first proof was pulled by the apprentice</u> so the master could judge the impression.
stem_md: Which choice best corrects the underlined portion?

choices.label: the apprentice pulled the first proof
the apprentice's first proof was pulled

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening phrase describes someone inking rollers, but this version makes 'the first proof' the doer — proofs cannot ink.
per_choice_rationale.B: Shortening the passive does not supply a doer; the modifier still dangles.
per_choice_rationale.C: This places the person who inked the rollers directly after the modifier, so the opener describes its true subject.
per_choice_rationale.D: A possessive is not a subject; the clause's subject is still 'proof,' so the opener still lacks its doer.

why_correct_md: An opening modifier must be followed immediately by the **doer** it describes.
why_tempted_md: The possessive version tempts because the person's title appears right after the comma, hiding that the true subject is still the proof.
rule_md: 1) Find the opening modifier and ask: who performs this action? 2) Look at the subject that follows the comma. 3) If the subject is not the performer, the modifier dangles. 4) Rewrite so the performer stands as the grammatical subject right after the comma. 5) Re-read to confirm the opener now describes its neighbor.

subject: act-english
context_html: Because every matrix was <u>reusable</u>, a foundry could cast thousands of identical letters from a single mold.
stem_md: Which choice is most effective and concise?

choices.label: reusable and could be used repeatedly

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Reusable' alone carries the full meaning; the sentence is already concise.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'More than once' merely restates what 'reusable' already means.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Could be used repeatedly' duplicates 'reusable' word for word in longer clothing.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Capable of repeated use' is a third way of saying 'reusable,' adding bulk but no information.

why_correct_md: Each longer version repeats the idea already inside 'reusable,' so the original is the only **non-redundant** choice.
why_tempted_md: The expansions tempt because extra phrasing feels more thorough, though it adds no new content.
rule_md: 1) Define the underlined word in plain terms. 2) Compare each added phrase against that definition. 3) Strike any phrase whose meaning is already inside the word. 4) Keep additions only if they contribute genuinely new information. 5) Re-read the leanest version to confirm nothing is lost.

subject: act-english
context_html: The museum's Albion handpress is <u>still in operation and continues to run</u> every Saturday afternoon.
stem_md: Which choice most concisely states the idea?

choices.label: in operation, and it continues to remain running,

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Continues to run' repeats what 'still in operation' already says.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'And running' still duplicates 'in operation' in a second form.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Still in operation' states the fact once, completely.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Continues to remain running' stacks three ways of saying the same thing.

why_correct_md: Everything beyond the single statement of the fact is **repetition**, so the leanest complete version wins.
why_tempted_md: The longer versions tempt because motion verbs feel more vivid than the plain statement.
rule_md: 1) Identify the core fact the span must convey. 2) Cross out any words that restate that fact a second time. 3) Read the shortest surviving version aloud for completeness. 4) If no meaning is missing, the shorter version wins. 5) Confirm grammar still holds.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Due to the fact that</u> wooden poster type swells in humid weather, printers stored it beside the stove.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most concise while preserving its meaning?

choices.label: In light of the fact that

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Due to the fact that' spends five words doing one word's job.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Because' delivers the causal link in a single word with no loss of meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In light of the fact that' is an even longer formula around the same simple link.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Being as how' is both wordy and nonstandard in written English.

why_correct_md: One exact word replaces the entire filler formula while keeping the **causal** link intact.
why_tempted_md: 'Due to the fact that' tempts because its formality sounds academic, though it adds only bulk.
rule_md: 1) Spot formula phrases built around 'the fact that.' 2) Ask what single word expresses the same link. 3) Substitute the single word and re-read. 4) If meaning and grammar hold, keep the substitution. 5) Scan the rest of the sentence for similar formulas.

subject: act-english
context_html: Without kerning, the letters 'A' and 'V' appear to <u>move</u> apart, opening an awkward gap in an otherwise even word.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely describes the visual effect?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Move' is generic; it names motion without capturing the slow, unintended visual separation.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Travel' implies purposeful journeying over distance, wrong for a static optical impression.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Drift' captures a gradual, unintended separation — precisely the optical effect of poor letter spacing.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Bolt' means to dash away suddenly, the opposite of a subtle spacing problem.

why_correct_md: The most **precise** verb matches the effect's character: gradual, unintended separation.
why_tempted_md: 'Move' tempts because it is safely accurate — but the question asks for precision, not mere accuracy.
rule_md: 1) Describe the intended effect in adjectives: sudden or slow? deliberate or accidental? 2) Test each verb against those adjectives. 3) Eliminate verbs too generic to commit. 4) Eliminate verbs whose specific flavor contradicts the effect. 5) Choose the verb whose connotation matches on every axis.

subject: act-english
context_html: Nineteenth-century foundries guarded their designs jealously; when a rival's new face sold well, competitors would <u>rip it off</u> within a season.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the formal tone of the passage?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Rip it off' is slang, clashing with the essay's formal historical register.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Jump on the bandwagon' is a colloquial idiom and also blurs the meaning from copying to mere trend-following.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Vibe' is casual contemporary slang, jarring in a sentence about the 1800s.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Imitate it closely' matches the formal register and states the action exactly.

why_correct_md: Formal prose requires the **standard-register** phrasing, which also preserves the precise meaning of copying.
why_tempted_md: 'Jump on the bandwagon' tempts because it is a familiar idiom for following success, but idioms of that stripe are conversational, not essayistic.
rule_md: 1) Establish the passage's register from its surrounding sentences. 2) Flag any candidate containing slang, casual idiom, or trendy diction. 3) Check that the surviving candidates preserve the original meaning. 4) Pick the one matching both register and meaning. 5) Re-read the sentence inside the paragraph to confirm the fit.

subject: act-english
context_html: Working alongside university partners, researchers at the observatory have <u>began</u> lowering rugged gas sensors directly into the steaming crater.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Uses the simple past form where the helping verb 'have' requires the past participle of this irregular verb.
per_choice_rationale.B: Pairs 'have' with an -ing form, which would need a form of 'be' ('are beginning'), not 'have.'
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: 'have' plus the past participle forms the present perfect.
per_choice_rationale.D: The bare base form cannot follow 'have' to build a perfect tense.

why_correct_md: **Have** must be followed by the past-participle form of the verb to build the present perfect.
why_tempted_md: The simple past form sounds natural on its own, so many students never test it against the helping verb *have*.
rule_md: 1) Find the helping verb (have/has/had). 2) Ask whether the next verb is in its past-participle form. 3) For irregular verbs, recite the three principal parts (base, past, participle). 4) Keep only the participle after have/has/had, then re-read the verb phrase to confirm.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each of the twelve solar-powered stations along the ridge transmits <u>their</u> readings to the observatory every ten seconds.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Their' is plural, but the true antecedent 'each' is singular, so the pronoun disagrees in number.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'It's' is the contraction of 'it is,' not a possessive, so it cannot show ownership of the readings.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a singular possessive pronoun matches the singular antecedent 'each.'
per_choice_rationale.D: 'They're' means 'they are' — a plural contraction, not a possessive of any kind.

why_correct_md: **Each** is grammatically singular, so the possessive pronoun referring to it must be singular.
why_tempted_md: The plural noun *stations* sits right beside the pronoun's slot, luring students into matching the nearest noun instead of the true antecedent *each*.
rule_md: 1) Find the pronoun and ask what it stands for. 2) Trace back to the true antecedent — with 'each of the X,' the antecedent is *each*, not X. 3) Decide singular or plural from that antecedent. 4) Separately test any apostrophe by expanding it ('it is' / 'they are') and re-reading the sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: Before raising the alert level, analysts confirm that tremor is intensifying, that the ground is swelling, and <u>gas output has risen</u>.
stem_md: Which choice best completes the series in the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: Drops the 'that' carried by the first two items in the series, breaking the parallel pattern of that-clauses.
per_choice_rationale.B: Substitutes an -ing phrase with no 'that' and no finite verb, so it is doubly non-parallel.
per_choice_rationale.C: Restores 'that' but leaves the clause without a complete finite verb, so it still cannot match the pattern.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it matches the series exactly — 'that' + subject + finite verb.

why_correct_md: The list is a series of **that**-clauses, so the final item must also be a *that*-clause with its own complete verb.
why_tempted_md: Dropping the final *that* sounds natural in casual speech, so the missing marker is easy to overlook after two long clauses.
rule_md: 1) Find the series and read each item in isolation. 2) Write down the pattern the first item sets (here: that + subject + verb). 3) Test every later item against that pattern slot by slot. 4) Fix the item that deviates, then re-read the whole series.

subject: act-english
context_html: A summit webcam records only what happens at the surface, in daylight and clear weather. <u>Similarly,</u> radar satellites can map a swelling flank through thick cloud and total darkness.
stem_md: Which transition word or phrase is most logical in context?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Similarly' claims the two tools work alike, but the second sentence stresses what the satellite can do that the webcam cannot.
per_choice_rationale.B: The satellite sentence is not an example or illustration of the webcam's limits.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the sentences set a limited tool against a more capable one, a relationship of difference.
per_choice_rationale.D: Nothing in the first sentence causes the satellite's abilities, so a result transition is illogical.

why_correct_md: The second sentence **opposes** the first — limits versus capabilities — so the transition must signal difference.
why_tempted_md: Both sentences describe monitoring tools, and that surface similarity makes a likeness transition feel safe.
rule_md: 1) State sentence 1's idea in five words. 2) State sentence 2's idea in five words. 3) Name the relationship: alike, example, cause, or opposed? 4) Match the transition to that named relationship, then re-read with your pick inserted.

subject: act-english
context_html: For three weeks, every instrument pointed to an eruption from the summit crater, and the observatory said so publicly. <u>Therefore,</u> the outbreak, when it finally came, tore open a fissure far down the volcano's northern flank.
stem_md: Which transition word best expresses the relationship between these two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Therefore' treats the flank eruption as the predicted outcome, but the eruption defied the summit forecast.
per_choice_rationale.B: The actual outbreak is not similar to the forecast; it departs from it.
per_choice_rationale.C: The second sentence does not restate the forecast in different words — it contradicts it.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: despite the confident forecast, the eruption broke the expectation, which calls for a concession.

why_correct_md: The eruption **defied** the forecast, so the transition must concede that the expected outcome failed to occur.
why_tempted_md: The first sentence builds a strong forecast, so a conclusion word feels like the natural payoff — until you notice the eruption happened in the wrong place.
rule_md: 1) Ask what the first sentence leads the reader to expect. 2) Ask whether the second sentence fulfills or breaks that expectation. 3) Fulfilled → result word; broken → concession word; restated → clarification word. 4) Insert your choice and re-read for logic.

subject: act-english
context_html: ____ When earthquakes multiply beneath the summit, the designation moves from green to yellow. If tremor becomes continuous and the flanks begin to swell, orange follows. Red is reserved for an eruption that is underway or expected within hours.
stem_md: The writer wants to open the paragraph with a sentence that introduces its main subject. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Observatories rank a volcano's restlessness on a four-color scale.
A four-color scale can never capture every nuance of a volcano's restlessness.
Observatories around the world watch volcanoes with a growing array of instruments.
Pilots depend on timely warnings whenever ash begins to rise.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: it names the color-coded ranking that the body then walks through level by level.
per_choice_rationale.B: Adopts a critical stance toward the scale that the explanatory paragraph never takes.
per_choice_rationale.C: Too broad — it gestures at monitoring in general and never mentions the ranking system.
per_choice_rationale.D: Previews only one late detail (aviation danger at the highest level) rather than the whole system.

why_correct_md: The body explains a **four-color ranking** step by step, and only this opener names that exact subject.
why_tempted_md: An opener about observatories and instruments sounds on-topic, but it never previews the ranking the paragraph actually explains.
rule_md: 1) Read the paragraph without its opener and name its subject in one phrase. 2) Check each candidate: does it name that subject? 3) Reject openers that argue a stance the body never takes, zoom out too far, or spotlight one detail. 4) Confirm the survivor lets every following sentence feel like an expansion of it.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Installing a seismometer on an active volcano begins long before anyone climbs the mountain. [2] Technicians first assemble and test each station indoors at the observatory. [3] They then pack the electronics into padded crates for the helicopter flight to the summit. [4] Once on site, the crew levels the sensor, buries it, and checks the radio link back to the observatory. [5] Every cable and connector is inspected twice during this indoor stage.
stem_md: For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, Sentence 5 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Leaves 'this indoor stage' pointing at outdoor summit work, a mismatch the reader trips over.
per_choice_rationale.B: Places the pointer phrase before any indoor work has been described, so it has no referent yet.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: it follows the sentence describing indoor assembly and testing, giving 'this indoor stage' a clear referent.
per_choice_rationale.D: Attaches the inspection to crate-packing and the flight rather than to the bench testing it describes.

why_correct_md: '**This indoor stage**' must directly follow the sentence that describes the indoor assembly and testing.
why_tempted_md: Packing can also happen indoors, so slotting the inspection after the packing sentence feels plausible until you ask when cables and connectors actually get checked.
rule_md: 1) Find the pointer words in the movable sentence ('this indoor stage'). 2) Ask which earlier sentence those words must refer to. 3) Place the movable sentence immediately after its referent. 4) Re-read the paragraph in the new order to confirm the timeline still runs start to finish.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] For most of the twentieth century, the observatory's records lived on paper. [2] Scientists inked each day's tremor onto smoked drums and filed the sheets in long rows of cabinets. [3] Retrieving a single week of records could swallow an entire afternoon. [4] Digital networks ended that era in the 1990s. [5] Today a researcher can pull up decades of waveforms in seconds and compare eruptions on opposite sides of the world.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide this paragraph into two paragraphs in order to separate its two main ideas. The best place to begin the new paragraph is at:

per_choice_rationale.A: Splits the paper era right after its topic sentence, stranding the details that support it.
per_choice_rationale.B: Separates the retrieval frustration from the paper filing system it complains about.
per_choice_rationale.C: Cuts the digital era in half, divorcing 'Today...' from the technological shift that produced it.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the arrival of digital networks begins the paragraph's second main idea.

why_correct_md: The paragraph's subject **turns** at the arrival of digital networks, so the second paragraph should begin there.
why_tempted_md: 'Today' sounds like a fresh start, tempting readers to break at the final sentence even though the digital era begins one sentence earlier.
rule_md: 1) Label each sentence with its idea in two or three words. 2) Find where the labels change subject. 3) Begin the new paragraph at the first sentence of the new subject. 4) Check both halves: each should read as one unified topic.

subject: act-english
context_html: Each morning the team's lead <u>scientist a specialist in volcanic gases,</u> reviews the overnight spectrometer readings before the daily briefing.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most effective punctuation?

choices.label: scientist, a specialist in volcanic gases
scientist a specialist in volcanic gases
scientist, a specialist in volcanic gases,

per_choice_rationale.A: Closes the appositive with a comma but never opens it — interrupters need punctuation on both sides.
per_choice_rationale.B: Opens the appositive but never closes it, letting the descriptive phrase crash into the main verb.
per_choice_rationale.C: Uses no commas at all, treating an extra, removable description as if it were essential.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: paired commas set off the nonessential appositive from the rest of the sentence.

why_correct_md: A nonessential appositive must be set off by a **pair** of commas — one before and one after.
why_tempted_md: Students often remember one comma of the pair and forget its partner, so a half-fenced appositive looks complete at a glance.
rule_md: 1) Find the interrupting phrase and try lifting it out of the sentence. 2) If the sentence still works, the phrase is nonessential. 3) Nonessential interrupters take punctuation on BOTH sides — count your commas. 4) Re-read with the phrase removed, then restored, to confirm the pair.

subject: act-english
context_html: Magma does not rise quietly<u>; it</u> cracks the surrounding rock and rattles distant sensors as it forces a path toward the surface.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English punctuation?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: a semicolon may join two closely related independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Because' turns the second statement into a subordinate clause left standing alone — a fragment.
per_choice_rationale.D: Removing all punctuation fuses two complete sentences into a run-on.

why_correct_md: A **semicolon** legally joins two related independent clauses, and both halves here can stand alone.
why_tempted_md: The clauses are short and tightly linked, so a comma feels sufficient — but brevity never licenses a splice.
rule_md: 1) Cover the punctuation and read each side: can both stand alone as sentences? 2) Two independent clauses need a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. 3) A comma alone = splice; nothing = fused. 4) If a subordinator is added, make sure the clause still attaches to a complete sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: After a decade of near silence, the duty analysts finally saw the signal they had been waiting <u>for: harmonic</u> tremor, a steady seismic hum that often precedes an eruption.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: a colon after a complete clause formally introduces the long-awaited signal.
per_choice_rationale.B: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but what follows is only a noun phrase.
per_choice_rationale.C: A comma weakly splices the naming phrase onto 'waiting for' and blurs the boundary of the reveal.
per_choice_rationale.D: With no mark at all, the naming phrase has no grammatical seat and collides with the clause.

why_correct_md: A **colon** may follow a complete clause to introduce the thing just promised — here, the awaited signal.
why_tempted_md: Semicolons and colons look interchangeable before a big reveal, but only one of them tolerates a mere phrase on its right side.
rule_md: 1) Check what's left of the mark: is it a complete sentence? 2) Check what's right: a list, name, or explanation (it need not be a clause)? 3) Complete clause + reveal → colon works. 4) Remember a semicolon needs full clauses on both sides, and a comma can't splice an object onto a preposition; re-test the sentence with each rule.

subject: act-english
context_html: Within minutes of the first blast, the ash column <u>went</u> ten kilometers into the sky, forcing controllers to reroute every flight in the region.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize how fast the ash column climbed. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Went' states motion without any sense of speed, so it cannot emphasize a rapid climb.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it conveys explosive upward speed, exactly the quality the writer wants stressed.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Drifted' implies slow, aimless motion — the opposite of the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Extended' is neutral and gradual, adding no urgency to the climb.

why_correct_md: Only this verb's **connotation** of explosive speed accomplishes the writer's stated goal.
why_tempted_md: The original verb is grammatically fine, tempting students who forget that the question is about the stated goal, not correctness.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's goal in your own words. 2) Ask of each verb: does it, by itself, carry that quality? 3) Eliminate verbs that are merely correct but neutral, then verbs that contradict the goal. 4) Keep the one whose connotation does the goal's work.

subject: act-english
context_html: Asked at the press conference whether the volcano would erupt within the month, the observatory's director <u>refused to guess</u>.
stem_md: The writer wants to portray the director as measured and professional rather than evasive. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Refused to guess' carries a blunt, stubborn edge that tilts the portrait toward uncooperative.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Kept dodging' openly paints the director as evasive — the very impression to avoid.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: it conveys courteous, disciplined restraint grounded in scientific caution.
per_choice_rationale.D: Total silence reads as stonewalling or concealment, not measured professionalism.

why_correct_md: The goal calls for **connotation** work: only this phrasing sounds courteous and disciplined rather than stubborn, slippery, or secretive.
why_tempted_md: The original sits closest to the key in meaning, and 'guess' even hints at scientific caution, but 'refused' carries a blunt, uncooperative edge.
rule_md: 1) Write down the two impressions in play (careful professional vs. evasive official). 2) For each phrase, list its connotations — blunt, courteous, secretive, cautious. 3) Discard any phrase whose connotation feeds the unwanted impression. 4) Choose the phrase whose every word supports the wanted impression.

subject: act-english
context_html: Gas sensors on the crater rim sample the volcano's breath around the clock. Rising magma releases dissolved gases long before it reaches the surface, so a shift in the plume's chemistry can be the earliest sign of trouble.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the last sentence of the paragraph: "At one closely watched volcano, sulfur dioxide output tripled in the week before fresh lava appeared." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it supplies a specific case of the early warning the paragraph describes.
Yes, because it explains how the gas sensors were installed on the rim.
No, because the paragraph has already given a specific case of a chemical warning.
No, because it shifts the paragraph's focus from gas chemistry to lava hazards.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the sentence grounds the paragraph's general claim in one concrete, striking instance.
per_choice_rationale.B: Reaches the right verdict for a false reason — the sentence says nothing about installation.
