per_choice_rationale.C: False — the paragraph so far speaks only in general terms, with no concrete instance.
per_choice_rationale.D: False — lava appears only as the endpoint proving the chemical warning came early.

why_correct_md: The sentence **illustrates** the paragraph's claim that chemistry shifts warn early, so it belongs — and this reason names that contribution accurately.
why_tempted_md: The word 'lava' makes the sentence look off-topic at a glance, so the focus-shift objection attracts hasty readers.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's claim in one line. 2) Ask what the proposed sentence contributes: proof, illustration, digression, or repetition? 3) Match the yes/no verdict to that contribution. 4) Then vet the stated reason: it must describe the sentence accurately, not just reach the right verdict.

subject: act-english
context_html: Acoustic flow monitors stand watch along the river valleys that drain the volcano's upper slopes. When a lahar — a fast-moving slurry of ash and meltwater — sweeps down a channel, its ground vibrations trigger an automatic alarm. One member of the team also leads popular weekend birdwatching hikes in the lower valley. Sirens in the towns below then give residents precious minutes to reach higher ground.
stem_md: The writer is considering deleting the sentence about weekend birdwatching hikes. Should the sentence be deleted?

choices.label: No, because it offers a detail that supports the paragraph's claim about the alarm's reliability.
No, because it provides a transition between the alarm and the sirens.
Yes, because it interrupts the description of the warning system with a detail unrelated to it.
Yes, because the description of the warning system belongs earlier in the essay.

per_choice_rationale.A: False — a colleague's weekend hobby says nothing about whether the alarm works.
per_choice_rationale.B: False — the sentence touches neither the alarm before it nor the sirens after it, so it bridges nothing.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the hobby detail breaks the vibration-alarm-siren chain and serves no purpose in it.
per_choice_rationale.D: Votes to delete for a false reason — the problem is relevance, not the placement of the system description.

why_correct_md: The sentence is a **digression**: it halts the vibration-alarm-siren sequence with material that serves no purpose in the paragraph.
why_tempted_md: One wrong option also votes to delete, so students who sense the problem may grab it without vetting whether its reason describes the actual flaw.
rule_md: 1) Summarize the paragraph's through-line in one phrase. 2) Ask whether the sentence advances that line. 3) If not, it should go — but 4) verify the stated reason: it must accurately name what the sentence does to the paragraph.

subject: act-english
context_html: Bolted to bedrock on the volcano's flank, a tiltmeter senses changes in slope as slight as the lift of a coin under a kilometer-long beam. When magma pushes upward, the flank leans outward by fractions of a degree, and the instrument logs every shift. During the last period of unrest, those readings let scientists trace the swelling, week by week, from a single silent point on the mountain.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to provide an overview of the full range of instruments scientists use to monitor volcanoes. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it describes in detail how a single station is used during a period of unrest.
No, because it focuses on a single instrument instead of covering the range of tools the goal describes.
No, because the essay never explains the range of readings the instrument can record.
Yes, because focusing on one well-chosen tool is an effective way to meet the goal.

per_choice_rationale.A: Accurately describes the essay but ignores that the goal demands breadth across instruments.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the goal asks for a survey of the whole toolkit, and the essay offers depth on exactly one device.
per_choice_rationale.C: Reaches the right verdict for the wrong reason — the shortfall is breadth across devices, not missing detail about this one.
per_choice_rationale.D: Rationalizes depth as a substitute for the overview the goal explicitly requires.

why_correct_md: The goal demands **breadth** — a survey of many instruments — while the essay offers depth on exactly one.
why_tempted_md: Everything the tempting 'yes' says about the essay is true, which hides the fact that the goal asked for a different scope.
rule_md: 1) Underline the scope words in the stated goal (overview, full range). 2) Summarize the essay's actual scope in one phrase. 3) Compare the two scopes: match → yes; mismatch → no. 4) Then check the reason: it must name the actual match or mismatch, not some other feature.

subject: act-english
context_html: A sparse network of microphones listens for <u>infrasound. Which travels</u> hundreds of kilometers through the atmosphere and can betray an eruption at a peak no one is watching.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: The period strands a 'which' clause on its own — a fragment with no independent clause.
per_choice_rationale.B: A semicolon, like a period, must be followed by an independent clause, and a 'which' clause is not one.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a comma attaches the nonrestrictive relative clause to the noun it describes.
per_choice_rationale.D: After the period there is still no subject or finite main verb — the fragment survives in new clothes.

why_correct_md: A relative clause cannot stand alone; a **comma** must attach it to the noun it modifies.
why_tempted_md: Swapping the period for a semicolon feels like a fix, but a semicolon carries the very same requirement the period does.
rule_md: 1) Read what follows each end-stop as if it were alone: subject? finite verb? complete thought? 2) A clause beginning with a relative pronoun can't stand alone. 3) Attach dependent add-ons to the noun they describe with a comma. 4) Re-read the joined sentence to confirm one complete main clause remains.

subject: act-english
context_html: The alarm from the tremor network sounded at 3 a.m.<u>, the</u> duty scientist reached the control room within four minutes.
stem_md: Which choice best corrects the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma form a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Therefore' is a conjunctive adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so the splice remains.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a comma plus the coordinating conjunction legally joins the two clauses.
per_choice_rationale.D: Deleting the comma fuses the two complete sentences with nothing between them.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses may be joined by a comma **plus a coordinating conjunction** — that pairing repairs the splice.
why_tempted_md: 'Therefore' feels like a connector, but it is an adverb, and with only a comma in front of it the splice survives.
rule_md: 1) Confirm both sides of the boundary are independent clauses. 2) Legal joins: period; semicolon; comma + FANBOYS conjunction. 3) Remember that words like 'therefore' and 'however' are adverbs — with only a comma they still splice. 4) Apply one legal join and re-read.

subject: act-english
context_html: By dawn the tremor beneath the summit had faded<u>; the</u> gas plume, however, kept thickening above the crater.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: a semicolon joins the two related independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Because' makes the second clause dependent, and a semicolon cannot be followed by a lone dependent clause; it also asserts a causal link the sentences don't support.
per_choice_rationale.D: With no punctuation, the two complete sentences fuse into a run-on.

why_correct_md: Both halves are **independent clauses**, and a semicolon is a legal join between closely related ones.
why_tempted_md: The interrupter 'however' tucked inside the second clause tricks readers into thinking a comma boundary is enough at the main seam.
rule_md: 1) Find the boundary and test both sides for independence. 2) Independent + independent → period, semicolon, or comma + coordinating conjunction. 3) Don't let a mid-clause interrupter like 'however' distract you from the main seam. 4) If a subordinator is added, confirm the clause pair still forms one grammatical sentence with sound logic.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Flying low over the churning lava lake, the intense heat forced the drone to climb</u> to a safer altitude before its cameras could finish mapping the vent.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: Flying low over the churning lava lake, the drone was forced by the intense heat to climb
The intense heat, flying low over the churning lava lake, forced the drone to climb
Flying low over the churning lava lake, it was the intense heat that forced the drone to climb

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening modifier dangles — it describes the drone, but 'the intense heat' occupies the subject slot.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the flyer, the drone, immediately follows the modifier that describes it.
per_choice_rationale.C: Relocates the modifier next to 'heat,' absurdly making the heat the thing that flies.
per_choice_rationale.D: The expletive 'it' still leaves the modifier with no true actor beside it — the dangler survives in disguise.

why_correct_md: An opening participial phrase must be followed **immediately** by the noun it describes — here, the machine that was flying.
why_tempted_md: Rearranging words feels like a repair, and 'it was the intense heat' sounds emphatic and formal, but the modifier still lacks its true actor.
rule_md: 1) Find the opening -ing modifier and ask: who or what performs this action? 2) Check the first noun after the comma — it must be that performer. 3) If it isn't, rewrite so the doer lands right after the comma (or give the modifier its own subject). 4) Re-read: the sentence should answer 'who was doing this?' instantly.

subject: act-english
context_html: After recalibrating the spectrometer, the chemists <u>revised</u> their estimate of the volcano's daily gas output.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most concise while preserving its meaning?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: one precise verb does the whole job.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Updated' merely repeats what 'revised' already says.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Went back and' adds nothing — revising an earlier estimate already implies returning to it.
per_choice_rationale.D: Doubles the redundancy and buries the action in weak noun phrases.

why_correct_md: One **precise verb** already carries the complete meaning; every alternative repeats it in extra words.
why_tempted_md: Pairing near-synonyms sounds thorough and official, so the doubled verbs feel like an upgrade rather than a repeat.
rule_md: 1) Circle the underlined words and ask what each adds. 2) Cut any word restating another's meaning; cut any phrase already implied by the main verb. 3) Prefer one exact verb over a noun-heavy paraphrase. 4) Re-read: if the meaning is untouched after a cut, the cut was right.

subject: act-english
context_html: The alert level can change <u>in a very rapid manner</u> once fresh magma reaches shallow depths beneath the crater floor.
stem_md: Which choice most concisely expresses the idea?

choices.label: at a rapid rate of speed

per_choice_rationale.A: Five words stand where a single adverb serves.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: one adverb delivers the full meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: Trims a little but keeps the wordy 'in a ___ way' scaffold.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Rate of speed' is internally redundant on top of the wordy frame.

why_correct_md: A single **adverb** replaces the entire prepositional scaffold with no loss of meaning.
why_tempted_md: The mid-length option looks trimmed compared with the original, so it feels like the concise pick even though the scaffold remains.
rule_md: 1) Ask what single word the whole phrase is standing in for. 2) Replace 'in a ___ manner/way' constructions with the matching adverb. 3) Check the survivors for internal redundancy. 4) Choose the shortest version that keeps the exact meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: The observatory<u>, as a matter of fact,</u> publishes every change in the alert level within minutes of the decision.
stem_md: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.label: , as it happens to be the case,

per_choice_rationale.A: 'As a matter of fact' asserts no contrast or emphasis the sentence needs — it is pure filler.
per_choice_rationale.B: Swaps one filler phrase for its twin, leaving the padding in place.
per_choice_rationale.C: Replaces the filler with an even wordier version of the same empty phrase.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the sentence is complete and stronger without the interrupter.

why_correct_md: The interrupter is **empty filler**: removing it changes nothing, so it should not stay in the sentence.
why_tempted_md: The phrase sounds authoritative, as if it strengthens the claim, so students keep it for its official ring.
rule_md: 1) Read the sentence without the underlined phrase. 2) Ask: did any meaning, emphasis, or logic disappear? 3) If nothing disappeared, the phrase is filler — cut it rather than replace it. 4) If something did disappear, choose the shortest phrase that restores it.

subject: act-english
context_html: Modern seismometers can <u>detect</u> ground movements far too faint for anyone standing on the volcano to feel.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most precise word for the context?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: this is the precise term for an instrument registering a faint signal.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Notice' implies casual human awareness, the wrong register for a machine's sensitivity.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Witness' implies seeing an event happen, not registering an imperceptible signal.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Uncover' implies revealing something hidden through investigation, not sensing in real time.

why_correct_md: The sentence needs the **technical** verb for an instrument registering signals below human perception.
why_tempted_md: In everyday speech we casually 'notice' small things, so that verb feels natural even though machines don't have casual awareness.
rule_md: 1) Identify the subject doing the action (person or instrument?). 2) List each verb's built-in scenario: casual awareness, eyewitnessing, investigative revealing, instrumental sensing. 3) Match the scenario to the sentence's actual situation. 4) Keep the verb whose connotation fits the subject and object exactly.

subject: act-english
context_html: When the tremor spiked just after midnight, the overnight crew <u>totally freaked out and</u> alerted civil-defense officials in the towns below.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the tone and style of the passage?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Totally freaked out' is slang that clashes with the passage's formal, factual register.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Seriously rattled' softens the slang but remains conversational rather than formal.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Hit the panic button' is an idiom too casual for the context, and it adds panic the facts don't state.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: formal and factual, it keeps the focus on the crew's swift official response.

why_correct_md: **Register** governs here: a factual report calls for neutral wording that centers the swift official response, not dramatized emotion.
why_tempted_md: The softened idiom sheds the most obvious slang and can masquerade as a formal revision while staying conversational at its core.
rule_md: 1) Identify the passage's register (formal report vs. casual talk). 2) Flag underlined idioms or slang that belong to the other register. 3) Prefer wording that states the verifiable action, not dramatized emotion. 4) Re-read the revised sentence in the passage's voice to confirm the tone matches.

subject: act-english
context_html: Even after passing the written exam, many interpreting students stay committed <u>to master</u> the facial grammar that gives American Sign Language much of its meaning.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Treats 'to' as the start of an infinitive, but in the idiom 'committed to,' the word 'to' is a preposition and must be followed by a gerund.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — after the preposition 'to' in 'committed to,' the verb takes the gerund form.
per_choice_rationale.C: The perfect infinitive wrongly suggests the mastering was completed before the commitment and still misreads 'to' as an infinitive marker.
per_choice_rationale.D: Swaps in a preposition that does not form a standard idiom with 'committed.'

why_correct_md: In **committed to**, the word 'to' is a preposition, so the verb that follows must be a gerund.
why_tempted_md: 'To master' sounds natural because 'to + base verb' is the most familiar verb pattern in English.
rule_md: 1) Find the expression before the verb (here, *committed to*). 2) Test whether *to* is a preposition by placing a noun after it: *committed to excellence* works, so *to* is a preposition. 3) A preposition takes the noun form of a verb — the -ing form. 4) Reject any option that treats *to* as an infinitive marker or that swaps the idiom's preposition.

subject: act-english
context_html: Under clinic policy, each on-call interpreter must confirm <u>their</u> assignment with the nursing station an hour before the shift begins.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Their' is plural, but the antecedent 'each on-call interpreter' is grammatically singular, so the pronoun and antecedent disagree in number.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — it matches the singular antecedent 'each ... interpreter' in number and refers to a person.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'One's' abandons the sentence's third-person reference to 'each interpreter' and shifts to an impersonal pronoun.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Its' is singular but refers to things, not to a person such as an interpreter.

why_correct_md: The antecedent **each ... interpreter** is singular, so the pronoun must be singular and personal.
why_tempted_md: 'Their' sounds natural in speech, so students miss that 'each' makes the antecedent singular under ACT conventions.
rule_md: 1) Circle the pronoun and draw an arrow to its antecedent. 2) Check the antecedent's number — words like *each*, *every*, and *neither* are singular. 3) Match the pronoun in number. 4) Then match it in kind: personal pronouns for people, *it/its* for things.

subject: act-english
context_html: A seasoned theater interpreter spends the month before opening night analyzing the script for wordplay, <u>attends</u> rehearsals to absorb each actor's timing, and building a signed translation that mirrors the production's rhythm.
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Attends' is a finite verb, but the series pairs it with the -ing forms 'analyzing' and 'building,' breaking parallel structure.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — it matches the -ing forms 'analyzing' and 'building,' making all three items in the series parallel.
per_choice_rationale.C: The infinitive 'to attend' is grammatical on its own but still fails to match the two -ing items in the series.
per_choice_rationale.D: Inserting 'she attends' turns the second item into an independent clause, which cannot sit in a series of -ing phrases.

why_correct_md: All three items in the series must share the same **-ing** form, matching 'analyzing' and 'building.'
why_tempted_md: 'Attends' agrees with the subject 'interpreter,' so it sounds fine until the whole list is read as a unit.
rule_md: 1) Find the series and bracket each item. 2) Label the grammatical form of the items before and after the underlined one. 3) Force the underlined item into that same form. 4) Reread the whole list aloud to confirm every item now starts the same way.

subject: act-english
context_html: Video relay services let Deaf callers conduct business by phone through an on-screen interpreter, and the connection takes only seconds to establish. <u>Likewise,</u> the system has limits: an interpreter unfamiliar with a caller's regional signs can slow a conversation considerably.
stem_md: Which transition provides the most logical connection between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Likewise' signals that a similar point is coming, but the second sentence pivots from the service's strengths to its limits.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — the passage turns from praise to criticism, so a contrast word is needed.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For instance' promises an example of the previous claim, but the sentence introduces an opposing point instead.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Consequently' claims the limits result from the fast connection, a cause-effect link the passage never makes.

why_correct_md: The passage shifts from an advantage to a drawback, so the transition must signal **contrast**.
why_tempted_md: 'Consequently' tempts readers who feel any flow between sentences must be cause and effect.
rule_md: 1) State the point of the sentence before the transition in five words. 2) State the point of the sentence after it in five words. 3) Name the relationship: same-direction, contrast, example, or cause-effect. 4) Pick the transition that names that exact relationship, and reject any that name a different one.

subject: act-english
context_html: Silent-era film clubs recorded dozens of Deaf lecturers so that distant audiences could watch celebrated signers. <u>Indeed,</u> several regional signs from the 1910s survive today only because those reels were preserved in university archives.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition in context?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — the second sentence intensifies and confirms the first, exactly the emphasis 'indeed' signals.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'On the other hand' announces a contrast, but the second sentence extends the first rather than opposing it.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In the meantime' imposes a simultaneous-time frame the sentences do not share; the second spans a century of preservation.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Granted' concedes a point to an opposing argument, but no counterargument follows.

why_correct_md: The second sentence **reinforces** the first with a stronger, more specific claim, which is what 'indeed' signals.
why_tempted_md: 'Granted' attracts readers who sense the second sentence qualifies the first, though it actually amplifies it.
rule_md: 1) Compress each sentence to its core claim. 2) Ask whether the second claim opposes, exemplifies, results from, or intensifies the first. 3) Match the transition to that relationship. 4) Confirm by deleting the transition: the surviving logic should equal the relationship you named.

subject: act-english
context_html: ____. During a full-day conference, an interpreter's arms may repeat the same motions thousands of times, and researchers have measured injury rates comparable to those of assembly-line workers. To protect themselves, professionals work in pairs, trading the active role every twenty to thirty minutes. Many also follow stretching regimens borrowed from athletic trainers.
stem_md: The writer wants an opening sentence that frames the paragraph's focus on the occupational strain of interpreting. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Interpreting may look effortless from the seats, but it taxes the body like an athletic event.
Interpreting requires years of coursework, mentorship, and supervised practice.
Sign languages differ from country to country, and even from city to city.
Conference interpreters usually earn more per hour than staff interpreters at schools.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — it names the physical toll directly, setting up the injury statistics, paired staffing, and stretching routines that follow.
per_choice_rationale.B: Focuses on training and credentials, which the paragraph never discusses.
per_choice_rationale.C: Raises language variation across regions, a topic unrelated to the paragraph's details.
per_choice_rationale.D: Introduces pay differences, which none of the following sentences address.

why_correct_md: The opener must preview the paragraph's actual content — **bodily strain** and how interpreters manage it.
why_tempted_md: The training option feels relevant because credentials often open essays about professions, but no later sentence supports it.
rule_md: 1) Read every sentence after the blank and list their shared subject in two or three words. 2) Turn that subject into a promise an opening sentence should make. 3) Test each option against the promise: does the rest of the paragraph deliver it? 4) Eliminate any opener whose promise the paragraph never keeps.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] The national certification exam for interpreters unfolds in two stages. [2] Candidates first sit for a written test covering ethics, linguistics, and Deaf history. [3] Those who pass advance to a filmed performance exam, interpreting recorded scenarios under time pressure. [4] Raters then score each film for accuracy, clarity, and professional judgment. [5] Because scoring can take several months, many candidates spend the wait working under a mentor's supervision.
stem_md: The writer wants the paragraph to present the certification process in the order a candidate would experience it. To accomplish that goal, Sentence 5 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — the wait for scores follows the rating stage described in Sentence 4, so the sentence belongs at the end of the sequence.
per_choice_rationale.B: Placing the scoring delay first would describe the end of the process before the exam has even been introduced.
per_choice_rationale.C: After Sentence 2, candidates have only taken the written test; no films exist yet to be scored.
per_choice_rationale.D: After Sentence 3, the films have been made but the rating step has not yet been described, so a delay in scoring would refer to nothing.

why_correct_md: Sentence 5's 'scoring can take several months' depends on the **rating step** in Sentence 4, so it must follow that step.
why_tempted_md: Placing it after Sentence 3 tempts readers because films are mentioned there, but scoring has not yet entered the narrative at that point.
rule_md: 1) Find the time or process cues in the movable sentence. 2) Identify what earlier information those cues depend on. 3) Place the sentence immediately after its dependency. 4) Reread the paragraph in order to confirm no step is referenced before it happens.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] For decades, television news reached Deaf viewers only through captions typed minutes behind the broadcast. [2] Captions also flattened tone, rendering an anchor's urgency and a weathercaster's reassurance in identical block letters. [3] Emergency coverage suffered most, since evacuation orders scrolled past faster than many viewers could absorb them. [4] Complaints about the delays filled station mailrooms after every major storm. [5] In the 1990s, several stations began placing live interpreters in an on-screen box during emergencies. [6] The interpreters could match the urgency of the moment, and viewers finally received warnings in real time.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide this paragraph into two paragraphs, so that the second paragraph focuses on the shift to on-screen interpreters. The best place to begin the new paragraph is at the start of Sentence:

per_choice_rationale.A: Sentence 2 continues describing captioning's weaknesses, the first paragraph's topic.
per_choice_rationale.B: Sentence 3 is still about captioned broadcasts and their delays, not about interpreters.
per_choice_rationale.C: Sentence 4 wraps up the complaints about captions, so it belongs with the first topic.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — Sentence 5 introduces the on-screen interpreters, the shift the second paragraph should feature.

why_correct_md: The break belongs where the topic turns — Sentence 5 is the **first** sentence about on-screen interpreters.
why_tempted_md: Sentence 4 tempts readers because the complaints feel like a new note, but they still concern captioning.
rule_md: 1) Label each sentence with a two-word topic tag. 2) Find where the tags switch from the first subject to the second. 3) Start the new paragraph at the first sentence of the new subject. 4) Verify: everything before the break shares topic one; everything after shares topic two.

subject: act-english
context_html: The workshop <u>leader, a certified Deaf interpreter</u> demonstrated how to voice a signed poem without flattening its rhythm.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most effective punctuation?

per_choice_rationale.A: Opens the appositive with a comma but never closes it, leaving the interrupter half-fenced.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — the appositive 'a certified Deaf interpreter' is extra information and needs a comma on both sides.
per_choice_rationale.C: Removing both commas fuses the appositive to the sentence as if it were essential to identifying the leader.
per_choice_rationale.D: A semicolon cannot close an appositive; semicolons separate independent clauses, and 'demonstrated how...' is not one.

why_correct_md: A nonessential appositive must be fenced by a **pair** of commas, one before and one after.
why_tempted_md: The single opening comma looks sufficient because readers pause there naturally and forget the interrupter must be closed.
rule_md: 1) Find the renaming phrase and cover it with your finger. 2) If the sentence still works, the phrase is nonessential. 3) Fence nonessential phrases with matching punctuation on both sides — two commas or two dashes. 4) Never mix a comma on one side with different punctuation on the other.

subject: act-english
context_html: Courtroom interpreters must render testimony exactly as it is spoken<u>, accuracy</u> in this setting can decide the outcome of a trial.
stem_md: Which choice results in a correctly punctuated sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Adding 'indeed' between commas does not fix the splice — conjunctive adverbs are not conjunctions.
per_choice_rationale.C: Deleting the comma fuses the two independent clauses together with no boundary at all.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — a semicolon legally joins two closely related independent clauses.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses need a **semicolon**, a period, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction — a bare comma is a splice.
why_tempted_md: The interrupter 'indeed' feels like glue, but a conjunctive adverb never licenses a comma to join clauses.
rule_md: 1) Cover the punctuation and read each side: can both stand alone as sentences? 2) If yes, a bare comma is illegal. 3) Legal joiners: semicolon; period; comma + FANBOYS conjunction. 4) Test the chosen option against that list before committing.

subject: act-english
context_html: Every gig bag she packs for an assignment holds <u>three essentials, a</u> water bottle, plain dark clothing, and a backup pair of glasses.
stem_md: Which choice provides the most effective punctuation of the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: A comma after 'essentials' buries the list in a string of commas, hiding where the announcement ends and the list begins.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — 'Every gig bag ... holds three essentials' is a complete clause, so a colon may introduce the list it announces.
per_choice_rationale.C: A semicolon must join two independent clauses; 'a water bottle...' is a list, not a clause.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Such as' flows into its examples and never takes a colon; the phrase also clashes with the exact count 'three.'

why_correct_md: A **colon** may introduce a list only after a complete independent clause, which 'Every gig bag she packs ... holds three essentials' is.
why_tempted_md: The semicolon looks like a strong list-introducer, but its job is joining clauses, not announcing items.
rule_md: 1) Read the words before the candidate mark: do they form a complete sentence? 2) If yes and a list or explanation follows, a colon fits. 3) Reject a semicolon unless a full clause follows too. 4) Never place a colon after 'such as,' 'including,' or a verb that flows directly into the list.

subject: act-english
context_html: As the valedictorian's speech sped up, the interpreter's hands <u>darted</u> through the fingerspelled names of a dozen scholarship donors.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize the quickness of the interpreter's movements. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — 'darted' conveys quick, agile motion, matching the speeding speech.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Moved' is generic and conveys no speed at all.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Worked' suggests effort, not quickness.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Proceeded' sounds slow and formal, the opposite of the intended emphasis.

why_correct_md: '**Darted**' is the only option whose core meaning contains speed and agility.
why_tempted_md: 'Worked' tempts readers because the hands are indeed working hard, but effort is not the stated goal.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's stated goal in one word (here: speed). 2) Test each option: does its dictionary meaning contain that idea? 3) Cut every option that is merely neutral or generic. 4) Keep the choice whose connotation delivers the goal on its own, without help from context.

subject: act-english
context_html: Support for a campus interpreting program <u>appeared</u> over three semesters, one persuaded administrator and one signed petition at a time.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize how gradually the program won support. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Appeared' marks that support existed but says nothing about a slow, additive build.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Materialized' suggests support popped into being, if anything implying suddenness.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Surfaced' implies hidden support becoming visible, not support growing bit by bit.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — it denotes piling up increment by increment, matching 'one administrator ... at a time.'

why_correct_md: Only a verb meaning **built up piece by piece** matches the sentence's one-at-a-time details.
why_tempted_md: 'Surfaced' tempts readers because emerging support feels gradual, yet the verb describes visibility, not growth.
rule_md: 1) Convert the stated goal into a test phrase (here: 'bit by bit over time'). 2) Ask of each verb: does its core meaning include that increment-by-increment sense? 3) Use the sentence's own details ('one ... at a time') as the tiebreaker. 4) Keep the verb the details could literally describe.

subject: act-english
context_html: Educational interpreters do more than translate lectures. They place themselves so a student can watch the teacher's demonstrations and the signed message in a single glance. During a chemistry lab, an interpreter may even stand beside the fume hood so the student never looks away from a live reaction.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the second sentence: "In one middle school, an interpreter moved her stool six times in a single class period to stay inside the student's sight line." Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it explains why schools began hiring interpreters with special training.
Yes, because it gives a specific example of an interpreter adjusting her position for a student.
No, because it repeats the chemistry-lab example in the very next sentence.
No, because it shifts attention away from the student and onto the interpreter.

per_choice_rationale.A: The anecdote says nothing about hiring or training; it depicts positioning during a single class.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — it supplies a vivid, concrete case of the positioning strategy the previous sentence describes in general terms.
per_choice_rationale.C: The stool anecdote and the chemistry-lab sentence describe different settings and details, so nothing is repeated.
per_choice_rationale.D: The anecdote exists to show the interpreter serving the student's sight line, so the student remains the focus.

why_correct_md: The sentence turns a general claim about positioning into a **concrete case**, which strengthens the paragraph.
why_tempted_md: Readers who see two examples of similar behavior often cry repetition, though the anecdotes differ in setting and detail.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's claim at the insertion point. 2) Ask: does the new sentence support, repeat, or derail that claim? 3) Supporting details add new specifics; repetition adds none. 4) Accept the addition only when the option's 'because' clause accurately describes what the sentence does.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Shadow interpreting places the interpreter onstage, moving in step with the actor she voices. [2] The approach demands weeks of blocking rehearsals so that the interpreter never masks a key gesture. [3] Directors who have staged it this way report that Deaf patrons follow plot twists without ever glancing away from the action. [4] Traditional placement, by contrast, parks the interpreter at the stage's edge beneath a small spotlight.
stem_md: The writer is considering deleting Sentence 3. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?

choices.label: Kept, because it names the directors who first staged a shadow-interpreted production.
Kept, because it reports a payoff of the technique for the Deaf patrons it is intended to reach.
Deleted, because it interrupts the paragraph's account of rehearsal schedules.
Deleted, because the reactions of Deaf patrons have little to do with the technique being described.

per_choice_rationale.A: Sentence 3 mentions unnamed directors' observations; it never identifies who pioneered the staging.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — it supplies the paragraph's only proof that shadow staging achieves its purpose for Deaf theatergoers.
per_choice_rationale.C: Only Sentence 2 concerns rehearsals; Sentence 3 turns to results, so nothing about schedules is interrupted.
per_choice_rationale.D: How Deaf patrons experience the show is the whole point of the staging, not a side issue.

why_correct_md: Sentence 3 is the paragraph's only **support** showing the staging works, so cutting it would leave the claim unproven.
why_tempted_md: The rehearsal option tempts readers who assume any sentence between two related sentences must be an interruption.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's main claim. 2) Ask what the target sentence contributes: proof, detail, or detour? 3) If it is the only support for the claim, keep it. 4) Accept a keep/delete option only when its 'because' reason matches that contribution exactly.

subject: act-english
context_html: My grandmother's kitchen table was my first classroom. There she drilled me on fingerspelling until my knuckles ached, corrected the slope of my signing space, and told stories about the Deaf club she helped found in 1968. Years later, when I raised my right hand to take the interpreter's oath, I could still feel that table's worn oak beneath my wrists.
stem_md: Suppose the writer's goal had been to provide an overview of the certification process for sign language interpreters. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.label: Yes, because it ends with the writer taking the interpreter's oath after years of preparation.
No, because it is a personal tribute to a single teacher rather than a survey of certification requirements.
No, because the essay shows that the writer never completed the certification process.
Yes, because the grandmother's lessons at the table cover each stage of the certification process.

per_choice_rationale.A: One closing image of the oath does not amount to an overview; no exam, rating, or requirement is ever explained.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — the essay honors a formative figure through memory and detail; it never outlines how certification works.
per_choice_rationale.C: The essay states the writer took the interpreter's oath, so the claim that certification was never completed contradicts the text.
per_choice_rationale.D: The lessons named — fingerspelling drills, signing space, club stories — are family teaching, not stages of any formal process.

why_correct_md: An overview would explain the **process**; this essay instead lingers on memory, gratitude, and a formative figure.
why_tempted_md: The oath in the final sentence tempts readers to count the essay as process writing, though the process itself is never described.
rule_md: 1) Restate the hypothetical goal as a checklist of content it would require. 2) Scan the essay for each checklist item. 3) Decide yes/no from coverage, not from a lone matching detail. 4) Then verify the option's 'because' clause states a fact the essay actually supports.

subject: act-english
context_html: Because the stadium's video-board interpreter needed a clear line of sight to the podium<u>. She</u> worked from a raised platform beside the sound booth.
stem_md: Which choice results in a complete, grammatically correct sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: The period strands 'Because ... podium' as a fragment — a dependent clause punctuated as a sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: A semicolon, like a period, requires an independent clause on each side; the 'Because' clause cannot stand alone.
per_choice_rationale.C: Adding 'Therefore' dresses up the second sentence but leaves the opening fragment untouched.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — a comma joins the introductory dependent clause to the main clause, completing the sentence.

why_correct_md: A clause beginning with **because** is dependent; it must attach to a main clause with a comma, not stand alone.
why_tempted_md: The semicolon feels like a compromise between period and comma, but it carries the same full-clause requirement as a period.
rule_md: 1) Underline the subordinating word at the start (because, although, when...). 2) That clause cannot end with a period or semicolon on its own. 3) Attach it to the neighboring main clause with a comma. 4) Reread from the capital letter to confirm one complete sentence remains.

subject: act-english
context_html: Demand for video relay interpreting has soared over the past decade<u>, the</u> national centers now schedule staff in overlapping around-the-clock shifts.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Consequently' is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction, so the clauses remain illegally spliced.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct — a period cleanly separates the two independent clauses into two sentences.
per_choice_rationale.D: Removing the comma fuses the clauses with no boundary at all.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses can be separated by a **period**; a bare comma or no mark at all cannot join them.
why_tempted_md: 'Consequently' seems to supply the missing connection, but adverbs cannot legally join clauses across a comma.
rule_md: 1) Test each side of the underlined punctuation as its own sentence. 2) If both pass, a bare comma is a splice. 3) List legal fixes: period, semicolon, or comma plus a FANBOYS word. 4) Match the options against the legal list and eliminate everything else.

subject: act-english
context_html: The platform interpreter wrapped up the keynote at noon<u>, then</u> she debriefed with the sound crew about the afternoon panels.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Then' is an adverb, not a conjunction, so a comma before it splices the two independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.B: Wrapping 'then' in commas adds a pause but leaves the same illegal splice in place.
per_choice_rationale.C: Dropping the comma fuses the clauses together with no boundary at all.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — a semicolon can join the two independent clauses, with 'then' acting as an adverb in the second.

why_correct_md: Because 'then' is **not** a coordinating conjunction, the clauses need a semicolon (or period) at the seam.
why_tempted_md: 'Then' feels like 'and then,' so students treat comma-plus-'then' as a legal joint between clauses.
rule_md: 1) Verify each side of the seam is an independent clause. 2) Ask whether the joining word is one of the seven FANBOYS. 3) 'Then,' 'however,' and 'therefore' are adverbs — they need a semicolon or period before them. 4) Keep the option whose punctuation, not its adverb, does the joining.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Signing at a furious pace, the audience struggled to follow the interpreter's poetry-slam rendition.</u>
stem_md: Which choice best conforms to the conventions of standard English?

choices.label: Signing at a furious pace, the interpreter's poetry-slam rendition confused the audience.
The audience, signing at a furious pace, struggled to follow the interpreter.
Signing at a furious pace, the interpreter delivered a poetry-slam rendition that the audience struggled to follow.

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening modifier attaches to 'the audience,' absurdly claiming the audience was doing the signing.
per_choice_rationale.B: A possessive cannot anchor the modifier; 'the interpreter's rendition' makes the rendition itself the signer.
per_choice_rationale.C: Moving the modifier next to 'audience' now states outright that the audience signed at a furious pace.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct — the doer of 'signing,' the interpreter, immediately follows the modifier.

why_correct_md: An opening participial phrase must be followed **immediately** by the noun performing its action — here, the person signing.
why_tempted_md: The possessive version tempts students because 'interpreter's' appears right after the comma, though the actual subject is 'rendition.'
rule_md: 1) Bracket the opening -ing phrase. 2) Ask: who performs that action? 3) The very first noun after the comma must be that performer — possessives don't count. 4) Reject any version whose post-comma subject could not logically do the action.

subject: act-english
context_html: To stay accurate during the eight-hour deposition, the two interpreters <u>alternated back and forth</u> every quarter hour.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most concise without changing its meaning?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Back and forth' restates what 'alternated' already means, creating redundancy.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — 'alternated' alone carries the full meaning of switching repeatedly.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In turn' duplicates the idea of alternation just as 'back and forth' does.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Took turns alternating' doubles the idea twice over — taking turns is alternating.

why_correct_md: 'Alternated' already means switched **by turns**, so any added phrase repeats it.
why_tempted_md: 'Back and forth' feels like helpful detail because the rhythm of switching is easy to picture.
rule_md: 1) Define the underlined verb in your own words. 2) Compare each added phrase to that definition. 3) Cut any phrase whose meaning the verb already contains. 4) Keep the shortest version that loses no information.

subject: act-english
context_html: The referral agency <u>screens</u> every freelance interpreter before adding a name to its on-call roster.
stem_md: Which choice expresses the idea most concisely while preserving the meaning?

choices.label: engages in the process of screening
makes it a point to screen

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — 'screens' delivers the full meaning in one word.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Conducts a screening of' swaps a crisp verb for a noun-heavy phrase with no added meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Engages in the process of' is pure filler wrapped around the same action.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Makes it a point to' adds words about intention without changing what happens.

why_correct_md: The single verb already says everything; every alternative pads it with **empty** words.
why_tempted_md: 'Conducts a screening of' sounds official, and students often equate formality with correctness.
rule_md: 1) Find the core action of the underlined portion. 2) For each option, cross out words that add no new information. 3) Whatever survives should match the core action. 4) Keep the version with zero crossed-out words.

subject: act-english
context_html: Agencies <u>generally</u> assign interpreters in pairs for any event scheduled to run longer than an hour.
stem_md: Which choice best expresses the idea clearly and without unnecessary words?

choices.label: as a general rule of thumb,

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — 'generally' states the qualification in a single precise word.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'In most cases, generally' says the same thing twice.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'As a general rule of thumb' swells one word into a five-word cliché with no gain.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'For all intents and purposes' is filler that means 'effectively,' not 'usually,' so it also distorts the meaning.

why_correct_md: One well-chosen adverb does the work; the alternatives add **filler** or blur the meaning.
why_tempted_md: The rule-of-thumb phrase sounds folksy and authoritative, so its bulk feels like substance.
rule_md: 1) Identify the qualification the sentence needs (how often? how sure?). 2) Ask whether each option states that qualification once, twice, or not at all. 3) Strike doubled or off-target qualifiers. 4) Keep the version that qualifies the claim exactly once, in the fewest words.

subject: act-english
context_html: At the board meeting's midpoint, the staff interpreter <u>condensed</u> an hour of debate into a two-minute signed summary for members arriving late.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely conveys how the interpreter handled the debate?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct — 'condensed' means compressed while keeping the essential content, exactly what a summary does.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Shrank' implies mere reduction in size, saying nothing about preserving the substance.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Deflated' connotes losing air or importance, an unwanted negative shade.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Abbreviated' suits shortening words or events, not distilling content into a summary.

why_correct_md: '**Condensed**' uniquely captures compressing material while retaining its essence.
why_tempted_md: 'Abbreviated' tempts because it also means shortened, but it lacks the sense of keeping the substance intact.
rule_md: 1) State exactly what the sentence's action requires (here: shorter but nothing essential lost). 2) List each option's core connotation. 3) Eliminate options that change size only, add a negative shade, or fit a different object. 4) Keep the word whose full connotation matches the requirement.

subject: act-english
context_html: When the panel discussion ran past its scheduled hour, the support interpreter <u>tagged in</u> so her partner could rest her hands.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the essay's consistent, professional tone?

choices.label: commenced the performance of her interpreting duties

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Tagged in' borrows wrestling slang, too casual for the essay's professional register.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Jumped into the mix' is even chattier slang, drifting further from the essay's tone.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct — plain, neutral phrasing that matches a professional description without stiffness.
per_choice_rationale.D: The stiff, legalistic pile-up of nouns overcorrects into pompous wording no natural essay would use.

why_correct_md: The essay's voice is professional but plain, so the replacement must be **neutral** — neither slang nor ceremony.
why_tempted_md: The formal-sounding option lures students who assume the fanciest phrasing is always the safest fix.
rule_md: 1) Read two neighboring sentences and label the passage's register (casual, neutral, formal). 2) Label each option's register the same way. 3) Eliminate both extremes: slang and stuffiness. 4) Keep the option matching the passage's label, at natural sentence length.

subject: act-english
context_html: By the time the doors opened on Saturday morning, the volunteers <u>had already began sorting</u> a mountain of weekend donations.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Uses the simple past *began* where the past-perfect construction requires the past participle *begun*.
per_choice_rationale.B: Supplies the right participle but shifts to present perfect, which clashes with the past-time frame set by 'By the time the doors opened.'
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: past perfect *had* plus the past participle *begun* places the sorting before the doors opened.
per_choice_rationale.D: Keeps the wrong participle *began* and swaps the natural gerund for an infinitive, so the verb form is still broken.

why_correct_md: After the helping verb *had*, the verb must take its **past participle** form, which for this verb is *begun*.
why_tempted_md: *Began* sounds familiar as a past tense, so pairing it with *had* feels natural even though the participle is required.
rule_md: 1) Find the helping verb (had/has/have). 2) A helping verb demands the past participle, not the simple past. 3) Recite the trio for the verb (begin-began-begun). 4) Check that the tense matches the sentence's time frame. 5) Pick the option that satisfies both.

subject: act-english
context_html: Every one of the donated appliances is tested and tagged before <u>they are</u> placed on the sales floor.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Matches the pronoun to the nearby plural *appliances* instead of the singular subject *Every one*.
per_choice_rationale.B: Doubles the error: plural pronoun plus a past-tense verb in a sentence describing a routine, present-time process.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the antecedent *Every one* is singular, and the present tense matches the habitual testing routine.
per_choice_rationale.D: Gets the singular pronoun right but shifts to past tense, breaking the sentence's present-time description.

why_correct_md: The true antecedent is the singular **Every one**, so the pronoun must be singular and stay in the present tense.
why_tempted_md: The plural noun *appliances* sits right before the pronoun, luring the ear toward a plural match.
rule_md: 1) Find the pronoun. 2) Ask exactly which noun it stands for — not the closest noun, the logical one. 3) Strip prepositional phrases like 'of the donated appliances.' 4) Match the pronoun's number to that antecedent. 5) Confirm the verb tense matches the rest of the sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: The manager credits the shop's longevity to three habits: pricing donations the day they arrive, rotating window displays before shoppers tire of them, and <u>tracking which sections outsell the rest</u>.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the grammatical pattern of the sentence?

choices.label: to track which sections outsell the rest
she tracks which sections outsell the rest
the tracking of which sections outsell the rest

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the third habit stays a gerund phrase, matching *pricing* and *rotating*.
per_choice_rationale.B: Switches the final item to an infinitive, breaking the gerund pattern of the first two habits.
per_choice_rationale.C: Turns the final item into a full clause, which cannot sit in a list of gerund phrases.
per_choice_rationale.D: Swaps in a heavy noun phrase, abandoning the -ing pattern and adding clutter.

why_correct_md: Items in a series must share one grammatical form, and this list is built on **gerund** (-ing) phrases.
why_tempted_md: An infinitive feels like a natural way to name a habit, so the shift away from -ing is easy to miss at the end of a long list.
rule_md: 1) Find the list. 2) Label the grammatical form of the first item. 3) Check that every later item wears the same form. 4) Reject any option that changes form, even if it sounds fine alone. 5) Prefer the version that keeps the pattern intact.

subject: act-english
context_html: Donations surge every January as households clear out their closets. <u>As a result,</u> the back room often overflows before the month is half over.
stem_md: Which transition provides the most logical link between these sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the overflowing back room is a direct consequence of the January surge, so a cause-effect transition fits.
per_choice_rationale.B: Signals contrast, but the second sentence follows from the first rather than opposing it.
per_choice_rationale.C: Promises an illustration, but the second sentence states an effect, not an example of the surge.
per_choice_rationale.D: Suggests two unrelated events unfolding at the same time, missing the causal link.

why_correct_md: The second sentence is the **effect** of the first, so the transition must signal cause and result.
why_tempted_md: Both sentences do happen in the same season, so a time-based connector can feel plausible at a glance.
rule_md: 1) Read the sentence before and after the transition. 2) State the relationship in your own words (cause? opposite? example? time?). 3) Match that relationship to the transition's job. 4) Reject any connector whose job doesn't match. 5) Re-read with your pick inserted.

subject: act-english
context_html: The shop's vintage denim sells within hours of reaching the rack. <u>Therefore,</u> the board games can sit untouched for a year.
stem_md: Which transition best fits the logic of these sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: Treats the second sentence as a conclusion drawn from the first, but slow-selling games do not follow logically from fast-selling denim.
per_choice_rationale.B: Signals similarity, yet the two sentences describe opposite sales fates.
per_choice_rationale.C: Claims the second sentence restates the first, but it introduces entirely new, opposing information.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the sentences set fast-moving denim against stagnant board games, a relationship of direct opposition.

why_correct_md: The sentences pit one item's quick sales against another's slow sales, so the transition must signal **opposition**.
why_tempted_md: Both sentences discuss how merchandise sells, and that surface continuity makes a cause-effect or similarity word feel harmless.
rule_md: 1) Summarize each sentence in five words. 2) Ask whether the second continues, opposes, restates, or results from the first. 3) Name the job of each transition option. 4) Keep only the option whose job matches your step-2 answer. 5) Re-read the pair to confirm.

subject: act-english
context_html: When the mill closed in 2009, Harper's Bend lost its only department store. The thrift shop that moved into the empty storefront now hosts a repair café on Saturdays, and retirees teach teenagers to patch jeans and rewire lamps. Neighbors linger in the aisles long after their purchases are rung up.
stem_md: The writer wants a concluding sentence that reinforces the paragraph's main idea about what the shop provides for Harper's Bend. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: The mill's machinery was eventually sold to a factory two states away.
Thrift shopping has grown steadily more popular across the country in recent years.
The shop also sells used furniture at reasonable prices.
In a town that lost its only department store, the shop has become a gathering place as much as a business.

per_choice_rationale.A: Follows the mill's equipment rather than the shop, ending the paragraph off-topic.
per_choice_rationale.B: Zooms out to a national trend, abandoning the paragraph's focus on one community.
per_choice_rationale.C: Adds a narrow sales detail instead of capturing the shop's social role.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it gathers the paragraph's details — the vanished store, the café, the lingering neighbors — into one closing statement of the shop's community role.

why_correct_md: A strong conclusion **synthesizes** the paragraph's specifics into a final statement of its central idea, here the shop's social role in the community.
why_tempted_md: The furniture detail stays on the subject of the shop, so it feels connected even though it ignores the paragraph's real point.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's main idea in one sentence. 2) List what each option emphasizes. 3) Eliminate options that drift off-topic, zoom too wide, or shrink to a stray detail. 4) Keep the option that echoes the main idea using the paragraph's own threads. 5) Read the paragraph with it appended to confirm the landing.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] The pricing team meets at a long table in the back room every Tuesday. [2] Each member specializes in one category, from costume jewelry to small appliances. [3] Disagreements are settled with a quick auction-site search and a show of hands. [4] The system looks casual, but it keeps prices consistent from one week to the next.
stem_md: For the sake of the logic and coherence of the paragraph, Sentence 3 should be placed:

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: disagreements arise from the specialists described in Sentence 2, and Sentence 4's verdict on 'the system' must follow the full description.
per_choice_rationale.B: Opens the paragraph with 'Disagreements,' which have no context before the team or its members are introduced.
per_choice_rationale.C: Places the dispute-settling before readers learn who the specializing members are, breaking the chain of reference.
per_choice_rationale.D: Strands the detail after Sentence 4's summary, which reads as the paragraph's wrap-up of the whole system.

why_correct_md: Sentence 3 depends on Sentence 2's specialists for context and must precede Sentence 4's **summary** of the system.
why_tempted_md: Moving Sentence 3 right after the opening feels tidy because both mention team logistics, but the reference to disputes needs Sentence 2 first.
rule_md: 1) Underline backward-pointing words in the movable sentence (here, 'Disagreements'). 2) Find the earlier sentence that creates those disagreements. 3) Place the sentence after its setup. 4) Check that any summary sentence still comes last. 5) Re-read the paragraph in the new order.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] The shop opened in a former hardware store whose original shelving still lines the walls. [2] Early volunteers sorted donations by lantern light during the building's first drafty winter. [3] A kitchen fire in 1994 nearly ended the operation, but neighbors rebuilt the interior in a single summer. [4] Today, the main floor is divided into wings for clothing, housewares, and media. [5] Hand-painted signs guide shoppers from the register toward each wing.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide this paragraph into two paragraphs, the first about the shop's history and the second about its present-day layout. The best place to begin the second paragraph is at:

per_choice_rationale.A: Splits the opening from the rest of the history, leaving Sentence 1 stranded and mixing eras in the second paragraph.
per_choice_rationale.B: Puts the 1994 fire — a historical event — at the head of the present-day paragraph.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: 'Today' marks the pivot from decades of history to the current layout, so the new paragraph starts there.
per_choice_rationale.D: Separates the signs from the wings they point to, splitting the layout description in half.

why_correct_md: The word **Today** in Sentence 4 signals the shift from past events to the current layout, exactly where the stem says the second paragraph should begin.
why_tempted_md: The fire feels like a dramatic turning point, so starting a new paragraph at Sentence 3 seems natural even though the fire still belongs to the history.
rule_md: 1) Label each numbered sentence as 'history' or 'present layout.' 2) Find where the labels flip. 3) Check for a time-shift signal word at that seam. 4) Start the new paragraph at the first sentence of the second label. 5) Confirm both halves read as unified paragraphs.

subject: act-english
context_html: Opened in 1987 by a coalition of church <u>groups the shop on Fenwick Avenue</u> has funded a neighborhood food pantry ever since.
stem_md: Which choice punctuates the sentence correctly?

choices.label: groups, the shop, on Fenwick Avenue
groups the shop on Fenwick Avenue,
groups, the shop on Fenwick Avenue

per_choice_rationale.A: Runs the introductory participial phrase straight into the subject with no comma, blurring where the description ends.
per_choice_rationale.B: Adds a second comma that severs the subject from the phrase identifying its location.
per_choice_rationale.C: Skips the needed comma after the opening phrase and instead wedges one between the subject and its verb.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: a single comma closes the introductory phrase, and the subject flows uninterrupted into its verb.

why_correct_md: An **introductory participial phrase** must be set off with a comma, and no comma may separate the subject from its verb.
why_tempted_md: Pausing before 'has' feels natural aloud, so a comma after 'Avenue' seems to mark the breath even though it splits subject and verb.
rule_md: 1) Bracket the opening phrase up to the subject. 2) Place a comma at the bracket's close. 3) Read subject to verb — allow no lone comma between them. 4) Reject options that pause where grammar doesn't. 5) Re-read the corrected sentence.

subject: act-english
context_html: The record bins draw collectors from three <u>counties, most arrive</u> before the store even unlocks its doors.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Joins two complete sentences with only a comma, creating a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: a semicolon legally joins the two related independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.C: Puts a semicolon before a phrase with no finished verb, leaving a fragment after the stronger mark.
per_choice_rationale.D: Swaps in a conjunctive adverb but keeps only a comma, so the splice survives — and the contrast word misfits the logic anyway.

why_correct_md: Two **independent clauses** may be joined by a semicolon; each side of the mark here can stand alone.
why_tempted_md: The clauses feel so closely related that a light comma seems sufficient to fuse them.
rule_md: 1) Cover the punctuation and read each side. 2) Ask: could each side end with a period? 3) If yes-yes, use a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. 4) If one side can't stand alone, a semicolon is illegal. 5) Match the option to the legal patterns.

subject: act-english
context_html: The shop's most contested treasures <u>are: vintage</u> cameras, first-edition paperbacks, and hand-stitched quilts.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Drops a colon right after the verb, interrupting the clause before it is complete.
per_choice_rationale.B: Uses a semicolon where no second independent clause follows, stranding the list.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the verb *are* flows directly into its complements, and no punctuation is needed.
per_choice_rationale.D: Inserts a comma between the verb and the first item it introduces, splitting the clause's core.

why_correct_md: A colon may follow only a **complete** independent clause; after the verb *are*, the sentence must run straight into the list.
why_tempted_md: Lists feel like they deserve an introductory colon, so students reach for one even mid-clause.
rule_md: 1) Cover everything after the possible colon. 2) Ask: is what remains a complete sentence? 3) If not, no colon (and no semicolon or comma) may interrupt. 4) Only insert a colon after a clause that could take a period. 5) Re-read the sentence without any mark to see if it flows.

subject: act-english
context_html: Sweaters <u>spill in bright tangles</u> from every shelf of the clothing annex.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize the cheerful abundance of the sweater display. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: 'spill in bright tangles' conveys both overflowing quantity and cheerful color.
per_choice_rationale.B: Reduces the scene to flat warehouse language with no sense of abundance or cheer.
per_choice_rationale.C: Merely notes visibility, giving no impression of quantity or color.
per_choice_rationale.D: Says only that the sweaters stay put, with no image of plenty at all.

why_correct_md: Only the original wording delivers concrete images of **overflow and color** that match the stated goal.
why_tempted_md: 'Can be seen' feels safely descriptive, but a goal question rewards vivid specificity, not neutral reporting.
rule_md: 1) Restate the writer's goal in your own words. 2) For each option, list what a reader can actually picture. 3) Cross out options that could describe any object anywhere. 4) Keep the option whose images match the goal's key qualities. 5) Confirm it fits the sentence grammatically.

subject: act-english
context_html: In its written appraisal, the auction house concluded that the donated violin was <u>a super cool find</u> worth far more than its two-dollar price sticker.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the formal tone established by the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Super cool' is casual slang that clashes with the formal register of a written appraisal.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: elevated, precise diction that matches the professional context.
per_choice_rationale.C: Intensifier-plus-slang phrasing even more casual than the original.
per_choice_rationale.D: Conversational slang ('awesome pickup') unsuited to a formal document.

why_correct_md: The sentence's professional context calls for **formal** diction, and only one option avoids slang.
why_tempted_md: 'Insanely great' sounds enthusiastic and vivid, so students mistake energy for appropriateness.
rule_md: 1) Identify the passage's register from clues like 'written appraisal.' 2) Read each option aloud and ask: would a professional write this in a report? 3) Flag slang, intensifiers, and chatty idioms. 4) Eliminate every flagged option. 5) Confirm the survivor fits the sentence's meaning.

subject: act-english
context_html: Every price at Second Chance Goods reflects a simple formula. The manager checks what similar items sold for online, subtracts a third, and rounds down to the nearest dollar. She reviews the formula each quarter to be sure the shop stays cheaper than its competitors.
stem_md: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the final sentence of the paragraph: 'The manager also enjoys hiking with her sister on her days off.' Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it helps readers picture the manager as a well-rounded person.
Yes, because it explains why the shop closes early on weekends.
No, because it contradicts the paragraph's earlier description of the manager.
No, because it introduces a personal detail unrelated to the paragraph's focus on pricing.

per_choice_rationale.A: Humanizing the manager is not the paragraph's job; the addition would blur its single topic.
per_choice_rationale.B: Invents a justification the sentence does not provide — hiking says nothing about store hours.
per_choice_rationale.C: Reaches the right verdict for a false reason; nothing in the sentence conflicts with earlier statements.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the paragraph is a tight explanation of how prices are set, and an off-duty hobby has no bearing on that.

why_correct_md: An added sentence must serve the paragraph's **single controlling idea**, and this one veers into the manager's off-duty life.
why_tempted_md: The manager appears in every sentence, so a fact about her feels on-topic even though the paragraph is really about her formula.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's controlling idea in one phrase. 2) Ask what the proposed sentence contributes to that idea. 3) If it contributes nothing, the answer is no. 4) Then vet the reason: it must describe the actual relationship, not an invented one. 5) Pick the verdict-plus-reason pair that matches your analysis.

subject: act-english
context_html: Volunteering at the shop has become an informal job-training program. Teenagers who start by folding sweaters learn to schedule shifts, balance a register drawer, and negotiate with donors. One former volunteer, Dara Okafor, parlayed three summers at the register into a bookkeeping job at a regional bank.
stem_md: The writer is considering deleting the final sentence of the paragraph. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?

choices.label: Kept, because it offers a concrete example of a volunteer gaining the job skills the paragraph describes.
Kept, because it explains how the shop recruits new volunteers each summer.
Deleted, because it repeats information stated earlier in the paragraph.
Deleted, because it shifts the paragraph's attention away from volunteer training.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: Dara's bookkeeping job is a specific case proving the paragraph's claim that volunteering builds job skills.
per_choice_rationale.B: Right verdict, wrong reason — the sentence says nothing about recruiting.
per_choice_rationale.C: The example adds a new, specific outcome; nothing earlier mentions Dara or the bank.
per_choice_rationale.D: The sentence is the payoff of the training idea, not a departure from it.

why_correct_md: The sentence supplies a **specific example** that proves the paragraph's general claim, the strongest reason to keep it.
why_tempted_md: Because the sentence names one person while the rest of the paragraph generalizes, it can look like a digression rather than evidence.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's claim. 2) Ask what the target sentence does for that claim (proves it, repeats it, or ignores it). 3) Keep sentences that prove or develop; cut ones that repeat or stray. 4) Then check the option's stated reason against your step-2 answer. 5) Select the verdict-plus-reason pair that matches.

subject: act-english
context_html: Prices at the shop routinely undercut even discount retailers. Because <u>the shop has certain advantages</u>, and because volunteers keep labor costs near zero, markdowns can go deeper than any chain could match.
stem_md: Given that all the choices are accurate, which one most effectively supports the paragraph's explanation of why the shop can keep prices low?

choices.label: the shop's sign was repainted by a local artist
its merchandise arrives free, as donations

per_choice_rationale.A: The founding year is background trivia with no bearing on low prices.
per_choice_rationale.B: The sign's artwork is decorative detail irrelevant to cost.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: goods that cost the shop nothing directly explain how prices can stay below competitors'.
per_choice_rationale.D: Mentions donations but emphasizes their timing, which doesn't explain cheapness.

why_correct_md: The paragraph explains **why prices stay low**, and only the cost-free supply of goods feeds that explanation directly.
why_tempted_md: The option about unpredictable donation waves mentions the same subject — donations — so it feels connected despite explaining nothing about price.
rule_md: 1) Name the paragraph's specific claim (not just its topic). 2) For each option, ask: does this fact help prove that claim? 3) Beware options that share the topic but not the point. 4) Eliminate decoration and background. 5) Keep the option that plugs directly into the paragraph's logic.

subject: act-english
context_html: Because the loading dock floods every <u>spring. The</u> staff moves donation intake to the covered side entrance.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: The period strands 'Because the loading dock floods every spring' as a fragment with no main clause.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: a comma joins the introductory dependent clause to the main clause that completes it.
per_choice_rationale.C: A semicolon demands independent clauses on both sides, but the 'Because' clause cannot stand alone.
per_choice_rationale.D: Adds 'so' on top of 'Because,' doubling the causal signal and garbling the clause logic.

why_correct_md: A **dependent clause** beginning with 'Because' must attach to the main clause with just a comma when it comes first.
why_tempted_md: The 'Because' clause is long enough to feel like a full sentence, so a period after it sounds fine to the ear.
rule_md: 1) Circle the subordinating word (Because, Although, When...). 2) That clause cannot end with a period or semicolon on its own. 3) Attach it to the main clause with a comma when it comes first. 4) Never add a second conjunction to the same joint. 5) Re-read the full sentence for one complete thought.

subject: act-english
context_html: Marisol refuses to price anything sight <u>unseen, she</u> inspects every seam and zipper herself.
stem_md: Which of the following alternatives best corrects the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Two independent clauses fused with only a comma — a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the semicolon legally joins the two closely related independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.C: Deleting the comma creates a fused sentence, an even harder crash between the clauses.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'However' is a conjunctive adverb, so a comma before it still leaves a splice — and the sentence's logic isn't contrastive.

why_correct_md: Independent clauses need a **period, semicolon, or comma plus coordinating conjunction** — the semicolon satisfies that here.
why_tempted_md: Removing the comma feels like removing the error, but no punctuation at all fuses the clauses even more tightly.
rule_md: 1) Find the spot where two clauses meet. 2) Test each side for stand-alone completeness. 3) If both stand alone, pick from: period, semicolon, comma + coordinating conjunction. 4) Rule out bare commas, bare adverbs, and no punctuation. 5) Confirm the chosen joint preserves the sentence's logic.

subject: act-english
context_html: The window display changes with the <u>seasons in October the</u> mannequins wear flannel and carry paper lanterns.
stem_md: Which choice best establishes the boundary between the sentence's two statements?

per_choice_rationale.A: Runs two complete statements together with no punctuation — a fused sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: Substitutes a comma for the missing boundary, producing a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a period ends the first statement, and a comma sets off the introductory phrase 'In October.'
per_choice_rationale.D: 'While' turns the second half into a dependent clause, which a semicolon cannot legally precede.

why_correct_md: Two independent statements need a full **boundary** — here a period — plus a comma after the introductory time phrase.
why_tempted_md: A comma marks the pause the ear wants, so it masquerades as a sufficient boundary between the clauses.
