why_tempted_md: 'Undertake ongoing surveillance of' sounds impressively official, so students confuse stiffness with formality.
rule_md: 1) Identify the document type and its register. 2) Rate each option: slang, plain professional, or inflated. 3) Reject both extremes. 4) Choose the wording a professional writer would actually use.

subject: act-english
context_html: As the tide slipped away, the crab scuttled <u>quickly</u> across the wet ledge toward a shaded crevice.
stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the adverb properly modifies the verb 'scuttled,' telling how the crab moved.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Quick' is an adjective and cannot modify the action verb 'scuttled' (adj_for_adverb).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Real quick' is a colloquial adverb phrase, doubly nonstandard in formal writing.
per_choice_rationale.D: A comparative form has nothing being compared, so it cannot describe the single action.

why_correct_md: An **adverb** is needed to modify the verb 'scuttled,' and the -ly form does that job.
why_tempted_md: The bare adjective sounds fine in speech, so students forget that modifying a verb requires the adverb form.
rule_md: 1) Find the word being described. 2) If it is a verb or action, use an adverb (often -ly). 3) If it is a noun, use an adjective. 4) Reject comparative forms unless two things are actually compared.

subject: act-english
context_html: When the biologist lifted the stone away from the sea star, <u>it was covered in tiny barnacles.</u>
stem_md: Which choice most clearly identifies what was covered in barnacles?

choices.label: this was covered in tiny barnacles.
the stone was covered in tiny barnacles.
they were covered in tiny barnacles.

per_choice_rationale.A: The pronoun could refer to either the object or the sea star, leaving the reference ambiguous (ambiguous_pronoun).
per_choice_rationale.B: A demonstrative is an even vaguer pointer that still fails to name which item was covered.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: naming the object removes all doubt about which one bore the barnacles.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'They' is plural and matches no plural noun in the sentence, adding an agreement error to the vagueness.

why_correct_md: Replacing the pronoun with the **specific noun** eliminates the ambiguity between two singular candidates.
why_tempted_md: The original pronoun reads smoothly, so students assume the nearest noun is obviously the referent.
rule_md: 1) Find each pronoun. 2) List every noun it could point to. 3) If more than one noun fits, replace the pronoun with the intended noun. 4) Confirm number agreement between pronoun and noun.

subject: act-english
context_html: By the time the researchers reached the shore at dawn, the highest pools <u>already dried</u> under the summer sun.
stem_md: Which choice best fits the sequence of events in the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: Simple past does not show that the drying finished before the past arrival, so a past perfect is required (tense_sequence).
per_choice_rationale.B: This drops the verb entirely, turning the clause into an ungrammatical fragment.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the past perfect shows the drying was completed before the past-tense arrival.
per_choice_rationale.D: Present perfect clashes with the clearly past verb 'reached.'

why_correct_md: An action completed **before** another past action takes the past perfect ('had' + past participle).
why_tempted_md: Both events are in the past, so students use simple past for both and miss the earlier-than relationship.
rule_md: 1) Identify the two past events. 2) Decide which happened first. 3) Put the earlier one in past perfect ('had' + participle). 4) Keep the later one in simple past.

subject: act-english
context_html: Tide pools look calm and inviting. <u>Therefore</u>, the animals in them survive crashing waves, blazing sun, and long hours with no water at all.
stem_md: Which choice best signals the relationship between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: This claims the second sentence is a result of the first, but harsh survival is a contrast, not a consequence (transition_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.B: This promises an illustration of calmness, yet the second sentence describes the opposite.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the transition marks the contrast between the calm appearance and the harsh reality.
per_choice_rationale.D: This signals similarity, but the two sentences oppose rather than echo each other.

why_correct_md: The two sentences oppose each other, so a **contrast** transition is required.
why_tempted_md: The result word feels logical because one sentence follows another, and students read sequence as cause.
rule_md: 1) State the idea in sentence one. 2) State the idea in sentence two. 3) Decide the logical link: add, contrast, cause, or example. 4) Pick the transition that names that exact link.

subject: act-english
context_html: The limpet clamps onto the rock so tightly that few predators can pry it loose. <u>For instance</u>, that same iron grip seals in moisture and keeps the animal alive through hours of blistering exposure.
stem_md: Which choice best signals the relationship between the two sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: This presents the second sentence as an example of the first, but it names a second, separate benefit (transition_wrong_logic).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the transition adds a further advantage of the grip to the one already stated.
per_choice_rationale.C: This signals opposition, yet both sentences describe benefits of the same grip.
per_choice_rationale.D: This claims the moisture benefit is caused by the predator benefit, but they are parallel effects of the grip, not cause and effect.

why_correct_md: The second sentence supplies an **additional** benefit, so an addition transition fits.
why_tempted_md: Both sentences discuss the same grip, so the example word feels like it is giving another case of one idea.
rule_md: 1) Summarize each sentence's point. 2) Ask whether sentence two adds, opposes, illustrates, or results from sentence one. 3) Note that two separate effects of one cause are additive, not causal. 4) Choose the matching connector.

subject: act-english
context_html: Tide pools are stacked in bands along the shore. Near the top, only the hardiest species endure long stretches of air and glaring sun. Farther down, where seawater lingers between tides, softer-bodied creatures flourish.
stem_md: The writer wants to conclude the paragraph by emphasizing that where a creature lives on the shore determines whether it can survive. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: The best pools attract crowds of curious tourists each summer.
The ocean supports an astonishing variety of living things.
Thus a creature's exact position on the shore, more than anything else, decides where it can hold on.
Twice a day the rising tide covers and uncovers these bands.

per_choice_rationale.A: This detail about tourists is off-topic and ignores the paragraph's biological point (add_offtopic).
per_choice_rationale.B: A sweeping claim about ocean diversity is too broad to cap a paragraph about shore zones (goal_too_broad).
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: it ties survival directly to an organism's location on the shore, matching the stated goal.
per_choice_rationale.D: This restates the tides' motion rather than emphasizing how location governs survival (goal_wrong_emphasis).

why_correct_md: Only this sentence links **location** to survival, which is exactly the emphasis the stem requests.
why_tempted_md: The tide sentence stays on the topic of bands, so it feels relevant even though it misses the survival-by-location point.
rule_md: 1) Underline the goal's key idea in the stem. 2) Check each option against that exact idea. 3) Reject options that are off-topic, too broad, or emphasize the wrong point. 4) Keep the one that states the requested idea directly.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] Reaching a good tide pool takes patience. [2] Printed tide charts tell visitors the hours when the ocean will pull back. [3] A careful walker waits at the edge as the final waves slide away. [4] Crabs and snails then edge out from their hidden cracks.
stem_md: The writer wants to add the sentence 'Only then does the shallow water settle enough to explore safely.' Where would it best be placed?

per_choice_rationale.A: Placed here, 'only then' has no prior event to point back to, so the reference dangles (order_illogical).
per_choice_rationale.B: After the charts, the settling has not yet been set up by the waves sliding away.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the water settles right after the final waves slide away, so the sentence follows Sentence 3.
per_choice_rationale.D: By Sentence 4 the creatures are already out, so noting the water can now be explored arrives too late.

why_correct_md: 'Only then' must follow the event it refers to — the waves sliding away — which is **Sentence 3**.
why_tempted_md: Sentence 4 also describes the calm aftermath, so the added line seems to fit alongside it.
rule_md: 1) Find the pointing words in the new sentence ('only then'). 2) Identify the event they refer to. 3) Place the sentence immediately after that event. 4) Check the flow before and after the new spot.

subject: act-english
context_html: [1] For six hours the exposed pools bake and shrink until the returning sea refills them. [2] Marine biologists plan their entire field day around this narrow window. [3] They hurry to the lowest water, record everything they can, and retreat as the waves climb back. [4] A single missed low tide can cost them a week of data.
stem_md: The writer wants to divide this paragraph into two. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

choices.label: Begin a new paragraph with Sentence 2.
Begin a new paragraph with Sentence 3.
Begin a new paragraph with Sentence 4.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: Sentence 1 describes the pools, while Sentences 2-4 shift to the biologists' routine, so the break belongs before Sentence 2.
per_choice_rationale.B: Sentences 2 and 3 both describe the biologists' work, so splitting between them cuts one idea in half.
per_choice_rationale.C: Sentence 4 continues the biologists' fieldwork, so a break here separates closely related points.
per_choice_rationale.D: The paragraph contains a clear topic shift, so leaving it whole buries that transition.

why_correct_md: A new paragraph should start where the **topic shifts** — from the pools to the people studying them — which is at Sentence 2.
why_tempted_md: Sentence 4's warning feels like a fresh idea, tempting students to break there instead.
rule_md: 1) Summarize each sentence in a few words. 2) Find where the subject changes. 3) Start the new paragraph at the first sentence of the new subject. 4) Confirm each resulting paragraph holds one main idea.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Sea stars which can regrow lost arms are</u> among the most resilient hunters in the pool.
stem_md: Which choice correctly punctuates the sentence?

choices.label: Sea stars, which can regrow lost arms are
Sea stars which can regrow lost arms, are
Sea stars, which can regrow lost arms, are

per_choice_rationale.A: The nonrestrictive clause needs commas on both sides; leaving them out runs the modifier into the sentence (missing_nonrestrictive_commas).
per_choice_rationale.B: This opens the clause with a comma but never closes it, so the modifier bleeds into the verb.
per_choice_rationale.C: This closes the clause but never opens it, misplacing a single comma before the verb.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: paired commas set off the nonrestrictive clause 'which can regrow lost arms.'

why_correct_md: A nonrestrictive 'which' clause must be **enclosed by a pair of commas**.
why_tempted_md: The single-comma version looks balanced enough that students accept just one.
rule_md: 1) Find the extra-information clause. 2) Test whether the sentence still makes sense without it. 3) If yes, it is nonrestrictive and needs a comma before and after. 4) Make sure both commas are present.

subject: act-english
context_html: The pool teemed with life<u>; a</u> single square foot of rock held hundreds of creatures.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the semicolon links two complete, closely related independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma between two independent clauses creates a comma splice (comma_splice).
per_choice_rationale.C: Dropping punctuation fuses the two independent clauses into a run-on.
per_choice_rationale.D: A colon should follow a clause that sets up a list or explanation, not simply join two equal statements.

why_correct_md: A **semicolon** correctly joins two independent clauses that could each stand alone.
why_tempted_md: The second clause explains the first, so a colon feels justified even though the clauses are equal statements.
rule_md: 1) Check that both sides are complete sentences. 2) If they are and are closely related, a semicolon joins them. 3) A comma alone cannot join two sentences. 4) Use a colon only when the first part introduces the second.

subject: act-english
context_html: The tide pool's fiercest hunters<u> include:</u> sea stars, crabs, and anemones.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?

per_choice_rationale.A: A colon cannot separate a verb from its objects; the verb should lead directly into the list (colon_after_verb).
per_choice_rationale.B: A semicolon links independent clauses, not a verb and its list.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the verb flows straight into the list with no punctuation.
per_choice_rationale.D: A comma after the verb wrongly separates it from the items it introduces.

why_correct_md: A colon or comma must not split a **verb from its direct objects**; the list follows the verb cleanly.
why_tempted_md: Colons often precede lists, so students insert one even when a verb already introduces the items.
rule_md: 1) Find what comes right before the punctuation. 2) Check whether that part is a complete sentence. 3) A colon needs a complete clause before it. 4) If a verb leads straight into a list, use no punctuation.

subject: act-english
context_html: Day and night, the heavy surf <u>hit</u> the rocks at the mouth of the cove.
stem_md: Which choice most vividly conveys the force of the surf?

per_choice_rationale.A: The original verb is accurate but flat, missing the chance to convey relentless force (weak_word_choice).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: this verb captures the heavy, repeated force of the surf.
per_choice_rationale.C: This verb suggests gentleness, the opposite of the intended force.
per_choice_rationale.D: This phrase describes position, not action, and conveys no force at all.

why_correct_md: The chosen verb supplies the **forceful, repeated impact** the stem asks the writer to convey.
why_tempted_md: The original is technically correct and unremarkable, so students leave it rather than seek a stronger verb.
rule_md: 1) Read the goal in the stem. 2) Rank each verb by how strongly it conveys that quality. 3) Reject verbs that are too weak or off-meaning. 4) Choose the verb that best matches the requested effect.

subject: act-english
context_html: The field report observed that the anemone's sting, though harmless to people, <u>totally wrecks</u> the tiny shrimp that drift too close.
stem_md: Which choice best maintains the passage's formal, scientific tone?

per_choice_rationale.A: The original is casual slang out of place in a scientific report (informal_register).
per_choice_rationale.B: This is a colloquial idiom unsuitable for formal writing.
per_choice_rationale.C: This is slangy and imprecise for a research context.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: this phrase is precise and matches the report's formal register.

why_correct_md: The passage is a scientific report, so a **formal, precise verb** fits its register.
why_tempted_md: The original vividly conveys damage, so students keep it for its punch despite the clash in tone.
rule_md: 1) Identify the passage's register from its surrounding words. 2) Label each option as formal or casual. 3) Eliminate slang and idioms in a formal context. 4) Keep the precise, register-matching choice.

subject: act-english
context_html: Sea otters crack open spiny urchins on their bellies using small stones. This constant snacking keeps urchin numbers in check, which in turn protects the kelp forests the urchins would otherwise devour. Sea otters also have the densest fur of any mammal.
stem_md: The writer is considering deleting the final sentence of the paragraph. Should it be kept or deleted?

choices.label: Kept, because it adds a memorable fact about the animal.
Kept, because it explains how the otters break open their prey.
Deleted, because it strays from the paragraph's point about how otters protect kelp.
Deleted, because it repeats a point made earlier in the paragraph.

per_choice_rationale.A: The fur fact is interesting but irrelevant to the paragraph's point about kelp protection (add_offtopic).
per_choice_rationale.B: The fur sentence does not explain how otters open urchins; that reasoning misreads it.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the fur detail wanders from the paragraph's main point, so deleting it restores unity.
per_choice_rationale.D: The fur fact is new information, not a repeat, so this reason is inaccurate.

why_correct_md: A sentence should be deleted when it **breaks the paragraph's unity**, as the fur fact does here.
why_tempted_md: The fur fact is genuinely interesting, so students want to keep it as a bonus.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's main point. 2) Ask whether the sentence supports that point. 3) If it wanders off, delete it. 4) Match your reason to the actual problem, not a false one.

subject: act-english
context_html: A shallow tide pool can heat up sharply on a sunny afternoon. Water trapped by the low tide may climb ten degrees in a single hour, stressing the animals that cannot escape to cooler depths. Their bodies have only limited ways to shed that extra heat.
stem_md: At this point the writer is considering adding the sentence 'Coral reefs, by contrast, endure heat stress across entire ocean basins.' Should the writer make this addition?

choices.label: Yes, because it offers a helpful comparison to another ecosystem.
Yes, because it explains why the tide pool heats up so fast.
No, because it shifts attention away from the trapped pool animals the paragraph describes.
No, because it repeats the earlier point about rising temperature.

per_choice_rationale.A: A comparison to reefs pulls the reader away from the tight focus on the pool (add_offtopic).
per_choice_rationale.B: The added sentence about reefs does not explain the pool's rapid heating at all.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the reef comparison diverts from the trapped pool creatures the passage is about.
per_choice_rationale.D: The reef sentence is new material, not a repeat of the temperature point.

why_correct_md: An addition should be rejected when it **derails the focus**, as the reef comparison does.
why_tempted_md: The reef sentence stays on the theme of heat, so it feels topically connected.
rule_md: 1) Name the passage's specific subject. 2) Check whether the new sentence stays on that subject. 3) Reject additions that widen or change the subject. 4) Verify your reason names the true flaw.

subject: act-english
context_html: A mussel stays put in the pounding surf by spinning dozens of tough fibers called byssal threads. It reaches out with its muscular foot and lays down each strand one at a time until it is firmly moored.
stem_md: Given that all the choices are true, which one best supports the paragraph's focus on how a mussel anchors itself?

choices.label: Mussels are a popular seafood in many coastal countries.
Each strand ends in a natural cement that grips even slick, wet surfaces.
Mussels draw in and filter large volumes of seawater as they feed.
A mussel's shell is built from two hinged halves.

per_choice_rationale.A: The seafood fact is true but unrelated to how the mussel holds on (add_offtopic).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it explains a feature of the strands that lets the mussel grip its spot, supporting the anchoring focus.
per_choice_rationale.C: Feeding by filtering is true but concerns nutrition, not attachment.
per_choice_rationale.D: The shell's structure is true but says nothing about how the animal stays anchored.

why_correct_md: Only this detail advances the paragraph's focus on **how the mussel attaches** to its surface.
why_tempted_md: The filtering fact is a familiar mussel trait, so it feels relevant even though it misses the anchoring point.
rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's focus from the stem. 2) Test each true detail against that focus. 3) Discard details about other traits. 4) Keep the one that develops the stated focus.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Barnacles strain food from the passing water with delicate, feathery legs.</u>
stem_md: Which choice is a complete sentence?

choices.label: Barnacles straining food from the passing water with delicate, feathery legs.
Because barnacles strain food from the passing water with delicate, feathery legs.
Which strain food from the passing water with delicate, feathery legs.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the subject and a full verb form a complete, independent sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: The -ing form is a participle, not a finite verb, so the group of words is a fragment.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Because' turns the clause into a dependent fragment that cannot stand alone.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Which' opens a relative clause with no main clause, leaving a fragment.

why_correct_md: A complete sentence needs a subject and a **finite verb**, and both are present here.
why_tempted_md: The -ing version reads like an action, so students mistake the participle for a working verb.
rule_md: 1) Find the subject. 2) Find the main verb and check it is finite, not an -ing or -ed form alone. 3) Make sure no word like 'because' or 'which' leaves the clause dependent. 4) Confirm the words can stand alone.

subject: act-english
context_html: The tide was dropping fast<u>, we hurried to reach the far pools</u> before the light failed.
stem_md: Which choice best corrects the underlined portion?

choices.label: , so we hurried to reach the far pools
we hurried to reach the far pools
, therefore we hurried to reach the far pools

per_choice_rationale.A: A comma alone joins two independent clauses, creating a comma splice (comma_splice).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the comma plus 'so' properly coordinates the two independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.C: Removing the comma fuses the clauses into a run-on.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Therefore' is a conjunctive adverb; after a comma it still leaves a splice.

why_correct_md: A comma with a **coordinating conjunction** ('so') correctly links two independent clauses.
why_tempted_md: 'Therefore' expresses the cause-effect logic, so students accept it despite the punctuation flaw.
rule_md: 1) Confirm both sides are complete sentences. 2) A comma alone cannot join them. 3) Add a coordinating conjunction (and, but, so...) after the comma, or use a semicolon. 4) Note that 'therefore' is not a coordinating conjunction.

subject: act-english
context_html: The shell of a limpet is far thicker than <u>a periwinkle</u> that shares the same rocky ledge.
stem_md: Which choice makes the comparison logical?

per_choice_rationale.A: This compares a shell to a whole animal, an illogical comparison (illogical_comparison).
per_choice_rationale.B: Inserting a verb compares the shell to the animal's existence, still illogical and awkward.
per_choice_rationale.C: The plural stand-in does not match the singular 'shell,' so the number is wrong.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the singular stand-in fills in for 'the shell of,' comparing shell to shell.

why_correct_md: A comparison must match **like with like**; the singular stand-in supplies the second shell.
why_tempted_md: 'Than a periwinkle' sounds natural in speech, so students miss that it compares a shell to an animal.
rule_md: 1) Find the two things being compared. 2) Check they are the same kind of thing. 3) If a possessed noun is compared to a whole thing, insert 'that of' (singular) or 'those of' (plural). 4) Match the number to the first noun.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>Clinging to the rock with a broad, muscular foot, the snail held firm.</u>
stem_md: Which choice is grammatically acceptable?

choices.label: Clinging to the rock with a broad, muscular foot, firmness was maintained by the snail.
Clinging to the rock with a broad, muscular foot, the crashing wave could not budge the snail.
Clinging to the rock with a broad, muscular foot, and the snail held firm.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the opening modifier logically describes 'the snail,' the subject that follows it.
per_choice_rationale.B: The modifier now describes 'firmness,' which cannot cling, creating a dangling modifier (dangling_subject).
per_choice_rationale.C: The modifier attaches to 'the crashing wave,' which is not what clings to the rock.
per_choice_rationale.D: Adding 'and' after the modifier breaks the connection and leaves a faulty construction.

why_correct_md: An introductory participial phrase must modify the **subject that immediately follows**, and 'the snail' clings correctly.
why_tempted_md: The passive version sounds formal, so students accept it despite the illogical modifier.
rule_md: 1) Find the introductory -ing phrase. 2) Identify who or what performs that action. 3) Make sure the noun right after the comma is that performer. 4) Reject versions where something else follows the comma.

subject: act-english
context_html: The anemone slowly drew in its tentacles <u>at a gradual, unhurried pace</u> as the shadow passed overhead.
stem_md: Which choice best corrects the underlined portion?

choices.label: in a slow and gradual manner
at a pace that was not fast

per_choice_rationale.A: The underlined phrase repeats the idea already carried by 'slowly' (redundant_synonym).
per_choice_rationale.B: This still restates 'slowly' with two more synonyms, keeping the redundancy.
per_choice_rationale.C: This wordy phrase again duplicates 'slowly' while adding empty bulk.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: removing the phrase eliminates the redundancy, since 'slowly' already conveys the pace.

why_correct_md: 'Slowly' already states the pace, so the added phrase is **redundant** and should be cut.
why_tempted_md: The added phrase sounds descriptive, so students keep it for detail without noticing the repeat.
rule_md: 1) Read the whole sentence for repeated ideas. 2) Locate the word already expressing the idea ('slowly'). 3) Cut any phrase that restates it. 4) Confirm the sentence still reads smoothly.

subject: act-english
context_html: The crab, <u>due to the fact that</u> it sensed a shadow overhead, darted into a narrow crevice.
stem_md: Which choice is most concise while keeping the meaning?

choices.label: in light of the fact that

per_choice_rationale.A: The underlined phrase is a wordy way of signaling a cause (wordiness).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: a single conjunction conveys the same cause with no padding.
per_choice_rationale.C: This is another inflated substitute for a one-word cause.
per_choice_rationale.D: This is equally padded and no clearer.

why_correct_md: The shortest phrase that preserves the causal meaning is best; **one word** replaces the four-word phrase.
why_tempted_md: The longer phrase sounds formal, so students equate its length with correctness.
rule_md: 1) Spot multi-word phrases that signal cause. 2) Ask whether a single conjunction says the same thing. 3) Replace padded phrases with the concise word. 4) Confirm the meaning is unchanged.

subject: act-english
context_html: <u>It is important to note that the</u> tide pool refills completely when the ocean returns at high tide.
stem_md: Which choice best eliminates unnecessary words?

choices.label: What is worth mentioning is that the
There is the fact that the

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening is an empty filler that adds no content (empty_phrase).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: cutting the filler leaves a clean, direct sentence beginning with the real subject.
per_choice_rationale.C: This swaps one hollow opener for another equally empty one.
per_choice_rationale.D: This filler is wordy and awkward, delaying the real subject.

why_correct_md: Empty **filler openers** should be deleted so the sentence starts with its real subject.
why_tempted_md: The filler sounds like it signals importance, so students think it strengthens the sentence.
rule_md: 1) Check the sentence opening for throat-clearing phrases. 2) Ask whether removing them loses any information. 3) If not, delete the filler. 4) Begin with the true subject.

subject: act-english
context_html: Over centuries, the retreating tide <u>made</u> a branching network of channels across the muddy flat.
stem_md: Which choice most precisely describes the tide's effect on the flat?

per_choice_rationale.A: The original verb is vague and misses the cutting action that shaped the channels (imprecise_word).
per_choice_rationale.B: This is even vaguer, a placeholder verb with no descriptive force.
per_choice_rationale.C: This verb implies handing over, which does not describe shaping channels.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: this verb precisely conveys the tide cutting the channels over time.

why_correct_md: The chosen verb captures the **precise action** of cutting channels, unlike the generic verbs.
why_tempted_md: The original is technically true, so students accept it without seeking a sharper verb.
rule_md: 1) Identify the exact action being described. 2) Rank the verbs by how precisely they name that action. 3) Reject vague, all-purpose verbs. 4) Choose the verb that pictures the action.

subject: act-english
context_html: The survey concluded that runoff pollution <u>had significantly reduced</u> the number of species living in the northern pools.
stem_md: Which choice best fits the passage's formal register?

choices.label: had put a big dent in

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the original is precise and matches the formal survey register.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Cut down on' is casual phrasing unsuited to a formal report (informal_register).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Really messed with' is slang, clashing with the formal context.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Put a big dent in' is a colloquial idiom out of place in a survey.

why_correct_md: The passage is a formal survey, so the **precise, formal** verb phrase is appropriate.
why_tempted_md: The casual phrases feel punchy and vivid, tempting students who overlook register.
rule_md: 1) Gauge the passage's register from its surrounding words. 2) Label each option formal or casual. 3) Eliminate slang and idioms in a formal report. 4) Keep the precise, register-matching phrase.
